28:
It means our pinnacle (the extreme limit). Therefore, the teacher said, "I have answered the question by the power of my own doctrine." 'Paraṃ' means excess (surpassing). 'Bhāsitassa' means of the spoken word or sound.

This distinction is stated with regard to merely concluding in the exposition of virtue (Sīlaniddesa). Therefore, the teacher said, "It was concluded as virtue alone." In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, although virtue is concluded, it is again concluded as the fruit of asceticism (Sāmaññaphala). Because all sublime minds (mahaggata-citta) are associated with knowledge, and because the jhānas are associated with that knowledge, it is called "attainment of wisdom" (paññāsampadā) in terms of meaning (essence). In the exposition of wisdom (Paññāniddesa), however, having made the wisdom of jhāna the basis, insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) is first concluded. Therefore, it was said, "By insight wisdom," and so forth.

## Commentary on the Conversation Regarding the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa Becoming a Lay Follower

In the phrase "daharo yuvā," the word 'dahara' indicates the Blessed One's state of being in the first stage of life. For one who has reached the first stage of life is called 'dahara' (young). A son's son is called a grandson. "Nappahoti" means not being sufficient, not even reaching the measure of sons and grandsons. To show the meaning of the phrase "āsanā me taṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ," it was said, "Because of my lack of respect," and so forth. 'Etaṃ' refers to the raising of joined palms (añjali). This Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa wanders about seeking gain by impressing others through hypocrisy and creating a reputation for himself among the masses. Therefore, to show his extremely deceitful (kuhaka) nature, it was said, "This person," and so forth. "Agāravaṃ nāma natthi" means there is no such thing as a disrespectful word; it does not mean he spoke "Ahañceva kho pana" out of disrespect for the Blessed One, but rather out of fear of losing his gains.

"Taṅkhaṇānurūpāya" means in accordance with the arising of his inclination at that time, derived by the method of omitting the middle term (majjhepada-lopa). Since at that time he did not yet have the maturity of knowledge based on the cessation of the round (nibbāna), only the meaning based on worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) was shown. Thus it was said, "Having shown the benefit in the present life and the future life," meaning having made it clear through direct perception. "Kusale dhamme" refers to the wholesome states belonging to the three planes. This is the primary meaning here. Figuratively, however, it is also appropriate to say "wholesome states belonging to the four planes" because supramundane (lokuttara) wholesome states can also be obtained in the future. Thus, it will be said, "In the future, for the sake of Nibbāna..."
29:
In the phrase "vāsanābhāgiyāya vā," "tattha" means in the wholesome states that one has well undertaken. "Naṃ" refers to the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa. "Samuttejetvā" means having well sharpened him progressively, bringing him to a state of keenness and clarity in performing meritorious deeds. Since such sharpening essentially causes effort in that merit, it is said, "Having made him energetic." "Having gladdened him" (sampahaṃsetvā) is connected with the aforementioned state of being energetic, because being energetic in performing merit in this way definitely accomplishes benefits in the present life and so forth. "And by other existing qualities" means that being endowed with such qualities definitely accomplishes benefits in the present life and so forth; thus, having gladdened him with other qualities present in that Brahmin, it means having brought him to a state of being well-elated and joyful.

To resolve the objection, "If the Blessed One rained down the rain of the Dhamma-gem, why did that Brahmin not attain the special distinction?" it was said, "Brāhmaṇo pana," and so forth. "Kuhakatāya" means because of his hypocritical nature as mentioned. This shows the lack of perfection in his application (payoga). To resolve the further objection, "If so, why did the Blessed One rain down the rain of the Dhamma-gem for him?" he said, "Kevalamassa," and so forth. There, "kevalaṃ" means being purely unmixed with the part of penetration (nibbedha) or the state of an adept (asekha). "Nibbānatthāya" means for the sake of attaining Nibbāna or for the sake of final Nibbāna (parinibbāna). The tendency (vāsanā), defined as the familiarity in performing meritorious deeds which serves as a means for attaining special distinction in the future, is called the "part" (bhāga). Because it occurs as a means for that benefit, it is called "vāsanābhāgiya" (conducive to the tendency). There is no Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, even a mere four-line verse, that is without benefit. Therefore, it was said, "All the preceding and following talk." Here, from the beginning until the end of the Brahmin's answer is the "preceding talk" (purimakathā). The Blessed One's words answering about virtue and wisdom are the "following talk" (pacchimakathā). Even the talk spoken by the Brahmin concerning the qualities of the Buddha and so forth is only "conducive to the tendency" (vāsanābhāgiya) for the sake of Nibbāna in the future. The rest is easy to understand.

Thus, the explanation of the hidden meanings (Līnatthappakāsanī) in the commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, in the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) named Sādhuvilāsinī—which clarifies the very subtle, deep, and difficult-to-understand meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, and which generates pure and extensive intellectual clarity—is finished.

## The Explanation of the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta is finished.
249:
Thinking, "He will not even dare to speak," he will surely uphold his pride. However, when speaking, if Ambaṭṭha’s birth and lineage are made clear through the course of the conversation, there will be a subduing of his pride. Thinking, "Come, I shall converse with this young man Ambaṭṭha," the Blessed One said this to the young man Ambaṭṭha—this is the meaning. They are called *ācariya* (teachers) because they teach training in conduct and behavior. The prominent teachers of those teachers are called *pācariya* (great-teachers). To show the meaning of "great-grandfather" (*papitāmaha*), it is said, "with the teachers and with the teachers of those teachers."

## Explanation of the First Discourse on the Low-born (Ibbha)

Although the words "or while lying down" and so forth should not really be spoken, to show that he speaks them out of pride, wishing to place himself on an equal footing, [the commentator] said, "Indeed, in the three postures" and so forth. In that context, "in the three postures" (*tīsu iriyāpathesu*) refers to standing, walking, and sitting. Only in those postures is it proper to converse with a teacher. It is not proper in the posture of lying down. This is because pupils who should show respect must not lie down in the presence of teachers who are to be respected. "Conversation" (*kathāsallāpa*) means talking for the purpose of competing through speech. Indeed, talking while lying down with a teacher who is lying down is not good conduct. Nevertheless, even though it is not proper conduct, speaking in a way that makes it equal to others is called "conversation" (*kathāsallāpa*) here.

The Blessed One, while speaking with Ambaṭṭha, made clear the impropriety of the conversation expressed as, "Master Gotama, a Brahmin who is lying down is fit to converse with a Brahmin who is lying down." Although this explanation of impropriety was not included in the Council (*Saṅgīti*) by way of the Pali text, it has been brought down to this day by the lineage of teachers who are not to be blamed. To show its connection with the subsequent Pali text beginning with "Those indeed, Master Gotama," [the commentator] said, "From that, it is said" and so forth. "*Gorūpa*" is said because of having a form like a cow, or because the word *rūpa* occurs in that sense. If he did not wish to revile, he would have said, "shaven-headed ascetics." Because he wished to revile, he added the suffix "-ka," which has a derogatory meaning, and said, "shaven-headed little ascetics" (*muṇḍakā samaṇakā*); to show this, it is said, "shaven-headed, shaven-headed" and so forth. "*Ibbhā*" is a word merely meaning "householders" (*gahapatikā*). Etymologically, however, it refers to the exertion of an elephant (*ibha*). By dropping the final word "exertion" (*payoga*), it becomes "*ibha*." Because they are worthy of the exertion of that elephant, they are called "*ibbhā*" (with a double 'b'). What is meant is this: just as an elephant-vehicle, called *ibha* because of its beautiful gait, proceeds according to the will of another (the mahout) and not its own, so too these *Suddas* (menials) who serve the Brahmins proceed only according to the will of another and not their own. They do not proceed according to their own will. Therefore, because they have exertion similar to an elephant, they are called "*ibbhā*." Alternatively, the teacher shows by the word "*gahapatikā*" that those called *ibbha* are householders who live in houses because they are wealthy. "*Kaṇhā*" means those of dark birth. "Only the Brahmins are of pure birth, others are not"—this is Ambaṭṭha's intention. Therefore, the teacher said, "dark ones" (*kāḷakā*). Because of being related as a kinsman in the capacity of a grandfather, he is called "*bandhu*." Therefore, the teacher said, "They call him 'grandfather' (*pitāmaha*)." "*Apacca*" means children. "Born from the mouth" means the ancestors of the Brahmins came out from the mouth of Brahmā. This is...
250:
[They] proceed only according to the will of another and not their own; therefore, they are called *ibbhā* because their exertion is similar to that of an elephant. The teacher shows the mere meaning that those very *ibbhā* are householders who reside in houses and are masters of the house because of their wealth, by this word "*gahapatikā*."

"*Kaṇhā*" means those of dark birth. "Only the twice-born are of pure birth, others are not"—this is the intention of that young man Ambaṭṭha. Therefore, he said, "dark ones" (*kāḷakā*). Because of being related as a kinsman in the capacity of a grandfather, he is called "*bandhu*." Therefore, they say, "They address him as 'grandfather' (*pitāmaha*)." "*Apacca*" means children. "Born from the mouth" (*mukhato nikkhantā*) means the ancestors of the Brahmins came out from the mouth of Brahmā; the intention is that this was their first appearance. In the remaining words, the method is the same.

The distinction here is this: having said "*ibbhā kaṇhā*," Ambaṭṭha then says "*bandhupādāpaccā*" (offspring of the kinsman's feet) to show that, by way of clan, the ascetics belong to the merchant class (*vessa*), but by way of their first appearance, they came out from the tops of the feet of Brahmā, and not from the navel like ordinary merchants. However, this statement of Ambaṭṭha is even more thoughtless than the statement "born from the mouth," etc., because the state of being an ascetic is possible for those belonging to all four classes. "*Aniyametvā*" means without specifying, having the sense of indicating generally.

"He spoke relying only on pride" means that, making pride his support, exalting himself and disparaging others, he spoke such words as "shaven-headed little ascetics." "I will make [him] know" means "I will make [him] understand by clearly revealing the extent of my lineage as it really is." "*Attha*" means benefit or the desired object; since that object is simply a task to be done, it is said, "the benefit known as the task to be done upon arrival." One who has that benefit is "*atthika*," like the word "*daṇḍika*" (one who has a staff). Since the second word "*atthika*," which denotes a person, also has a suffix in that sense, by the first "*atthika*" only the mind that has that benefit as its object is understood; therefore, [the commentator] said, "the mind of that young man." The mind that desires that benefit belongs to this young man Ambaṭṭha, therefore he is called "*atthikavā*," like the word "*guṇavā*" (one who has virtue).

That the phrase "*yāyeva kho panatthāya*" is spoken by way of gender-transformation is shown by the phrase "*yeneve kho panatthena*." Therefore, it is said, "That very purpose"—this is spoken by way of the masculine gender. For, by showing the natural gender in that phrase, the establishment of the unnatural gender here is accomplished. In this matter, there is another method from the Commentary: "*yāya atthāya*" is the dative case in that sense by way of the masculine gender; the meaning is "for the sake of the benefit known as the task to be done." "Of him" (*assa*) means...
251:
Making a connection with the young man Ambaṭṭha means showing the connection in relation to him. 'Others who have come into the presence' refers to virtuous people who approach those in positions of respect. 'Vattaṃ' refers to the good practice or conduct of those virtuous people. By the context itself, the meaning is understood as 'in the teacher's house.' 'Avusitavā' is also spoken of as the state of being uneducated through common usage, just as it is said 'he covered the gift of robes with three robes.' Therefore, it is said, 'one who has not lived in the teacher's house, one who is uneducated.' Because of being uneducated, he is one of little learning (appassuta). Since the word is incomplete in relation to the term 'vusitamānī,' the remaining text 'samāno' is shown by the phrase 'being one of little learning' (appassutova samāno). Indeed, great learning (bāhusacca) should be desired only for the sake of calming the defilements. Because that calming is absent, this young man Ambaṭṭha is known as one who has not lived [under a teacher], one who is uneducated, and one of little learning. Thus, wishing to clarify the reason through the implied meaning, it is said: 'What other reason is there besides not having lived [under a teacher]?' This connection is also shown by 'Etassa hi,' etc. Directly, however, this is a demonstration of the cause for the lack of calm through the practice of harsh speech. Here, the construction (yojanā) is: this reason, 'not having lived [under a teacher],' is the cause for this young man Ambaṭṭha’s practice of harsh speech. There is also a reading 'pharusavacanasamudācārena'; the meaning is the cause spoken of by way of such speech. Others also construe it thus: setting aside the state of not having lived [under a teacher], what other cause is there for this person’s practice of such harsh speech? The former construction is more appropriate here as it should be construed according to the text. Because of the connection with the particle 'aññatra,' the word 'avusitattā' is an ablative case used in the sense of the accusative. That very reason is completed by 'in the teacher's house,' etc.

'One whose mind is not his own' (asakamano) means one whose mind follows the will of another, namely, anger. 'Mānanimmadanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of crushing conceit, or for the purpose of being free from the intoxication of conceit. 'Dosaṃ uggiletvā' means having performed the vomiting out of the faults of wind, bile, and phlegm, which are soiled by the drinking of oil. 'Lineage by lineage' (gottena gottaṃ) refers to [crushing] the lineage now considered faultless by means of the faulty ancient lineage spoken of by the young man Ambaṭṭha himself when questioned by the Blessed One. In the phrase 'clan designation by clan designation' (kulāpadesena kulāpadesaṃ), the method is the same. 'Uṭṭhāpetvā' means having raised him from the faulty lineage, or in other words, having extracted him. Here, 'lineage' (gotta) should be taken by way of the first man (ancestor), while 'clan designation' (kulāpadesa) should be taken by way of a famous man born in that lineage, such as 'Ādicca' or 'Māghava.' The Ādicca lineage of the Sakyans is the son of the goddess named Aditi...
252:
...it depends on the first man; they also call it the 'Gotama lineage.' As said in the Pabbajjā Sutta: 'By lineage I am an Ādicca, by birth a Sakyan; from that clan I have gone forth, I do not long for sensual pleasures.' (Sn 425). The Māghava clan, however, depends on the famous man from the village of Macala in that lineage. Because of the blameworthiness of the root of the lineage, showing that it is not a basis for pride, it is said: 'I will cut down the banner of conceit from its root.' 'Ghaṭṭento' means striking or insulting by way of birth and lineage. 'Hīḷento' means performing disparagement or blame. The intention is that when faults such as fierceness are attributed to the Sakyans by saying 'The Sakyan breed is fierce, Master Gotama,' etc., the ascetic Gotama will also be attributed with those faults.

The clan in which those with great pride and those with great anger are mutually stubborn and harsh is called 'fierce' (caṇḍa); this is shown by the phrase 'endowed with anger based on pride.' Here, the state of being 'based on' is by way of strong natural condition (pakatūpanissaya) and object condition (ārammaṇa), not by way of conascence (sahajāta), etc. 'Kharā' means being harsh in mind and speech. 'Lahukā' means those who are young and whose deeds are not mature. Therefore, it is said 'only by a little,' etc. 'Alābukatāhaṃ' is the unbroken shell of a gourd fruit. To show a method outside of the Commentary, the Teacher said: 'Some say bhassā means those who act or speak impulsively; others say it means those who provoke or threaten others.' 'Samānā' means 'being'; this meaning is by way of the word 'asa.' Therefore, it is said: 'Santā is merely a synonym of the preceding word.' 'They do not honor' (na sakkaronti) conveys the meaning 'to the Brahmins...' etc. 'Apacitikammaṃ' means the act of paying homage. In the latter sentence 'If these Sakyans' (yadime sakyā), the indefinite 'ya' sound which refers to the verb should be understood as being determined by the 'ta' sound in the previous sentence 'This, Master Gotama' (tayidaṃ bho gotama); thus it says 'That which these Sakyans,' etc. 'Nānulomaṃ' means being unsuitable for one's own birth.

## Explanation of the Second Accusation of Menial Status (Ibba)

The definition of the word 'santhāgāra' (council hall) has already been stated below. At that time, referring to the large number of consecrated Sakyan kings, it is said: 'the consecrated Sakyan kings.' Indeed, in the Sakyan royal clan, whoever is the eldest of all and is capable of ruling, he alone [receives] the consecration...
253:
Some individuals, having been consecrated, think: "This kingship involves many duties and much anxiety," and becoming weary of that kingship, they hand it over to the person next in age to them. Sometimes, that recipient also hands it over to another. Because of this successive handing over, there were many Sakyan kings at that time who had been previously consecrated; this is the teacher's intended view (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.265). Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say this referring to the abundance of Sakyan kings consecrated in various suitable positions. They are indeed called "kings." As it was said: "Kings mean universal monarchs, regional kings, local rulers, district governors, judges, high ministers, or those who govern by inflicting punishments such as cutting off limbs; these are called kings" (Pārā. 92).

A couch decorated with movable figures of wild beasts is called a pallanka. A stool woven with cane is called a vettāsana (bhaddapīṭha). A mere smile is mihitamatta; a mere laugh is hasitamatta. "Anuhasanti" means they laugh loudly, directed at me; this is the explanation of the word "anujagghantā" (mocking). The word "jaggha" occurs in the sense of loud laughter, as in "I will not go amidst the houses laughing loudly" (Pāci. 586).

They know the family lineage handed down successively from Kaṇhāyana through oral tradition. Those who are proud of their family usually cite the high or low lineage of others in various ways, and they also know their own family lineage. Similarly, Ambaṭṭha also knows his family. That is why later, when questioned by the Blessed One, he told his family lineage as it truly was, out of fear of the thunderbolt-bearing spirit (Vajirapāṇi). "Olambetvā" means wearing the cloth hanging down in the shape of an elephant's trunk, etc. "Tato" means because of such knowledge and because of going. "Mamanyeva manye" means he thinks they are laughing only at me.

## Commentary on the Third Statement about Menials

"Khettaleḍḍūnaṃ" refers to small birds known as "leḍḍukikā" (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.266) because they live among the clods of earth turned up by plowing in the field. In the commentary on the Leḍḍukikopama Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, they are called "cātakasakuṇikā" (Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.150), while in the lexicons (nighaṇṭu), they are called "lāpasakuṇikā." "Kodhavasena laggituṃ" means to harbor a grudge or to bind malice.
254:
Saying "He makes us equal to swans, cranes, and peacocks," the following words—"Just as no swan, crane, or peacock comes and prevents you, saying 'Why do you cry out?'"—although not included in the Council (Saṅgīti), were indeed spoken by the Blessed One at that time. Indeed, it is fitting to say that He made such a comparison while speaking then. Ambaṭṭha thinks that the words "Are you like this?" etc., and "You are indeed one who has not practiced" etc., were spoken by the ascetic Gotama out of pride; with this intention, the teacher says, "Thinking: 'Now he has become one without pride.'"

## Commentary on the Statement about the Son of a Slave Girl

In the word "nimmādeti," the letter 'a' is changed to 'ā' for the description; or it is shown by the word "nimmadeti" (he crushes pride) because it is derived from the word "mada" in the sense of intoxication or madness. "Nimmāne" means among those whose pride is gone. "It would be good if I were to ask about the lineage" is the meaning. Desiring to make it clear, he spoke with a loud voice three times. The question "Why did he speak?" is an inquiry into the reason for speaking thus even though he knew the impurity (of Ambaṭṭha's birth). Only the name that serves as a lineage name is intended, not the lineage separately; thus he says, "Belonging to both mother and father (the property of parents)." In reality, a lineage (gotta) is "pettika," obtained from the father, not "mātāpettika" from the mother. Brahmins do not desire marriage within the same lineage; however, the lineage name is established by birth (jāti), not an artificial name (kittima) or a name based on qualities (guṇa). Since birth involves both parents, it is "mātāpettika," not merely "pettika" from the father. "Nāmagotta" is a name that is a lineage name, not an artificial or qualitative name; it is said this way because the qualifier follows, as in the word "ajyāhita." The name itself is also the lineage because it proceeds by way of succession; thus it is "nāmagotta." Among those two, the designation "Kaṇhāyana" is well-known; referring to that designation, he says, "A name by way of designation." However, that name has come down through the family succession starting from the sage Kaṇha and is not well-known only in this (Ambaṭṭha's) family; thus it is said, "A lineage by way of succession." The definition of the word "gotta" has already been stated below.

In the phrase "to one who remembers," not just mere remembering is intended, but rather by way of investigating the purity of the family; thus he says, "to one who purifies the end of the family," meaning one who purifies the peak of the family. In the word "ayyaputta," the word "ayya" means lord (master), so he says "sons of the lord." Among the four...
255:
Among the slave-girls, the one named Disā was a household-born slave-girl of King Okkāka. Therefore, it was said, "the son of a slave-girl." In this matter, the young man Ambaṭṭha, relying on his birth, was arrogant and stubborn. If his true lineage were not clearly revealed, it would not be possible to subdue his pride. If his pride were not subdued, he would offend the Triple Gem through the power of that pride. However, once his pride is subdued, he will later gain faith in the Triple Gem. Such speech, because of the gentleness of the mind, is not what is called harsh speech (pharusavācā). The Abhaya Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa is the evidence here. Some people, when spoken to with harsh words, become soft, just as iron and such become soft by fire. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to make the young man Ambaṭṭha free from the poison of pride, said: "The Sakyans are your masters; Ambaṭṭha, you are the son of a slave-girl of the Sakyans."

In passages such as "In this Dispensation, some evil bhikkhu learns the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata and bears (dahati) it in himself," the word "daha" has the meaning of bearing (dhāraṇa). Here, bearing means making known by way of the ancestors; thus it is said, "King Okkāka is our ancestor," and so on. Scholars of grammar recognize the word "daha" in the sense of reducing to ashes and in the sense of bearing. It is said that rays of light emit; thus, because of such meritorious deeds, the teeth are radiant and appear as such, which is called "pabhassara."

"Te" refers to the elder princes. "Paṭhamakappikānaṃ" means those who arose at the beginning of the first eon. Here, the word "kira" is used in the sense of hearsay (anussava), indicating the variation in opinions of some teachers regarding the royal lineage to be described. Only by words of hearsay is the variation in opinion of those such as the dwellers of the Uttara Vihāra, which was not heard through tradition, rejected. "Mahāsammata" refers to the king so named because he was designated and appointed by the great multitude, saying "This person shall be our king," according to the method to be described in the Aggañña Sutta. Referring to that king, the teachers say:

Born of the Solar lineage, a mine of extremely pure virtues,
There was a king of great majesty, named Mahāsammata.
He was like the eye of the world, shining with the rays of his virtues,
Dispelling the darkness, he shone like a second sun.
256:
That King Mahāsammata, desiring the welfare of the world, established boundaries and regulations. People are unable to transgress those regulations. People call that King Mahāsammata 'Manu'—he who was illustrious, powerful, the protector of the world's boundaries, the first of his kind, and a great hero.

Referring to the lineage of sons and grandsons of that King Manu, they say:

The son of that King Mahāsammata was the mighty lord of the earth named Roja. The son of that King Roja was Vararoja, excellent among the assembly of kings.

The son of that King Vararoja was the one of good qualities named Kalyāṇa. The son of that King Kalyāṇa was the king named Varakalyāṇa.

The son of that King Varakalyāṇa was the great hero, King Mandhātu, the Universal Monarch, who was supreme among those who enjoy sensual pleasures, and who was honored by Sakka, the king of gods, with half of his kingdom.

The son of that King Mandhātu was the one of great majesty named Varamandhātu. The son of that King Varamandhātu was the one of great following named Uposatha.

There was a king of great majesty named Vara; the son of that King Vara was Mahāvara. The son of that King Mahāvara was the king of great strength named Upavara.

The son of that King Upavara was the lord of the earth named Maghadeva, who was like a god. The lineage of sons and grandsons of that King Maghadeva numbered eighty-four thousand.

The last of those kings was the one famous as 'Okkāka', who was of great fame, great majesty, and not insignificant among the assembly of kings.

This is the statement that is not in contradiction with the Commentaries. However, what is said in the Dīpavaṃsa is:

The first anointed king, the protector of the earth, the possessor of splendor,
The Khattiya named Mahāsammata, ruled the kingdom.

His son was the king named Roja. Besides him, Vararoja, Kalyāṇa, Varakalyāṇa, and Uposatha were also lords of the earth.
257:
Among those kings, King Mandhātu, the ruler of the four continents, was the seventh. The sons of King Mandhātu were King Vara, King Upavara, and King Cetiya, the rulers of the earth, and so forth. In the Mahāvaṃsa and other chronicles, it is stated: 'The Great Sage (the Buddha), a descendant of King Mahāsammata, was once King Mahāsammata at the beginning of the aeon. There were King Roja and King Vararoja. Furthermore, there were the two kings, Kalyāṇa and Varakalyāṇa. There were King Uposatha and King Mandhātu. There were the two kings, Vara and Upavara,' and so forth.

All these statements mostly contradict the Commentaries. In the Commentary, King Mandhātu is said to be the sixth, and King Makhādeva is said to be the eleventh. Among the eighty-four thousand kings who were the descendants of King Makhādeva, the last king is said to be King Okkāka. In those accounts, King Mandhātu is called the seventh, and King Makhādeva is called the last of many thousands of kings, and King Okkāka is called the last of the thousands of kings who were the descendants of King Makhādeva; thus, the Commentary refutes these contradictory statements in various ways. Did we not say that 'the word kira here is used in the sense of hearsay (tradition), indicating the differences of opinion among some regarding the royal lineage being discussed'? The phrase 'after those kings' means in the later period of the eighty-four thousand khattiyas ending with King Kaḷārajanaka, who were of the lineage of Makhādeva; this was stated by the Teacher according to what had been heard through tradition.

In the Dīpavaṃsa and other chronicles, however, it is stated: 'Among the thousands of kings who were the descendants of King Kaḷārajanaka, the last king was named Sujāta; his son was King Okkāka.' In the later period of the thousands of kings of the Makhādeva lineage, the first King Okkāka appeared. In the later period of the thousands of kings of his lineage, the second King Okkāka appeared. In the later period of the thousands of kings of that lineage, the third King Okkāka appeared. Referring to that third King Okkāka, it was said, 'There were three lineages of Okkāka,' and so forth.

Because performing auspicious ceremonies such as naming on the fifth day after birth is a worldly custom, it is said, 'having decorated [the child] on the fifth day.' Because [the king] reached great joy upon seeing his son and wished to give a gift out of delight without reflecting quickly, it is said, 'he immediately granted a boon.'
258:
(The King), having reached great joy and satisfaction, quickly granted a boon out of a desire to give out of delight, without investigating or reflecting, saying, 'Take whatever boon you desire.' She was the mother of Prince Jantu. 'She wishes to divert the kingship' means she wishes to take advantage of the boon I granted to transfer this kingship (to her son).

'They will cause the kingship to be exercised' means causing the kingship to be exercised by the great multitude, or causing the great multitude to exercise the kingship. 'They would not be able to oppress' means they would not be able [to find a place] for dwelling.

He was named the Brahmin Kapila because he had a dark (or mottled) complexion. 'Having gone forth' means having departed from the household life and from sensual pleasures. Sāka is the name of a specific excellent tree (teak) which is entirely heartwood, from which palaces and such are made; it refers to a forest grove consisting of a collection of those trees. Because it occurs in the earth, it is called bhumma; it illuminates or makes clear the virtues and faults of that earth; or, by that [knowledge], the virtues and faults of the earth become bright and evident; therefore, it is called Bhumma-jālā (the Earth-net). In this context, 'and below,' the word 'and' (ca) pulls in the phrase 'eighty cubits.' 'In this place' refers to the teak forest grove. By virtue of the arrangement of their trunks, they [the trees] wind to the right. By virtue of the arrangement of their branches, they face the east. 'By those' refers to deer, pigs, frogs, and mice. 'Those' refers to lions, tigers, snakes, cats, and so forth.

'Herein' means in the city thus created. The construction is: 'Even a single man included among your men, the enemies—even a hundred or a thousand other men—will not be able to oppress.' 'By the power of a Cakkavatti' means by way of having the power and strength of a Universal Monarch. 'Is excellent' means it would be exceedingly noble. Because it was the dwelling place of the sage Kapila, it is called Kapilavatthu.

The connection is: 'It would be in their presence.' 'In a dissimilar union' means because of the household union of those who are not similar by way of birth (caste/lineage). This is because the remaining princes entered into household life with their own younger sisters.

The word 'growing' is in the genitive case used in the sense of disregard (anādara); the meaning is that while the sons and daughters were growing up without any danger, [leprosy] arose (in the eldest sister). Because they were red like blood, they resembled kovilāra flowers. Since leprosy generally has a contagious nature like scabies or smallpox, it was said, 'This disease is contagious.' After covering it from above with a plank and making a heap of dust over it...
259:
"Nāṭakitthiyo" refers to dancing women. The king's wives are called "Orodhā" (harem). "Tassa" refers to [the interior] of a hollow tree. In the phrase "migasakuṇādīnaṃ," the word "ādi" includes forest-dwelling petas and so forth.

The words should be connected as "tasmiṃ rāmaraññe nisinne." "Padare" means on a wooden plank. By speaking of the king's artifice, he made his own kingship known.

"Mātikaṃ" means coming from the mother. "Pābhataṃ" means original capital or a gift. "Rañño" refers to King Rāmarājā, the eldest son, the King of Bārāṇasī. "Tattha" means in the city of Bārāṇasī. "Idheva" means only at the foot of the Himalayas. "Nagaraṃ" means the great city which is the royal capital. The tree named "Kolarukkho" is a special kind of tree used as medicine for leprosy. "Vyagghapathe" means on the tiger's path or on the road.

"Mātulā" means mother's brothers (uncles). "Kesaggahaṇaṃ" means tying the hair in a bun. "Dussaggahaṇaṃ" means the manner of wearing clothes. "Nhānatitthaṃ" means the bathing place of the aforementioned pond. To show that even now their race is unmixed, he said "evaṃ tesaṃ" and so on. "Āvāha" means taking a bride. "Vivāha" means giving a bride. "Tattha" means among those Sakyans and Koliyans. Since roots (dhātu) have many meanings, the word "samu" has the meaning of dwelling, thus he said "vasanti" (they dwell). The word "agge" is in the locative case (bhamma) with the sense of the accusative (upayoga); the word "agga" also exists in the sense of "beginning," and it is shown as an adverb (kriyāvisesana) by "taṃ aggaṃ" and so forth.

In this matter, the Blessed One said: "Ambaṭṭha, then King Okkāka uttered this inspired utterance: 'Indeed, sirs, the princes are capable; indeed, sirs, the princes are very capable.' Ambaṭṭha, from the time of that inspired utterance, the Sakyans became well-known." This is a demonstration of a natural derivation both by word and by meaning. Because they were able (sakkuṇanti) to preserve their family lineage without mixing the race by cohabiting even with their own sisters, they are called "Sakya." Those same princes are also called "Sākiya" due to a specific grammatical formation.

As stated in the Sanskrit Nighaṇṭu texts:
"Because those princes formerly dwelt in a place covered by teak (sāka) trees,
Therefore, those born of that lineage are famous on earth as 'Sakya'."
This statement is merely based on the word and is an unnatural derivation. It is also said: "They are called Sakya or Sākiya because they lived in the teak forest (sākavana) where the hermit Kapila resided."
260:
He is called "Kaṇha" because of his dark complexion (kāḷavaṇṇa), as stated by "kāḷavaṇṇa" and so on. The hair growing on the chin is called the beard (massu); the hair growing on both sides of the upper lip in the manner of tusks is called the moustache (dāṭhikā). This statement is made only according to the meaning; however, by the power of the word, just as nowadays yakkhas are designated as "pisāca," so at that time they were designated as "kaṇha." Therefore, because he spoke as soon as he was born and resembled a pisāca, he was called Kaṇha. For that reason, it was said: "Ambaṭṭha, just as nowadays people see pisācas and recognize them as 'pisāca,' even so, Ambaṭṭha, at that time people recognized pisācas as 'kaṇha'," and so forth. In that passage, "pisāco jāto" is a synonym (vevacana) for the previous word "kaṇha" to make it easily understood by the name well-known today. As in passages such as "I will not speak with a mouth full of food," the word "hara" with the power of a prefix has the meaning of making a sound; again, when joined with the second prefix (u), it signifies making a loud sound, therefore it is said, "he made a loud sound."

"To free themselves from reproach" means for the teacher (Pokkharasāti) and the youth Ambaṭṭha to remove the blame that would fall upon them. The word "attano" here is a word showing the elision of a repeated word (vicchā). "Will cause division" means he will cause division by making known his ill-will, or he will bring about slander (pesuñña). Because it is the means for making the meaning known, the making of speech alone is called "vākkaraṇa" by the method of nirutti (etymology); because that person has good speech-making, he is called "kalyāṇavākkaraṇa." In the phrase "in this speech," the word "ta" (this/that) certainly refers to the doctrine of birth (jātivāda) previously mentioned by Ambaṭṭha, such as "Master Gotama, these four varnas...", but Ambaṭṭha should respond to that doctrine of birth only according to the method stated in the Vedas. Therefore, to show that only the words of the three Vedas, which are well-known as the reason for the response, should be referred to, it is said: "in the words of the three Vedas learned by himself." Now, to show the reference to the words spoken by the Blessed One, "Ambaṭṭha, your ancient ancestral lineage...", he said: "or else, in this speech about being the son of a slave-woman." Furthermore, in the phrase "to respond," "paṭimantanā" means answering a question or speaking further (excessively). Therefore, it should be understood that the word "ta" refers to that subject in accordance with both meanings.

"First" means even before the consultation, even before the consultation was made. "Hard to know" means difficult to understand, even at first to lift the head...
261:
Because of being unable to answer the question, because of the difficulty in knowing the lineage, and because of the difficulty in explaining the meaning, it is implied that Ambaṭṭha wished to free himself on his own. By calling the Sakyans 'menials' (ibbhā), he brought blame upon himself; thus it is said, 'a bag tied by himself,' meaning a bundle tied by himself.

'Dhamma' here means 'cause,' as in 'Dhamma-paṭisambhidā' and so on. Because it occurs together with a cause, it is called 'Sahadhamma.' This same 'Sahadhamma' is 'Sahadhammika,' expressed through synonyms like 'Sahetuka.' Alternatively, the originating cause is called 'hetu,' and the supporting cause is called 'kāraṇa.' Referring to speaking one irrelevant word with another irrelevant word, it is said 'Yo hi' and so on.

'Tato' means after being urged twice, even before the third urging arrives, he would depart.

Because he is worthy of worship, Sakka, the king of devas, is called a 'Yakkha.' Being endowed with the natural appearance of fire, 'āditta' (blazing) means the color of fire. 'Kandala' is a specific flowering tree; its flower is white, and its bud is also white and shaped like a tusk. 'Virūparūpa' means a frightening and distorted form.

Referring to the state of being unconcerned (appossukkata) while staying at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree in the eighth week—a practice common to all Buddhas—it is said 'Ahañceva' and so on. 'Avattamāne' means not practicing or not following. Because of that promise, Sakka came to frighten Ambaṭṭha and make him answer the question, just as in the meeting with Saccaka the Wanderer in the Mūlapaṇṇāsa.

In the phrase 'Only the Blessed One and Ambaṭṭha saw,' the two reasons why others did not see are shown by 'Yadi hi' and so on. The word 'hi' is a particle indicating a cause. The connection should be made as: because it was not a burden, and because others would talk. It was not a burden because it was common to others as well. 'Āvāhetvā' means summoning by the power of a mantra. 'Tassa' refers to Ambaṭṭha. 'Antokucchi' refers to the interior of the belly, such as the large and small intestines. 'Vādasanghaṭṭe' refers to the clash of words. 'Maññamāno' means due to thinking or perceiving. This shows the connection.

'Seeking a shelter' (tāṇaṃ gavesamāno) means seeking the Blessed One as a refuge (tāṇa), thinking, 'Only this ascetic Gotama is the one who will save me from this danger of the yakkha.' In the remaining two terms, 'seeking a cave' (leṇaṃ gavesamāno) and 'seeking a refuge' (saraṇaṃ gavesamāno), the connection should be understood in the same way. 'Tāyati' means it protects from the danger that has arisen, thus it is said 'rakkhati' (protects); this term is in the agentive sense (kattu-sādhana). 'Nilīyati' means it is a place to hide when oppressed by an evident danger, thus it is called 'leṇa' (cave/refuge); this term is in the locative sense (adhikaraṇa-sādhana). The word 'sara' is used in the sense of destruction. That destruction refers only to the destruction of danger. Therefore, it is said, 'it destroys danger.' This term is in the agentive sense (kattu-sādhana).

The explanation of the talk about the son of a slave girl is finished.

## Commentary on the Lineage of Ambaṭṭha

274. 'Gaṅgāya dakkhiṇe' means in the region south of the Ganges river. 'Brāhmaṇatāpasā' refers to ascetics of Brahmin lineage. Bamboo, or spears...
262:
...seeking, approaching is what is meant. In the other two terms as well, this is the method. 'Tāyati' means it protects from the danger as it has appeared. Therefore it is said 'rakkhati' (protects); this is an agentive derivative (kattu-sādhana). 'Nilīyati' means one is hidden, being oppressed by the danger as it has appeared; this is a locative derivative (adhikaraṇa-sādhana). The word 'sara' is in the sense of harming/destroying, and that destruction is intended as 'dispelling'; thus it is said 'it harms or dispels danger'; this is an agentive derivative (kattu-sādhana).

## Commentary on the Story of the Ambaṭṭha Lineage

'Gaṅgāya dakkhiṇato' means in the southern part of the river named Gaṅgā. 'Brāhmaṇatāpasā' are ascetics of Brahmin birth. Due to the power of a mantra, the hand of one who wishes to throw an arrow or a spear etc. at another does not turn (cannot move). If the hand itself cannot move, how could the weapon turn? Referring to such inability to move, it is said 'the weapon does not turn.' 'Bhadraṃ bho' is an expression of acceptance, meaning 'Very well.' That an arrow shot by a bow cannot reach its mark is expressed as 'the bow cannot reach' by way of the sasamphārakathā method (metonymy), just as it is said 'one shoots with a bow, one sees with the eye.' Because it causes [weapons] to stay in the bodies of beings, it is called 'Ambaṭṭha' science by way of etymology (nirutti); it means a mantra-science that has acquired this name. Because that ascetic possessed the Ambaṭṭha science, the Kaṇha Rishi was known as 'Ambaṭṭha.' Because he was born in that lineage, this youth is also called 'Ambaṭṭha.' It is said that the Kaṇha Rishi, loathing his low birth and thinking, 'How is it that I was born from the womb of a slave girl named Disā?', went forth thinking, 'Now I shall purify this birth by whatever means.' Therefore it is said, 'Now I shall fulfill my heart's desire.' This was his heart's desire: 'From the time I frighten the king by the power of science and obtain his daughter, this slave-birth of mine will be purified.'

'Seṭṭhamante' means in the excellent Vedic mantras. The meaning is: 'Being the son of a slave girl, for what reason does he ask for a daughter of such smooth beauty?' It is called a 'khurappa' arrow because it cuts (khurati), or because it drinks/destroys the razor (khuraṃ pāti/pivati), or because a razor is fixed at its tip. By the power of the mantra, the king's arms became merely stiff; because of that stiffness of the arms, the king became afraid, suspicious, and terrified, thinking, 'Who knows? What will happen?' Therefore it is said, 'He stood trembling with fear.'
263:
In the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, King Okkāka appeared after King Daṇḍakī and others. The story of these kings has been well-known everywhere for a long time; this is the intended meaning of the words beginning with "Daṇḍakīrañño". The same applies to King Daṇḍakī, King Nāḷikera, and King Ajjuna, who committed offenses. Although there were rains of sand and such, they reached destruction only through a rain of weapons; this is the meaning of the term "āvudhavuṭṭhiyā". It should be understood that the ministers, thinking, "This ascetic Kaṇha is also a person of such great power," spoke thus out of fear.

"Undriyissati" means it will break apart. Here, the word "pathavī" (earth) is used in the sense of a passive-agent (kammakattu), as in the phrase "the granary breaks by itself." Therefore, it means "bhizzissati" (it will break). "Thusamuṭṭhī" refers to a handful of straw or a handful of chaff. Why? Because it means "merely enough to stop an arrow," and so forth.

Those who are terrified by danger have trembling bodies and their hair stands on end. However, those who are not terrified or frightened because there is no danger have bodies that do not tremble and their hair remains flat (not standing up). They remain in safety and well-being. By that state of the hair remaining flat, the safety and well-being of that person are made manifest. Therefore, to make the cause known through the effect, the word "pallomo" is used in the Pāḷi text, which is explained by the words beginning with "pannalomo". The formation of the word according to the method of Nirutti is like that found in the Bhayabherava Sutta: "I attained extreme calmness for the sake of dwelling in the forest." "Idaṃ" is the concluding word. The promise, "If the Great King gives that girl, the prince will be safe and his hair will lie flat (he will be calm)," is clear from the context. "Tena" refers to the ascetic Kaṇha. "Mante" refers to the mantra known as the science that pacifies the mantra which makes the arms stiff. For such mantras that cause danger and harm, there certainly exist mantras that pacify them, just as in the case of the Kusumāraka science and others. "Parivattite" means when recited. To free his daughter from the foul smell (reproach), he made that ascetic Kaṇha a free man (bhujissa). To establish him in a position of authority suitable for that daughter, he placed the ascetic in a noble position. "Ekena pakkhena" means from the mother's side. The Blessed One spoke out of compassion to provide relief, not to show that he was of noble birth. Therefore, he said the words beginning with "Atha kho bhagavā".

## Description of the Excellence of the Khattiyas
"Brāhmaṇesu" is merely a conventional expression. It means that one should receive seats and so forth that are to be received by Brahmins in the presence of Brahmins. Therefore, it is said "brāhmaṇesu". "Saddha" (alms-food) is so called because it is performed in accordance with the Vedas for those who have gone to the next world, without longing for anything in return. To show this meaning, it is said "food prepared for the deceased" (matake uddissa katabhattaṃ). In the term "maṅgalādibhatte", the word "ādi" includes food prepared for festivals, the propitiation of deities, and so forth. "Yaññabhatte" refers to food prepared through restraint from evil and so forth. Here, the fire sacrifice (aggihoma) is called "yañña". "Pāhunakānaṃ" refers to the gift of food given to arriving guests. "Anivāraṇaṃ" means non-prohibition (anāvaṭaṃ). Because he was not born purely from both parents, he did not attain the status of a Khattiya (noble). Therefore, it is said "parisuddho" (impure). In the phrase "iti vā idaṃ katthaṃ", the performance of a general action is called "karaṇa".
264:
"Brāhmaṇānaṃ antare". To show the definition of "saddha" as that which should be done only out of faith for those who have gone to the next world in accordance with the Vedic scriptures, without desiring anything else, it is said "food prepared for the deceased". In the term "maṅgalādibhatte", the word "ādi" includes food prepared for festivals, the propitiation of deities, and so forth. "Yaññabhatte" refers to food prepared by means of restraint from evil and so forth. Here, the fire sacrifice (aggihoma), which is said to be "food prepared for restraint from evil and so forth," is called "yañña". "Pāhunakānaṃ" refers to the food of guests. Since the gift of food given even to those who are not regular visitors is called "pāhuna", it is also called "gift-food" (paṇṇākārabhatta). "Āvaṭaṃ" means prohibition; "anāvaṭaṃ" means non-prohibition. Because he was not well-born from both parents, he did not reach the status of a Khattiya. Therefore, he is called "an impure person" (aparisuddho).

In the phrase "itthiyā vā itthiṃ karitvā", "karaṇa" (making/doing) is used because the roots "kar" and "bhū", which have the general meaning of action, are included in the meaning of all roots; thus it means "having sought out". Having sought out and taken a Brahmin girl who is the wife of a Khattiya prince, one should apply the Pāḷi: "Khattiyas are superior to the women of Brahmins; Brahmins are inferior." In the phrase "purisena vā purisaṃ karitvā", the teacher says the method is the same. There too, having sought out and taken a Brahmin youth who is the husband of a Khattiya princess, the construction is: "Khattiyas are superior to the men of Brahmins; Brahmins are inferior." In the phrase "kismiñcideva pakaraṇe", "pakaraṇa" means "cause", as in "on this account, for this reason". Therefore, it means "on account of a slip due to passion and so forth." In essence, that is an offense. Since that offense is the doing of what should not be done, it is said "in some fault" and so forth. The word "bhassa" is a synonym for "bhasma" (ashes). It is called "bhassa" (ashes) because it is discarded as useless. The meaning of the word "vadhitvā" is "okiritvā" (having scattered/strewn).

He is called "janita" because he is brought into existence by kamma and defilements, or because he is born from them. That "janita" itself is "janeta" (a person/human). Thus it is said, "Those who, relying on lineage, remember." This is like the word "pajā" (beings/progeny), where the singular is used for the plural by the power of the word "jāti"; therefore, it means "the assembly of beings." It is also appropriate to say "in this assembly of people." "Paṭisaranti" means that relying on lineage, they make a refuge (remember), saying "I am of the Gotama lineage, I am of the Kassapa lineage," and so forth; they investigate and reflect.

## The Description of the First Recital Section is finished.
265: ## Explanation of the Discourse on Knowledge and Conduct (Vijjācaraṇa) However, when this verse is brought forth, those who hold Brahmā in high regard will come to have faith. The youth Ambaṭṭha, upon hearing the phrase 'endowed with knowledge and conduct' (vijjācaraṇasampanno), will ask about knowledge and conduct. Seeing that this teaching, which clarifies knowledge and conduct, would be beneficial to the masses, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, brought forth this verse spoken by the Brahmā Sanankumāra. To clarify this meaning, the teacher said, 'By this verse...' (imāya pana gāthāya), and so on. If it were not so (if he merely relied on another's words), the Blessed One would be one who is not all-knowing and one who depends on others; but it is not fitting for the Blessed One to be dependent on others because of his status as a Sammāsambuddha. Therefore, he said, 'I too, Ambaṭṭha, say this' (ahampi hi, ambaṭṭha, evaṃ vadāmi), and so on. 'Established in the Brahmin tradition' (brāhmaṇasamaye siddhaṃ) means well-known in the Brahminical view. It is connected with the talk on birth (jātivāda) and so forth in the manner to be described. The teacher (the sub-commentator) stated that 'connecting' (saṃsanditvā) means joining together and making it non-contradictory. Currently, in some manuscripts, the reading 'rejecting' (paṭikkhipitvā) is found, but that is inappropriate. Why? Because in the Pali, the Blessed One does not reject the knowledge and conduct established by the Brahmin tradition; rather, he connects that very knowledge and conduct contemplated by Ambaṭṭha, making it non-contradictory, and then teaches the unsurpassed knowledge and conduct. 'Vāda' means a view or a verbal expression. Therefore, he said, 'Brahmin... etc... the initial word.' Even a view is just a word because it is something to be spoken. 'Idaṃ' (this) includes the meaning that activities such as studying, teaching, sacrificing, and officiating at sacrifices are not suitable for a trader (Vessa), a noble (Khattiya), or others besides them, by the word 'ādi' (etc.). 'Everywhere' (sabbattha) refers to the talk on lineage (gotravāda) and the talk on pride (mānavāda). Among those two, 'gotravāda' is talk based on lineage, meaning words such as 'this matter is suitable only for the Kassapa lineage, not for the Kosiya lineage.' 'Mānavāda' is talk based on pride, through self-exaltation and disparaging others, meaning words such as 'this matter is suitable only for a Brahmin, not for a low-caste person (Sudda).' 'Bound by birth-talk' (jātivāde vinibaddhā) refers to those who are attached to views based on birth or caste. 'Everywhere' refers to being bound by lineage-talk and so on. 'Bound by lineage-talk' means those attached to lineage-talk. 'Bound by pride-talk' means those attached to pride-talk; those who proceed by self-exaltation and disparaging others, saying 'studying, teaching, sacrificing, and officiating are for Brahmins alone,' are also bound by pride-talk. 'Bound by marriage' (āvāhavivāhavinibaddhā) refers to those attached to the ceremonies of giving and taking daughters in marriage. Those who, by the power of the three types of attachment, are prone to say, 'Are you worthy to ask me, or are you not worthy?' are also bound by marriage. Intending this remaining meaning, it is said, 'This...
266: ...method' (eso nayo). To clarify the state of being bound by marriage, it is stated in the Pali, 'Are you worthy to ask me, or are you not worthy?' This should be connected with the three terms such as birth-talk. By the method of repetition (āvutti) and so on, birth-talk and the others express the meaning twice. Therefore, the teacher said, 'Those views which are bound by marriage are the ones that, by the power of the three connections, are prone to say, "Are you worthy to speak to me, or are you not worthy?"' To clear the objection as to why knowledge and conduct are asked about again when they were already asked about previously, he said, 'Then Ambaṭṭha...' (tato ambaṭṭho), and so on. There, 'where' (yattha) refers to the attainment of that knowledge and conduct. It is said with reference to what is established in the Brahmin tradition. 'We will be stuck' (laggissāma) means we will be attached or included within. 'Then' (tato) means from that attainment of knowledge and conduct. 'He disparaged' (avakkhipi) means he spoke down. One who holds things that are not truly knowledge and conduct as 'knowledge and conduct' through wrong knowledge, when the true knowledge and conduct are analyzed, is said to be far removed from them. 'Where' (yattha) refers to the attainment of that knowledge and conduct, spoken with reference to the unsurpassed knowledge and conduct. Although it is an object (kamma) when connected with the action of knowing, the subject (kattā) alone is appropriate when connected with the action of suitability. Since factors (kāraka) depend on the principal action, it is said, 'It is proper for us to know this attainment of knowledge and conduct.' In such cases, it should be noted thus. 'From the beginning' (samudāgamato) means starting from the initial arising. Although it is proper to conclude by way of conduct (caraṇa) because it is included in conduct, the Blessed One concludes only by way of virtue (sīla) to prevent Ambaṭṭha from traveling on an uneven path. To clarify this meaning, it is said, 'Even though included in conduct' (caraṇapariyāpannampi). Virtue is of three types, such as minor virtue (khuddaka-sīla), according to the method taught in the Brahmajāla Sutta. 'Only by way of virtue' (sīlavaseneva) means only by the method of virtue. 'Some slight virtue' (kiñci kiñci sīlaṃ) refers to the minor virtue of Brahmins, characterized by restraints (yama-niyama) such as non-violence, which is established by their birth. Because it exists thus, the intention is that one might be stuck by relying on even that mere virtue existing in oneself. The teacher said, 'One might be stuck as "conduct" (caraṇa) in only that mere virtue established in the Brahmin tradition.' That statement should be examined because the manner of speaking is already mentioned in the Commentary itself, or it is just a demonstration of the intention. The meaning here is: 'One might be stuck there' means one might be stuck in the place connected with the mere virtue existing in oneself, thinking 'We too are endowed with conduct.' Therefore, it is connected that he concludes only by way of virtue. Because there is no such possibility of straying, further on, only by way of conduct...
267:
To show the meaning of the word 'niyyāteti' (completes/leads out), the phrase beginning with 'Yaṃ panā' is stated. Since the immaterial attainments (arūpāvacara jhānas) are already explained by the explanation of the fourth fine-material attainment (rūpāvacara jhāna), it is said that 'the eight attainments are led out as conduct (caraṇa).' These immaterial attainments are also essentially fourth jhānas due to the similarity of their factors (aṅgasamatāya). 'Niyyātitā' has the meaning of being taken out without remainder, or being shown. 'From insight knowledge onwards' refers to the method: 'When his mind is thus concentrated, pure, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana),' and so on, meaning from the stage of insight knowledge.

## Description of the Four Ways to Ruin

'Asampāpuṇanto' refers to one who, despite making an effort, cannot complete or cannot enter (the attainment). 'Avisahamāno' refers to one who is unable even to begin the effort. 'Khārī' is the name for the requisites of ascetics; since there are many varieties, 'araṇī' and others are mentioned to distinguish them. Among them, 'araṇī' refers to the two fire-sticks, lower and upper, used for producing fire. 'Kamaṇḍalu' is a water-pot (pitcher). 'Sujā' is a ladle used in fire offerings.

In fact, the word 'sujā' applies to the fire offering itself and to the ladle made for scooping sacrificial food and so on. This is as stated in the Kūṭadanta Sutta: 'When the first or the second person holds up the sujā.' In this very context, the Teacher (the sub-commentator) stated: 'Sujā is a ladle.' It is called 'sujā' because it arises for the purpose of easily taking sacrificial food and so on. Some, without considering this meaning, take the meaning of sewing and read it as 'sucī' (needle). Since the Teacher did not explain it in that way, such a reading is inappropriate.

'Camaro' is a special kind of animal (yak/chowry-deer) that eats, and a fan made from its tail is called 'cāmarā.' By the word 'ādi' (etc.), one should include the triple staff, small pots, and so on. It is called 'kājo' (carrying pole) because it arises in a despicably curved shape. Alternatively, it is called 'kāco' because it binds a load. Grammarians accept both of these terms. 

'Khāribharitaṃ' means being filled with khārī (requisites). In the view of the teachers who read it as 'khārivividhaṃ' by adding the syllable 'vi', the phrase 'Ye panā' etc. is stated to show the meaning through a conjunctive compound (samuccaya-samāsa).

For monks, are not laypeople and novices within the Dispensation (even an Arahant novice) technically only attendants (paricāraka)? What then need be said of external ascetics? Based on this inquiry, 'Kāmañcā' etc. is stated to show the distinction among such attendants. 'Vuttanayenā' means 'by the method already mentioned, starting with kappiya...'.
268:
"By virtue of performing duties (vatta-karaṇa)," by the method thus stated, and by virtue of undertaking hundreds of thousands of restraint disciplines (saṃvara-vinaya), an Arahant novice is said to be an attendant to a worldling (puthujjana) monk because of the superior nature of the state of a fully ordained monk.

"Nine thousand crores, one hundred and eighty crores, five million, and again another thirty-six thousand—these restraint disciplines were proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One; they are the trainings in the restraint of the Vinaya, briefly indicated by way of repetition (peyyāla)."

Upasampadā (Higher Ordination) is the supreme fulfillment attained by well undertaking and training in these numerous hundreds of thousands of restraint disciplines. Because of this fulfillment of Upasampadā, this worldling monk is called 'upasampanna' (ordained).

"Ayaṃ pana" refers to the ascetic with the characteristics mentioned above. Ascetics are those who hold the doctrine of action (kammavādī) and the doctrine of the efficacy of action (kiriyavādī); they are not enemies of the Dispensation. Therefore, for those ascetics who come to ordain, ordination is permitted in the Khandhaka without the probation for other sectarians (titthiya-parivāsa). Because they possess austerity (tapa), the letter 'ta' is lengthened to form 'tāpasa.' Grammarians accept the suffix 'sa', as in the word 'lomasa' and others. The meaning is this: although an Arahant novice is technically an attendant to a worldling monk, he is an attendant only by performing duties, not because of an inferior state. An ascetic, however, is an attendant due to an inferior state both in terms of virtue and in terms of performing services (veyyāvacca), not just by performing duties. Thus, referring to this difference between them, only the ascetic's status as an attendant is mentioned.

With the word "Kasmā" (Why?), the questioner asks for the reason. With the word "Yasmā" (Because), the Teacher answers by showing the reason. To elaborate on the meaning thus briefly answered, "Imasmiñhi" etc. is stated. "Asakkontaṃ" refers to a shameless (alajjī) monk who practices wrongly because he is unable (to restrain himself). "Khuradhārūpamaṃ" has the simile of walking by treading upon the edge of a razor. "Bahujanasammatā" refers to one who is regarded as noble by many people. "Aññေ" refers to other monks. "Idha" refers to the ascetic ordination. "Chandena saha caranti" means they live according to their own desires, hence they are called "sachandacārī," meaning those who act as they please. "Anusikkhanto" means training by following the example seen. The ascetics are many, but the monks are not many.
269:
The etymology of kudālapiṭaka (hoe and basket) has been mentioned below. Bahujanakuhāpanattha means for the purpose of amazing the multitude. Aggisāla refers to a hall for fire-worship (fire-hut). Nānādārūhi means with various kinds of fuel such as branches and wood. Homakaraṇavasena means by way of performing sacrifices. In this context, pānāgāra (water-hall) is mentioned by way of water. Therefore, it is said 'having prepared drinking water,' etc. The phrase 'yaṃ bhattapuṭaṃ vā yāni taṇḍulādīni vā' should be connected. Ambilayāgu is gruel mixed with sour liquids such as fermented rice-water. Because they are handled with craving, etc., robes and such are called āmisa. Vaḍḍhiyā means by way of increase, such as double or triple. Kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapeti means establishing wealth.

The phrase 'Idaṃ panassa paṭipattimukhaṃ' is said because the aforementioned meaning is shown in the Pāḷi merely as an illustration. This Pāḷi statement means that this is only the beginning of the deceptive practice (kohaññapaṭipatti) of the fourth type of person. Why is that? Because he stays there amazing the world with various kinds of deception. Therefore, it is said 'Iminā hi,' etc. Evaṃ is intended in the manner stated as 'having prepared drinking water there,' etc.

To explain the phrase 'Sabbāpi tāpasapabbajjā niddiṭṭhā' (all types of ascetic renunciation are indicated), which was shown by the method of teaching according to the Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), by the method of teaching according to the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), the phrase 'Aṭṭhavidhā hi,' etc., is said. Uñchā is the gleaning and collecting of rice, green gram, black gram, sesame, etc., by standing near people at threshing floors and such in the manner of alms-gathering. Those whose habit of livelihood is such gleaning are called uñchācariya. Those who live by begging for rice cooked by fire are called aggipakkika. Those who do not beg for fire-cooked rice but live by begging only for raw rice are called anaggipakkika. The difference is that uñchācariya go to threshing floors and accept the first-fruits of grain offered by people, whereas anaggipakkika do not accept such grain but only raw rice. Those who do not cook themselves but live only on alms-food that is already cooked are called asāmapāka. A stone about the size of a fist, as hard as iron, is called ayamuṭṭhi; those who live by means of it are called ayamuṭṭhika. Tree bark peeled off with the teeth is called dantavakkala; those who live by it are dantavakkalika. Those whose habit is to eat fruit that has naturally fallen from trees are called pavatta-phalabhojī. The word paṇḍupalāsa has two meanings by the method of ekasesa: withered yellow leaves and [fruits/flowers] similar to them by being ripe and yellow...
270:
In the phrase 'pupphaphalādi ca,' flowers, fruits, etc., are also included. Therefore, [the commentator] will say: 'They subsist by eating naturally fallen flowers, fruits, withered leaves, etc.' Because they live by those flowers, fruits, and leaves, they are called paṇḍupalāsika; they are ascetics who habitually eat naturally fallen leaves, flowers, and fruits. Now, to show these eight types of ascetics in their specific forms, the word 'Tattha' etc., is said. The story of the ascetic Keṇiya should be taken from the Vinaya commentary (Khandhaka-vaṇṇanā).

Saṅkaḍḍhitvā means making into one collection by way of alms-gathering.

Taṇḍulabhikkhā is alms-food consisting of raw rice. It is called bhikkhā because it is begged for, or because it is the property of those who beg (monks/ascetics). Thus, the word bhikkhā is traditionally established for raw rice and such. Therefore, it is said 'they cook and eat' because they receive raw rice as alms.

Bhikkhā-pariyeṭṭhi nāma dukkhā means that searching for alms by going from house to house of others is miserable because it is a lowly way of living.

Certain ascetics think, 'For a renunciant, the grasping of a stone (or tool) is suffering,' and so they peel off bark using only their teeth and eat it; they are called dantavakkalika. This is a method not directly found in the Commentary (aṭṭhakathāmuttaka).

The word paṇḍupalāsa also applies to flowers and fruits by way of metaphorical similarity; this is shown by the phrase 'pupphaphalapaṇḍupalāsādīni'.

Te refers to the paṇḍupalāsika ascetics. This is merely an illustration, as such variations are possible among other ascetics as well. Pāpuṇanaṭṭhāne means in a place within reach [of the hand]. Ekarukkhato means from the tree first approached.

Since the objection 'How are all types of ascetic renunciation indicated by only these [four]?' has not yet been resolved, the phrase 'Imā pana' etc., is said. 'Catūhi yeva' means only by the four types of ascetic renunciation taught in the Pāḷi starting with 'khārividhamādāya,' namely: pavatta-phalabhojanika, kandamūla-phalabhojanika, ajjāgārika, and āgārika. Agāraṃ bhajanti means they resort to a house for the purpose of dwelling. By this phrase, it is shown how those ascetics are included in the fourth type of ascetic renunciation taught here in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, starting with 'having built a house with four doors, he stays,' etc. Similarly, the connection with the remaining ascetics should be understood in reverse order. By way of serving the fire, [they resort] to the fire-hut (ajjāgāra)...
271:
They attend to them. Thus, the commentator, speaking of the inclusion of those hermits, should be understood as showing that each of these hermits also has two types, corresponding to those four divisions.

Because he lives together with his teacher, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, he is called 'Sācariyaka' (one with a teacher), referring to that Ambaṭṭha. 'Apāyamukha' means a cause of ruin. What need is there to speak of its manifestation in the attainment of knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampadā)? Here, the word 'pi' is used in the sense of reproach. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Do you, together with your teacher, appear in this unsurpassed attainment of knowledge and conduct?" etc. In that Pali text, the following method is one outside the commentary (aṭṭhakathā-mutta-naya). Rejecting the manifestation in knowledge and conduct by saying "Not so, Master Gotama," Ambaṭṭha spoke "Who am I..." etc., to clarify only the state of non-manifestation. "Who am I, being of such a nature with my teacher, that I could appear in the unsurpassed attainment of knowledge and conduct? What is the nature of the unsurpassed attainment of knowledge and conduct that it should appear in me with my teacher? I am far away..." etc., this should be connected with the rest of the Pali text.

One who is engaged in the cause of ruin is called 'āpāyika'. Because he cannot fulfill the state of a hermit engaged in that cause of ruin, he is called 'aparippūramāna', meaning incomplete in that state. Although he himself is one associated with ruin, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, not fulfilling that state, spoke these words; because it is connected by meaning, this word 'āpāyika' is in the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti) in the sense of the agent (kattā); thus it is explained as 'āpāyikena api aparippūramānena'. Alternatively, although he is associated with the ruin of knowledge and conduct which he himself has not fulfilled, being himself an unfulfilled person associated with ruin, Pokkharasāti spoke these words; because the meaning is appropriate, this word 'āpāyika' is also said to be in the nominative case in the sense of 'characteristic state' (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). Indeed, the order of words is one thing, and the order of meaning is another. Some teachers say this is said to show the instrumental sense (karaṇa); that is not appropriate, because those two words have the same meaning as the subject (kattā), and words with the same meaning cannot stand in an instrumental relation to each other. There is no need for further elaboration.

## Commentary on the Practice of Ancient Sages

Because it is given, it is called 'datti'; that same 'datti' is called 'dattika', thus it is explained as 'dinnaka' (given). Because it is an art that makes one who does not wish to give, wish to give, and turns (confuses) others in one's presence, it is called 'Sammukhāvaṭṭanī'. Therefore, it is said: "He cannot say 'I do not give'." Again, 'tassa' means 'of the Brahmin'. Because of reaching fulfillment for kings according to the cause, "Why..."
272:
In the phrase "me dinno", "saṅkhapalitakuṭṭha" refers to white leprosy (vitiligo) that is white like a washed conch shell. It is said so because his body is white like a white lotus or silver, similar in quality to the planet Venus. "Anugacchati" means it follows after another or is contagious.

If, for two reasons, the King did not grant the Brahmin an audience face-to-face, then why was the approach of that Brahmin not forbidden? To answer this, it was said "Yasmā pana" etc. "Khettavijjā" refers to the Nīti treatises (treatises on policy/ethics), as the teacher said. In the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta below, it is also said: "Khettavijjā refers to Nīti treatises such as Abbheyya, Māsurakkha, and Rāja treatises." Here, "dussa" means a curtain (screen). Therefore, it is said: "Standing inside the curtain-wall." The word "anta" is used to augment the word without adding meaning, so "dussanta" is formed like the word "vananta". "Payāta" refers to rice (alms) offered out of faith dedicated to the deceased (saddha-feeding) or rice given constantly. Therefore, the teacher said "brought and given in front"; it should be understood to mean alms brought in the form of food for the dead or regular food. The phrase "Ayaṃ pana" etc., is spoken by way of implication (atthāpatti). "Niṭṭha" means decision/conclusion. Why did the Blessed One speak such unpleasant and piercing words to the Brahmin? To show the reason and clarify this, "Idaṃ pana" etc., was said. It should be connected as: "He revealed even the secret and hidden piercing words."

"Rājāsana" (royal seat) refers to the area of the elephant's back; thus the Pali says "sitting on the neck of the elephant". "Rathူpatthara" is the place spread on top of the chariot. Therefore, the teacher said "in the chariot" etc. "Uggatuggata" refers to those who are exceedingly eminent among the eminent. Worldly teachers do not favor the repetitive compound (vicchā-samāsa). The offspring of a king is called "rājañña" (prince). It is said "rājaññehi" either because of the state of being many or by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa). "Pākaṭamantana" means public consultation. Here, only that public consultation is intended, not secret consultation, because it is desired that even the poor (Suddas) etc., should hear it. Therefore, it was said: "If a Sudda or a slave of a Sudda should come" etc. "Only with such people" means only with those whose appearance is like the King's. Just as the King spoke words capable of achieving that purpose, it should be connected as: "Does he also speak words capable of achieving that purpose?"

"Pavattāro" means those who speak by way of proclaiming the scriptures (Vedas); this is the literal meaning. Since those sages were the originators of the mantras in that way...
273:
Therefore, to show the meaning by intention, it is said 'pavattayitāro' (promulgators). Indeed, the formation of the word 'vattāro' (speakers) should be understood through the root 'vada' and the suffix 'tu'; likewise, the formation of the word 'pavattayitāro' through the root 'vatu'. This is the view of the teacher Venerable Dhammapāla and the teacher Venerable Sāriputta Thera. Some teachers also say that the formation of the word 'pavattāro' is shown by the root 'vatu' alone. Because the two words have the same locus (tulyādhikaraṇa), it is said 'mantam-eva' (only the mantra). Indeed, because the mantras alone are the cause for attaining various benefits when spoken in secret after excluding the Shudras (suddas), they are called 'pada' (words/steps); thus, they have the same locus. The term 'mantapada' is also explained as the means of attainment (pada) for the act of whispering (mantana-kiriyā) which should be spoken secretly because it is not shared with those who are not initiated; this is a method outside the Commentaries.

'Gīta' (sung) means recited and chanted by way of singing. Here, singing is intended only by way of fulfilling the high and low tones, etc.; thus, it is said 'sara-sampatti-vasesana' (by way of vocal perfection). It is spoken to others as a form of teaching (pāvacana). That Veda is caused to be taught by way of making others speak it. It is well-compiled by way of collecting and arranging them in layers. It is categorized by way of the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, etc.; and therein also by way of individual mantras, Brahmanas, etc.; and by way of chapters (ajjhāya) and sections (anuvāka), etc. It is placed in a collection by the aforementioned method. 'Aññesaṃ vācitaṃ anuvācenti' means that the Brahmins of today make others recite the mantra-verses which were taught to those others (the students) by those rishis.

'Tesaṃ' refers to the rishis who were the authors of the Vedas. 'Dibbena cakkhunā' (with the divine eye) is said with reference to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa), which is an attendant of the divine eye, and the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa), which is similar to the divine eye because it sees clearly. Therefore, the meaning should be taken as: having observed the beings' ownership of kamma, etc., with the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma, and having observed the Brahmins' ritual of teaching the Vedas in past aeons with the knowledge of recollection of past lives. Indeed, since only present visible forms are the objects of the divine eye, that (the past) would be impossible here. 'Pāvacanena saha saṃsanditvā' means having compared and made it consistent with the words concerning the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) spoken by the Kassapa Buddha. Indeed, the meaning concerning the cessation of the round (nibbāna) was not evident to those rishis. 'Ganthiṃsu' means they composed it in the Sanskrit language by way of verse (pajja) and prose (gajja). 'Aparā pare' means others who were later, appearing during the time of King Okkāka and so on, other than the rishis like Aṭṭhaka. 'Pāṇātipātādīni pakkhipitvā' means having inserted words connected with defilements such as killing (pāṇātipāta) into the very mantra-verses composed by rishis like Aṭṭhaka. 'Viruddhe akaṃsu' means according to the method found in the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta...
274:
...they made it contradictory by illustrating meanings that cause defilements. The word 'isi' (seer/rishi) is just an illustration. It should be said, 'either a seer or one who has practiced to become a seer.' Why, in this context, is it not included in the sequence of the discourse by way of taking an admission? To answer this, he said 'idha bhagavā' and so on. 'In this place' (idha) refers to the place where it was said, 'I will study the mantras; do you consider yourself one with a teacher?' Without taking an admission means, just as an admission was taken below, 'What do you think, Ambaṭṭha, would you then be a seer or one who has practiced to become a seer, one with a teacher? No, indeed, Master Gotama'—thus, without taking an admission in this place (is the meaning).

'Nirāmagandhā' means free from the stench caused by the impurities of defilements. 'Anitthigandhā' means free from the scent of women, being unable to endure even the mere scent of women. 'Rajojalladharā' means bearing natural dust, sweat, and such dirt. 'Pākārapurisagutti' means the protection of walls and the protection of men. Here, by the word 'nirāmagandhā', he shows that those ten Brahmins had defilements suppressed by jhāna. By the words 'anitthigandhā, brahmacārino', he shows their solitary living.
