By 'rajojalladharā', he shows the absence of grooming and decoration. By 'araññāyatane pabbatapādesu vasiṃsu', he shows their living in seclusion, having abandoned human settlements. By 'vanamūlaphalāhārā vasiṃsu', he shows the rejection of excellent food such as sāli rice and meat. By 'yadā' etc., he shows the rejection of vehicles and carriages. By 'sabbadisāsu' etc., he shows the rejection of guards and protection. By showing this, in comparison to the livelihood of Ambaṭṭha who belongs to the side of wrong practice, the livelihood of those Brahmins, though belonging to the side of good practice, is still only wrong practice when compared to the right practice in the Noble Discipline (Ariya Vinaya). How could they possibly be endowed with the practice of effacement (sallekha)? By the words 'evaṃ su te' etc., the Blessed One clarifies that he is threatening and rebuking Ambaṭṭha. This is the illustration of the summary meaning of the Pali text to be spoken later.

'Dussapaṭṭikā' means a strip of cloth. 'Dussakalāpo' means a bundle of cloth or a braid of cloth. 'Veṭhakehi' means with ribs made by wrapping with cloths. 'Kappetuṃ' means to cut with scissors. In the phrase 'kappitavālehi', the method is the same. As in 'Monks, the beard should not be caused to be cut (kappāpetabbaṃ)', the word 'kappa' is used in the sense of cutting. 'Yuttaṭṭhānesu' means on the neck, head, and tail. 'Vālā' means the hairs growing in those places. They are so called either by way of association or by the name of the location.
275:
“Kuttavālā” is said. Some teachers, considering the reading “vālayuttattā,” say the meaning is “because of being associated with the figures of wild beasts.” The fault of those teachers is their disregard for the Pali text. In the Pali, it is said: “kuttavālehi vaḷavārathehi” (with chariots drawn by mares with trimmed tails). “Samantānagaraṃ” means from all around the city. The place where plasterwork is done at the lower part of the wall is called “upakārikā” because it is made near the city and because it provides benefit (upakāra). These plastered areas provide benefit to the city; therefore, they are called “nagarūpakārikāyo.” The feminine gender is used in reference to the capital (rājadhānī). Therefore, it is said: “idha pana,” and so on. “Mati” means knowledge that is not certain, by way of doubt. Desiring to show the reason for the non-increase of the teaching above, it is said: “idaṃ bhagavā,” and so on. In the Pali, “so maṃ pañhena” means that person should purify me with a question, and I too will purify him with an answer; the meaning should be understood according to the appropriate context.

## Description of the Vision of the Two Marks
The word “nisinnānaṃ” and so on is the genitive case in the sense of disregard, or it is an adjective. Because the marks cannot be known without remainder in a crouched posture, it is said: “na sakkoti” (he is not able). However, because they can be well-discerned by walking, it is said: “sakkoti” (he is able). It should be understood that the habit of walking was practiced for the sake of ease in searching for the marks. For those two reasons, it is said: “tena.”

“Gavesī” means he made a search with wisdom. “Gaṇayanto” means calculating and combining with wisdom. “Samānayī” means he brought together well. Because the meaning of the word “kaṅkhatī” is “he desires” (ākaṅkhatī), it is said: “aho vata,” and so on. Even a word without a prefix (upasagga) can, in some places, express a special meaning as if it had a prefix, such as the word “gotrabhū.” “Tato tato” means from various parts of the body. “Kicchatī” means he is weary. Therefore, it is said: “na sakkoti daṭṭhuṃ” (he is not able to see). “Tāyā” refers to the doubt mentioned as “he is weary while investigating.” “Tato” is because of not being able to reach a conclusion. Having thus shown the meaning of “kaṅkhatī” as longing, now, desiring to show the meaning as doubt, it is said: “kaṅkhāya vā,” and so on. There, “kaṅkhāya” refers to the doubt expressed by the word “kaṅkhatī.” A verb (ākhyāta) primarily expresses action. This method should also be understood for the remaining words. Doubt that has reached various states is called “tīhi dhammehi,” meaning by three kinds of doubtful states. “Kālusiyabhāvo” means the state of turbidity which is the cause of lack of clarity.
276:
The sheath of the male organ located at the bladder (or pelvic region), which is the lower part of the navel, is called “vatthikosa.” Just as in “aṇḍakosa” (eggshell/pouch) and so on, the word “kosa” is used in the sense of a surrounding pouch. It is called “vatthaguyha” (the organ) because it should be hidden by cloth. The Blessed One’s male organ, enclosed in a sheath, is a unique attribute (āveṇika) of all Buddhas, not shared with others, and resembles the radiance of a perfectly pure golden circle. Due to the beauty of its shape and position, it possesses the supreme charm of the noble organ of a thoroughbred Gandha elephant. It has the splendor of the radiant whorl of filaments of a blooming golden lotus. It surpasses with its own glory the beauty of the full moon seen amidst the waters colored by the evening glow. Because of being unstained by external or internal impurities, having practiced the holy life (brahmacariya) for a long time, and being endowed with a perfect shape, although it is an organ that should be concealed (kopīna), it is like one that need not be concealed. Therefore, it is said: “bhagavato hi,” and so on. “Varavāraṇasseva” means like that of a noble Gandha elephant. “Pahūtabhāva” refers to the extensiveness and largeness of the tongue. It was regarding this tongue that the youth Ambaṭṭha had doubt. However, there was no investigation into the qualities of the tongue such as its thinness, softness, and delicacy.

Because “tathārūpaṃ” is a compound (samāsa) word, it is explained as “taṃrūpaṃ.” “Ettha” means in the creation by psychic power, just as the youth Ambaṭṭha saw the male organ enclosed in a sheath. By this word “ettha,” the Pali text “tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhari” and so on is referred to. Therefore, in this context, the reason for showing the male organ along with the method of psychic creation is made clear by the text of the Milindapañhā. Some teachers refer to it as “vatthaguyhadassane,” but such a reference is inappropriate. This is because such a statement is found neither in the Pali nor in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) to be referred to in that way; if it were so, the method of psychic creation would not be made clear. There is nothing for others to say here, because it should be accepted exactly according to the method taught by the Venerable Nāgasena Thera, who was a master of debate, possessed the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and the six higher powers (abhiññā). Here, it is called “hirikaraṇa” because shame (hiri) is produced there; that “hirikaraṇa” itself is the place of shame (the organ). “Uttarassa” refers to the youth Uttara who appears in the Sutta Nipāta. The story of all these people should be taken from the Sutta Nipāta.

“Chāyā” means an image or reflection. To the questions “How did he show it?” or “What was it like?”, it is said: “iddhiyā,” and so on. “Chāyārūpakamatta” means it was merely a reflected image of the Blessed One, not the actual physical organ. Since that image is separate from the Buddha’s own continuity (santāna), it is merely a representation, a psychic image having a color, shape, and parts similar to the Blessed One. By doing so, the word specially qualified with the letter “ka,” which has the sense of “diminutive” or “imitation” (appaka), is appropriate. Having created a mere reflected image by psychic power...
277:
The word "dassesi" should be connected. Teachers say: "The Blessed One, while showing that shadow-image, did so in such a way that his own actual Buddha-form was not visible." This statement of the teachers is consistent and in agreement with the words of the Venerable Elder Nāgasena, who spoke of "showing only a shadow-image created by supernormal power," just as milk blends with milk or the water of the Ganges with the water of the Yamunā. By saying this, it is effectively established that the rest of the Buddha-form was not shown at that moment. However, here, by the words "nivāsananivatthata" etc., it is shown that although the shadow-image of the male organ is distinct from the Buddha's physical continuity, it does not go outside the undergarment he is wearing. One should not ask, "How does the Blessed One show the shadow-image that is inside the undergarment he is wearing, and how does Ambaṭṭha see it?" For the scope of supernormal power is unthinkable.

"Chāyaṃ diṭṭhe" means when the shadow-image of the male organ is seen. "Etaṃ" refers to the shadow-image. The intention is that if there were someone capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths, he would even show his heart-flesh, which is the basis of life. "Ninnitvā" means having taken out. Or, this "nīharitvā" is the only reading. "Kallosi" means "You are skillful and clever in answering the problem," or it means "The aforementioned way of answering the problem is appropriate and correct." Some read it as "kusalo," but that is not suitable. Because in the Milindapañha, at the end of every answer, only "kallo" is found.

"Ninnāmetvā" means having extended it towards the ear-holes etc., by way of taking it out from the mouth. To show the intention, "nīharitvā" is said. "Kathiṇasūciṃ viya" means making it like a hard needle by making it dense and subtle. "Tathākaraṇena" means by making it like such a hard needle. Here, the softness, length, and thinness of the extensive tongue are shown. The teacher said that a tongue that is not soft cannot be made dense and subtle. The meaning here is: since only a soft tongue can be made dense and subtle, by doing so, its softness is shown, just as fire is known by smoke. Since only a soft tongue, by becoming dense and subtle, can reach far, its length is shown by touching the ear-holes. Since only a soft tongue, by becoming dense and subtle, can be thin, its thinness is shown by touching the nostrils. Since a tongue that is not broad cannot cover in that way, its broadness is shown by covering the forehead.

"Patthento" should be connected with "udikkhanto" (looking on with longing and expectation).
278:
Original speech is called "kathā," and responsive speech is called "sallāpa."

As in words like "uddhumātaka" (bloated), the suffix "-ka" has the sense of disgust; therefore, it is said, "disgusting even that person." "Tam-eva" means either his state of being a wise man or the youth Ambaṭṭha himself. It is said this way with reference to the youth Ambaṭṭha. Thus it is said in the Pali: "Thus... he said this to the youth Ambaṭṭha." Although it is said with reference to Ambaṭṭha, it should be understood that he speaks in the plural because he wishes to reproach him without specifying him by name and clan. The fact that this word "evarūpena" is a definite statement for the indefinite statement "yad-eva kho tvaṃ" is shown by "yādiso" etc. In the sense of the locative case marking one state by another, the instrumental case is used, as in the phrase "edise atthacarake." "Na aññatra" means not in any other happy destination (sugati). Here, by the word "atthacarakeṇa," it should be understood that by the method of exclusion (vyatireka), it clarifies only the state of one who does not act for welfare. "Upaneyya upaneyya" is a repetitive word (vīcchā) ending in the suffix -tvā; therefore, it is said "brāhmaṇo kho pana" etc. Thus, "upanetvā upanetvā" means repeatedly bringing up this or that fault. Therefore, it is said, "having properly attributed the status of a slave etc." "Pātesi" means causing to fall (knocking down) by way of rolling. The phrase "and where he went" is connected by "having cut off that place (position) known as such going of that Ambaṭṭha."

## Description of Pokkharasāti Approaching the Buddha

292-3-6. Because it was asked how long that time was, it is said, "There was no time even for friendly conversation." "Āgamā nu" means "Has he come?" "Kho" is a mere particle. "Idha" means here (in your presence). "Adhivāsetu" means "may he accept" (may he be pleased). Since that acceptance here is only a mental acceptance and not by body or speech, it is said "sampaṭicchatū" (may he receive). To show this meaning of merit and joy occurring today, "yaṃ me" etc. is said. "Kāra" means a favor or an act of honor. "Acopetvā" means without moving (steadfastly).

"Sahatthā" is a word with an ablative ending in the sense of the instrumental. Therefore, it is said "sahatthena" (with one's own hand). "Suhita" means satisfied or having reached happiness because of the absence of the suffering of hunger. "Yāvadatthaṃ" means as much as desired, referring to what was done with food at that time. Here, "pavāraṇā" in the sense of refusal is intended, not "pavāraṇā" in the sense of invitation; therefore, "alaṃ" (enough) etc. is said. "Hatthasaññāya" (by a hand signal) is a mere example. In other places, refusal [is shown] by a change in facial expression or by speech...
279: Because rejection is stated through facial expressions or verbal utterances in other places, and because such rejection can be obtained in that manner even in a single moment (the signal by hand is merely an example). The Noble One who has removed his hand from the bowl is called 'onītapattapāṇi'. This is a bahubbīhi compound of three words with different referents. In the variant reading 'oṇittapattapāṇi', it is shown by the letter 'ṇ' and the geminate 'tt' that the word 'oṇitta' expresses the meaning of being free from or cleansing, as in 'oṇittapattapāṇinti pi pāṭho' and so forth. Alternatively, the word 'oṇitta' is used in the sense of cleansing. Because he has a bowl and hands that have been cleansed by removing food remnants, he is called 'oṇittapattapāṇi'. Therefore, it is said, 'having washed both hands and the bowl'. In the Sāratthadīpanī, it is stated: 'The Noble One who has a bowl that is free from the hand or cleansed by removing food remnants'. In that statement, the latter part should be considered as it does not harmonize with the commentary's phrase 'having washed both hands and the bowl'. 'Evambhūtaṃ' means being in the manner already described as 'bhuttāviṃ onītapattapāṇiṃ'. 'Anupubbikathā' means a discourse to be preached in successive order. Therefore, it is called 'anupaṭipāṭikathā'. That discourse consists of virtue (sīla) and so forth immediately following giving (dāna). This meaning should be understood: the discourse on giving (dānakathā) should be preached first because it is common even among those with little wisdom, universal to all, easy to practice, and serves as a means for establishing oneself in virtue. Indeed, a person who is accustomed to giving, being free from attachment to material objects, easily undertakes the precepts and becomes well-established in them. After the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā) should be preached because virtue shows the purity of the donor and the recipient, expresses the benefit to others, speaks of abstaining from harming others, distinguishes between what should be done and what should not be done, and shows the cause for the accomplishment of wealth and the accomplishment of existence. To show that such giving and virtue are based on the round of rebirth and that the accomplishment of existence is their fruit, the discourse on heaven (saggakathā) is preached after the discourse on virtue. By that discourse on heaven, it is shown that 'through these meritorious actions consisting of giving and virtue, which are distinguished as superior and most superior, these immeasurable divine splendors in the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth, which are also distinguished as superior and most superior, can be obtained'. To show that while heaven is defiled by lust and so forth, the Ariyan Path is entirely undefiled by them, the discourse on the Path (maggakathā) is preached after the discourse on heaven. In preaching the Path, the danger (ādīnava), the degradation (okāra), and the defilement (saṅkilesa) of sensual pleasures, and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma) must be preached to show the means of its attainment. Even all sensual pleasures pertaining to heaven are full of danger, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change; what then need be said of other sensual pleasures?
280:
The fault in other sensual pleasures, the baseness of all sensual pleasures being low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and associated with harm, is called 'okāra'. Because all states of existence are the basis for defilements, they are called 'saṅkilesa'. The benefits of 'nekkhamma', which is Nibbāna free from all defilements, should also be preached. This meaning should also be understood from 'bodhi' (knowledge). In this context, in the word 'maggo', the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'beginning etc.', and thus the explanation is made that the faults of sensual pleasures and so forth are also included. Therefore, it was said: "What is this? — He reveals the talk on giving, the talk on virtue, the talk on heaven, the danger, baseness, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefits of renunciation." The details should be taken from the Sāratthadီpanီ-ṭီkā.

The word 'kasi' occurs in the sense of 'taking with knowledge', hence it says "gahitā" etc. By the word 'sāmaṃ', the meaning to be excluded is shown by the phrase "not shared with others (asādhāraṇa)". This means it is not shared with others because, in attaining the supramundane Dhamma, there is an absence of instruction from others (upadesa), and because he alone first fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) in the world. In this context, 'dhammacakkhu' refers only to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). It does not refer to the lower three paths as in the Brahmāyu Sutta, nor to the destruction of taints (arahattamagga) as in the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta. Why is it said, "to show the manner of the arising of that path"? To resolve the objection that "the path-knowledge has only the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) as its object and not the conditioned (saṅkhata)", it says "tañhi" etc. 'Kiccavasena' means by the power of the function of penetrating without confusion.

## Explanation of the Declaration of Lay Discipleship by Pokkharasāti

In the Pali, among the words beginning with "diṭṭhadhammo", since 'seeing' (dassana) can also mean seeing with the eye etc. other than knowledge, the word "pattadhammo" is used to exclude that seeing with the eye. Since 'attaining' (patti) can also mean physical going etc. other than attaining through knowledge, the word "viditadhammo" is used to show the distinction from that. Since that 'knowing the Dhamma' (viditadhammatā) can also occur partially, the word "pariyogāḷhadhammo" is used to show the knowing of the Dhamma without remainder (entirely). By that word, it points only to Pokkharasāti's penetration of the Truths. For the path-knowledge, while accomplishing the four functions such as full understanding (pariññā) by way of a single realization (ekābhisamaya), is said to have completely plunged into the Dhamma of the Four Truths without remainder. Therefore, it is said: "Because the Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by this path-knowledge, he is called 'diṭṭhadhammo'." (If it is asked:) "How does a single knowledge function while accomplishing four tasks in a single moment? Such a thing has not been seen in the world, nor is there such a scripture (āgama)." (The answer is:) It should be known that just as a lamp in a single moment performs the burning of the wick, the consuming of the oil, the dispelling of darkness, and the manifesting of light, so too is this path-knowledge. The scriptural passage stating that the knowledge of a person endowed with the path occurs in the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), in the truth of the origin (samudayasacca), in the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca), and in the truth of the path (maggasacca) should be cited regarding the arising of path-knowledge.

"Tiṇṇavicikiccho" means that this Brahmin Pokkharasāti has crossed over the sixteen-fold doubt and the eight-fold doubt, which are like a dangerous and difficult journey. "Vigatakathaṅkatho" means...
281:
It should not be said that it 'does not exist.' Just as a lamp, in a single moment, burns the wick, consumes the oil, dispels the darkness, and produces light (simultaneously), so too should this Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) be understood (as completing four functions at once). The scriptural passage from the Vibhaṅga should be cited here as evidence: 'The knowledge of one possessed of the Path is this very knowledge regarding suffering, this very knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, this very knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and this very knowledge regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering.'

'Crossed over doubt' (tiṇṇā vicikicchā) means that this person has crossed over the sixteen-fold doubt and the eight-fold doubt, which are like a perilous wilderness. 'Gone is indecision' (vigatā kathaṃkathā) means that the indecision occurring as 'Is it thus? Is it not thus?' regarding the process of existence and so forth has been removed and utterly cut off for him. 'Attained to confidence' (visāradabhāvaṃ patto) means he has reached confidence (proficiency) because of the abandonment of unwholesome states that cause timidity, and because of being well-established in virtues such as morality (sīla) which are the opposites of those unwholesome states. If it is asked where that confidence is established, he says, 'Where? In the Teacher’s Dispensation,' intending to show it is in the Buddha's Dispensation. The meaning is that because he has personally realized and attained it through direct experience, there is no need to rely on another for conviction. This meaning is expressed by the words 'not of another' (na parassa) and so on. 'Does not proceed' (na vattati) means it does not occur or does not practice. The term 'independent of others' (aparappaccaya) is also appropriate because he no longer follows others or relies on (longs for) others. It should be understood by the wise that any points left unexplained in this Ambaṭṭha Sutta were omitted either because they were explained previously or will be explained later.

Thus, the 'Explanation of the Hidden Meaning' (Līnatthappakāsanā) of the Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta is concluded. It is contained within the sub-commentary named Sādhuvilāsinī, which clarifies the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-understand meanings of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī (the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya) and generates pure and vast intellectual proficiency. This work was composed by the Great Elder (Mahāthera) named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati, the Sangharaja and teacher of the Great King of Dhamma (King Bodawpaya). He was endowed with virtues such as uprightness, gentleness, serenity, faith, mindfulness, stability, wisdom, patience, and energy; he moved with fearless knowledge, unattached, through the Tipitaka along with its commentaries; he was able to penetrate the forest of his own doctrines (saka-samaya) and other doctrines (samayantara) in their many varieties; he was a leader of many groups and a master of great grammar.

## The Explanation of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta is finished.
282:
## 4. Explanation of the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta

Having explained the Ambaṭṭha Sutta in the manner stated, the Commentator now begins the explanation of the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta. To demonstrate that the opportunity for sequential explanation has arrived, or to show that the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta is the sutta recited (in the Council) immediately after the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, he said: 'Thus have I heard... among the Angas... the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.' The princes are called 'Anga' because they possess excellent limbs (qualities) in abundance. Since the derivative suffix (taddhita) denotes an extraordinary possession, it primarily refers to the princes, but by convention (ruḷhi), it also refers to the district (janapada), as stated in 'Angā nāma' and so on. This is also the intention here in the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, not only in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. The phrase 'At that time, it is said' (tadā kira) and so on, states the reason for the Buddha's journey. It implies that he would not allow them to come by pointing out the faults in coming to the Buddha (as a rejection).

Because it is mixed with trees such as the blue Asoka, Kaṇikāra, Kovilāra, Kundara, and Rājarukkha, that Campaka grove appears as if adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue. Although some say that it is not only the Campaka trees that bloom with five-colored flowers like blue, due to such a specific nature (dhātu), the Campaka trees themselves bloom with flowers of five colors. Even now, they are seen in some regions, so the literal words of the Commentary are quite appropriate. As previously explained, it has a fragrant scent from the perfumes of the mixed trees or the pure Campaka flowers. By saying this, he shows that Campaka trees were not only abundant in that city at the time of its founding but also in later periods. Because of the abundance of Campaka trees at the time of its founding, the city received the name 'Campā.' He is called 'Issaratta' because of his lordship (sovereignty). Because this king has an army (senā), he is called Senika; that very Senika is Seniya. Here, the derivative suffix highlights an extraordinary possession in the sense of 'many,' hence it is said, 'because he is endowed with a great army.' It is also said because he resembles excellent gold. However, in the Commentary on the Cūḷadukkhandha Sutta, it is stated that 'Seniya' is the king's name, and 'Bimbi' is the name of his body (attabhāva). Because the king was endowed with a substantial, beautiful, and pleasing body, he was called 'Bimbisāra.'

301-2. 'Assembled' (saṃhatā) means joined together or gathered by way of meeting. 'From each direction' (ekekissāya disāya) means from each individual region. In the Pali text, since it refers to the brahmins and householders, it is said 'possessing a group' (saṅghino)...
283:
In the word "saṅghī", the teacher shows that although it refers to a plurality (etesaṃ), the singular form is used. Although the teacher (Venerable Dhammapāla) said this, the plural usage of "saṅghī" with a long vowel (dīgha) is also commonly seen. "Agaṇā" refers to those who are not a group or have no organization. Although there is a variant reading "agaṇanā", only this meaning [agaṇā] is correct because the meaning of 'number' is inappropriate. This is because they have no number. The meaning of this statement is: although they previously did not have a group inside the city, they later became a group outside the city; this is what "gaṇībhūta" means. In the sense of 'becoming what was not' (abhūtatabbhāva), when associated with the roots √kar or √bhū, the 'a' vowel is changed to 'ī', or the 'ī' suffix is applied. A man who holds the staff or rod of kings and princes is called "khattā" according to the etymological method (nirutti) because he protects (tāyana/rakkhana) the kings from various places. He, in the place where he is sent by them, removes their faults and is capable of answering the questions asked with appropriate skill. Therefore, it is said: "one capable of answering the questions asked." Because he has a great measure or scale in terms of lineage etc., he is called "mahāmatta" (great minister).

## Explanation of the Talk on the Qualities of Soṇadaṇḍa

The places where the authority of a king extends are called "rajja" (kingdoms). Exceptional kingdoms are called "virajja", and they are also called "verajja". Various and diverse kingdoms are also called so. Because they are born in those kingdoms etc., the three types of derivative (taddhita) definitions are shown. This is because derivative functions (taddhitavutti) are diverse. "Yaññānubhavanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of experiencing the benefit of some sacrifice. "Te" refers to the Brahmins who have come from various countries. "Tassa" refers to the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa. "Uttamabrāhmaṇa" means a Brahmin who is very noble or excellent, being endowed with [perfection of] birth, wealth, and knowledge. "Āvaṭṭanီmāyā" (enticing magic) has been mentioned before. Because of being oppressed by stinginess regarding gains (lābhamacchere), there will be no assembly.

"Aṅga" means 'reason' (hetu) because it makes its own result known, or because it is known by itself. Therefore, it is said "because of a reason". To show that others also stated other reasons by reflecting on the nature of the world, it says "evaṃ" etc.

"Dvီhi pakkhehi" means the two sides of relatives: the mother's side and the father's side. In the phrase "well-born from both sides", if only this much were said, it might be understood as being well-born from any two parts. Since the word "sujāta" is also a synonym for perfection of physical stature in such phrases as "sujāto cārudassano" (well-born and lovely to behold)...
284: ...to clarify the state of being well-born specifically by birth, the Blessed One said, 'from the mother's side and from the father's side'. Therefore, the commentator said, 'The mother of the venerable one is a Brahmin woman,' and so on. 'Evaṃ' means in the manner described, through the three generations of relatives on each side, the mother's and the father's. By the phrase 'saṃsuddhagahaṇiko' (of pure conception), the meaning already stated as 'from the mother's side and from the father's side' is further established; thus the commentator said, 'The womb of your mother is pure.' This means it is pure because of not being shared with other men. Indeed, in the world, the designation of parents is sometimes seen even when the child is not biological (orasa); however, here, to show that he is desired specifically as a biological son, 'saṃsuddhagahaṇiko' is said. 'Gahaṇī' is that which receives and carries the fetus; it is the region of the mother's belly known as the womb, described as the third cavity. 'Samavepākiniyā' means that which causes even digestion. In this context, 'Gahaṇī' refers to the 'digestive fire' (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) known in the world as 'udara-aggi' (stomach fire), which, as in the Mahāsudassana Sutta, receives food by digesting it and does not discard it. 'Pitupitā' means the father's father (grandfather). The word 'Pitāmaha' is formed as a derivative (taddhita) with the suffix 'āmaha'. As in 'catuyuga' and so on, 'yuga' refers to a specific time because it is associated with those respective meanings. Expressing the span of life with this word 'yuga' is merely a conventional worldly expression; however, according to the intended meaning, only the grandfather is meant by the term 'pitāmahayuga' because he is the primary one intended. 'Tato uddhaṃ' means above the grandfather. Therefore, the commentator said 'pubbapurisā' (ancestors), meaning the six preceding men remaining from that grandfather. The use of the word 'purisa' (man) here should be understood as being made by way of an excellent description. Only in this way is the Pali statement 'mātito' (from the mother's side) fully established. In describing that lineage, this is the method outside the commentaries (aṭṭhakathāmuttaka-naya): Mother and father are 'pitaro'; the parents of those parents are 'pitāmahā'; their pair is 'pitāmahayuga'; therefore, it should be understood as 'up to the seventh pair of grandfathers'. By taking 'pitāmaha' (grandfather), the 'mātāmaha' (maternal grandfather/grandmother) is also included. The word 'yuga' here is an 'ekasesa' (elision of similar terms) as in 'yugo ca yugo ca yugo'; thus, the pair of grandfathers is taken in each respective generation of relatives. This phrase 'up to the seventh pair of grandfathers' is connected to both sides (grandfather and grandmother) like a crow's eye (kākāpekkha); thus the commentator said 'Evaṃ' and so on. As long as there is the seventh generation of men...
285:
The phrase "not rejected or reviled on account of birth" refers to the connection of the sentence. 'Akkhiitto' means the rejection of a fault that has not been reached, or simply not being rejected. 'Anavakkhiitto' means not being discarded in things such as rice-cooking pots and so on. 'Na upakuṭṭho' means not being reviled. The word "jātivādena" is used to show that it is in the instrumental case (kāraṇa) in the sense of cause (hetu), as in "for what reason?" and so on. "Itipi" means "for this reason also." In this text, by the phrase "on both sides... up to the seventh generation," the absence of birth-defects (yoni-dosa) of the brahmin is shown by describing the purity of the mother's womb. By the word "akkhiitto," the absence of fault in conduct (kiriya-aparādha) is shown. For beings reach rejection because of faults in conduct. By the word "anupakuṭṭho," the absence of association with unsuitable persons is shown. For beings receive reviling and reproach because of association with unsuitable persons.

'Issaro' means one who has the habit of ruling by the power of kamma that leads to lordship. That lordship (issaratā) becomes manifest due to the attainment of wealth and prosperity. Therefore, wishing to show it by the synonym of being wealthy (aḍḍhabhāva), it is said, "A wealthy person is a lord." He is called 'mahaddhana' (one of great wealth) because his wealth, both buried in the ground and stored above ground, is vast. "Tassa" means "of that particular quality"; this is the reading currently found. "Aguṇaṃ yeva dassema" means that after stating the quality of that brahmin by way of accordance (anvaya), we shall now show, by way of contrast (vyatireka), only the lack of quality which is the reason for not approaching the Blessed One.

'Adhikarūpo' means one of distinguished appearance, having an excellent body. Because he is worthy of being seen, he is 'dassanīyo'; thus it is said, "worthy of being looked at." Because he inspires confidence, he is 'pāsādiko'. Therefore it is said, "because of generating confidence." Here, the word 'pokkhara' is established in the sense of "beautiful" (sundara) and "body" (sarīra). "Vaṇṇassa" means "of the element of complexion." Because the word 'vaṇṇa' occurs in the sense of the element of complexion due to a clear and pure sign, that sign itself is 'vaṇṇatā' (having complexion). Since that 'vaṇṇatā' depends on the complexion, it is said without distinction, "with an excellent and pure complexion."

The body (sarīra) is a specific structure consisting of the collection of hands, feet, neck, head, and so on. That body is also perceived by the sign of its shape, which is its component part. Therefore, that sign itself is 'pokkharatā' (perfection of bodily form); thus it is said, "by the perfection of bodily form." It should also be connected as "by the perfection of the excellent bodily form." This is because the gender and case endings may change according to the sense. Since among all complexions, the golden complexion is the most excellent, it is said, "endowed with a golden complexion, which is the most excellent even among pure complexions." Accordingly, Buddhas and Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) are golden-colored. Since the word 'vacchasa' occurs in the sense of bodily radiance, 'brahmavacchasī' means having a sublime bodily radiance, a golden radiance. Intending this very meaning, it is said, "with a body like the body of Mahābrahmā..."
286:
In the word 'samannāgato' (endowed with), it does not mean having a straight body like a Brahma. 'Okāsa' (space/scope) refers to the location of all major and minor limbs. It means that the visible area is not small because of the perfection of height and circumference, and the fullness of the body parts. Therefore, it is said, 'sabbāneva' and so on.

'Sīla' (virtue) refers to the virtue that is constantly observed. This virtue is specifically called 'vuddhasīlī' (one of mature virtue) because it has been developed through the seniority of the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, who knows the passage of nights. 'Vuddhasīlena' means with mature and constant virtue because it is always well-practiced. By doing so, although these three terms are distinct in their intended meaning, with regard to the literal meaning, it is said, 'This is merely a synonym for the term vuddhasīlī.' It is said to be 'merely the five precepts' because there is no virtue beyond the five precepts in that Brahmin, and because they [the Brahmins] do not know of any higher virtue.

The state of being rounded and complete in words, syllables, and sentences of speech is itself a beautiful state; therefore, it is said, 'sundarā parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā' (beautiful, rounded words and syllables). Because of the perfection of the places of articulation and the perfection of training, without any deficiency, the words, syllables, and letters are rounded; thus, it is called 'parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā.' Only the letter that is delimited by the capacity to express various meanings is called 'pada' (word). Alternatively, only the word is called 'byañjana' (syllable/expression) because it expresses the meaning. The roundedness of words and syllables occurs through the completeness of letters such as 'sithila' (unaspirated) and 'dhanita' (aspirated). Because such rounded words and syllables exist in this speech, it is so called. In another way, it is called 'pada' because the meaning is understood through words such as nouns. It is called 'byañjana' (sentence/expression) because it expresses the intended meaning. Because those words and sentences are complete, it is called 'parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā.' Speech itself is the instrument (karaṇa) in making the meaning known; to show this identical meaning, it is called 'udāharaṇaghosa' (utterance of sound). It means the sound of vocal expression. It is called 'porī' (polite/urban speech) because it is endowed with the qualities of that Brahmin or the meaning to be spoken by him, or because it occurs in a state full of qualities in a city. Again, 'pure' means occurring in the royal capital or because of growth. 'Sukhumālattanena' means by way of delicacy. This term expresses the softness and smoothness of that speech. 'Apalibuddhāya' means not obstructed (or not covered) by bile, phlegm, and so on. This term is an adjective expressing the cause. Only because there is no such obstruction by bile and phlegm, the aforementioned faults do not exist.

Speaking only a part, as if biting the lip, is called 'sandiṭṭha.' Speaking slowly and for a long time is called 'vilambita.' There is also a variant reading 'sanniddhavilambitādi.' Speech that does not produce sound is called 'sanniddha.' Alternatively, stuttering, known as 'mammaka,' or pronouncing a single letter two or three times, is called 'sanniddha.' By the word 'ādi' (etc.), it includes speaking incorrectly by slipping and speaking by repeatedly dragging out sounds. 'Eḷāgaḷena' means by the dripping of saliva (or tongue fluid). To show two kinds of meaning for the term 'eḷā gaḷanti,' it is said 'lālā vā' (or saliva). Just as in the passages 'daseṭṭhamukhaṃ uragaṃ dubbhinnaṃ' and so on, the word 'e' is also used in the sense of 'lālā' (saliva)...
287:
...it is said 'paggharantī' (dripping) and so on. As in the Jātaka Pali passages such as 'passeḷamūgaṃ uragaṃ dujivhaṃ,' the word 'eḷa' occurs in the sense of saliva and also in the sense of snot or phlegm. 'Kheḷaphusitāni' means drops of saliva. Here, the method outside of the Commentary (Atthakathā) is: as in 'yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā' and so on, 'eḷa' is said to be a fault. When unwise people speak words with faults, they cause faults to flow; therefore, their speech is called 'eḷagaḷā.' It means speech that is the opposite of that (faultless speech). By the phrase 'making the beginning, middle, and end clear,' it speaks of the completeness of the meaning of that speech. This should be connected with the word 'viññāpana' (making known).

'Jarājiṇṇatāya jiṇṇo' means having reached the state of broken teeth, grey hair, and so on. 'Vuddhimariyādappatto' means having reached the limit or the end of growth. 'Jātimahallakatāya' means being elderly by birth (conception). Therefore, it is said, 'one who has existed for a long time.' The word 'addha' is a synonym for 'addhāna' and expresses a long time. How long is that time? It is said, 'two or three reigns,' meaning the period of the successive reigns of two or three kings. Although it is said 'addhagato' (gone a long way), the use of 'vaya' (age) is in consideration of the final stage of life; thus, it is said, 'one who has reached the last stage of life.' 'Pacchimavaya' (the last stage of life) is the third and final portion when a hundred years are divided into three parts. In each part, months and days exceeding 33 years are also divided; therefore, the last stage of life should be known starting from the appropriate months and days from the 67th year onwards. The teacher Elder Sāriputta also intended this very meaning when he said, 'The portion of the last stage of life starts from the 67th year.' Otherwise, it would contradict the Commentary's statement that 'the last stage of life is the final third of a hundred years.'

Having thus stated the first alternative by way of mere birth, the second alternative is undertaken with 'apica' (moreover) to speak by way of being mixed with qualities. In that context, this old age is not merely by years, but rather it is being ancient by way of lineage; thus, it is said, 'jiṇṇo means an ancient person' and so on. 'One who has a lineage that has existed for a long time' means having a succession of lineage that has continued for a long time; by that speech, it refers to the state of being increasingly prominent and famous by way of lineage. Because 'vayoanuppatto' will be spoken of as growth by birth...
288:
He is called "Vuddho" (Grown/Elder) because he is endowed with growth in virtues such as virtue (sīla) and conduct (ācāra). This statement is made by taking the remainder in consideration of what is to be said later. Likewise, regarding greatness in birth, he is also spoken of by that same word; and because he is exhaustive in the greatness of wealth, "Mahallako" (Great/Elder) means one endowed with greatness of wealth. "Maggapaṭipanno" (One on the path) shows the meaning as one who has arrived by way of conduct without deviating from the appropriate path of practice for Brahmins, as indicated by the words beginning with "Brāhmaṇānaṃ". He has reached greatness in birth, and that too, he has reached the final stage of life (pacchimavaya); this should be construed with the intended meaning. Thus, it shows greatness in birth by way of the final stage of life.

## Buddhaguṇakathāvaṇṇanā

"Even placing [myself] on par with such powerful beings is not fitting for wise people like me, let alone placing [myself] in a superior position; this is not appropriate for a Brahmin," showing this, he said the words beginning with "Na kho pana metaṃ". In that passage, the connection is: even those virtues that are similar to his own virtues, he declares them while considering them to be far superior. "Sadisā" (Similar) means similar in one part. Indeed, no virtues are found in others that are in every way similar to the virtues of the Buddhas. The words beginning with "Ko cāhaṃ" show the manner of being far superior. The intended meaning is: "Who am I to be similar, and what are the virtues of the ascetic [Gotama] to be similar?" Some teachers make a new reading, but this alone is the original reading, as in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta: "Who am I, O Gotama, with my teacher, and what is the unsurpassed endowment of knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampadā)?" "Itare" refers to virtues dissimilar to his own virtues, and it should be connected with the word "pakāseti" (declares). "Ekanteneva" (Exclusively) is because there is no possibility [of similarity] as there is with similar virtues.

In this way, Sonadaṇḍa the Brahmin, while making this determination, clarifies this meaning. In the phrase "Yathā hi", the word "hi" is used in the sense of cause. Therefore, he said, "Therefore, we alone are worthy." "Gopadakaṃ" means like water standing in a cow's hoofprint. "Guṇe" means even in similar virtues (if it is like water in a cow's hoofprint), what need is there to speak of dissimilar virtues?

"Saṭṭhikulatasatasahassaṃ" means one hundred and sixty thousand families. However, in the Dhammapada Commentary and other texts, the statement that the Blessed One has eighty thousand families in some places should be understood as referring to only one side (either maternal or paternal).
289: 'Sudhāmaṭṭhapokkharaṇiyo' refers to lotus ponds that have been finished with plaster. 'Sattaratanānaṃ' means 'with the seven jewels.' When associated with the word 'pūra' (full), the genitive case (saṭṭhī) is frequently used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa). 'Pāsādanīyūhādayo' refers to the ends of beams and so forth located at the top of the palace. The term 'sattaratanānaṃ' follows by way of repetition. Here, although there is no distinction, it is spoken of as if there were a distinction. 'Kulapariyāyena' means by way of the lineage of King Suddhodana's unmixed warrior (khattiya) family. 'Tesu pi' means in the four treasure jars as well. Whenever wealth is taken from those treasure jars, the place is refilled and remains just as it was; it does not decrease. 'Bhaddakena' means 'with good' or 'auspicious.' The first stage of life (paṭhamavaya) should be understood in the same way as the final stage of life (pacchimavaya) was described. Going forth into homelessness without the parents' consent is indeed called 'disrespect' (anādara); the genitive case (sāmivacana) is used here in a sense associated with that disrespect. 'Etesaṃ' refers to the parents. 'Kanditvā' means having lamented and wept, saying 'Where are my dear sons?' and so forth. 'Aparimāṇo yeva' means immeasurable because no one can delimit it with knowledge, saying 'It is this much.' Since it means two bamboo-lengths are only as high as the lower waist, it was said 'only the height of the waist above two bamboo-lengths.' It is because of the power of his perfections (pāramī) that it appeared so to the Brahmin; it seems it was said 'it appeared' to show that the Blessed One was actually of normal stature at that time; this should be taken after investigation. Some teachers say that it shows this immeasurability is due to the power of perfections alone, not due to the power of psychic potency (iddhi), by the words beginning with 'Na hi'. 'Atulo' means incomparable, having no equal. The reading in some versions 'He spoke the verse in the Dhammapada' is incorrect. This is because this verse is not found in the Dhammapada Pali. However, this verse appears in the Sudhāpiṇ|iyatthera Apadāna and other works, but that verse is in a different story, not in this story. Therefore, it should be understood that this verse is merely a miscellaneous teaching (pakiṇṇakadesanā) that was not included in the formal rehearsal (saṅgīti) according to the Pali canon.In that verse, the words 'te tādise' are synonymous terms, as in 'Life is short, a hundred years, it exists now and at this time' and so forth. Although some read 'etādise', that is not good because it is not found that way in the Apadāna and other works. The meaning is: for one who honors such persons who have attained Parinibbāna through the extinction of defilements and who have no fear from anywhere, this merit cannot be calculated by anyone, even one of great power.
290:
"Bāhantara" means the space between the two arms. "Dvādasa yojanasatāni" means twelve hundred (1,200) yojanas. "Bahalantarena" means by the measurement of the body's circumference all around. "Puthulato" means by breadth. "Aṅgulipabbāni" means individual finger joints. "Bhamukantaraṃ" means the space between the two eyebrows. The mouth is two hundred yojanas in breadth, as it is mentioned separately from the circumference. "Yathākathaṃ" is so called because it is appropriate to the talk spoken by others that "The Blessed One is of such a nature." By this, it shows that [Rāhu Asurinda] came with the desire to behold the Blessed One after hearing the talk of praise spoken by others. Or, "yathākathaṃ" means "of what kind?" As in passages such as "How (yathākathaṃ) then, monks, did you spend the vassa in harmony, in mutual courtesy, without disputes, and in comfort?", this is a combination of particles or a single particle used in the sense of a question.

"Gandhakuṭipariveṇe" means in the precinct of the Perfumed Chamber, inside the precinct outside the Perfumed Chamber. "Tattha" means on the couch. "He took the lion's posture (sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi)": The teacher says that just as Rāhu Asurinda could not grasp the limits of the Blessed One's physical body in terms of length, breadth, and height, so the Blessed One, while performing a psychic feat of form, took the lion's posture. That statement is completely contradictory to the commentary's words: "O Asurinda, I did not fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) with my face down; I gave gifts only by making them upright." They say that this is a demonstration of the accomplishment of the power of perfections, as in the opening of the door of the Perfumed Chamber; otherwise, that very word should have been spoken. This should be accepted after careful consideration. "Adhomukhena" (Face down) is said with reference to having retreating energy. "Uddhaggameva" (Upright) means having non-retreating energy, meaning having made it reach the highest point. Because Rāhu then declared his status as a lay follower (upāsaka), he said "On that day," etc.

Because of being far from defilements, he is called "Ariya" (Noble) by way of the system of linguistics (nirutti); for this very reason, it is said to be "supreme and pure." "Kusala" (Wholesome) is in the sense of being faultless, not in the sense of having happy results, because that [result] is impossible for an Arahant. "Kusalasīlena" means with virtue that is faultless and has destroyed defilements along with latent tendencies (vāsanā). In this way, these four terms are distinguished by their intended meaning. With reference to the mere literal meaning, it is said, "This is a synonym for it."
291:
In some Suttas, it is said that there were eighty-four thousand beings, and in others, immeasurable devas and humans. With this meaning in mind, it is stated: "In a single Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One," and so forth. Indeed, in discourses such as the Mahāsamaya Sutta and the Maṅgala Sutta, at twenty-four places, incalculable and immeasurable devas and humans drank the nectar of the Paths and Fruits. Even by counts such as a hundred thousand crores, they are many; however, this is stated by way of illustration. Therefore, because he is the one who teaches the unsurpassed supramundane training, the Blessed One is the Teacher (ācariya) of many beings. Because he is the teacher of those disciples who are themselves teachers, he is also the Teacher of Teachers (pācariya) for the disciples to be tamed. For the disciples, established in the method granted by the Blessed One, tame those who are to be tamed; thus, the Blessed One alone is their primary Great Teacher.

The intended meaning of the speaker is the standard (authority), not the scope of the modes of conveying (hāra) or characteristics (lakkhaṇa); thus, it is said: "But the Brahmin (brāhmaṇo pana)," and so forth. Having placed an ellipsis (peyyāla) at the end of the Pali "of this foul body," it is said: "ornamenting and re-ornamenting (kelanā paṭikelanā)." This is taken by way of ellipsis in the Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga Pali as "the decorating of external requisites," and so forth. In that Pali, "of this foul body" means this human body. Just as even a jackal born that very day is called an "old jackal," and even a creeper the size of a thigh is called a "stinking creeper" (pūtilatā), so too, even a human body with a golden complexion is called a "foul body" (pūtikāya); its decoration is the meaning. "Kelanā" means playing or sporting. Some also read it as "kelāyanā." "Paṭikelanā" means repeated playing. Frivolity or fickleness is called "cāpalya" or "cāpalla." A person endowed with such frivolity, even if a hundred years old, is like a child born that very day; it should be understood that this name "cāpalya" is a designation for that frivolous person.

Because one performs non-evil (the opposite of unwholesome) states first, or because one does not perform evil first, it is called "apāpapurekkharo" (having non-evil as one's precursor). To show the meaning in two ways through proper and improper compounds (yutta/ayutta-samāsa), it is said: "non-evil, the nine supramundane states," and so forth. "Apāpa" means the opposite of the unwholesome, or states devoid of the unwholesome. Because they are born in the Noble Birth by way of the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, who is the Excellent (brahma), or because they are the offspring of the Blessed One (the Brahma) through reverence and so forth, and through practicing according to the instruction, or because they know the Excellent Noble Path, they are called "brahmaññā"—referring to the assembly of Noble Disciples. Therefore, it is said: "Sāriputta, Moggallāna," and so forth. "Brahmaṇapajā" means the assembly of beings whose evil has been expelled. In this context of "apāpapurekkharo," it is shown that the word "purekkharo" is the principal term.
292:
In the phrase ‘Prioritizing this assembly of beings’, the word ‘ca’ has a conjunctive meaning (samuccaya). It means, ‘Not only prioritizing the absence of evil, but indeed, prioritizing the assembly of beings connected to the knowledge of the noble path (Brahmanya).’ The passage beginning with ‘Ayañhi’ is merely to show the intended meaning. The term ‘Apāpapurekkharo’ (prioritizing the absence of evil) should be connected only with the term ‘Brahmanyāya pajāya’ (the assembly of beings connected to Brahmanya), and it does not indicate a separate meaning. To show that the meaning of this term can also be understood by the power of the natural Brahmin caste, he said ‘Api ca’ and so on. This compound is an Ayutta-samāsa. ‘Pāpa’ means evil unwholesome kamma, which is non-beneficial and suffering. Because that term depends on a connection, the question ‘Prioritizing the absence of evil of whom?’ arises; to show this, the passage beginning with ‘Kassā’ was spoken. The passage beginning with ‘Attanā’ is an explanation of that meaning. ‘Brāhmaṇapajāya’ refers to beings of the Brahmin caste.

‘RaṦṭha’ (country) is so called because kings frequent this place for judicial matters; these are the great kingdoms such as Kāsi and Kosala which are the realms of a single king. ‘Janapada’ (district) is so called because people attain a happy livelihood there; these are the smaller districts such as Uttarapatha and Dakkhiṇapatha which are parts within a single king’s realm. ‘Tattha’ means among those who have arrived in that way. ‘Pucchāya’ means by the question prepared by oneself. ‘Vissajjanāsampaṭicchane’ means in accepting the answer with one’s own wisdom. The meaning is that the Blessed One, having known the perfection of the strong supporting conditions (upanissaya), the maturity of wisdom, and the mental disposition of certain individuals, personally generates the effort to ask and then causes the answer to be given.

The Pali beginning with ‘Tattha katamaṁ sākhalyaṁ’ is the Pali found in the NikkhepakaṇḎa of the Dhammasaṁgaṇī. ‘Addhānadaratha’ refers to the fatigue and exhaustion caused by traveling a long distance. ‘Assa’ means of the Blessed One, and it should be connected with ‘Mukha-padumaṁ’ (lotus-like face). His face blooms just like when touched by the rays of the newly risen sun. Indeed, in the world, the sun is well-known as the ‘friend of the lotus’ (padmabandhū), while the moon is the ‘friend of the water-lily’ (kumudabandhū). Because it has a splendor equal to the splendor of the full moon, it is called ‘Puṇṇacandasassirika’ (having splendor like the full moon). For the question of why there might be a face like an overturned pot, he said ‘Sampattāya’ and so on. Here, by the term ‘Ehi svāgata-vādī’, he shows the quality of speaking endearing words, having first engaged in pleasant conversation. By the term ‘Sakhila’, he shows the quality of having gentle speech; by ‘Sammodaka’, the quality of being skilled in courtesy (paṭisanthāra); by ‘Abbhākuṭika’, the quality of having a clear face at all times; by ‘Uttānamukha’, the quality of being easy to talk to; and by ‘Pubbabhāsī’, he shows the quality of being well-intentioned by providing the opportunity to exalt the Dhamma.
293:
In the term ‘Yattha kira’, the word ‘kira’ is a particle used to indicate dissatisfaction.

‘Those objects such as visible forms, which do not come into the range of the senses because of the brevity of the thought-moment’s duration,
are called Dhamma-objects (dhammārammaṇa); in the view of some teachers, the word ‘kira’ (it is said) is used.’

As in the verse from the Abhidhammāvatāra Commentary and so on, it shows that in the region where the Blessed One dwells, the absence of danger for humans is not due to the power of devas, but rather, it is due to the power of the Buddha. Indeed, those devas themselves take up protection only through the power of the Buddha. ‘Paṁsupisācakādayo’ refers to earth-dwelling ghosts and so on. By the word ‘ādi’, beings such as Bhūta, Rakkhasa, and Pisāca are included. Now, to clearly demonstrate the power of the Buddha, the passage beginning with ‘Api ca’ was spoken.

The entire assembly of beings to be trained (veneyya) who are to be instructed is called the ‘Anusāsitabba-saṁgha’. The assembly of Noble Ones (ariya-puggala) who are produced by oneself is called the ‘Sayaṁ-uppādita-saṁgha’. By the term ‘Tādiso’, the alternative (vkappa) already mentioned as ‘Sayaṁ vā uppādito’ is referred to. Considering it as a prohibition of the preceding rule of ‘Anusāsitabba’, the teacher said, ‘Or it belongs only to the preceding term,’ taking another alternative. The intention there is this: although the term ‘Gaṇī’ is a synonym for the term ‘Saṁghī’, in order to show just the meaning, only the second alternative among the two mentioned alternatives is referred to, and because it was said ‘Such a group (gaṇa) exists for him,’ it was said ‘It is only a synonym of the preceding term’ to include the remaining first alternative as well. Some also say this: the term ‘Tādiso’ and so on were spoken referring to the groups of individual elders such as the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta), or to groups such as the Suttantikas. In that case too, the entire group of monks is called ‘to be instructed’ (anusāsitabba), while the group of Noble Ones that has arisen is called ‘self-produced’ (sayaṁ-uppādita). Therefore, referring to both alternatives with the term ‘Tādiso’ is appropriate. Having thus shown the specific meanings of the two terms, he said ‘Purimapadassvā’ and so on to show that they have the same meaning in every way. Among many teachers of other sects (titthakara) such as Pūraṇa and Makkhali, this term is in the genitive case used for selection (niddhāraṇa). ‘Because of such reasons as being an Acelaka (naked ascetic)’ means by a reason characterized by the attribution of fewness of wishes, contentment, etc., merely by such things as being unclothed.

‘Navaka’ means those who are new. ‘Pāhunaka’ means those who are worthy of receiving gifts (pahaṇaka). By this term, among the two kinds of visitors (āgantuka), they are ‘Atithi’ (guests) here by virtue of having arrived earlier.
294:
It is shown that one is not called an "abbhāgata" (guest) merely by arriving at mealtime. "Pariyāpuṇāmi" means knowing by delimitation; however, "jānāmi" (I know) is stated here to show only the basic meaning of the root.

"Kappampi" means for a whole life-aeon (āyukappa); it should be understood in connection with the phrase "if one were to speak." The construction (yojanā) is that although an aeon may be exhausted over a long period, the virtues of the Blessed One are not exhausted even in a long interval of time. Here, although "ciraṃ" should have been said, the vowel was shortened and the niggahita dropped for fear of breaking the poetic meter. Alternatively, "ciradīghamantare" is said with reference to an extremely long time, and it should be connected to both. Just as in connection with verbs and so on, a verse foot with extra syllables is not to be faulted when used with the word "antara." This verse is stated in the commentaries as a hypothetical reflection (abhūtapari-kappanā), because there was no such actual teaching in that manner.

"Naṃ" refers to the teacher (ācariya). The word "alaṃ" here has the meaning of "worthy" (araha), as in "alaṃ eva nibbindituṃ" (it is indeed worthy to be weary of) and so on. Therefore, it is explained as "yuttameva" (it is indeed fitting). Provisions for a journey are called "puṭaṃsa" because they are carried in a bag (puṭa) and consumed. By the words "taṃ gahetvā" (having taken that), the instrumental case (karaṇavacana) is shown in the sense of a characteristic attribute (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). In the Pali, "tena puṭaṃsena" is stated to show the connection: "the clansman carrying the bundle of provisions on his shoulder." "Aṃsena" and so on are merely to show the intended meaning. The meaning is that it is indeed fitting for a clansman carrying a bundle of provisions to approach.

## Description of Sonadanda's Reflection

306-7. Here, the word "tiro" does not mean "outside" as in "tirokuḍḍe" (outside the wall) or "tiropākāre" (outside the rampart). Thus, it is said, "of one who has gone inside the forest grove." By the words "of one who has entered inside the monastery," it is shown that the monastery is also included within the forest grove. Those sitting with palms joined are those belonging to both sides (ubhatopakkhika) due to the power of wrong view. It is understood by implication that the others belong to one side (ekatopakkhika) due to the power of right view. The meaning is that they acted thus because they were obscure in terms of name and clan due to poverty or the loss of relatives, and they wished to become well-known. "Kerāṭikā" means those who are deceitful. "Tattha" means among those two people. "Tato" means due to intimacy or due to giving.
295:
## Description of the Designation of a Brahmin

The stiffness of the body is due to an upright posture (anonatakāya), not due to pride. Therefore, it will be said in the Pali, "having raised the body" (abbhunnāmetvā). With reference to the thought in the mind, it is said "he knew the mind" (cittaṃ aññāsī), taking the mind as the head. "Vighāta" means mental distress.

"Sakasamaya" means in the Brahminical doctrine. "Mīyamāna" means one who is dying. "Diṭṭhisañjānanena" means simply by recognizing one's own doctrine. "Suja" is the sacrificial ladle; its definition has already been stated. "Gaṇhantesu" means among those who take it up for the purpose of making an offering; the meaning is among those proficient in the Rig Veda (iruvijjā). Indeed, because they perform the fire-offering by the power of the Rig Veda, the sacrificers are called "iruvijjā." "Paṭhamo vā" means the Brahmin who is most prominent among all the Brahmins assembled there in the act of using the ladle. "Dutiyo vā" means the Brahmin who is immediately next to him. Since this word "sujaṃ" is in the accusative case (upayogavibhatta) in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇattha), the teacher said "sujāya" (with the ladle). Because the sacrifice has the fire-offering as its head, the gift given in the sacrifice is offered by means of the ladle. It is also said: "Sacrifices have the fire-offering as their head; the Sāvitrī is the head of poetic meters." Therefore, the teacher (in the Ṭīkā) said that the remaining Pali "diyamānaṃ" (being given) should be understood. Furthermore, this is said to show the meaning of "suja" by way of a derivative (taddhita) as that which is given by the ladle. "Porāṇā" refers to the teachers of the commentaries. Between these two views, in the former view, it is the first or second Brahmin by way of giving, while in the latter view, it is by way of taking; this is the distinction between those views.

"Visesato" means due to the distinction of knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇa), not merely due to the knowledge and conduct desired by the Brahmins. "Uttamabrāhmaṇa" refers to an excellent Brahmin because he is worthy of the unsurpassed gift. Indeed, the Blessed One spoke the words "Brahmin, among these five factors" and so on, only to provide an opportunity for the words "But what, Brahmin, is that virtue? What is that wisdom?" which illuminate the distinction of knowledge and conduct as intended. Therefore, it should be understood that the words "But the Blessed One" and so on are stated to show the connection consistent with the principal statement.

"Apavadati" means speaking by setting aside beauty (color/caste) and so on; "paṭikkhipati" (rejects) is said to show only the general meaning. "Idaṃ" refers to the words "Let not the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa speak thus" and so on. "Brāhmaṇasamaya" means the Brahminical doctrine. "Mā bhindi" means do not destroy.

Being just equal, he is called "samasamo" (exactly equal) because he is equal; the meaning is equal in every respect. Indeed, the doubling of synonyms illuminates an intensive meaning, such as "dukkhadukkhaṃ" (extreme suffering) or "rūparūpaṃ" (pure matter). However, by way of only a single part, the youth Angaka and those Brahmins'...
296:
Because of the similarity between the young man Angaka and the Brahmin, the teacher (sub-commentator) said "leaving aside a portion" etc., wishing to preclude that similarity. "Kula-koṭi-paridīpana" means explaining the origin of the lineage. Since no one can fail to know the parents of the young man Angaka, who is his own nephew, he does not speak referring merely to his parents, but refers to the pinnacle (origin) of the lineage. By the word "Atthabhañjanaka", he refers to reaching the course of action (kammapatha). "Guṇa" refers to the aforementioned Five Precepts. "Atha pi siyā" means: you might have such a thought: even if one is of broken virtue, when he stands again in natural virtue, his status as a Brahmin is accomplished by his appearance and so on. In the text "sādhēti", the teacher points out "vaṇṇa" (appearance) as the subject; this is just an example. The same method should be understood regarding the Vedas (mantas) and birth (jāti). "Sīlam-eva" means: only virtue, which has become natural again, will accomplish the state of a Brahmin. Why? Because it is said, "Without that virtue... appearance and so on..." In that context, "appearance and so on are just confusion" means that saying appearance, Vedas, and birth are factors for being a Brahmin is just great confusion; this is spoken without proper reflection.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Virtue and Wisdom

317. "The Brahmin spoke the question" means the question asked regarding the two factors, starting with "he is virtuous," was answered correctly according to reality. "Herein" refers to the meaning answered, or the two factors. "His" refers to the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa. If one factor is set aside, it cannot stand; if not set aside, it can. This was said only to test whether this Brahmin would be able to do so or not, not because one factor should actually be set aside. Therefore, He said: "O Brahmins, it is so," etc. "Purified by virtue" means purification occurs only because of cleansing; it means being entirely pure and unstained due to the fulfillment of virtue. Where can there be wisdom in an immoral person? Because he lacks concentration (stability). Or where can there be virtue in a dull-witted, drooling person who lacks wisdom? Because he does not know the divisions of virtue or the means to purify virtue. One from whose mouth saliva (eḷā) flows is called "eḷamūga"; by changing the letter 'kha' to 'ga', it is also "elamukha" or "elamūka". Thus, there are various readings as stated in the Commentary to the Bhayabherava Sutta. Noble and excellent knowledge is called "paññāṇa"; it is called "paññāṇa" to exclude ordinary knowledge. Here, knowledge such as insight (vipassanā) is intended; that knowledge is called "paññā" because it knows in various ways (prakāra). Therefore, it is said "only by wisdom".
297:
Washed by the fourfold purification of virtue means washed and purified from all stains of defilements by the fourfold purification of virtue, which is the proximate cause of concentration. Therefore, He said "How then," etc. In that context, "dhōvati" means it becomes pure. "Sixty or eighty years" means for sixty years or eighty years. Even at the time of death, let alone at other times. Like the Elder Mahāsaṭṭhivassa (or the Elder Mahādahavāsī).

In the phrase "even the mere comprehension of feeling," the comprehension of feeling (vedanāpariggaha) refers to insight (vipassanā) practiced by observing the feeling that has arisen according to its nature and essence, and then, through its proximate cause, applying the three characteristics: "This feeling arises depending on contact; that contact is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change." Indeed, one who sees thus can easily endure that feeling, thinking "feeling itself feels."

"Having suppressed the feeling" means following the painful feeling that has arisen, beginning insight, and dispelling that painful feeling through insight that has entered the cognitive process (vīthi). "Like a fallen crocodile" means like a crocodile lying on the ground on its chest. With the words "Not I," etc., he speaks considering that guarding virtue alone is difficult. For one established in virtue, Arahantship is already in hand.

As the Blessed One taught: "Established in virtue, the wise man... should disentangle this tangle." This is the domain of the person of quick intuition (ugghāṭitaññū) among the four types of individuals; therefore, it is said "by way of quick intuition." Washing virtue with wisdom means making virtue well-purified by wisdom, ensuring it is unbroken, etc., in the beginning, middle, and end. The story of the minister Santati is mentioned in the Dhammapada.

## By the words "Why did he say," the reason for the above teaching is asked.

Shame (lajjā) refers to being known in the assembly as "He answered the question asked by the ascetic Gotama by revealing the merits and faults of virtue and birth." That shame will be destroyed because of the inability to answer in that way. It means that although he was not ashamed at first, he will be ashamed now. "Parama" means limit or measure. To show the identical reference of the words "We are only this much," it is said "Those we."

This is what is meant: "The words 'virtue and wisdom' are our limit. There is no discerning knowledge of the five precepts, the explanation of the three Vedas, and wisdom through their characteristics, etc., which are the meanings of those words; we are merely supreme in words in that regard." However, here is the method outside the commentary: "Ettakapparamā" means having this much as the highest point (ukkaṃsakoṭi). Only the first answering of the question...
298:
It means our pinnacle (the extreme point of excellence). Therefore, the Teacher said: "I have answered the question by the power of my own doctrine." "Paraṃ" means excess (surpassing). "Bhāsitassa" means of the spoken word or sound.

This distinction, however, is stated in the Description of Virtue (Sīlaniddesa) with regard to merely bringing it to a conclusion. Therefore, the Teacher said: "It is concluded as virtue alone." In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, although virtue is concluded, it is again concluded as the "Fruit of Recluseship" (Sāmaññaphala) alone. Because all lofty (mahaggata) minds are associated with knowledge, and because the jhānas are associated with that knowledge, it is called "fulfillment of wisdom" (paññāsampadā) in terms of essence. In the Description of Wisdom (Paññāniddesa), however, having made the wisdom of jhāna the basis, insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) is first brought to a conclusion. Therefore, it was said: "By insight-wisdom," and so forth.

## Commentary on the Account of the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa Attaining the Status of a Lay Follower

In the phrase "daharo yuvā" (young and youthful), the word "dahara" shows the state of being in the first stage of life. For one who has reached the first stage of life is called "dahara" (young). A son's son is called a grandson. "Nappahoti" means it is not sufficient, meaning it does not even reach the measure of sons and grandsons. To show the meaning that has arrived for the phrase "āsanā me taṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ" (that rising from my seat), it is said: "due to my lack of respect," and so forth. "Etaṃ" refers to the act of raising the hands in salutation (añjali). This Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa wanders about seeking to generate gain by impressing others with wonders and creating a reputation for himself among the masses; therefore, to show his extremely deceitful (kuhaka) nature, it is said: "This person indeed," and so forth. "Agāravam nāma natthi" means there is no such thing as a disrespectful word; it does not mean this Brahmin spoke "But if I..." and so forth out of lack of respect for the Blessed One, but rather it means he spoke only because he was afraid of the loss of his gains.

"Taṅkhaṇānurūpāya" means in accordance with the way his disposition arose at that time; the meaning is derived by the method of dropping the middle term. At that time, because that Brahmin did not yet have the maturity of knowledge based on the cessation of the round (Nibbāna), the Blessed One showed only the meaning based on worldly prosperity (abhyudaya); thus, it is said: "Having shown the benefit in the present life and the future life." It means having made it clear through direct perception. "Kusale dhamme" refers to the wholesome states belonging to the three planes. This is the literal meaning here. Figuratively, however, it is also appropriate to say "wholesome states belonging to the four planes," because supramundane wholesome states can also be obtained in the future. Thus, it will be said: "In the future, for the sake of Nibbāna..."
299:
In the phrase 'vāsanābhāgiyāya vā', 'tattha' refers to the wholesome states (kusaladhamma) in which one has been well-established. 'Naṃ' refers to the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa. 'Samuttejetvā' means having properly sharpened [his mind] step by step, bringing it to a state of sharpness and clarity in performing meritorious deeds. Since this sharpening, in its true sense, is simply the generating of effort in that merit, it is said 'having made it with effort' (sa-ussāhaṃ katvā). 'By being with such effort' means that since having effort in performing merit consistently accomplishes benefits such as those in the present life, it should be connected with 'having gladdened' (sampahaṃsetvā) through the aforementioned state of having effort. 'By other existing qualities' means that being endowed with such qualities certainly accomplishes benefits in the present life and so on; thus, it means having gladdened and brought him to a state of being truly joyful and delighted by those existing qualities and other qualities.

To resolve the objection, 'If the Blessed One rained down the rain of the Dhamma-treasure, why then did that Brahmin not attain any distinction?', the passage beginning with 'brāhmaṇo pana' is stated. 'Kuhakatāya' means due to the state of being a hypocrite as previously mentioned. By this, the lack of perfection in effort (payoga-sampatti) in that Brahmin is shown. To also resolve the counter-objection, 'If that is so, why did the Blessed One rain down such a rain of the Dhamma-treasure upon him?', the passage beginning with 'kevalamassa' is stated. Therein, 'kevalaṃ' means being purely unmixed with the stage of penetration (nibbedha) or the stage of a non-learner (asekkhabhāgiya). 'Nibbānatthāya' means for the sake of attaining Nibbāna or for the sake of final Nibbāna (parinibbāna). The habitual tendency (vāsanā), characterized by the practice of performing meritorious deeds which serves as a means for attaining distinction in the future, is called the 'portion' (bhāga). Because it occurs as a means toward that benefit of attaining distinction, it is called 'conducive to habitual tendencies' (vāsanābhāgiyā). Indeed, there is no Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, even a mere four-line verse, that is without benefit. Therefore, it is said, 'all the former and latter talk.' Here, from the beginning until the end of the Brahmin's answers is the 'former talk' (purimakathā). The Blessed One's answers regarding virtue and wisdom are the 'latter talk' (pacchimakathā). Even the talk spoken by the Brahmin concerning the Buddha's qualities and so on is indeed 'conducive to habitual tendencies' for the sake of Nibbāna in the future. The remaining words are easy to understand.

Thus ends the 'Explanation of the Inner Meaning' (Līnatthappakāsanā) in the sub-commentary named Sādhuvilāsinī, which clarifies the extremely subtle, deep, and difficult-to-understand meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, and which generates clear and extensive intellectual clarity, specifically for the Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.

## The Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta is finished.
300:
## 5. Commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta

Having thus commented on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, the author now wishes to comment on the Kūṭadanta Sutta. To demonstrate that the opportunity to comment has arrived according to the sequence of the Suttas, or to show that the Kūṭadanta Sutta is the one recited immediately after the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, he says: "*Evaṃ me sutaṃ... pe... Magadhesu*" (Thus have I heard... among the Magadhans), referring to the Kūṭadanta Sutta. Regarding the words "*Magadhā nāma janapadino rājakumārā*" (The Magadhans are the royal princes of the country) and so forth, the method we stated in the commentary on the Kosala country in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta should be applied accordingly. The distinction here is: they are called "Magadha" because those princes run (*dhāvanti*) together with deer (*maga*). Alternatively, according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*), they are called "Magadha" because they are greedy (*gijjhanti*) for meat (*maṃsa*). Grammarians, however, say that by way of usage (*ruḷhī*) or through the dropping of a suffix, there is no augmentation (*vuddhi*) in the name of the country which is the dwelling place of those princes. It is said, "*Tasmiṃ Magadhesu janapade*" (In that country among the Magadhans), using the plural inflection only for the name of the country, while the word *janapada* does not take the plural because it is a generic term (*jātishadda*). "*Ito paraṃ*" (After this) refers to the words "*cārikaṃ caramāno*" (wandering on a journey) and so forth, which follow the word "*Magadhesu*." "*Purimasuttadvaye*" (In the two previous Suttas) refers to the two Suttas, the Ambaṭṭha and the Soṇadaṇḍa. "*Vuttanayam-eva*" (Just as the method stated) means that the explanation of the meaning in this Sutta, which is similar to what appeared in those two Suttas, is exactly as the method already stated; it should be understood by the method stated therein. Because it was already stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta as "*taruṇo ambarukkho ambalaṭṭhikā*" (a young mango tree is *ambalaṭṭhikā*), he says, "*Ambalaṭṭhikā* is just like what was stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta."
