Having caused the sacrificial pit to be prepared and intending a great sacrifice, the requisites for the sacrifice, both animate and inanimate, were set up. With this meaning in mind, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "*Mahāyañño upakkhaṭo*" (A great sacrifice was prepared). That the preparation of those sacrificial requisites was done in such a manner is shown by the word "*sajjito*" (prepared). "*Vacchatarasatāni*" (Seven hundred bull-calves) refers to seven hundred strong young calves that have reached the state of youth. Because they are a special kind of calf, they are called "*vacchatarā*"; they are indeed just calves, not yet trained oxen (*damma*) nor full-grown bulls (*balībadda*); thus he says "*vacchasatāni*." This is the teacher's opinion. Alternatively, considering the suffix "*tara*" to be redundant, he says "*vacchasatāni*." In this way, all varieties of calves are included. "*Ete*" (These) refers to the animals starting from bulls (*usabha*) and ending with goats (*urabbha*). "*Anekesaṃ*" (Of many) refers to beasts and birds of many species. "*Migapakkhīnaṃ*" (Of beasts and birds) refers to beasts such as buffaloes, elk, spotted deer, hog-deer, and gaur, as well as birds such as peacocks, pigeons, quails, partridges, and snipes. To define the great number by the count of seven hundred, it is said: "*Satta sattasatāni*" (Seven times seven hundred), meaning seven hundred each...
301:
...and seven hundred each. *Thūṇa* (post) is the pillar for binding the beasts and birds that are requisites for the sacrifice. It is also named *yūpa*. Therefore, he says: "known as *yūpa*."

*Vidhā* (methods/ways) refers to the dispelling of remorse (*vippaṭisāravinodanā*). For if there is any defilement (*upakkilesa*) of the merit known as sacrifice, the dispelling, preventing, and ceasing of that defilement are called *vidhā*, which are the dispelling of remorse. These are also called "*ṭhapanā*" (establishment) because they establish the flow of merit without interruption. Indeed, it is only through the absence of remorse that the flow of merit proceeds higher and higher. These establishments are of three types (*tippakāra*) according to their occurrence in the three times: the beginning, the middle, and the end of the sacrifice; thus he says "*tiṭṭhapana*." Here, the word *parikkhāra* (requisite) is a synonym for *parivāra* (retinue/accompaniment), in the sense that "they prepare (*parikaronti*) and arrange the sacrifice." Therefore, he says: "having sixteen accompaniments."

## Commentary on the Account of King Mahāvijita’s Sacrifice

That which occurred in the past is "*bhūtapubba*" (it has been). Just like the word "*diṭṭhapubba*" (seen before), he says "*pubbacarita*" (past conduct). It means the practice of merit that was well-accumulated in his own previous births and which served as the equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*). This is indeed true; the illustration of the merit that follows one like a shadow as a stable, eternal treasure is very appropriate. However, experts in grammar say: "This word *bhūtapubba* is an indeclinable term (*nepātika*) used in the sense of the locative of time (*kālasattami*)." According to their view, it means "in a time long past." "*Assa*" (to him) means to this king. It should be connected as: "the great circle of the earth was conquered (*vijita*)." Or it means: "to that king, there is a conquered great circle of the earth." For the word *vijita* is used in the sense of a kingdom (*rajja*), as in "*antoraṭṭhe*" (within the country), meaning in the country where he dwells. By this, he shows the king's status as a sole sovereign (*ekarāja*), but not as a Universal Monarch (*cakkavatti*), because the possession of the seven treasures is not mentioned.

In the Pāḷi, to show that he was not wealthy merely with some indefinite property, after saying "*aḍḍha*" (prosperous), he says "*mahaddhana*" (of great wealth). Therefore, he says "*yo koci*" (whoever) and so forth. Prosperity (*aḍḍhatā*) means being endowed with riches (*vibhava*), and it is said in reference to that. Likewise, to show that his great wealth had reached its full strength and pinnacle, he says: "by a count that is immeasurable." Because of the sense of being enjoyed, the sensual pleasures (*kāma*) here are specifically called wealth (*bhoga*). He shows this by the words: "by way of the five cords of sensual pleasure." *Piṇḍapiṇḍavasena* means without dividing into vessels, ornaments, etc., but simply by way of portions and masses.

A *māsaka* is an object made to the measure of a *māsa* (bean), whether a mark is stamped on it or not. By the word "*ādi*" (and so forth), vessels and such are included. "By the count of many tens of millions" means...
302: The phrase (apari māṇasaṅkhyena) is said with reference to the extent of one hundred crores of coins and so forth. This is because one can only reach the status of a Khattiyamahāsāla (a wealthy noble) with a minimum amount of one hundred crores. Tuṭṭhī means the joy and gladness of the mind. Here, the word upakaraṇa is a synonym for cause (kāraṇa). If one asks what that cause is, it is said to be 'of various kinds, such as ornaments, gold vessels, silver vessels, and so forth.' By the word ādi (and so forth), clothing, bedding, dwellings, and so forth are included. Gold, silver, rubies, pearls, cat's-eyes, diamonds, and coral are called the seven treasures (satta ratanāni). It has also been said: 'Gold, silver, pearls, rubies, cat's-eyes, diamonds, and coral—these are the seven treasures.' The seven kinds of grain, such as sali rice and paddy, are considered the primary crops to be eaten first and are called pubbaṇṇa (early crops). Other than those, the remaining items such as green gram and black gram are called aparanna (later crops). They are called pubbaṇṇa because they occur before the aparanna, and aparanna because they occur after that time. Grammarians also call them pubbaṇṇa and aparaṇṇa by changing the 'nna' sound to 'ṇṇa'. The priority and posteriority of these crops should be understood by their appearance or non-appearance in the beginning of the aeon (ādikappa). The previously mentioned statement, 'He is rich, of great wealth, with much gold and silver,' was said in terms of daily expenses, receiving wealth, and wealth and grain used in trade. However, the current statement, 'He has much wealth and grain,' is said in terms of wealth buried in the ground and grain that has been stored. This method is shown with reference to this distinction. Daily usage of twenty coins, twenty ammaṇa (baskets), and so forth is also a characteristic of a Mahāsāla wealthy person. Now, to show the distinction by the opposite method of what was said, the second method is begun with 'atha vā' (or else) and so forth. By this method, it is established by meaning that the previous statement refers to buried wealth and stored grain. Therein, 'this statement' refers to the phrase 'He has much wealth and grain.' 'His' refers to King Mahāvijita. That which is to be used every day is called 'devasikaṃ'; this is a neuter noun expressing an action. Giving wages and provisions to slaves, workers, and servants is called 'paribbaya-dāna'. Taking wealth and grain for the purpose of clearing debts and so forth is called 'gahaṇa'. By the word ādi, the giving of loans and so forth is included. 'By the power of wealth and grain used in trade' means wealth and grain that are to be exchanged through buying and selling. In some versions, a reading without the word 'ca' is found. In that case, the term 'paribbayadānaggahaṇādivasena' should be connected with the term 'parivattana', and the meaning should be understood as 'by the power of wealth and grain to be exchanged here and there by such a method.'
303: The place where grain is kept is called 'koṭṭha'; that very place is a building (house). Therefore, it is said, 'one who has a koṭṭhāgāra (granary) full of grain.' Thus, having shown the treasury where essence (wealth) is kept as 'kosa' and the place where grain is kept as 'koṭṭhāgāra', now, to show that kosa in another way, 'atha vā' and so forth is said. In that sentence, just as the sheath that protects the sharpness of a sword is called 'kosa', the fourfold army is also called 'kosa' because it carries out the sharpness of the King's authority; thus it is said, 'the fourfold kosa' and so forth. Here, elephants and so forth, described by characteristics such as 'an elephant with twelve men,' should be taken. By taking the koṭṭhāgāra where clothing is kept, all places where kuppabhaṇḍa (utensils/goods) are kept are included; therefore, it is said, 'the koṭṭhāgāra is of three kinds' and so forth. Base materials other than gold and silver, such as copper, iron, wood, horn, and clothing, are called 'kuppa' (changing the 'ga' to 'ka') because they must be guarded securely. The place where gold and silver are stored is called 'dhanakoṭṭhāgāra'. Wandering about and looking at treasures in various places is called 'ratanavilokanacārikā'. Although the King truly knows that matter, he asks in this way by having the treasurer speak, for the purpose of preventing the assembly from making sounds of blame. If he does not have him speak in that way, the assembly will complain, 'Why does the King destroy the ancestral family wealth?' and from that, public unrest will occur. However, if he has him speak in that way, they will understand, 'He is discarding that wealth for this reason,' and will become silent. Then, public unrest cannot occur; therefore, it should be understood that he asks in that way. 'Maraṇavasaṃ' means (falling into) the power of death, or (reaching) the domain known as death. To make known the meaning of the word 'āmantetvā' in the Pali as 'wishing to consult,' it is said, 'having consulted with a wise man.' Here, the prefix (upasagga) follows the meaning of the root; in some places, there is a special meaning depending on the context, such as in the Pali: 'Monks, a monk who wishes to train should know, should inquire repeatedly, should weigh repeatedly.' In the Padabhājanī of that Pali, it is stated: 'sikkhamānena means one who wishes to train; aññātabbaṃ means that which should be known,' and so forth. 'Āmantesi' means he has become one who wishes to consult. The Brahmin thought for the sake of the country being free from danger and for the sacrifice to proceed for a long time without interruption; thus he said, 'This King,' and so forth. It should be connected as 'the houses of the people who are bringing (items)'; or, that word 'āharantānaṃ' is a genitive case in the sense of anādara (disregard).
304:
Because they destroy the welfare and happiness of beings, bring about harm and suffering, and are like thorns, bandits are here called "thorns" (kaṇṭaka). Therefore, it is said, "with thorns, namely bandits."

Just as those who kill villagers are called "village-destroyers" (gāmaghātaka) either literally or figuratively—since the name of the village also applies to the people residing there—similarly, bandits who rob and oppress travelers are called "road-oppressors" (panthaduha). One who habitually performs unrighteous and improper acts is called an "unrighteous doer" (adhammakārī). Alternatively, it refers to one who habitually fails to practice the royal duties of a kshatriya, which involve protecting the people of the countryside within his realm from various harms.

"Dassu" is a name for bandits. Because they destroy (viddhaṃsenti), they are called "dassu" through the dropping of the nasal (niggahīta). Since these bandits are like stakes, they are called "bandit-stakes" (dassukhīla). Just as a stake in a field obstructs the ease of plowing and the growth of crops in due course, similarly, bandits obstruct the exercise of royal authority and the prosperity of the countryside within a kingdom.

To show the sacrifice of life, it is said "by killing" (māraṇena). To show oppression, it is said "by beating" (koṭṭanena). The word "vadha" also carries the meaning of oppression, as in "he strikes (vadhati) but does not cry, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," etc. It means striking with elbows and so on. "Addu" refers to a specific type of binding instrument made of wooden logs (stocks). It means binding with such stocks. By the word "and so on" (ādi), it includes binding with ropes, chains, imprisonment, and so forth. The derivation of the word "jāni" (loss) from the root "hā" is shown by the term "by decline" (hāniyā). That this decline refers specifically to the loss of wealth is stated by "take a hundred," and so on.

Shaving the head while leaving five top-knots is called "pañcasikhamuṇḍakaraṇa." This practice is also referred to as "making crow's wings" (kākapakkhakaraṇa). Pouring cow-dung water on the head is called "gomayasiñcana." "Kudaṇḍaka" refers to a short stick less than four cubits in length; it is also called "gaddula." Binding with such a stick is "kudaṇḍakabandhana." By the word "and so on," it includes shaving the head with a razor and binding with a bag of ashes, etc. Since the word "sammā" has the meaning of cause (ñāya), it is stated as "by cause" (hetunā), etc.; this is a synonymous expression. "Ūhanissāmi" means I will remove or extract. Because of previous familiarity with that task, they exert effort. Regarding the term "anuppadetu," with the meaning of "give repeatedly," it is said "if what is given is insufficient," and so on. Farming implements include plowshares, goads, yokes, plow-poles, etc. By this statement, it is shown that in the Pāḷi text, only seeds and provisions are mentioned as examples.
305:
Witnessing and the writing of contracts on palm leaves and so on are practices that occur when giving to someone with the intention of taking it back, whether with or without interest. However, in this case, because there is no intention of taking it back, it is said "without making a witness," etc., meaning both are absent. Therefore, it is said, "by way of cutting off the root (capital)." "Witness" (sakkhi) refers to the people present at the time of giving. "Without putting it on paper" means without recording it on palm leaves or other leaves as is customary. In other contexts, the word "pābhata" also means a gift or present, but here it means the capital for goods; thus it is said "of the capital for goods," and so on. Capital is called "pābhata" because it brings in (ābharati) various types of profitable goods. Those skilled in grammar say it is "pābhata" because it is brought (ābhata) even before the profit. As for a gift, it is called "pābhata" because it is brought by those desiring a particular benefit. Here, the prefix "pa-" expresses the sense of desiring.

By saying "as it is said" (yathāha), etc., the meaning of the word "pābhata" as capital is proven by the text of the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka. The commentary there states: "Appakenapi" means even with a little or a small amount. "Medhāvī" means a wise person. "Pābhatena" means with capital. "Vicakkhaṇa" means one skilled in trade. "Establishes himself" means producing great wealth and followers and establishing oneself therein. How? Just as one blows a small fire; as a wise man gradually adds cow-dung powder and so on to a small fire and, blowing with the breath of his mouth, establishes and increases it into a great mass of fire, even so, a wise man, having obtained even a little capital, manages it through various means to increase wealth and followers. Having increased them, he establishes himself there. Or rather, by the greatness of that wealth and followers, he establishes himself, meaning he makes himself well-known and famous.

That which is to be given daily is "devasika." That which is to be given monthly is "māsika." By the word "and so on," it includes giving on non-uposatha days, etc. To each person, according to their skill, according to their work, and according to their bravery—the word "according to" (anurūpa) appearing after the compound should be applied to each term. Here, being according to one's proficiency is "according to skill" (kusalānurūpa). In some versions, the word "kula" (family/caste) is seen; this is also appropriate, as giving according to family, such as to the families of Jāṇussoṇi and others, is also fitting. Positions such as general (senāpati) and so on are mentioned here merely to indicate rations and wages. Because of being devoted to their own work and because of the absence of calamities, they are those who accumulate heaps of wealth and grain. Safely...
306:
"Ṭhitā" means existing without danger or harm. Therefore, in the word "abhayā," it means being free from any kind of danger. "Modā modamānā" refers to rejoicing through joy itself, and does not merely mean associating. In phrases such as "bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodī," the word "muda" can also occur in the sense of associating. Alternatively, it means that because some are rejoicing, others also live in a state of joy. Therefore, it is said, "having hearts that rejoice with one another." Even though there is no physical union, because the intention to be so arises as knowledge, there are two versions of the text. "Iddhaphītabhāvaṃ" means the state of being prosperous and abundant.

## Description of the Four Requisites

They are called "anuyantā" because they follow and perform various duties. Just as "anubhāva" is also called "ānubhāva," "anuyantā" is also called "ānuyantā." There is also a reading "ānuyuttā," and according to the method already mentioned, they are called "ānuyuttā" because they strive in various duties. "Assa" means of the king. "Te" refers to those following khattiyas and others. This is to prevent them from feeling dissatisfied, thinking, "We are being excluded here."

"A village where a constant and abundant revenue comes is called a market town (nigama). A village with particularly increased revenue is a large village (mahāgāma)," says the Teacher. In the Vinaya commentaries, however, it is said: "A village with shops but without a surrounding wall is a nigama; a town with a wall and shops is a city (nagara); a place contrary to these two is a village (gāma)." It is called "gāma" because people delight or consume (madanti/gasanti) there; if that village is prominent, it is an excellent village called "nigama." Here, the prefix "ni" denotes excellence (bhusa), and because it is a proper name, it is shortened (rassa), according to grammarians. The meaning of "janapada" has already been stated.

Among the seven constituents of a kingdom (rājapakati)—namely, the lord (king), minister, friend, treasury, fort, territory, and army—the great increase of welfare and happiness occurs through the power of the six constituents other than the king. Referring to the followers (anuyantā) who are a part of these constituents, it is said "yaṃ tumhākaṃ," etc.

They are called "amaccā" (ministers) because they are with (amā) the king in various matters. Grammarians say that the indeclinable "amā," meaning "together" as in "amāvāsī," is formed into a derivative (taddhita) with the suffix "ca." The term "piyasahāyakā" (dear friends) shows that when administering state affairs, they are the king's beloved and close associates. They are called "pārisajjā" (courtiers) because they are in the king's assembly (parisā). Who are they? They are the "remaining subordinates who follow orders."

Even if there are gifts to be given, if one is not endowed with power and a retinue, one cannot give such a gift. In old age, both that power and retinue tend to decline even for such kings. How much more so if there are no gifts to be given? To show this, the phrase starting with "deyyadhammasmiñhi" was said. The construction is: "one is unable to give when there are no gifts and in old age." "Etena" means because of the two aforementioned reasons. "Anumatiyā" means by permission. "Pakkhā" means the constituents of the sacrifice along with consideration. Because they prepare and arrange the sacrifice, they are called "parikkhārā" (accessories/requisites); since they are parts of that sacrifice, they are like a retinue; thus it is said, "parivārā bhavanti" (they become the retinue).
308: (Being a master) he gives. This is a figurative expression where the name of the cause is applied to the effect (kāraṇopacāra). The same method should be understood for what follows. Because he cannot be pulled away by greed for the object to be given, he is neither like a slave nor like a friend (but gives only as a master). To explain this meaning through both exclusion (vyatireka) and inclusion (anvaya), the phrase beginning with "Yo hi" is stated. In this context, it is shown by excluding the two undesirable types: the slave (dāsa) and the friend (sahāya). Among various foods and edibles, only the sweet is considered excellent, thus it is said, "He eats what is sweet." Alternatively, this is merely an illustration, meaning "He enjoys what is excellent." He gives like a slave because he has fallen into the state of slavery to craving. He gives like a friend because he cannot relinquish the beloved nature of the object to be given. In that act of giving, he gives like a master because he has liberated himself from slavery to craving and acts by overcoming it. As for the statement made by the teacher (the sub-commentator), "It is similar to the enjoyment of a master," this was said with reference to the common quality of transcending slavery to craving. The meaning that only the gift of an Arahant is called the "master of the gift" (dānasāmī), just as the enjoyment of an Arahant is the "enjoyment of a master" (sāmīparibhoga), is not fully complete. Otherwise, this statement might be a scribal error (pamādalikhita) made during later copying. "Tādiso" refers to one who has the nature of a master of the gift (dānasāmī). In this context, the ascetic (samaṇa) who has calmed evil and the brahmin (brāhmaṇa) who has expelled evil are mentioned by way of an exalted designation (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa). Alternatively, it should be understood that those who are ascetics merely by ordination and brahmins merely by birth are included under terms such as "kapaṇa" (the poor). "Duggata" refers to those who have reached a difficult livelihood, those who live with hardship. Therefore, it is said, "poor human beings." "Pathāvino" refers to travelers. "Vaṇibbaka" refers to those who beg by praising the virtues of the donors or by speaking of the fruits of kamma. To show the meaning as including those such as naked ascetics (acelaka), the phrase beginning with "Ye iṭṭhaṃ dinnaṃ" is stated. Only through those two modes can the praise of the gift's merit occur. It should be construed that those who wander about are called "vaṇibbaka." "Pasatamatta" (a handful) is said in terms of paddy, rice, etc., while "sarāvamatta" (a bowlful) is said in terms of gruel, cooked rice, etc. A public watering place common to all, such as a river or a lake, is called "opāna" because one descends into it to drink. Because he is like a watering place, he is "opānabhūta." Therefore, it is said, "become like a well," and so on. "Hutvā" is used in the sense of being. "Sutam eva sutajātaṃ" means simply that which is heard (suta). The word "jāta" does not express a distinct meaning, similar to the term "kosajāta" (born in the sheath). The ability to contemplate the results of the past and so on should be understood as being by the power of that king's inference (anumāna) and by the power of how things should be done, and not by direct perception (paccakkha) as in the case of the Buddhas. To show this, the phrase beginning with "Atīte" is stated. In this context, the contemplation of the benefits of merit and the consequences of demerit...
309:
It should be understood by the power of knowing the context. 'Puññassa' means of the merit of sacrifice (yañña-puñña). 'Dāyakacittampi' means the mind of the donors, or the mind of one who desires to give.

Among these eight factors, let the five factors such as wealth be the requisites of the sacrifice, for without them the sacrifice cannot be accomplished. However, since the sacrifice can be accomplished even without being well-born from both parents and being handsome, how could these two be requisites of the sacrifice? To address this objection and show that all eight factors are requisites through both the method of presence (anvaya) and the method of absence (vyatireka), the passage beginning with 'ete hi kira' is stated.

In this regard, some teachers say: 'Just as the five factors like wealth are definitely (ekaṃsato) factors of the sacrifice, being well-born and being handsome are not so. To show that these two are factors only indefinitely (anekaṃsato), the word "kira," which indicates a lack of preference, is used.' Those teachers say this because they consider the statement 'this person is ill-born,' etc., to be indefinite. This is without essence (incorrect). This is because the demonstration of these being factors of the sacrifice through the method of absence is done by way of what is common to all. This is stated only for the purpose of showing that there is no room for the objection that 'some might have such a thought.' Since it does not show them as being indefinite factors only by way of what is common to both, that statement is without essence.

Here, the word 'kira' should be understood as having the meaning of indicating the manner of thinking of the Brahmin chaplain at that time. Because it is said that 'this Brahmin, having thought thus, said "these eight factors also are the requisites of that sacrifice,"' his manner of thinking is indicated by the word 'kira.' In the phrase 'evamādīni,' by the word 'ādi,' the following phrases should be included: 'This person is ugly; for how long will he give? Now he will become displeased and cut off the gift. This person is poor, of little influence, without faith, of little learning, does not know the benefit, is not wise; for how long will he give? He will cut off the gift.'

## Explanation of the Four Requisites, etc.
In the phrase 'sujaṃ paggaṇhantānaṃ,' regarding the two alternatives mentioned in the Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, the passage beginning with 'mahāyāgaṃ' is stated to refute the second alternative. By that, by showing the chaplain himself holding the ladle, it indicates that the state of being intensely devoted to giving respectfully with one's own hands is desired.

In the phrase 'evaṃ dujjātassa' as well, one should not take it as 'this is showing being well-born as an indefinite factor,' but the meaning should be taken only by way of what is common to all, according to the method mentioned below. By the word 'ādi,' the following phrases should be included: 'Thus, the gift performed by the arrangement of one who does not desire the sacrifice... one who is immoral... one who is unwise, for how long will it continue?'
310:
The summary of these words should be understood as: "How long will a gift persist when it is performed under the direction of one who lacks wisdom?" "Tasmā" means for those two reasons.

## Explanation of the Three Stages (Tissa-vidhā-vaṇṇanā)

"Tiṇṇam thānānam" refers to the meaning of the three stages or moments known as the beginning, the middle, and the end of the gift. "Calanti" means they shake; they do not remain in their former state as before. Because it regards the word 'karaṇīya' (to be done), this genitive case (of the Brahmin) exists only in the sense of the agent (kattā), not in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa). Generally, according to the nature of the case ending that indicates the instrument, only the unexpressed agent (anuttakattā) is to be understood here as having the sense of the instrument.

To show the means of not producing subsequent remorse, it is said: "Before... should be established." In that passage, "acalā" (unshakable) means firm, without shrinking or retreating due to any cause. "Patiṭṭhapetabbā" means it should be made well-established. Desiring also to show the means of such establishment, the words beginning with "Evañhi" are spoken. By thus making [the prior volition] unshakable, just as that gift is accomplished according to one's desire at the present time of giving, so also in the future it yields great fruit by being of vast benefit. This is because it is not defiled by subsequent remorse.

"Dvīsu ဌာနေသု" (In two places) refers to the time of sacrificing and the time after the sacrifice. Intending the meaning "remorse... should not be felt," it is said: "Eseva nayo" (This is the same method).

"Muñca-cetanā" refers to the volition of relinquishing. The stability (niccala-bhāva) of that volition is the state of being a liberal giver, which is grand by the power of prior preparation. "Pacchā-samanussaraṇa-cetanā" is the subsequent volition (the volition that arises after giving). Its stability is to be known by the power of respectfully reviewing one's gift, thinking, "Oh, it is wonderful that I have given this gift; it is truly good."

To show the means of making both those volitions unshakable by way of the opposite, it is said: "Tathā... hoti." In that passage, "tathā akaro ntassa" means for one who does not make the muñca-cetanā and pacchā-samanussaraṇa-cetanā unshakable, but instead produces subsequent remorse. The words "nor does the mind incline towards grand wealth" show the means of making only the pacchā-samanussaraṇa-cetanā unshakable by way of the opposite. Only when shown in this way is the stated illustration complete.

In that passage, "uḷāresu bhogesu" (in grand wealth) refers to the grand wealth obtained because the gift was made in a superior field (khētta-visēsa), namely the recipient. Because the mind is defiled by subsequent remorse later on, it does not incline [towards enjoying those riches]. To show who it is like, the words beginning with "Mahāroruvaṃ" are spoken. The story of that merchant householder appears in the Kosala Saṃyutta and the Mayhaka Jātaka. Because it appears there, the Blessed One spoke thus in the Kosala Saṃyutta: "Great King, in the past, a certain merchant householder offered almsfood to a Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī."
311:
"Great King, in the past, a certain merchant householder offered almsfood to a Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī. Having said, 'Give almsfood to this ascetic,' he rose from his seat and departed. But after giving, he felt subsequent remorse, thinking, 'It would have been better if slaves or workers had eaten this almsfood.'"

It is said that although the merchant had seen that Paccekabuddha on other days, the thought of giving did not arise in him. However, on the day of that alms-giving, this Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, the third son of Queen Padumavatī, having spent time in the bliss of fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana, emerged from that attainment in the morning. He washed his face at Lake Anovatatta, dressed in his lower robe on the Manosilā plateau, fastened his girdle, took his bowl and robes, and entered the fourth jhāna which is the basis for supernormal knowledge. Then, ascending into the sky by psychic power, he descended at the city gate, donned his upper robe, and holding his bowl, he arrived at the merchant's door in due order with a graceful gait, as if placing a bundle of a thousand coins at the doors of the city dwellers.

On that day, the merchant had risen early, eaten excellent food, and was sitting at the entrance of his house cleaning his teeth after having a seat prepared. When he saw the Paccekabuddha, because he had already eaten early that morning, the thought of giving arose. He called his wife and instructed her, "Give almsfood to this ascetic," and then departed to attend upon the King.

The merchant's wife, being wise, thought: "For such a long time, I have never heard the word 'Give' from this merchant. Today he asks to give, and he does not ask to give to just anyone, but to a Paccekabuddha who is free from lust, hatred, and delusion, who has discarded all defilements, and who has laid down the burden of the aggregates. Therefore, I will not give just any ordinary food, but I will give excellent almsfood." She went out from the house, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha with the five-point prostration, took his bowl, and invited him to sit on the seat prepared inside the house. She prepared almsfood with very pure fine rice, and having prepared suitable snacks, curries, and bean soup, she filled the bowl. She decorated the outside of the bowl with perfumes, placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, and paid homage.

The Paccekabuddha, thinking, "I shall also show favor to other Paccekabuddhas," did not eat there but spoke words of appreciation (anumodanā) and departed. The merchant, having returned after attending upon the King, saw the Paccekabuddha and asked, "Venerable Sir, I departed after instructing them to give you almsfood. Did you receive the almsfood?" When the Paccekabuddha replied, "Yes, merchant, I received it," the merchant said, "Let me see," and craned his neck to look.
312:
The wealthy man looked; as he looked, the scent of his alms-food arose and struck his nostrils. Being unable to restrain his mind, he felt remorse after giving. The manner in which this remorse arose is already explained in the Pāḷi starting with "Varaṃ etaṃ" and so on. However, due to the merit of giving alms-food, he was reborn in the happy heavenly realms seven times, and seven times he was born into a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. This present life is his seventh existence. Yet, because of the remorse he felt after giving, his mind does not incline toward grand luxuries. This matter is taught in the Varalañcaka Sutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya as follows:

"Great King, after that wealthy householder gave alms, he felt remorse, thinking, 'It would have been better if my slaves or laborers had eaten this alms-food.' Due to the result of that kamma, his mind does not incline toward enjoying excellent food, nor does it incline toward enjoying excellent clothes or vehicles, nor does it incline toward enjoying the five excellent cords of sensual pleasure."

In the Mayhaka Jātaka, it is also stated: "Great King, in this way, although the visiting wealthy man obtained great wealth due to the offerings made to the Tagarasikhī Paccekabuddha, because he was unable to make his subsequent volition (aparacetanā) noble after giving, he was unable to enjoy noble luxuries."

Furthermore, this wealthy man had previously killed his brother's only son for the sake of wealth. Due to that kamma, he suffered in hell for many years and was born without children for seven lifetimes. Even now, because of that same kamma, he has returned to the Mahāroruva Hell. Therefore, it is said, "Like the wealthy householder who went to the Mahāroruva Hell." In this context, the meaning should be understood through the power of the preceding and subsequent volitions. This is because a single volition cannot produce two rebirth-linkings (paṭisandhi).

## Explanation of the Ten Aspects (Dasa Ākāra)
It is called "Ākāra" because it produces a result that has a boundary or limit appropriate to itself. Therefore, it is taught as "by ten reasons," using the sense of cause. Here, the prefix "ā" denotes the sense of boundary (mariyāda). Remorse can arise not only toward those of poor virtue but also toward those possessed of virtue. In both cases, remorse should not be allowed to arise.
313:
The particles "api" or "pi" are used to perform a conjunction. The statement "it arises only because of the recipient" refers to a very strong remorse. However, weak remorse can also arise because of the gift (deyyadhamma) or because of the attendants. "Fit to arise" means it is worthy of occurring. It should be connected as "he also dispels remorse." "Only to them" refers only to those who take life. In this context, "yajana" (sacrifice) is intended only as "dāna" (giving), not as the ritual of tending the fire; therefore, it says, "May the venerable one give." "Let him relinquish" means let him give by way of liberated generosity (mutta-cāga). "Within" refers to the internal (ajjhatta) states within one's own continuity.

## Explanation of the Sixteen Aspects (Soḷasa Ākāra)

Only the factors such as the side of approval, having been made the basis of the sacrifice below, are called the "sixteen requirements" (soḷasa-parikkhāra). However, here, because the effort is made to gladden by way of showing (sandassana) and so on, it is called "by sixteen aspects" (soḷasa-ākāra). "Having shown" means showing the fruit as if it were present before the eyes through the power of his own teaching. Because of showing many times, the phrase "having shown, having shown" is a distributive expression. The teacher states that this is an iterative (āmeḍita) expression due to the sense of repetition. The same method applies to phrases like "having encouraged, having encouraged." "That meaning" refers to the meaning connected with kamma and its fruit through the power of the fruit of giving. "Having encouraged" means not merely hearing, but just as a king takes that meaning to heart and holds it well, so he causes him to take it up respectfully.

"By dispelling remorse" is merely an illustration. Greed, hatred, delusion, envy, stinginess, and pride are also defilements (upakkilesa) of the mind of giving. By dispelling those defilements, that mind is said to be incited (samuttejita) because it reaches a state of sharpness and clarity. Remorse is specifically mentioned because it is very close to the act. For when a gift is being given, the possibility of remorse exists. To bring about a state of great joy through qualities that truly exist is called "gladdening" (sampahaṃsana); thus, it is said "it is excellent," and so on. "Righteously" means truthfully. To show that meaning, it is said "by a righteous and even cause." Truth is called "dhamma" because it does not depart from righteousness, "sama" (even) because it is a practice of peace, and "kāraṇa" (cause) because it is appropriate.

In that sacrifice, if there was not even the cutting of trees or grass, how could there be the killing of living beings? To strengthen the fact that there was no killing of beings, and to show that it was not corrupted by any perverted views, the Buddha, after saying "neither were cattle slaughtered," etc., also taught "neither were trees felled," and so on.
314:
Even though it was taught, "Cows should not be killed," and so forth, the phrase "Ye yūpanāmake" and so on is stated to show that it was also said, "Trees should not be cut," and so forth. "Barihisatthāya" means for the purpose of demarcation. "Vanamālāsaṅkhepena" means by the sign of a garland woven with forest flowers. This is what the Teacher (the Sub-commentator) stated. It means in the manner of a forest grove. "Bhūmiyaṃ vā pattharanti" means they spread it out in various places, surrounding the sacrificial ground. The ground prepared with mantras and so forth is called "Vedī" (altar) because it causes one to obtain gains and honors. "Te pi rukkhā te pi dabbā" should be connected. Both of these can be either the agent of the action (kammakatā) or the expressed object (abhihitakamma). According to the speaker's intention, the grammatical roles (kāraka) function according to their capacity. The phrase "Kiṃ panā" and so forth is shown to strengthen the fact that there is no killing of beings by the aforementioned method, and to show that it is not corrupted by wrong views.

"Antogehadāsa" refers to a slave born within the house. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), one should include slaves who are bought, those captured in raids, and those who voluntarily accept slavery. "Pubbameva" means even before performing the hired work. "Dhanaṃ gahetvā" means taking it according to the daily work performed. "Bhattavetanaṃ" refers to the daily food and the monthly wages or allowance. This meaning has already been stated. "Tajjitā" refers to those who are threatened. "Parikammāni" means all types of tasks, implying both high and low or superior and inferior duties. "Piyasamudācāreneva" means only with endearing speech. "Yathānāmavaseñeva" means in accordance with their well-known names. In the phrase "sappitelananavanītadadhimaduphāṇitena ceva," the word "ca" has the sense of including what has not yet been mentioned. By that word "ca," one should include various kinds of excellent food and snacks, clothing, vehicles, flowers, scents, ointments, beds, and dwellings. Therefore, it is said, "paṇītehi sappitelādisammissaheva" and so forth. It should be connected as "with rice gruel... (pe)... drinks, etc., appropriate for those various times." "Sappiādīnaṃ" means with ghee and so forth.

Wealth is called "saṃ" because it is stored up and because it is one's own property. Because he is the master of that wealth, it is called "sapati" (owner of wealth) with the elision of the niggahita. Because it brings benefit in the present life and the future life, the benefit of that owner of wealth is called "sāpateyya" (property). It refers to that very wealth. Therefore, it is said, "pahūtaṃ dhanaṃ" (abundant wealth). "Akkhayadhammameva" means having a nature that is inexhaustible. "Gāmabhāgena" means either by way of fame or by way of the portions to be taken in the village. Thus the Teacher stated. It also means by way of the respective village portions. In the remaining terms, the same method should be understood.
315:
Yaññāvāṭa is a designation for the place of sacrifice, such as the Assamedha (horse sacrifice), which is a dug-out pit. However, in this context, by way of metaphorical usage, it refers to the alms-hall itself. The phrase "puratthimato nagaradvāre" and so forth is stated to show the meaning that since that alms-hall was built near the eastern city gate, it is in the eastern part. The phrase "yathā" and so forth is said to show that the place is neither too far nor too near the King's alms-hall. This is because, having eaten breakfast there, they can reach the King's alms-hall in the evening without being exhausted. The same method applies to the phrases "dakkhiṇena yaññāvāṭassa" and so forth. In the phrase "yāguṃ pivitvā" (having drunk the rice gruel), the meal eaten in the morning (breakfast) is meant, using rice gruel as the primary example.

Madhura means having a sweet taste. "Upari vattabbamattha" refers to the meaning that will be stated later, such as "api ca me bho evaṃ hoti" and so forth. "Parihārena" means either by showing respect to the Blessed One and avoiding disrespect, or by avoiding direct questioning and asking the intended meaning through circumlocution (vaṅkavutti). Therefore, it is said, "If one asks directly, it is as if one is being disrespectful."

## Description of Constant Alms and Customary Sacrifice

By the word "uṭṭhāya," the exertion of energy in giving is meant. By "samuṭṭhāya," the constant performance of that giving is meant. The intention is that if one does not perform work such as farming or trading, one will perish by falling into misfortune such as poverty. Although it is stated briefly in the Commentary as having fewer materials (requirements) and greater fruit, in the Pāḷi text it appears as "appatthatara, appasamārambhatara, mahapphalatara, mahānisaṃsatara." Among these, "appasambhāratara" means having very few materials or materials that are not difficult to prepare. "Appatthatara" means having very few duties; here "attha" means duty. There is also a variant reading "appaṭṭhatara" by changing 'ttha' to 'ṭṭha'. "Samārambha" is that by which a sacrifice is well-undertaken; it refers to the oppression of beings that occurs through the gathering of materials. A sacrifice with little such oppression is called "appasamārambha"; if it is very little, it is "appasamārambhatara." It is called "mahapphala" because it has a great result known as the ripening (vipāka); if it is very great, it is "mahapphalatara." It is called "mahānisaṃsa" because it has a great result known as the consequence (nissanda); if it is very great, it is "mahānisaṃsatara." "Dhuvadāna" refers to gifts that are given constantly and without interruption. In the term "niccabhatta," all four requisites are included, using food as the primary example. "Anukulayañña" refers to gifts given by following the family lineage.
316:
Therefore, the teacher said "Amhākaṃ," and so forth. Those offerings that are caused to proceed should be understood as "anukula-yañña" (offerings made according to family lineage). "Nibaddha-dāna" refers to offerings that are established and maintained through tradition.

A voting ticket (salākā) made of ivory is called "dantamaya-salākā." On which the names of the donors are marked; by this, it is shown that the regular meal is offered by means of a ticket-offering (salāka-dāna). "Taṃ kulaṃ" refers to the family of Anāthapiṇḍika. "Dāliddiyena" means because of the state of poverty. By the words "unable to give more than one ticket," it is said that even with a single ticket-offering, the regular gift is maintained without interruption. "Rañño" refers to King Setavāhana.

In the phrase "ādīni vatvā," the word "ādi" includes words of concern in making equal offerings, such as "Why do you snatch it like a hawk pouncing on a piece of meat?" and so forth. "Galaggāhā" refers to seizing by the neck. By the words "kammaccheda-vasena," it is shown that taking away the opportunity for one's own work is also a form of oppression. Since the word "samārambha" here has the meaning of oppression, it is said, "samārambha is known as oppression (pīḷā)."

Through the donor's power, there are three factors: the fulfillment of the volition before giving (pubba-cetanā), the volition while giving (muñca-cetanā), and the volition after giving (apara-cetanā). Through the recipient's power, there are three factors: the practice of being free from lust, hatred, and delusion. Thus, the offering is endowed with six factors. The Nandamātā Sutta in the Chakka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya is the evidence that establishes this meaning.

Merit that arises, flowing and rushing from here and there like a great river or a great flood by the power of successive volitions, is called "puññābhisanda" (overflow of merit). By the word "tathāvidhaṃ," it is said that it is not easy to measure the extent. It should be understood that because the cause is great, the result is also great. Because it is like a great flood occurring due to rain at the upper reaches of a river, "tasmā" and so on are said.

"Navanavo" has the meaning of being always new. Because there is the donor's effort every day, it is said "ekena" and so on, meaning there is no end to the task. Because a leaf-hut (paṇṇasālā) that has been undertaken can be completed in a few days, it is said "paṇṇasālaṃ" and so on, meaning there is an end to the task. To show the means by which there is an end to the task even in a great monastery, it is said, "having relinquished wealth once."

"Suttantapariyāyena" means by the method of the Suttas, such as the Sabbāsava Sutta. "Navānisaṃsā" refers to the nine benefits counted according to reflection, beginning with the warding off of cold and ending with delight in seclusion. These benefits are stated in a brief measure.
317:
Because one who gives a dwelling (āvāsa) is said to have given all requisites. As stated in the excellent seal of the Saṃyutta Nikāya: "He who gives a shelter gives everything." This giving of a dwelling is also a means for the constant increase of merit. In that same Saṃyutta Nikāya, it is said: "For those who give a shelter, merit increases always, both by day and by night."

Indeed, even a monk who has wandered through two or three villages for alms and returned without receiving anything, upon entering a park (ārāma) endowed with shade and water, bathing, lying down for a moment in the dwelling, and then getting up and sitting down, it is as if strength has been brought from somewhere and placed into his body. The complexion of a monk wandering outside becomes exhausted due to wind and sun; when he enters the dwelling, closes the door, and lies down for a moment, the disagreeable continuity (of mind and body) subsides, and the agreeable continuity is established; it is as if the complexion has been brought from somewhere and placed (into him).

For a monk wandering outside, thorns may pierce his feet, he may strike against stumps, and dangers from scorpions, lice, etc., as well as the fear of thieves, may arise; when he enters the dwelling, closes the door, and lies down, all those dangers are no more. Because there is no outward distraction, for a monk who recites and studies, the joy and happiness born of the Dhamma arise; for a monk who applies his mind to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), the happiness of tranquility arises.

Sweat pours from the body of a monk wandering outside, and his eyes quiver; at the moment of entering the dwelling, he cannot see the couch, stool, etc. But after lying down for a moment, it is as if clarity of vision has been brought and placed (in him), and he can see the door, window, couch, stool, and so on. Seeing him residing in this dwelling, people respectfully serve him with the four requisites. For that reason, I have said: "One who gives a dwelling... is," and "This giving of a dwelling is also a means for the constant increase of merit." Therefore, all the aforementioned benefits should be understood.

Speaking by way of the Khandhaka method means by the method of the Vinaya Pali found in the Senāsana Khandhaka. In that Pali, it is stated:

"It wards off cold and heat, and also wild beasts,
Scorpions, lice, mosquitoes, and the cold winds and rains.
Furthermore, it wards off the fierce wind and sun that arise.
(A dwelling is given) for the sake of seclusion, for the sake of living happily,
And for the sake of practicing jhāna and vipassanā.

The Buddha praised the offering of a monastery to the Saṅgha as the highest. Therefore, a wise person, seeing his own benefit..."
318:
One should have delightful monasteries built and have learned monks dwell there. To those upright ones, with a clear mind, one should give food, drink, clothing, and lodgings. They teach him the Dhamma that dispels all suffering; having understood that Dhamma in this life, he attains Parinibbāna, free from taints.

The Buddha showed the verses of appreciation (anumodanā) in brief regarding the donation of monasteries by the merchant of Rājagaha and others. In those verses, 'cold' and 'heat' are spoken of in terms of seasonal imbalance. In the phrase 'sisire cāpi vuṭṭhiyo', 'sisira' refers to drizzle accompanied by wind. 'Vuṭṭhi' refers to straight, heavy rainfall. All these terms should be connected with the word 'patihanti' (wards off).

'Is warded off' means it is warded off by the monastery. 'For the purpose of shelter' (leṇatthaṃ) means for the purpose of secluded dwelling. 'For the purpose of happiness' (sukhatthaṃ) means for the purpose of living happily without dangers such as cold. The two terms 'to meditate' (jhāyituṃ) and 'to practice insight' (vipassituṃ) should also be connected with the term 'for the purpose of happiness'. This means: the gift of a monastery is for the purpose of happiness; what kind of happiness? The happiness that arises from meditating and practicing insight. Alternatively, it should be connected with the subsequent term: the gift of a monastery is for the purpose of meditating and practicing insight. The Buddha praised the gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha as the highest among all gifts, given with the thought, 'Here they will meditate and practice insight.' For it was said: 'He who gives a dwelling gives everything' (SN 1.42).

Because the gift of a monastery was praised as the highest, the verse beginning with 'A wise man...' was spoken. In the phrase 'have learned monks dwell there,' it means one should have monks who are learned in both the scriptures (pariyatti-bāhusacca) and realization (paṭivedha-bāhusacca) dwell in the monastery. 'To those [monks] food...' and so on refers to all suitable food, drink, clothing, and lodgings such as couches and stools. 'To those who are upright' means to those whose minds are not crooked. 'One should give' means one should bury a treasure-trove of merit. Furthermore, one should give with a clear mind, without letting the clarity of mind be disturbed. To one who gives with such a clear mind, those monks teach the Dhamma... up to... attains Parinibbāna free from taints; this is the method of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

The method of the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) explained by the Elders Dhammapāla and Sāriputta is: 'cold' refers to cold arising either from the disturbance of internal elements or...
319:
...from cold arising due to external seasonal change. 'Heat' (uṇhaṃ) refers to the heat of fire; it should be understood that this occurs in forest fires and the like. 'Patihanti' means it wards off or prevents; the monastery acts so that there is no oppression of body and mind by both cold and heat. Indeed, when the body is oppressed by cold and heat, a monk with a distracted mind is unable to strive by the proper method. 'Vāḷamigāni' refers to fierce wild beasts such as lions and leopards. Indeed, for a monk who has entered a secure dwelling in the forest and sits with the door closed, those dangers do not occur. 'Sarisape' refers to long-bodied creatures that crawl on their bellies, such as snakes. The word 'makase' (mosquitoes) is just an illustration; by this, gadflies and other such creatures are also included. 'Sisire' refers to the extremely cold touch arising from the cold season or from seven-day continuous rain and the like. 'Vuṭṭhiyo' refers to heavy rainfalls that occur at any time; it should be noted that the construction is 'wards off [heavy rains].'

'Vātātapo ghoro' refers to fierce winds, with or without dust, that uproot and break trees and bushes, and the fierce heat of the sun that arises during the hot summer season; these are warded off. 'For the purpose of shelter' (leṇatthaṃ) means for the purpose of withdrawing the mind from various sense objects for the sake of delighting in seclusion. 'For the purpose of happiness' (sukhatthaṃ) means for the purpose of living comfortably due to the absence of the aforementioned dangers. 'To meditate' (jhāyituṃ) means to fix the mind on any one of the thirty-eight meditation objects and contemplate it closely. 'To practice insight' (vipassituṃ) means to contemplate conditioned formations through characteristics such as impermanence.

'Vihāre' refers to dwellings to be relied upon. 'Kāraye' means one should have them built. 'Ramme' refers to monasteries that are delightful to the mind and comfortable for living. 'Have learned monks dwell there' means that after having the monastery built, one should have monks who are learned, virtuous, and of good conduct dwell there. To those learned monks, one should give food, drink, clothing, and lodgings so that they do not suffer fatigue regarding the four requisites. One should give to those who are upright and endowed with wholesome intention, with a clear mind that has faith in kamma, its results, and the qualities of the Triple Gem.

Now, to show the mutual benefit between the laity and the monastics, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with 'Te tassā...'. In that verse, 'te' refers to the learned monks dwelling in the monastery. 'Tassa' refers to the lay devotee (upāsaka). 'They teach the Dhamma' means they teach the True Dhamma that dispels all the suffering of the round of rebirth. 'Having understood that Dhamma here' means that lay devotee, having understood the True Dhamma in this Dispensation through right practice, attains the path of Arahatship, becomes free from taints, and attains Parinibbāna by the extinguishing of the eleven fires; he becomes cool as the eleven fires of defilements are extinguished.
320:
Seventeen benefits are taught regarding the donation of a monastery, starting from the dispelling of cold and ending with vipassanā (insight), including obtaining food and so on, hearing the Dhamma, realization of the Dhamma, and Parinibbāna.

The fruit of the donation of a monastery by donors should also be understood in accordance with the fruit arising through the power of the monastery for the recipients. Since they generally receive results similar to their actions, it is said "Therefore," and so on. By the phrase "because it is relinquished to the Saṅgha," he speaks primarily of a saṅghika monastery. A saṅghika monastery is one built for the Saṅgha of the four directions. Regarding this, it is said in the Padabhājanīya: "A saṅghika monastery is one given and relinquished to the Saṅgha." In a monastery where a cetiya is established, where the Dhamma is heard, where monks coming from the four directions wash their feet without asking anyone, open the door with a key, prepare the lodgings, and stay as they please—even if it is a leaf-roofed hut of only four cubits—it is called a monastery built for the Saṅgha of the four directions.

For one who cannot suppress greed, it is difficult to relinquish. The passage "even to a single monk," etc., is said to show the practice and the very firm undertaking of the upāsakas (lay devotees) in taking refuge in that manner. Teachers say that the refuge undertaken by those upāsakas themselves is indeed well-undertaken. It should be connected as "in the presence of the Saṅgha or a group." Here (tattha) means in the refuge as taken. There is also a reading "tassa," meaning "of the refuge as taken." The statement that it need not be done repeatedly is said with reference to wise people. For wise people, their skill in the meaning of the refuge and so on remains unshakable like lion's fat in a golden jar. The phrase "merit made by sacrificing life" is said regarding one who has taken the refuge so firmly that even if someone were to take their life with a sharp weapon, saying, "If you do not break the refuge you have taken, I will kill you," they would still say, "I will never say the Buddha is not the Buddha, the Dhamma is not the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha." The phrase "it gives fulfillment in heaven" is just an illustration. The fruits and benefits of it have already been stated in the explanation of the saraṇagamana.

By the method to be explained, the unwholesome state such as killing (pāṇātipāta) is called "vera" (enmity) because it is a cause of enmity. It is called "veramaṇī" because it forbids that unwholesome state, as if threatening, "Why do you come while I am standing here?" Or, it is called "viramaṇī" because that virati (abstinence) abstains from that unwholesome state. Even though it is so called, by the method of linguistics (nirutti), the letter 'i' is changed to 'e', and it is called "veramaṇī." In the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, it is said that they recite it in two ways: "veramaṇi sikkhāpadaṃ" and "viramaṇi sikkhāpadaṃ." In this pāṇātipātā veramaṇī training rule, only the virati associated with wholesome consciousness is desired, not the virati associated with the fruit (phala), because it is connected with sacrifice. For one who has not undertaken the precepts, abstaining from an object of transgression that has come before them is called "sampatta-virati." The virati arising by the power of undertaking the training rule is called "samādāna-virati." The Noble Path is called a bridge (setu); the virati that is included in that path and acts to destroy unwholesome states by cutting them off completely...
321:
...is called "veramaṇī" because it prevents; or it is called "viramaṇī" because one abstains from unwholesome states by it. When it should be said as "viramaṇī," by the method of linguistics, the letter 'i' is changed to 'e' and it is called "veramaṇī." In the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, it is said: "They recite it in two ways: veramaṇi-sikkhāpadaṃ and viramaṇi-sikkhāpadaṃ." Here, only the virati associated with wholesome consciousness is intended, not that associated with the fruit, because of the context of sacrifice (killing). For one who has not undertaken the precepts, abstinence from an object of transgression that has appeared before them is sampatta-virati. Virati arising by way of undertaking is samādāna-virati. The Noble Path is called a bridge (setu); the virati that, being included in that path, proceeds to kill unwholesome states by way of cutting them off (samuccheda) is called setughāta-virati. In other texts, it is also called samuccheda-virati. Now, to show those types of virati by their nature, the passage beginning with "tattha" is said. "Birth... etc." refers to birth, lineage, family, etc., which are to be pointed out. By the word "etc." (ādi), age, great learning, etc., are to be included. "He avoids" (pariharati) means he abstains by way of non-transgression; sampatta-virati should be understood like that of Cakkana Upāsaka in the island of Sīhaḷa. 

In the passages "I do not kill living beings," etc., by the word "iti" in the sense of "etcetera," or by the word "vā" in the sense of "alternative," the individual meanings such as "I do not take what is not given, I abstain from taking what is not given, I undertake the abstinence," etc., should be included. Therefore, instead of saying "sikkhāpadaṃ" (singular), it is said as "sikkhāpadāni" (plural). It should be connected as "pāṇātipātā veramaṇīṃ." "I undertake" (samādiyāmi) means I take well, with the intention of non-transgression, and it means I take it by making it unbroken, without holes, unspotted, and unspeckled. Samādāna-virati should be understood like that of the upāsaka living on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna. "Associated with the path" (maggasampayuttā) means associated with the path of Right View, etc. Now, among the many decisions in various places regarding states (dhamma), groups, objects, feelings, roots, undertaking, and divisions, the decision by way of object is shown briefly by the passage beginning with "tattha." The "former two" are sampatta-virati and samādāna-virati. "The object such as the life-faculty" refers to "life" (pāṇa) in the ultimate sense; in the conventional sense, it should be said as "beings, etc." Only in this way does it agree with the words of the Khuddaka Nikāya Commentary: "Abstaining from killing and unchastity by taking only beings as the object." Here, by the word "etc." (ādi), objects not given, objects of touch, objects of falsehood, and objects of intoxicants should be included by way of beings and formations (saṅkhāra).
322:
By way of beings and formations, the object of theft, and likewise the object of touch, the object of falsehood, and by way of formations alone, the object of intoxicants—the inclusion of these objects should be understood. The phrase 'They arise taking those objects as their objective support' means that they arise by way of abstaining from the object to be abstained from, known as the volition of transgression, by taking as an objective support the aforementioned object of transgression. The final abstinence is Setughātavirati (abstinence by destruction of the bridge, i.e., supramundane abstinence). Although it takes Nibbāna as its object, it is so called because it accomplishes the function of abstinence in that same way. By this statement that it only takes Nibbāna as its object, it should be understood that among the three teachers' views (ācariyavādas) mentioned in that Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā, two are rejected and only one is accepted.

Some teachers say: 'Sampattavirati (spontaneous abstinence) and Samādānavirati (abstinence by undertaking) arise taking as their object only one's own unwholesome states such as killing (pāṇātipāta) which they abandon.' Others say: 'Samādānavirati arises taking as its object the unwholesome states such as killing, either of oneself or of others, from which one abstains. Sampattavirati, however, arises taking as its object the very objects of those unwholesome states such as killing.' Still others say: 'Both of these abstinences arise taking as their object the object of transgression which is the objective support of those unwholesome states such as killing. Indeed, taking the object of transgression, which is the meaning of the preceding term, as the objective support, one abstains from the object to be abstained from, which is the meaning of the succeeding term.' Among these views, the first view is incorrect. Why? Because one's own unwholesome states such as killing are neither present nor external (bahiddhā). In the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga, it is stated that the five precepts have present objects and external objects. Likewise, the second view is also incorrect. Why? Because it is mixed with the previous view, it is not definitive regarding the taking of others' unwholesome states as objects, and it asserts a distinction between the objects of the two terms. The third view, however, is correct as it is favored by all the Reciters (bhāṇakas). Therefore, it should be understood that only that view is accepted. Thus it is said: 'Among the three teachers' views, two are rejected and only one is accepted.'

Here, a question may be raised: 'If these two abstinences arise taking only the object of transgression, such as the life-faculty, as their objective support, then it would follow that while thinking of one thing, one does another; and one would not know the state that one is abandoning. This would lead to an undesired conclusion.' It is replied: One who acts by way of accomplishing a function is not said to be 'doing one thing while thinking of another' or 'not knowing the state that one abandons.' For example, just as the Noble Path abandons defilements while taking only Nibbāna as its object, so too these two abstinences, having objects such as the life-faculty, abandon immoralities (dussīlya) such as killing. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
323:
## 
'The Noble Person standing on the Path, taking the Deathless (Nibbāna) as the object and abandoning all evils, is the illustration in this matter of abstinence.' (This is found in the Ekatanānanatā-vinicchaya of the Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā).

Now, in order to show the decision regarding the undertaking and the breaking of precepts in brief, the passage beginning with 'Ettha' is stated. One undertakes and receives the precepts collectively by saying, 'I undertake the virtue endowed with five factors,' and so forth. Even when undertaken collectively in this way, the fivefold nature of these precepts is understood by way of their function. Since they are undertaken collectively, if one is broken, all are broken. At that time, the possession of the five factors of virtue is no longer achieved. However, one is bound by kamma only through that specific precept which was transgressed. One receives them individually and separately by saying, 'I undertake the precept of abstinence from taking life,' and so forth. The term 'Veraamaṇīsikkhāpadaṃ' is stated as a compound (samāsa) in the Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā; however, in the Pali texts, it is seen as a separate word 'Veramaṇiṃ' ending with a niggahīta. This statement is made with reference to laypeople. For novices (sāmaṇeras), however, no matter how they undertake them, if one is broken, all are broken because it is equivalent to an offense of defeat (pārājika). Thus, the distinction between collective undertaking and individual undertaking is stated here. But in the Khuddakanikāya-aṭṭhakathā, this distinction is stated: 'For one undertaking them collectively, there is only one abstinence and only one volition, but their fivefold nature is understood by way of function. For one undertaking them individually, there are five abstinences and five volitions.' Regarding the breaking of precepts, it is also said: 'No matter how they undertake them, if one precept of the novices is broken, all are broken. For those precepts stand in the place of pārājika for them. However, one is bound by kamma only by that precept which was transgressed. For laypeople, if one is broken, only that one is broken, because for them, the possession of the five factors of virtue can be achieved again simply by re-undertaking that broken precept.' The view of the Dīgha-reciters (Dīghabhāṇakas) as mentioned before is treated there as the 'Alternative View' (aparevāda).

There is no such thing as the breaking of Setughātavirati (supramundane abstinence), because it is of an unshakable nature (akuppa) due to the total eradication of opposing states. To show this meaning, the passage beginning with 'Bhavantarepi' is stated. There, by the word 'Bhavantarepi' (even in other lives), it makes known the meaning: 'even if one does not know one's own state as a Noble One (ariya).' Even for the sake of life, they would not kill, much less for other reasons. The phrase 'He neither kills a living being nor drinks intoxicants' is an elliptical mention in the middle (majjhepeyyāla), or it is stated by the method of the deer's footprint (migapadavaḷañjananaya). The word 'Surā' is a mere indication. In reality, they do not consume any kind of intoxicant. In the term 'Surāmeraya' and so forth, those two, Surā and Meraya, are the names.
324:
It has been stated (in the Commentary): The word *surā* is merely an indication. In truth, one does not engage in the practice of consuming all ten types—the five kinds of *surā* and the five kinds of *meraya*—which are the basis for negligence through intoxication. It is stated in the *Samyutta Mahāvagga Commentary*: "Only those two (liquor and spirits) are called *majja* (intoxicants), or any other intoxicating substance apart from liquor is also called *majja*." In the *Khuddakapāṭha Commentary* as well, it is stated: "Only those two are called *majja* because of their intoxicating nature; or if there is any other substance that, when drunk, causes one to be intoxicated and negligent, it is called *majja*."

A specific distinction is shown in that same Commentary with the words "If one should drink," and so on. Even if a Noble Disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) does not know they are a Noble One, only milk enters their mouth, not liquor; how much more so for one who knows. *Koñcasakuṇa* refers to cranes. It should be connected thus: "If water mixed with milk is placed in their beaks (they drink only the milk and leave the water)."

If someone should say, "In this example, the comparison and the thing compared cannot be connected because it is accomplished by the nature of the cranes' birth (*yonisiddha*)," the teacher says "*Idaṃ*," and so on. Accomplishment by birth (*yonisiddha*) means being accomplished by the nature of the species, such as the vertical or horizontal length of humans and animals, or cranes conceiving by the sound of thunder, or hens conceiving by the wind. This is the meaning if someone should say so.

Some teachers, stating that there is also a reading "*ceva*," desire the sense of conjunction. Accomplishment by natural law (*dhammatāsiddha*) means being accomplished naturally, such as the virtue of a Bodhisatta’s mother while he is in the womb, or her passing to the celestial realm after his birth. Alternatively, it should be understood as being accomplished by the power of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) through the nature of the Path. This is how one should answer.

Straightening one's view (*diṭṭhijukamma*) is extremely difficult. Therefore, taking refuge (*saraṇagamana*) is a much greater task than undertaking the training rules (*sikkhāpada*); it is not a lesser task. This is the intention. "*Etaṃ*" refers to the training rule. Whether one undertakes that training rule without respect or undertakes the virtues with great respect, it is still a lesser task and requires lesser effort (compared to taking refuge). It means that one need not exert double the effort. Here, virtue (*sīla*) is called *dāna* (giving) because it is the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*). Alternatively, it is called *dāna* because it protects (*dayati*) the entire community of beings without exception.

This is the method not directly mentioned in the Commentary: One who has gone for refuge must respectfully worship the Triple Gem with body, speech, and mind, and must carefully avoid defilement of the refuge. The training rules, however, consist merely of undertaking them and merely abstaining from an object when it appears. Thus, virtue should be understood as a lesser task and requiring lesser effort than taking refuge. However, because it involves laying down the rod by giving the gift of life to all beings, and because it is the foundation for all mundane and supramundane qualities, the great fruit and great benefit of that virtue should also be seen. Desiring to complete that meaning with the Pāli, the teacher says "*Puttañca etaṃ*," and so on. In that passage, they are called *agga* (foremost) because they are known to be excellent. They are called *rattaññū* (of long standing) because they are known by the fact of having many nights (seniority).
325:
Desiring to prove that meaning with the Pāli, he said "*Vuttañhetaṃ*," and so on. There, "*aggāni*" means they are the foremost types because they are known to be noble. They are "*rattaññāni*" because they have been known for a long period of time (many nights). They are "*vaṃsaññāni*" because they are known as the "lineages of the Noble Ones." They are "*porāṇāni*" because they are the possessions of the ancient people of old. They are "*asaṃkiṇṇāni*" because they have not been mixed with or abandoned by the virtuous in any way whatsoever.

This "unmixed" method is the same for those virtuous ones in the present and future as it was in the past; therefore, he said "*asaṃkiṇṇapubbāni*," and so on. The state of not having been abandoned in the past is shown by "*asaṃkiṇṇapubbāni*"; that they are not abandoned in the present by "*na saṅkiyanti*"; and that they will not be abandoned in the future by "*na saṅkiyissanti*." Precisely because they are not abandoned, they are not loathsome (*appaṭikuṭṭhāni*) and not rejected (*na paṭikkhittāni*). This is because wise recluses and brahmins never permit evil states such as violence.

It is said "He gives fearlessness (*abhayaṃ deti*)" because he gives the gift of fearlessness to immeasurable beings. Because he has laid down the rod toward all beings, he gives the state of being without fear to the entire community of beings. Indeed, no fear ever arises from a Noble Disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). "*Avera*" means the absence of enmity. "*Abyāpajjha*" means the absence of suffering. The words "Having given fearlessness to immeasurable beings," and so on, show the benefits. Here, the suffix "*-tvā*" (having) is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), as in the phrase "He cries having remembered his mother."

Since everything characterized by relinquishing is called a "sacrifice" (*yañña*), he said "*Idañca pana*," and so on. Are not the five precepts to be practiced at all times? Even during times when no Buddha has arisen, the wise undertake those five precepts. However, because they are also undertaken by those outside the Buddha's teaching, they are not strictly a basis for liberation (*vimuttāyatana*). Taking refuge, however, is caused by the arising of a Buddha and is strictly a basis for liberation. If that is so, why are the five precepts said to have greater fruit than taking refuge? He answers with "*Kiñcāpi*," and so on. "*Jeṭṭhaka*" means supreme because of the state of having great fruit. By the words "Only by being established in the taking of refuge," he shows that because that virtue is prepared (*abhisaṅkhata*) by the taking of refuge, it has greater fruit than that (refuge alone). Likewise, he shows that virtue not prepared by refuge has little fruit.

"Only of such a nature" means being the opposite of defilement. To answer the inquiry, "Should not only the sacrifices of the first jhāna and so on be taught? Why does he begin the teaching from the arising of a Buddha?", he said "*Tividha... pe... dassetukāmo*." For one established in the fulfillment of the three types of virtue, these sacrifices are of lesser effort but of greater fruit. Therefore, desiring to show that, he begins the teaching from the arising of a Buddha. Thus he said "*Tattha*," and so on.
326:
The qualities mentioned below refer to those such as taking refuge (saraṇagamana), perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā), and guarding the doors of the senses (indriyesu guttadvāratā), which were stated below starting with 'Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.' The phrase should be construed as 'one does not become weary in producing the first jhāna.' 'Tāni' refers to the first jhāna and so forth. Knowing that in the Pāḷi text, the description of the jhānas is given specifically in terms of the superior ones, it is said 'one aeon, eight aeons,' and so forth. Here, the meaning should be taken in terms of great aeons (mahakappa). However, the inferior first jhāna gives a lifespan of one-third of an incalculable aeon (asaṅkheyyakappa). The medium first jhāna gives a lifespan of half an incalculable aeon. The inferior second jhāna gives two aeons, the medium second jhāna gives four aeons, and so the meaning should be understood. Alternatively, in this context, only the superior jhānas are intended because the teaching primarily aims to show the state of having great fruit. Therefore, it should be understood that only the superior jhānas are described by 'the first jhāna for one aeon,' and so forth.

'Tadeva' refers to the fourth jhāna itself. This is because the teaching comes by way of the fourfold method. If so, one might ask why it becomes a formless attainment (āruppa); thus it is said, 'it is developed by the power of attainments such as the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana).' Because it is so developed, the fourth jhāna itself becomes a formless attainment and gives a lifespan of twenty thousand aeons and so forth. This is the teacher's opinion. Alternatively, 'tadeva' refers to the fourth jhāna which is called formless (āruppa). If asked why that formless fourth jhāna gives a lifespan of twenty thousand aeons and so forth, it is said, 'because it is developed by the power of attainments such as the sphere of infinite space.' Because it is so developed, it gives such a lifespan. Another method: if 'tadeva' is said, it might be understood as only the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara); to prevent that meaning, it is said, 'it is developed by the power of attainments such as the sphere of infinite space.' Because it is so developed, it means that only the formless jhāna, which is called the fourth jhāna due to the equality of factors, is intended.

Vipassanā, which proceeds by way of thoroughly dispelling opposing states such as the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) and which well-assembles the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) that occur in the preliminary stage of the path, brings much joy (pīti) and happiness (somanassa) to the person practicing insight. Therefore, it is said, 'Because there is no happiness equal to the happiness of insight, it is of great fruit.' As the King of Dhamma, the Buddha, said in the Dhammapada:

'Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
one attains joy and gladness;
that is the Deathless for those who know it.'
327:
However, because this teaching is set forth in this sequence by way of a person producing these insight-knowledges, it is said, 'established in insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa),' making each lower knowledge the basis for each higher knowledge. The creation of a form similar to oneself is a specific function of the supernormal power of the mind-made body (manomayiddhi), not shared with other supernormal powers; thus it is said, 'one's own... is of great fruit.'
