The creation of various forms such as elephants and horses is called transformation (vikubbana), because one is able to show that transformation. 'Desired place' refers to the part of the aggregates desired in previous births. Since the happiness of the path is completed only by the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), it is said, 'exceedingly... is of great fruit.' 'Samāpento' means finishing or concluding.

## Commentary on the Exposition of Kūṭadanta’s Attainment of the Status of a Lay Follower, etc.

354-8. The words 'Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent!' and so forth are words of appreciation for the teaching, while 'I go to the Blessed One...' and so forth are words for taking refuge. To show the connection between both, it is said, 'By the teaching...' and so forth. 'Tanu' (slender/diminished) means little, due to the increase of bodily and mental happiness. 'All those living beings' refers to all those living beings mentioned as 'seven hundred bulls,' and so forth. 'That occurrence' refers to the manner of releasing those living beings. 'Agitation' (ākulabhāva) refers to the state of mental agitation in the Brahmin Kūṭadanta, who, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, established compassion for living beings and thought, 'How is it that I have caused so many living beings to be bound for the purpose of slaughter?' It should be construed that because there was such agitation, the teaching was not [immediately] given. There is also a variant reading 'udapādi' (arose). 'Having heard' means having heard the words reported as 'Sir, those living beings have been released.' 'Mental wandering' (cittacāra) is the occurrence of the mind. The five terms 'ready mind, soft mind, mind free from hindrances, uplifted mind, and confident mind' are intended by the phrase 'ready mind and so forth.'

In that context, by the power of the progressive discourse (anupubbī-kathā) taught as 'talk on giving, talk on virtue,' and so forth: by the departure of sensual desire (kāmacchanda), there is a ready mind, a healthy mind; by the departure of ill-will (byāpāda), there is a soft mind, a non-harsh mind through the power of loving-kindness; by the departure of restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), there is a mind free from hindrances because of the absence of distraction, and thus a mind unstained by them; by the departure of sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), there is an uplifted mind through the power of exertion, an unstained mind; by the departure of doubt (vicikicchā), there is a confident mind, an unclouded mind, due to the state of not being unreleased from the right practice. Therefore, it is said, 'It is said with reference to the hindrances being suppressed by the power of the progressive discourse.' Here, the terms not analyzed in terms of meaning are easily understood.

Thus, the commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta is finished in this Ṭīkā (sub-commentary) of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, which is an explanation of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, showing the very subtle and profound meaning and producing pure wisdom in the manner stated.
328:
Thus, in the sub-commentary named Sādhuvilāsinī, which clarifies the hidden meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī—which in turn illustrates the meanings that are extremely subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend, and generates the swift power of pure and extensive wisdom—the explanation of the hidden meanings of the Kūṭadanta Sutta is concluded.

## The Explanation of the Kūṭadanta Sutta is Finished.

Having explained the Kūṭadanta Sutta in the manner stated above, the commentator now says, "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... Vesāliyaṃ" (Thus have I heard... at Vesālī) in order to clearly show that it is now the turn to explain the Mahāli Sutta in sequence, or alternatively, to show that the Mahāli Sutta is the one recited in the Council immediately following the Kūṭadanta Sutta.

Regarding the phrase "because of reaching expansion repeatedly," the summary is as follows: The chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī gave birth to two children, a boy and a girl, from a single lump of flesh. These two children were married to each other and, through the power of offspring, gave birth to two children at a time for sixteen consecutive times. Subsequently, as those children grew up along with their retinues, the city was expanded three times, each by one gāvuta, because the parks, gardens, dwellings, and retinues were insufficient. Because that city reached expansion through three layers of surrounding walls repeatedly, it came to be called "Vesālī" alone.
329:
## 6. Mahālisutta-vaṇṇanā
## Brāhmaṇadūtavatthu-vaṇṇanā
Thus, having explained the Kūṭadanta Sutta, the commentator now speaks the Mahāli Sutta starting with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... pe... Vesāliyaṃ" to show that the opportunity to explain it in sequence has arrived, or alternatively, to show that the Mahāli Sutta is the sutta recited in the Council immediately after the Kūṭadanta Sutta.

Regarding the phrase "punappunaṃ visālabhāvūpagamanato" (because of repeatedly reaching a state of extensiveness), the summary is this: Two children, a daughter and a son, were born as a lump of flesh to the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Through their marriage to each other, they gave birth to pairs of children sixteen times. Later, as those children grew up along with their retinues, the space in the parks, gardens, and residences became insufficient to accommodate them and their retinues. Therefore, the city was expanded three times, each time by a distance of one gāvuta. Thus, because the city reached a state of extensiveness through these repeated three-layered wall enclosures, it came to be called "Vesālī." Therefore, the teacher said, "In the city named Vesālī because of repeatedly reaching a state of extensiveness." Detailed accounts regarding this city of Vesālī should be taken from the commentaries on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta and the Ratana Sutta.

"Outside the city" means outside the city limits, not inside the city like Ambapālī's mango grove. "Self-grown" (sayāñjāta) means a forest that grew naturally without being planted by humans. "Because of its greatness" refers to the vastness of the trees and shrubs, as well as the area where it stands. For this reason, the teacher said, "Being continuous with the Himālaya."

According to the view of the masters of the Vinaya as stated in the Vinaya Commentary: "There, the forest named Mahāvana is a naturally grown, unplanted, large forest with defined boundaries. However, the Mahāvana near Kapilavatthu is continuous with the Himālaya, without boundaries, and extends to the Great Ocean; this [Vesālī Mahāvana] is not of that nature." This statement is also the common view of the masters of the Majjhima Nikāya and the Saṃyutta Nikāya. It is stated thus in the Majjhima Commentary and the Saṃyutta Commentary. In this commentary [on the Dīgha Nikāya], it should be understood that it is stated according to the view of the masters of the Dīgha Nikāya. If in some versions the reading "ahutွာ" (not being) is found, then [the views of all Nikāya masters would be the same].

In brief, because it was constructed with the feature of a hall with a peaked roof (kūṭāgāra), covered in a circular manner like Mount Haṃsa and adorned with a pinnacle, the mansion itself is called "Kūṭāgārasālā." By extension of this name, the entire monastery (saṅghārāma) is also called "Kūṭāgārasālā." Alternatively, it is stated in the Vinaya Commentary: In the monastery established depending on the Mahāvana forest, the Kūṭāgārasālā hall—which contains a mansion with a pinnacle inside, is covered in a circular manner like Mount Haṃsa, and is complete in all aspects—should be known as the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) of the Blessed One.
330:
The views of all the Elders who are reciters of the Nikāyas should be the same. To summarize the 'Kūṭāgārasālā' (Gabled Hall), it is a hall with a peaked roof constructed in the manner of a 'swan-round' (hamsa-vaṭṭaka) design, which is described as a circular swan-like shape. Because it was built in that specific way, the mansion (pāsāda) itself is called the 'Kūṭāgārasālā'. By that designation, it refers to the entire Saṅghārāma (monastery). However, in the Vinaya Commentary, it is stated: 'The Kūṭāgārasālā should be understood as the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) of the Blessed Buddha, which was built within the monastery situated near the Mahāvana forest, featuring a peaked roof and constructed with a swan-round covering, complete in every aspect.'

Those born in the Kosala region, or those residing there, are called 'Kosalaka'. Similarly, they are called 'Māgadhaka'. Words denoting a region are generally in the masculine plural. An action is called 'Karaṇīya' (duty/obligation) because a person would suffer great loss by not performing it; thus, it is worthy of being done. Therefore, the teacher said, 'by an act that must certainly be performed.' If there is no coincidence of causes, it is acceptable not to perform it; therefore, it is meant that when the causes coincide, it is called a 'kicca' (task) because it must be done.

Regarding the diverse perceptions (nānatta-saññā) that are worthy of arising in the Buddhas, it is said 'due to wandering among diverse objects,' which means due to the occurrence of diverse objects. Only that which is possible is prohibited, not that which is impossible. 'Paṭikkamma' means withdrawing (from the object) and not allowing the mind to arise in such a manner. 'Sallīna' means being absorbed in a single object through meditative attainment (jhāna-samāpatti). The word 'Nilīna' is a synonym for that same 'Sallīna'. Therefore, it is said 'the state of being alone,' and so on. Even if there is a retinue, because one is like a single person at that time, it is called 'ekībhāva' (the state of being alone); one reaches that state of being alone. With reference to the place where the Venerable Nāgita was, it is said 'from that place.'

## Explanation of the Story of Oṭṭhaddha Licchavī
'Addhoṭṭhatāya' means because of having half a lip. It is heard that because the upper lip of that Mahāli Licchavī was so small and short, it appeared as if it had been split crosswise and half of it removed; it could not cover the four front teeth and the two canine teeth. Therefore, people called him 'Oṭṭhaddha' (Hare-lipped). Some teachers, however, speculate on the Pali text using the word 'Adho' and interpret it as 'Oṭṭhādho' because the lower lip was hanging down. That is improper because such a reading is not found and it was not explained by the Sub-commentary teacher. This Licchavī king was a donor who habitually observed the Uposatha...
331:
That Licchavī king was a master of giving, a person of faith who believed in the Triple Gem and the law of kamma and its results, and one who greatly cherished the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Therefore, the teacher mentioned 'purebhatta' (before the meal) and so on. In accordance with the method found in the Khandhaka of the Mahāvagga and the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, it is said: 'having colors such as blue, yellow... resembling the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.'

This city of Vesālī, during the time of the Blessed One, was prosperous and had reached a state of great abundance. In that city, there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven (7,707) kings. Likewise, there were the same number of viceroys, generals, treasurers, and so forth. Mansions, gabled houses, monasteries, and lotus ponds were also in that same number. It was a city filled with many people, crowded with various inhabitants, and where almsfood was easily obtainable. Therefore, it is said 'together with a great assembly of Licchavīs.'

Regarding the origin of that clan, whatever milk entered the stomachs of the children born from the lump of flesh (maṃsapesi) could be clearly seen from the outside as if it were in a jewel vessel. Just as the skin of the Buddha-to-be's mother's abdomen was extremely clear while the Bodhisatta was dwelling in her womb in his final birth, the skin of those children's abdomens was also extremely clear, so they were 'Nicchavī' (as if having no skin). Others, however, say: 'Because their skin was joined together as if sewn, they were Līnacchavī.' Thus, they were known as 'Licchavī' either because of being 'Nicchavī' or 'Līnacchavī'. Here, the formation of the word should be understood according to the method of Nirutti (etymology). All those born in that royal lineage were also called 'Licchavī'. Therefore, in the phrase 'Licchaviparisāya', it means the assembly of Licchavī kings or the assembly belonging to the Licchavī lineage. He is called 'Mahāli' because he acquires (lāti) great (mahantaṃ) fame and retinue (yasaṃ), similar to the name 'Bhaddāli'. 'Mūlanāma' (original name) refers to the name given by the parents.

One who is 'exerted in the Dispensation' means one who repeatedly practices Samatha and Vipassanā meditation. Although the Blessed One's conduct is like that of a lion in all matters, when there is a large assembly, there is a special quality in the Dhamma teaching delivered in accordance with the inclinations of that assembly; thus it was said, 'He will preach the Dhamma with great effort.'

After saying 'one who is intimate,' the phrase 'ayañhi' and so on was said to clarify his state of intimacy. 'Thūlasarīro' means one who has a stout body. Since the Venerable Nāgita was an Arahant, it should not be said that 'he had not yet abandoned laziness'; however, with reference to the residual impressions (vāsanā), it was said as if 'he had not yet slightly abandoned it.' This is because disciples (sāvakas), unlike the Buddhas, cannot abandon defilements along with their residual impressions (vāsanā). With reference to the aforementioned mansion itself, it was called 'Kūṭāgāramahāgeha'. 'Pācīnamukhā' means facing towards the East.
332:
The display of the miraculous powers (pāṭihāriya) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, occurs without conflicting with the beings who are to be tamed; with this meaning, the words beginning with “Atha kho” are spoken. Indeed, at the time of departing from the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), the six-colored Buddha-rays emerged in clusters and pairs, being exceptionally brilliant. By these rays, people recognized His departure from the monastery as if it were being announced, “The Blessed One is departing.” Therefore, it is said, “saṃsūcitanikkhamano” (one whose departure is well-indicated).

The day immediately preceding the day called “ajja” (today) is called “purima” (the previous day). Similarly, the day before yesterday is called “purimatara” (the more previous day) because it is excessively previous. Thus, in these two days, the status of being previous and more previous is determined respectively. Even so, in this context, whatever day is called “purimatara,” any day on this side (internal) of it is called “purima,” and any day on that side (external) of it is called “purimatara”; to show this, the words beginning with “tato paṭṭhāya” are spoken. The status of being previous and more previous is established in relation to one another, just like the status of this shore and that shore, or like directions and intermediate directions. “Mūladivasato” means from the very first day. The word “agge” is a locative case used in the sense of the accusative case, or it is the substitution of “e” for the accusative case; this is shown by the word “agga,” meaning “the beginning.” That beginning here refers only to the other past limit; thus it is said, “parakoṭiṃ katvā.” The word “yaṃ” is an indeclinable (nipāta) in the sense of delimitation, and because of its association with “yaṃ,” the word “viharāmi” is in the present tense, but its meaning should be understood in the past tense; to show this, it is said, “yāva vihāsiṃ.” “Tassa” means of that day. In the first alternative, the word “viharāmi” should first be directly connected with the word “yadamagge,” and then the expression of duration “naciraṃ tīṇi vassāni” should be applied. In the second alternative, however, it should be connected with the words “naciraṃ tīṇi vassāni” in a convoluted (oblique) manner. “Naciraṃ” is an adverb (bhāvanapuṃsaka) or an accusative of duration (accantasaṃyoga). To specify that period by measure, it says “tīṇi vassāni.” Therefore, it is said, “naciraṃ vihāsiṃ tīṇiyeva vassāni” (I lived for a short time, only three years).

“Ayaṃ” refers to this bhikkhu Sunakkhatta. “Piyajātikāni” means objects that are desirable by nature. “Sātajātikāni” means objects that are pleasurable by nature. Because of its similarity to a sweet taste, a delightful object is called “madhura” (sweet/agreeable). They are called “kāmūpasaṃhitāni” because they are connected with sensual desire (kile-sakāma) that takes them as objects; they are objects desired by sensual lust. Therefore, it is said, “kāmassādayuttāni” (associated with sensual gratification). It means they are associated with the gratification called sensual desire that grasps the object, or they are suitable for sensual gratification. “Sarīrasaṇṭhāne” means in the physical form of the body (in the body). Here, the word “saṇṭhāna” is in the locative case in the sense of a support (ādhāra). Therefore, by the word “saddena,” it means by the sound that arises depending on that body...
333:
...by the sound. Furthermore, without depending on the rest of the text, it should be connected only with the word “bhavitabba.” “Madhurena” means with what is desirable and pleasurable. “Kaṇṇasakkhaliyaṃ” means in the outer ear (ear-flap).

“Ettāvatā” means merely by not explaining the preliminary practice (parikamma) which is the cause for attaining the divine ear-element (dibba-sota-ñāṇa). Thinking, “Though he knows it himself, he does not tell me; what is the use of staying in this Buddha’s dispensation?” he became angry and bound himself with ill-will toward the Blessed One, and along with that anger, his jhānas and supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) declined. “Cintesi” means he pondered and reflected, “Why indeed did he not tell me that preliminary practice?” and thought with unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). “Anukkamena” means that according to the method found in the Pāthika Sutta and the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, by continually thinking, speaking, and doing what is improper, and because of his bound ill-will toward the Blessed One, he found no footing in the Sasana, returned to the lay life (gihibhāvaṃ patvā), and spoke of that matter.

## Description of Concentration Developed on One Side

366-371. The word “ekaṃsāya” is in the dative case in the sense of purpose; it means for the sake of one portion. Here, the word “aṃsa” is a synonym for “koṭṭhāsa” (part/portion). That “aṃsa” should be understood through the context (adhikāra) by the power of seeing divine forms and hearing divine sounds; thus it is said, “ekakoṭṭhāsāya,” etc. The word “vā” here is used in the sense of an alternative (vikappa), because only one portion is intended. “Anudisāya” means in the four intermediate directions such as the southeast, etc. “Ubhayakoṭṭhāsāya” means for the purpose of seeing divine forms and for the purpose of hearing divine sounds. “Bhāvito” means developed in such a way that the divine-eye knowledge (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) and the divine-ear knowledge (dibba-sota-ñāṇa) are well-attained.

There is nothing to be said regarding the accomplishment of these supernormal knowledges through separate preliminary practices; even when they are accomplished together, the task is completed only sequentially. This is because it is impossible for the task to be completed simultaneously in one go. Indeed, in the Pali, the statement “for the seeing of divine forms and for the hearing of divine sounds” is merely to show that one [concentration] is capable of both, not to show the possibility of simultaneous completion of the task. By the words “ekaṃsabhāvito samādhi hetu,” it is shown that because Sunakkhatta had performed the preliminary practice only for the divine-eye knowledge, he did not hear divine sounds even though they were present.

Thinking that the divine-ear knowledge is superior to the divine-eye knowledge, Mahāli asked about this matter. Therefore, the teacher said, “Idaṃ dibbasotena... pe... manye.” “Apaṇṇakaṃ” means unerring or faultless. Because concentration itself is that which should be developed...
334:
Development of concentration (Samādhibhāvanā). Thinking that "the divine ear knowledge is supreme," Mahāli included the divine eye knowledge along with the divine ear knowledge and asked with a plural expression, "Venerable Sir, these..." and so on. To show this, it is said, "of the two types of developed concentration." These developments of concentration are outside the Dispensation (Sāsana) because they do not lead to liberation from the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Indeed, these developments of concentration are also achieved by those outside this Dispensation (titthiyas). They are not internal (to the Sāsana) because they were not taught by the Blessed One as the Sāmukkaṃsika teaching (the exalted teaching of the Noble Truths discovered by his own self-evolved knowledge). Indeed, these developments of concentration are not Sāmukkaṃsika teachings like the Truths. 'Yadatthaṃ' means for the benefit of those Noble Fruits; although there is no distinction, this is a statement of distinction, or it means for the benefit of that which is a qualifier (Noble Fruit). 'Te' refers to the Noble Fruits. Currently, there is also a reading as 'taṃ'. Indeed, those Noble Fruits should be realized. By the passage, "Mahāli, there are other things... for the sake of realizing which the monks lead the holy life under me," the things to be realized are taught in this context.

## Commentary on the Four Noble Fruits (Catu-ariyaphala-vaṇṇanā)

'Saṃyojenti' means they bind. 'Tasmā' means because they connect beings to the danger of suffering in the round of rebirth, they are called fetters; therefore, it is so. In some versions, there is a reading "vaṭṭadukkhamaye rathe," but that is not an ancient reading because the Teacher did not comment on it in that way. One has entered the stream of the Noble Path, not the stream of faith and so on. Indeed, it is said, "Monks, 'stream' (sota) is a designation for the Noble Path." 'Āpanno' means having reached at the beginning, because the prefix 'ā' functions in the sense of beginning an action. However, this statement is made by way of one established in the Fruit. The word 'āpanno' is a past tense term; however, at the moment of the Path, one is said to be entering the stream of the Noble Path. For that very reason, it is taught in the Dakkhiṇavibhaṅga Sutta: "He gives a gift to a Stream-enterer; he gives a gift to one practicing for the realization of the Fruit of Stream-entry." 'Apatanadhammo' means having the nature of not falling (into lower realms). 'Dhammaniyāmena' means by the fixed law of the higher Paths. Alternatively, being fixed by the nature of not being reborn beyond the seventh existence at the minimum is a method outside the commentary (aṭṭhakathā-muttaka-naya). It means that for such a person, there is a destination (gati). 'Anena' is a word showing the third bahubbīhi compound again; here, the word 'vā' is indicated as being elided.

Thinness (tanutta) means the slowness and sparseness of occurrence; this is stated by "tanuttā" and so on. 'Karahaci' is merely an indeclinable (nipāta), or a synonym for 'kadāci'. As in the passages "thinking that a month of the summer remains, he should seek a rains-cloth within the ora (seven months)," the word 'ora' does not mean 'excess'; thus it says "heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ," meaning the things that are beneficial as causes for the lower realm of the sense-sphere (kāmabhava).
335:
"Suddhāvāsabhūmiyaṃ" (in the Pure Abodes)—this statement shows the place of rebirth of those monks who have abandoned the lower fetters. 'Opapātika' means one who is reborn spontaneously, one who excels in spontaneous rebirth. Therefore, the Teacher said, "This is a statement excluding the remaining modes of birth." 'Parinibbānadhammo' means one whose nature is to attain final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder. It is called 'vimutti' (liberation) because it is liberated from defilements. Since the mind itself is liberated from defilements, it is called 'cetovimutti' (liberation of mind) in such terms as "cittavisuddhi" (purification of mind). Here, concentration is taken by using 'mind' as the head, as in the verses: "A wise man, established in virtue, developing the mind (concentration) and wisdom..." The same method should be understood for the term 'paññāvimutti' (liberation by wisdom). Therefore, the Teacher said, "The wisdom of the fruition of Arahantship itself is liberation by wisdom." 'Sāmaṃ' means by oneself, without depending on others. By the word "abhijānitvā," the elision of the letter 'ya' caused by the suffix 'tvā' etc. is shown. By the word "abhiññāya," it should be understood that the elision of the letter 'ya' caused by the 'nā' case ending is shown. The word 'sacchi' is a particle in the sense of 'witnessing' (direct experience). Realization (witnessing) means taking the object in its true form, letting go of thinking based on hearsay, logic, and so on.

## Ariyaaṭṭhaṅgikamaggavaṇṇanā

374-5. 'Uppatitvā' means having flown up through the sky. A Noble Disciple practices to reach Nibbāna and the Noble Fruition through this path, so it is called 'paṭipadā' (the way). Since that practice is only the preliminary part of that path, the Noble Path is taught here by the name 'pubbabhāga-paṭipadā' (preliminary practice). It has five factors by way of the 'ātata' drum, 'vitata' drum, etc., and it has eight factors by way of the regions established in the cardinal and intermediate directions. There is no other path called 'eightfold' that is separate from the eight factors. Therefore, the Teacher said, "It is only the eight factors," and so on. Indeed, there is no such thing as a whole that is separate from its parts. Therefore, the Teacher said that instead of making an 'Aññapadattha-samāsa' (Bahubbīhi compound) as "the path which has eight factors," the word should be formed by way of a 'Samāsagabbha-taddhita' (a derivative containing a compound) as "the eight factors are the 'aṭṭhaṅga'; these factors are in this path, thus it is 'aṭṭhaṅgika'." Here, the intention should be considered. If an 'Aññapadattha-samāsa' is made, it is not possible to distinguish between the 'eight factors' and the 'eightfold path' even by interchanging them, because in a sentence, the meaning of both words becomes primary and the meaning is reached through the numerical limitation of eight. However, if a 'Samāsagabbha-taddhita' is made, it is possible to distinguish them by interchanging them, because the meaning is reached through the numerical limitation of eight without the meaning of the subsequent word being primary in the compound. Indeed, a compound has the characteristic of having a single unified meaning. In the Commentary on the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, the Teacher said: "Because..."
336:
The designation 'Path' (Magga) applies to the collection of path-factors. The whole is also endowed with its constituent parts. Therefore, it is called 'Eightfold' (Aṭṭhaṅgika) because it possesses eight factors which are its own parts. Between these two methods, in the first method, the 'eightfoldness' of the factors is stated by way of the possessor of factors (aṅgī). In the second method, however, the 'eightfoldness' of the possessor of factors is stated by way of the factors (aṅga). This is the distinction between these two methods.

Now, wishing to show the analysis of the Eightfold Path by way of characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (kicca), moment (khaṇa), object (ārammaṇa), variety, and sequence, he said 'Tattha' and so forth. The characteristic of Right Seeing (Sammādassana-lakkhaṇā) is the nature of seeing the four Noble Truths (Ariyasacca) directly and correctly as they really are. The characteristic of Right Directing (Sammā-abhiniropana-lakkhaṇā) is the nature of correctly directing the mind towards the object of Nibbāna. The characteristic of Right Embracing (Sammā-pariggahaṇa-lakkhaṇā) means that speech endowed with four factors supports people; therefore, Right Speech (Sammāvācā), which has the nature of abstinence (virati) from the opposite of those four factors, has the function of embracing people and associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) by abandoning wrong speech (micchāvācā) that causes division. Thus, it has the nature of correctly embracing. The characteristic of Right Originating (Sammā-samuṭṭhāpana-lakkhaṇā) is as follows: just as the work of tailoring a robe etc. brings about a task to be done, or as the action (kammanta) called volition (cetanā) which completes various activities brings about movements such as those of the hands and feet; similarly, by abandoning wrong action (micchākammanta) which originates faulty activities, Right Action (Sammākammanta) has the function of originating blameless actions. It occurs only while originating associated states. Therefore, it has the nature of correctly originating. The characteristic of Right Purifying (Sammā-vodāpana-lakkhaṇā) is the nature of correctly purifying by abandoning wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) which is the cause of defilement for body, speech, and the continuum of aggregates (khandha-santāna). The characteristic of Right Upholding (Sammā-paggaha-lakkhaṇā) is the nature of correctly upholding the mind associated with it, not allowing it to fall into the side of defilement. The characteristic of Right Establishing (Sammā-upaṭṭhāna-lakkhaṇā) is the nature of correctly appearing in that object with the characteristic of the state of steadfastness (tādi-bhāva). The characteristic of Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhāna-lakkhaṇā) is the nature of correctly placing the mind on the object by destroying distraction (vikkhepa).

Because they exist in the same single arising of consciousness (cittuppāda), ignorance (avijjā) and others which exist in the same arising of consciousness as wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) are called its own opposing defilements other than wrong view. 'Passatī' (he sees) means he manifests; he penetrates through the penetration of function. Therefore, he said 'Tappati... pe... asammohato'. This is the demonstration of the manner of seeing of that Right View. Indeed, by that factor called Right View, reflection occurs in that Path. The two preceding functions are common to all path-factors; thus he said 'Sammāsaṅkappādayopi' and so forth. By the word 'Tatheva', he includes the meaning 'together with its own opposing defilements'.
337:
'In the preliminary stage' (pubbabhāge) means at the moment of access (upacāra). Because there are moments of consciousness occurring many times by the power of access-development (upacāra-bhāvanā), there are multiple moments. Because they have characteristics such as impermanence (anicca) as their object, there are multiple objects. Because the Path (Magga) occurs in a single moment of consciousness, it has a single moment. Because it takes Nibbāna as its object, it has a single object. 'By way of function' (kiccato) refers to the function performed by the knowledges that understand the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) etc. in the preliminary stage of the Path, which arises excellently in this arising of Path-consciousness; or, it refers to the function of manifesting the Truth of Suffering etc. by this Path-knowledge itself. It receives four names because of the completion of the function to be performed regarding the four Truths. It receives three names because of the completion of the abandonment of sensual intention (kāma-saṅkappa) and so forth. In the Vibhaṅga of Precepts (Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga), it is said: 'Abstinence-volitions (virati-cetanā) and all associated states are precepts.' In that Vibhaṅga, by the power of the predominant abstinence-volitions, it is said: 'There are abstinences and there are volitions.' It should be applied such that at the time of abstaining from false speech etc., they are abstinences, and at the time of speaking well-spoken words etc., they are volitions. Since volitions are not path-factors, he said: 'At the path-moment (maggakkhaṇa), however, there are only abstinences.' Just as a single Path-knowledge exists as the knowledge of the Truth of Suffering etc., and just as a single abstinence exists as the abstinence from false speech etc., it should be understood that this was said because it is impossible for a single volition to accomplish the three functions of Right Speech etc., and thus the state of Right Speech etc. cannot be established; and if that is not established, the state of being the three path-factors cannot be established. By this, he shows both the two-fold variety and the non-differentiation of those states. 'By the power of Right Exertions and Foundations of Mindfulness' means by the power of the state of the four Right Exertions and the four Foundations of Mindfulness.

Although Right Concentration (Sammāsamādhi) is analyzed by way of the four Jhanas through the power of initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and equanimity (upekkhā), which have the functions of directing towards the object, repeated examination of the object, being pleased, increasing happiness, and being peaceful, which are helpful to concentration; yet, just as Right Effort (Sammāvāyāma) accomplishes the four functions of effort such as preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and just as Mindfulness (Sati) accomplishes the four functions of mindfulness that abandon the perception of beauty (subha) etc. in the body etc. which are actually foul (asubha), painful (dukkha), impermanent (anicca), and non-self (anatta); similarly, a single concentration cannot accomplish the concentration-function of the group of four Jhanas. Therefore, even in the preliminary stage, the first Jhana concentration is only the first Jhana concentration. Likewise, at the path-moment and in the preliminary stage, the second Jhana concentration is only the second Jhana concentration. Likewise, at the path-moment and in the preliminary stage, the third Jhana concentration is only the third Jhana concentration. Likewise, at the path-moment and in the preliminary stage, the fourth Jhana concentration is only the fourth Jhana concentration. Therefore, he said: 'Both in the preliminary stage and at the path-moment, it is only Right Concentration.'

'Therefore' means that because it is the light of wisdom, it destroys the darkness of ignorance, and because it is the weapon of wisdom, it slays the thieves of defilements; thus it should be applied accordingly. Because in this beginningless Saṃsāra, this yogi has never before uprooted...
338:
There is the group of defilements and the Noble Path that eradicates that group of defilements. In this Noble Path, this Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi) is the forerunner and is highly beneficial because it occurs by way of full understanding (pariññā-abhisamaya) and so forth. Therefore, to show that very quality of being highly beneficial as a cause, it is said, "Because it is highly beneficial to the yogi." "Tassa" refers to Right View.

Having said "It is highly beneficial," and wishing to clarify that benefit through an analogy, he said "Just as," and so forth. This coin is a counterfeit because it is made of a mixture of copper, bronze, and so on. A skilled money-changer knows it because of rejecting that counterfeit and because of its great essence. In this way, just as the hand is another instrument that greatly assists the money-changer in distinguishing coins after seeing them with the eye to complete the task, so too, vitakka (thought) is another factor that greatly assists the yogi in distinguishing phenomena after observing them with wisdom, acting as a forerunner. This is because one penetrates and knows that phenomenon with wisdom only after thinking about it with vitakka. Therefore, the meaning is that Right Intention (Sammā-saṅkappa) is of great benefit to Right View.

In the second analogy: In this way, just as a carpenter uses a hatchet to plane a piece of timber given to him by another, turning it over and over, and uses it in tasks such as building a house, so too, the yogi, after defining phenomena as they really are by thinking about them through their characteristics and so forth with vitakka, applies them to tasks such as full understanding (pariññā-abhisamaya). This should be so connected.

Vitakka, which assists in the breaking of speech (vocalization), also assists Right Speech (Sammā-vācā), which performs the functions of restraining from blameworthy speech and engaging in blameless speech. Thus, he said, "That [vitakka]," and so forth. By saying "As it was said," and so forth, he shows the passage from the Cūḷavedalla Sutta (M. Ni. 1.464) spoken by the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā to the householder Visākha as evidence. "Bhindati" means he utters.

Speech that regulates vocalization assists Right Action (Sammā-kammanta), which regulates bodily actions. To make this meaning clear in the world, he said "Because," and so forth. "The two types of good conduct" are good conduct of body and good conduct of speech. "Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla" (morality with livelihood as the eighth) is the morality of the beginning of the holy life (ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla) taught by making Right Livelihood the eighth along with the four types of good conduct of speech and three types of good conduct of body. Referring to that Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla, it was said: "Previously, his bodily actions, vocal actions, and livelihood are very pure."

"Immediately after those two" means immediately after Right Speech and Right Action, which abandon the two types of misconduct and are the causes for the fulfillment of the two types of good conduct. "By sleeping and being negligent" means by sleeping without concern and by being negligent. "This effort" refers to the four types of Right Effort (Sammappadhāna-vīriya). "In the body and so forth" means in the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. Equanimity of the faculties and so forth are beneficial to concentration (samādhi).
339:
Factors that are the opposite of that [concentration] are not beneficial. "Gati" refers to outcomes, or the nature of functions and so forth. "Samanvesitvā" means investigating and reflecting. Here, the suffix '-tvā' is used in the sense of cause (hetu).

## Commentary on the Story of the Two Renunciants (Dvepabbajita-vatthu-vaṇṇanā)

376-7. To the question "Why was [this sutta] begun?"—inquiring about the reason for the connection—he said "This, it is said," and so forth to answer that question. By saying this, he shows that this subsequent teaching proceeded by the power of the disposition (ajjhāsaya) and connection of King Mahāli. "Tena" means because of having such a view. "Assa" refers to the Licchavī king. "Desanāyaṃ" refers to the teaching as it was taught, which is subtle, delicate, and connected with emptiness (suññatā). "Nādhimuccati" means he does not believe or have confidence.

"Tantidhammaṃ nāma kathento" means that although the Dhamma is preached for the sake of certain people, even if they have not yet attained the penetration of the Path, he preaches by making it the scriptural tradition (Tantidhamma), which is the lineage or the Pariyatti (scriptural study) in the Sasana. By preaching thus, he shows that those people had not yet attained the penetration of the Path at that time. "Evarူpassa" refers to the Teacher (the Buddha) who has such a manifest Dhamma-kāya because of being a Perfectly Enlightened One and having an unerring teaching.

"Assa" is a question: Is it appropriate for a son of good family, whose mind is concentrated through the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth, to hold the view of annihilation (uccheda) and so forth, such as "that soul is the body"? Since they were not yet freed from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) merely by the attainment of jhāna in terms of their view, when those two wanderers replied, "It is appropriate for him to hold such a view," the meaning should be taken that the Buddha rejected that annihilationism or eternalism by saying, "I do not say..." and so forth, asserting that it is indeed inappropriate to hold such a view even for one who has attained jhāna.

"Etaṃ" refers to the first jhāna and so forth. "Evaṃ" is according to the method already mentioned. "Atha ca pana" means because of knowing and seeing in this way. Although the view of one practicing insight (vipassanā) and so forth is shown in the Pali text, he said, "Having shown the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) above," to show that the teaching was concluded with the pinnacle of Arahantship. Those two renunciants, starting from the stage of practicing insight, said, "It is not fitting for him to say that."

"Imassa" refers to the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava/arahant). Although it is not explicitly stated in the Pali text that "they were delighted," their delight should be understood from their answer, "It is not fitting," and so forth; thus he said, "Te mama," and so forth. In that context, because an Arahant is free from delusion and has crossed over doubt, the certainty arose that it is inappropriate for him to speak in such a (wrong) way; therefore, they were delighted upon hearing my words. That Mahāli Licchavī also became delighted because his conviction became firm just like those two renunciants. Therefore, the commentator said, "When this was said, that King Mahāli was also delighted."

In this Mahāli Sutta, the words that I (the sub-commentator) have not explained are only those that are easy to understand. In the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, which explains meanings that are very subtle, profound, and difficult to see, and which generates pure and extensive wisdom...
340:
The meaning is "they have become." That Licchavi King Mahāli also became delighted and joyful because a firm conviction had arisen in him in that manner, just as it had in those two wandering ascetics. Therefore, it was said, "When this was said, that king also became delighted and joyful." What is not explicitly analyzed here in terms of meaning is easily understood.

Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the Mahāli Sutta in the Līnatthappakāsanī (Ṭīkā)—which clarifies the hidden meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sādhuvilāsinī, which illustrates the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-comprehend meanings, and which generates pure and extensive clarity of wisdom—is completed.

## The Explanation of the Meaning of the Mahāli Sutta is Finished.
341:
## 7. Jāliya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
## Dvepabbajita Vatthu Vaṇṇanā
Having thus commented on the Mahāli Sutta, the commentator, now wishing to comment on the Jāliya Sutta, said, "Thus have I heard... at Kosambī," in order to show that the opportunity to comment in due order has arrived, or to show that the sutta recited in the Council immediately after the Mahāli Sutta is the Jāliya Sutta. By the word "Ghositena" and so forth, he shows a compound with the middle term elided (majjhelopa-samāsa); it can also be said as "the monastery of the merchant Ghosita." Indeed, if said in this way, it amounts to mentioning and praising the donor, as in "in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika" and so forth. However, it is stated in other texts that by praising in this way, the Venerable Ānanda is also urging others to follow the example of that merchant. Regarding the question of who this merchant named Ghosita was, why he built this monastery, and how the Blessed One resided there, the commentator said, "In the past, it is said..." and so forth, wishing to show the entire answer in brief from the beginning. Although the text "the country of Allakappa" is found in many palm-leaf manuscripts, in some versions it is written as "the country of Addila" or "the country of Damiḷa." "Tato" means from the country of Allakappa. This statement, "the son... went..." was also said to make it known that his abandoning of his son was an unwholesome kamma. "Tadā" means on the day they entered the village. "Balavapāyāsaṃ" means a large quantity of very delicious rice gruel. "Jīrāpetuṃ" means to be digested by the digestive fire that cooks evenly. "Asannihite" means while having gone elsewhere outside the house. "Bhussati" means barking; it means making the sound of a dog as "bhu bhu." This too was one of that dog's kammas.

When the Paccekabuddha went to another place for the purpose of robe-making, the dog's heart broke. Animals are of an upright nature; they are not crooked. Human beings, however, think one thing in their hearts and say another with their mouths. Therefore, it was said, "Venerable Sir, humans are a thicket (hidden nature), but animals are open (manifest nature)."

Thus, that dog, due to its affection for the Paccekabuddha, its upright view, and its lack of crookedness, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven when it passed away. Referring to that, it is said, "That person... was reborn." When that deva spoke near someone's ear, the sound spread for sixteen yojanas. His natural speaking voice, however, spread throughout the entire city of the devas in Tāvatiṃsa, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent. Being endowed with such a loud voice, he became known as "Ghosaka Devaputta." This loudness of voice was the result of his barking out of affection and devotion for the Paccekabuddha. "Having passed away" means passing away due to the exhaustion of nutriment. Devas in the celestial realm pass away due to four causes: exhaustion of life-span, exhaustion of merit, exhaustion of nutriment, and through anger. For this deva, however, passing away occurred due to the exhaustion of nutriment while he was heedlessly enjoying sensual pleasures...
342:
The voice of that deva spread to a distance of sixteen yojanas. His natural speaking voice, however, spread throughout the entire city of the devas, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent. Due to this perfection of voice, he was known only as "Ghosaka Devaputta." This was the result of that deva's barking with a mind of affection and devotion toward the Paccekabuddha in his past life. "Having passed away" means passing away due to the exhaustion of nutriment. Devas in the celestial realm pass away due to four causes: exhaustion of life-span, exhaustion of merit, exhaustion of nutriment, and anger. As for this deva, while enjoying sensual pleasures, he became unmindful and passed away due to the exhaustion of nutriment.

That deva took rebirth in the womb of a courtesan in the city of Kosambī. Courtesans, it is said, look after a daughter but not a son. This is because only daughters can continue their lineage. Therefore, that woman also had the boy thrown away on a rubbish heap. This was the result of his kamma of abandoning his son in a previous life. Indeed, one should not despise an evil kamma, thinking "it is only a little." A certain man, seeing the child surrounded by crows and dogs, thought, "I have gained a son," and took him home. From that man's hand, the merchant of Kosambī purchased the child for a thousand kahāpaṇas. Referring to that matter, it was said, "He was born in the house of a family in Kosambī," and so forth. The fact that he faced attempts to be killed seven times was also the result of the kamma of abandoning his son.

"The merchant's daughter's" refers to the daughter of a regional merchant. "By the maturity of wisdom" means due to the sharpness of her intellect. She saved his life by tearing up the death warrant sent by his father and instead writing and tying a marriage proposal. Due to that perfection of voice, he became known as the merchant Ghosita.

"To refresh the body" means to strengthen the body, which was exhausted from eating only roots and fruits in the Himālaya, by consuming salt and sour foods. When the ascetics, thirsty and physically exhausted, reached a great banyan tree, they rested beneath it. Then, the senior ascetic, seeing the magnificent beauty of the banyan tree, thought, "The deity residing here must be of great power. It would be good if this deity would dispel the fatigue of the journey for this group of sages by providing drinking water and so forth." The deity, knowing his thought, gave the group of sages water for drinking and bathing, and food. Therefore, it was said, "Therein," and so forth. Attributing the thought of the senior ascetic to everyone generally, it was said, "Hoping for assistance." By the phrase "stretching out the hand," it shows the accomplishment of whatever was desired by merely stretching out the hand. The deity said (spoke because of being repeatedly questioned), although she did not venture to speak out of shame because her own merit was small.
343:
That deity guarding the banyan tree, being repeatedly urged and oppressed by the ascetics, spoke thus. "That person" refers to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. "To the hirelings" means to the slaves, servants, and laborers who perform various tasks for wages. "Only the usual meal-wages" means that although they did not work on that day because they were observing the Uposatha, he gave them the same meal-wages usually given on a working day, and not less than that. In the Dhammapada Commentary, according to the view of the Elders who recited the Khuddaka Nikāya, it is said, "He came to eat in the evening," but in this commentary, according to the view of the Elders who recited the Dīgha Nikāya, it is said, "He came to eat breakfast at midday."

"A certain" should be connected to either "a certain hireling" or "a certain task of a hireling." Because it was midday, he said, "Half the day has passed." It is shown that because it was undertaken for only half a day, that Uposatha is called a "Half-Uposatha" (upaḍḍhūposatha). In the Dhammapada Commentary, the Half-Uposatha is described in terms of the night portion, but in this commentary, it refers either to the day portion starting from midday, or to the remaining day and night portion from that morning. Indeed, the word "upaḍḍha" (half) can also apply to unequal parts. The phrase "on that very day" is said with reference to the time of dawn.

Upon hearing that "Even the sound 'Buddha' is rare in the world," joy and rapture arose. "On that very day" means only on the second day from the day of arrival in the city of Kosambī. "Go quickly" means "Venerable sirs, please travel swiftly." With reference to the "Come, Bhikkhu" (ehibhikkhu) ordination, it is said, "having gone forth." "Arahatship" (arahatta) refers to the state of an Arahant adorned with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Those three wealthy merchants also, having established themselves in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), gave alms for about half a month, and upon their return, they had three monasteries built. The Blessed One stayed in one monastery each day. In whichever merchant's monastery He stayed, He would wander for alms only at that merchant's house. At that time, however, He was staying at the monastery of the merchant Ghosita. Therefore, it is said, "He was staying at the Ghositārāma in Kosambī."

He is called a "preceptor" (upajjhāya) only by way of external sectarian tradition, not by the characteristics of a preceptor as in the Dispensation (Sāsana). Approaching and oppressing another with words is called "reproach" (upārambha); it means attacking by way of pointing out faults. Therefore, it is said, "wishing to find fault." Because one speaks with the intent to disparage, that fault is called "vāda" (argument/accusation). It means wishing to place that fault or defect upon [the other]. How did they wish to accuse? It is said, "Thus, it is heard," and so on. "That soul is that body" means that whatever object is perceived as the soul (jīva) is the very same object perceived as the body. This is [the view] "regarding form as self..."
344:
...regards [form as self]," they speak by grasping this stated view. They speak either by way of regarding form and self as one and the same, not as two, or with reference to a self imagined by external sectarians as a "being." For this reason, it is said, "A being is destroyed right here in this life." "Assa" means of the ascetic Gotama. "Bhijjati" means it is destroyed by way of cessation and disappearance. By saying this, it amounts to admitting the non-difference between the soul and the body, and it serves to show the destruction of the body. Here, just as the destruction of the unseen soul is stated because it is non-different from the body which has a visible destruction, likewise, it is impossible to say that the body does not destroy because it is non-different from the soul which has an unseen destruction. This is because the destruction of the body is proven by direct perception, and because there is no body that is separate from the great essential elements and derived matter. With this intention, He said, "It becomes a doctrine of annihilation" (ucchedavāda).

"The soul is one thing, the body is another" means the object called soul is one, and the object called body is another. This is spoken by grasping the view that proceeds in the manner of "regarding the self as possessing form," and so on. Since only the destruction of form is seen, and such destruction does not exist in the self, the meaning "the self is eternal" is arrived at. With this intention, He said, "The being falls into the eternalist view" (sassatavāda).

379-380. This view of theirs is like imagining the height or shortness of the son of a barren woman; therefore, this question is to be set aside (ṭhapanīya). It is not connected with the goal, not connected with the Dhamma, not the beginning of the holy life, and does not lead to disenchantment, etc. The Poṭṭhapāda Sutta is the evidence here. Having overlooked that question as if closing the eyes like a king, the Teacher began the further Dhamma teaching to them with the words, "Therefore, friends, listen," etc.; with this in mind, it is said, "Then the Blessed One," and so on. The eternalist view and the annihilationist view are the two extremes. The Noble Path is the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā). "Tassāyeva paṭipadāya" refers only to the wrong practice (micchāpaṭipadā).

"One gone forth through faith" (saddhāpabbajita) means one who has entered the monkhood with faith, thinking, "In this way, I shall escape from this suffering of the round of rebirths," and who, having fulfilled the virtue appropriate for that monkhood, has a mind concentrated through the first jhāna. "This" (etaṃ) refers to the words based on the defilement of views, such as "That soul is that body," which illustrate the increase of the round of defilements. "He is not one without doubt" means he is not one who has crossed over doubt regarding the dhammas; the meaning is that doubt arises in him by way of wavering and hesitation in various objects.
345:
"I know this thus" means that by whatever state that monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna, I, the Buddha, know that state together with its associated states as "mahaggata consciousness." Therefore, [the commentator] says, "He established the perception that 'this is mahaggata consciousness'." "I do not say thus" means that just as those with wrong views hold the nature of that state along with its basis as being non-different, saying "the soul is the same as the body," or hold both as being different, saying "the soul is one thing, the body is another," and thus declare their own wrong views—I do not say so, because I have fully understood that state with penetrative knowledge. Therefore, [the commentator] says "Atha kho," and so on. Since those outside the Dispensation mostly produce only kasiṇa jhānas, it is said, "for one who develops the kasiṇa preliminary work."

Because the attainment of jhāna occurs through the power of meditation, and meditation occurs by taking the knowledge of the earth kasiṇa, etc., as the starting point, it is pointed out by way of perception (saññā). Therefore, [the sub-commentator] says, "arisen by the power of perception." Thus, it is said, "one perceives the earth kasiṇa," and so on. Because the Blessed One said in various sections, "However, I do not say thus," the two wanderers, taking the Blessed One's words as a guideline, said, "This statement is not fit for him," with the intention that "this should not be said by this Great Man who is perfect in all qualities." To show that they did not speak from their own intuition, it is said, "they spoke while imagining." The remaining words are easy to understand because they follow the method already mentioned in the previous sutta and because they are clear.

Thus ends the Līnatthappakāsanā Ṭīka, the explanation of the difficult meanings of the Jāliya Sutta in the Sumangalavilāsinī, the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, which clarifies the extremely subtle, deep, and difficult-to-understand meanings, and which generates pure and extensive wisdom and courage.

## The Explanation of the Jāliya Sutta is finished.
346:
## 8. Mahāsīhanāda Sutta
## Explanation of the Story of Acela Kassapa

Having thus explained the Jāliya Sutta, now wishing to explain the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, [the commentator] said, "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... pe... uruññāyaṃ viharati," in order to show that the opportunity to explain in sequence has arrived, or to show that the sutta recited immediately after the Jāliya Sutta is the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. "Etadeva nāmaṃ" means that in whatever country that city is located, the name of that country and the name of the city where the Blessed One stayed are both "Uruññā." Therefore, the meaning of the word "uruññāyaṃ" should be understood by the method of repetition (āvutti), etc., as "in the janapada named Uruññā, in the city named Uruññā." By this, he shows this meaning: words denoting a janapada do not always have a fixed masculine plural form in all places. In some places, they may have an unfixed masculine plural form, like the text "āḷaviyaṃ viharati" (staying in Āḷavī). Some teachers say it refers only to the janapada; to refute that statement, it is said, "Bhagavā hi," and so on.

"Ramaṇīyo" means it is delightful because of having a charming ground area, being endowed with shade and water, and being secluded from people. Because it gives safety to animals in this forest, it is called "Migadāya" (Deer Park). Therefore, it is said, "So hi," and so on. "Cela" means cloth; because that person does not have that cloth, he is called "Acela" (a naked wanderer). "Nāmaṃ" refers to the clan name (gotta). Heating or exhausting the body is called "tapa" (asceticism); because he has that practice, he is called "tapassī" (an ascetic). Because he relies on asceticism in such a manner, and because that asceticism also relies on him, it is said, "tapanissitaka" (one who relies on asceticism).

In this context, "muttācārādī," by the word "ādī," includes practices such as licking the hands, etc., which appear later in the Pali text. Because he lives by a livelihood that is rough, harsh, devoid of the conduct esteemed by the virtuous, and uninspiring, he is called "lūkhājīvī" (one of rough livelihood); this is a method not explicitly in the commentary. "Uppaṇḍeti" means to mock by way of laughing and joking. "Upavadati" means to disparage with a mind of contempt. Therefore, it is said, "hīḷeti vambheti" (he scorns and despises). Just as in "knowledge of the cause is the discrimination of Dhamma" (hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā), the word "Dhamma" is a synonym for "hetu" (cause); therefore, it is said, "kāraṇassa anukāraṇaṃ" (the subsequent cause of a cause). According to the meaning already stated, the word "kāraṇa" here is due to being a cause (hetu). Indeed, the use of a word is employed according to its meaning. When that very meaning of the word is spoken by others, it is called "anukāraṇa" because it is an occurrence of a cause that conforms to, is similar to, or follows after that cause. "Parehi" refers to those others to whom you have spoken this cause. "Vuttakāraṇena" means...
347:
If you (Venerable Sirs) did not speak in the same way they (others) spoke, then would your doctrine, being with cause due to what they said, or any subsequent criticism of that cause, not reach a point of being censurable by the wise, even in the slightest? Why does it not reach such a point? This is how it should be construed. With the words "This is the meaning..." and so forth, he shows that same meaning in brief.

Now, the Blessed One, referring to the Vibhajjavāda (Analytical Doctrine), said in brief, "These people do not speak according to what I have said," and then, to show that doctrine analytically, he said, "Kassapa, here in this world, I..." and so forth. Desiring to show that division, he said, "Here in this world, a certain person..." and so forth. Indeed, the Blessed One censures the useless bodily exhaustion that does not lead to the subsiding of defilements, saying, "Devotion to self-mortification is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial," and so forth. However, he praises the beneficial bodily exhaustion that leads to the subsiding of defilements, saying, "He is a forest-dweller, he is a wearer of rag-robes," and so forth. "Appapuññatāya" means because of the lack of merit (glory). Here, the word "appa" expresses the meaning of non-existence (abhāva), as in the Pali passages such as "standing in a place where there is no grass (appaharite) near a monastery with two or three roofs, one should determine."

Because of being a wrong view holder, rejecting kamma and its results, and being led by wrong view with thoughts like "There is no result of giving," he fulfills the three types of misconduct for the sake of livelihood; referring to this, it is said, "having fulfilled the three types of misconduct."

"Bhiyyosomattāya" means excessively, beyond measure. This term "bhiyyoso" is an indeclinable (nipāta) with the same meaning as the word "bhiyyosadda." "Anesanavasena" means by the power of wrong livelihood (micchājīva), which is sought by practicing as one pleases with the desire to be praised for qualities one does not possess, while established in pretension (kuhana-vatthu). It means fulfilling the three types of misconduct for the sake of livelihood according to the method already mentioned. "These two persons" refers to the two individuals who commit misconduct, described as "one with little merit" and "one with merit."

In the second method, "these two persons" refers to the two individuals who perform good conduct, described as "one with little merit" and "one with merit."

In the third and fourth methods, the meaning should be understood respectively, just as mentioned in the first and second methods. It should be understood that in the first and third methods, they are those who hold the doctrine of non-causality (ahetukavāda) and the doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda). In the second and fourth methods, they are those who hold the doctrine of kamma (kammavāda) and the doctrine of action (kiriyavāda).
348: Appadukkhavihārī means one who usually dwells with little suffering. Bāhirakācārayutto means one who is associated with the practices of the titthiyas (outsiders), which are external to the practices of the Sāsana. Attānaṃ sukhetvā means making oneself happy or creating happiness for oneself through the happiness derived from requisites obtained by unrighteous and improper seeking. Currently, there is a reading 'sukhe ṭhapetvā' (having established in happiness). By the words such as 'Now there is no one equal to me,' it refers to the fulfillment of misconduct through the power of the three types of conceiving (maññanā), namely craving (taṇhā), pride (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi). Alternatively, it should be connected as: having fulfilled the three types of misconduct while generating gain and honor. Micchādiṭṭhivaseṇa means by the power of wrong view that arises as 'There is no fault in sensual pleasures.' Paribbājikāya refers to a female ascetic who has entered an external renunciation, or a clothed wandering nun. This is because in the word 'aparo,' the meaning of 'an ascetic or a clothed wanderer' also follows. Daharāya means one of young age. Mudukāya means one who is soft and delicate. Lomasāya means one with little hair due to having thin red hair. Because that wandering nun has hair, she is called 'lomasā.' Indeed, grammarians desire the formation of words with the 'sa' suffix in all three genders. Kāmesu refers to the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma). Pātabbataṃ refers to the state of being enjoyed or consumed. Here, the word 'pā' has the meaning of consuming, and the word 'tabba' is a bhāva-sādhana (abstract noun formation). The word 'tā' occurs in its own sense, just like in the word 'devatā.' Alternatively, 'pātabbataṃ' means the state of one who consumes; in this case, the word 'tabba' is a kattu-sādhana (agentive formation). For example, in the Pañcattaya Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pali, it is said: 'Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins designate the perfection of this base by merely the formations that are seen, heard, sensed, and cognized,' it is like the word 'viññātabba.' Regarding this, it is stated in that commentary (Aṭṭhakathā): 'It is called viññātabba because it cognizes; merely seen, heard, sensed, and cognized (merely the arising of perception in the five doors) is the meaning here.' In the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) of that commentary, it is also said: 'Just as the word niyyānika is a kattu-sādhana because it leads out, so too here the word viññātabba is a kattu-sādhana,' and it is explained as 'viññātabba because it cognizes.' The word 'tā' is in the sense of bhāva (state). Sensual lust (kilesakāma) that stands on the side of being enjoyed is also included within the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma). Therefore, enjoying those sensual pleasures as one pleases is the meaning here. This stated meaning is the analysis of the specific meanings spoken by way of the four methods. Although the teacher (Venerable Dhammapāla) said, 'It comes by way of the titthiyas because it is analyzed thus in the commentary,' it should be understood that it is analyzed in the same way in the Pali text as well. Sāsane pi means 'also in this Sāsana.'
349:
To the question, "In this Dispensation, how is it obtained?" the words beginning with "Ekacco hi" (A certain person indeed) are spoken. Because it cannot be obtained [rightfully], it should be connected with the words "having practiced wrong livelihood (anesana)," and so forth. It is obtained by directly claiming arahantship which does not clearly exist in oneself, saying "It exists in me," or by resorting to the three grounds for deception (kuhana-vatthu) known as hinting for requisites (sāmantajappana), using meager requisites (paccayapaṭisevana), and relying on artificial postures (iriyāpathasannissita).

"Such a person also" means one who has a meager livelihood by virtue of undertaking ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). The phrase "by virtue of wrong livelihood (anesana)" is merely an example. In fact, it should also be said, "by claiming arahantship," and so forth.

For a being born in woeful states (duggati), the meaning is the intention: "I shall be one who has happiness that is difficult to obtain." In this context, the word "anta" in "asakkonto" (being unable) is used in the sense of a state (bhāva-lakkhaṇa); it means "while being unable."

"From such a place" means from such a birth. "They have come" means they have come to this present life by virtue of rebirth. "And now the place to be gone to" means the birth to be gone to in the future, also by virtue of rebirth. "From there" means from the past life. "Rebirth again" means rebirth again in the life immediately following in the future, and rebirth again in the life immediately following that one; it refers to repeated birth. In the phrase "For what reason shall I blame?", a person who does not know the truth might blame any doctrine by the power of desire and anger; I do not blame in that manner. Rather, being one who knows the truth, for what reason shall I blame all these doctrines? To show this intention that there is no reason to blame all these practices, the words "It is only that which should be blamed," and so forth, are spoken. "Bhaṇḍika" refers to a bundle. In the context of the simile, it is like a cloth washed clean and a cloth not yet washed. In the context of the thing illustrated (upameyya), it means being pure due to having praiseworthy qualities, and likewise being impure otherwise. "That meaning" refers to blaming those who deserve blame and praising those who deserve praise.

Because of the importance of proceeding by way of accomplishing the welfare of the present life and the welfare of the future life, no one says it is "not good." "Fivefold enmity" refers to the fivefold enmity such as killing living beings. That is called "enmity" (vera) because it is the opposite of the five precepts (pañca-sīla) and because it is the cause of enmity for beings. For that very reason, no one says it is "good," and likewise because it does not accomplish the welfare of the present life and so forth, and because it corrupts the goodness of beings. "Should not be restrained" means it should not be prevented in the taking of visual objects. Their intention is that the acquisition of the eye has the benefit of seeing visible objects. In this same way...
350:
In the case of the ear and so forth, it should be understood in this same way. Because it means that non-restraint in their five sense-doors is good, and restraint in those five sense-doors is not good, it is said, "Again... pe... non-restraint."

Here is another method apart from the Commentary: In the statement "Some say it is good," the ascetics and brahmins called "some" are the sectarians (titthiya) who say that practices such as devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) are "good"; we say that such practice is "not good." In the statement "Some... pe... say it is not good," they say that the use of blameless requisites and the right practice of being well-clothed and well-robed are "not good"; we say that such practice is "good."

Thus, to make it known that the fourfold set (catukka) shown based on the doctrines of others (paravāda) is again shown as a fourfold set based on one's own doctrine (sakavāda), the words "In this way," and so forth, are spoken. Whatever is similar to something is indeed similar to it. Whatever is dissimilar to something is indeed dissimilar to it; thus it is said, "similarity and dissimilarity." Here, "similarity" means mere similarity. Indeed, the abandoning of states to be abandoned without remainder and the fulfillment of states to be fulfilled are seen only in one's own doctrine, not in the doctrines of others. Therefore, it is said, "I, having approached them, speak thus," and so forth. The meaning should be understood by way of the five precepts and so forth, according to the method already mentioned, in accordance with one's own doctrine and the doctrines of others.

## Samanuyuñjāpanakathāvaṇṇanā

"Anta" is the fifth (imperative) middle voice (attanopada) suffix in the sense of a command. "One who asks about the doctrine" refers to one who asks about the claimed conclusion, thus: "Does the ascetic Gotama live having abandoned the defiling states without remainder, or do other teachers of groups? First, state your own doctrine here." "One who asks for the reason" refers to one who asks for the cause, thus: "When it is said that only the ascetic Gotama lives having abandoned the defiling states without remainder, do you also practice by taking this meaning through reason?" "One who asks for both" refers to one who, when the claimed meaning is being established by stating the reason "This is the reason here," asks for the two examples and illustrations of similarity and dissimilarity to strengthen the reason through both positive (anvaya) and negative (vyatireka) concomitance. Furthermore, it should be understood that when the claimed meaning is established perfectly with the three characteristics by way of cause, simile, and illustration, one who speaks well afterwards and concludes is also said to "concur" (samanubhāsati). "Having brought together" (upasaṃharitvā) is the remainder of the Pali text. "What is yours?" and so forth...
351:
It is a demonstration of the manner of presentation. In the second phrase, 'saṅghena vā saṅghaṃ' (by the Saṅgha or the Saṅgha), it is also said, 'in this very way,' referring to the remaining words and the manner of presentation. 'Tam-atthaṃ' refers to the meaning of practicing by completely abandoning the states to be abandoned and the meaning of practicing by completely undertaking the states to be undertaken. It should be understood by associating it with terms such as 'akusala' (unwholesome). They are known as 'akusala' in the sense of being born from lack of skill, and for that very reason, they are known as 'akusala.' In this context, the word 'saṅkhāta' is suitable in the sense of 'known' or 'reckoned as a group'; thus, it is said, 'known, or placed as a group.' Here, the former term refers to strictly unwholesome states, while the latter term refers to the associated states (sampayutta-dhammā) that arise with those unwholesome states, as well as the states on the opposite side. Only such grouping is appropriate. Defining something by its nature as belonging to the unwholesome side is called 'grouping.' The word 'avajja' has the meaning of 'fault' because it is a synonym for 'blameworthy.' Since the prefix 'a-' occurs in the sense of having that fault, it is said, 'those with faults.' Those called 'Ariyas' (Noble Ones) are faultless. These unwholesome states, however, cannot be faultless for any reason; therefore, they are not worthy or capable of being 'Ariya' in the sense of being faultless.

386-392. This word 'yaṃ' is shown to be in the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti) in the sense of cause by the word 'yena.' 'Yaṃ vā pana' is a statement expressing impossibility, meaning 'even a little bit.' 'Pahāya vattanti' is stated as 'they live having abandoned even a little bit,' which is a plural transformation based on the sense of the meaning. Here, the 'gaṇācariyas' (teachers of a sect) are Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, and others. Since the Saṅgha has the Teacher as its source, the perfection of the Teacher is also manifested through the perfection of the Saṅgha; thus, it is said, 'saṅghena vā saṅghaṃ... siddhito.' Since that praise is rooted in confidence (pasāda), the phrase 'pasīdamānāpi' and so on are stated to show it through the aspect of confidence. There, with the word 'pi' in the sense of inclusion, it includes those who are not confident, showing that 'even those who are not confident do not have confidence in this way.' Just as confidence arises in the disciples due to the perfection of the teacher, and in the teacher due to the perfection of the disciples through accordance (anuloma), it should be understood that through divergence (vyatireka), lack of confidence arises in the disciples due to the failure of the teacher, and in the teacher due to the failure of the disciples. 'Tathā hi' and so on is the explanation of that point. 'Sārīrasampatti' means 'rūpasampatti,' the perfection of the physical body. This is said with reference to beings who measure by form (rūpappamāṇa). 'Dhamma-desanaṃ vā sutvā' is said with reference to those who measure by voice (ghosappamāṇa) and those who measure by Dhamma (dhammappamāṇa). 'Bhikkhūnaṃ panācāragocaraṃ' and so on, however, is said with reference to those who measure by Dhamma and those who measure by austerity (lūkhappamāṇa). Through conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara), the Dhamma is manifested; through right practice, austerity is manifested.
352:
Therefore, in the first phrase 'bhavanti vattāro,' those who measure by form, those who measure by voice, and those who measure by Dhamma should be associated; in the second phrase, only those who measure by Dhamma should be associated. 'Kīvarūpo' means 'of what kind of nature?' (of what caste or class?). The phrase 'yā saṅghassa pasansā' (what is the praise of the Saṅgha) is brought in and connected, or this very text is the original.

In that praise, the praiseworthiness of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas is illuminated, as well as the absence of such praiseworthiness in other sectarians (titthiyas). Desiring to show that praiseworthiness by extracting it through the power of summarizing abstinence (virati), abandoning (pahāna), and restraint (saṃvara), the phrase 'ayam-adhippāyo' and so on is stated. In that statement, because 'setughāta-virati' (abstinence by cutting the bridge) is associated with the Noble Path, it is said, 'it is not at all present.' 'Vikkhambhana-pahāna' (abandoning by suppression) through the power of the eight attainments, and 'tadaṅga-pahāna' (abandoning by substitution of opposites) through the power of insight (vipassanā), should be associated as applicable. 'Through the power of insight alone' means through the power of merely seeing in various ways as 'impermanent' or 'suffering,' but not through the power of contemplating formations (saṅkhāra) by applying the three characteristics preceded by the defining of mentality-materiality and the discerning of causes. This is because the defining of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) and the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) do not exist for sectarians outside the Dispensation. The remaining three—'samuccheda-pahāna' (abandoning by uprooting), 'paṭippassaddhi-pahāna' (abandoning by tranquillization), and 'nissaraṇa-pahāna' (abandoning by escape)—are completely non-existent for them because these are the nature of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. All 'sīla-saṃvara' (restraint of virtue) other than the mundane five precepts; the extremely pure 'khanti-saṃvara' (restraint through patience) taught as 'he is able to endure cold and heat' and so on; 'ñāṇa-saṃvara' (restraint through knowledge) known as Path-knowledge which completely cuts off defilements, taught as 'by wisdom these streams are shut' and so on; the extremely pure 'indriya-saṃvara' (restraint of faculties) which functions by closing the faculties with the mind as the sixth; and 'vīriya-saṃvara' (restraint through effort) known as Right Effort (sammappadhāna), taught as 'for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states' and so on—referring to these five kinds of restraint, it is said, 'the rest is completely non-existent.'

Taking up the aforementioned virtue (sīla) again with the phrase 'Monks, these five are the recitations of the Pātimokkha' and so on is for the purpose of showing the abundance of virtue in the Dispensation and showing that others (sectarians) stand only in a small portion of that virtue. Currently, there is the reading 'uposathuddesā.' 'Prajñāyati' means it is manifest by being established; therefore, it should be associated as 'By me... it is not.' 'Sīhanāda' (lion's roar) means a noble sound, a fearless sound, a doctrine that cannot be refuted by anyone. As for the words they say—
353:
"The terms such as byaggha (tiger), puṅgava (bull), usabha (ox), kuñjara (elephant), sīha (lion), saddūla (leopard), and nāga (serpent/elephant) are used as subsequent members of a compound (uttarapada) to denote the sense of 'excellent' or 'noble,' and they occur in the masculine gender when expressing this meaning."

This statement should be understood as being generally applicable.

## Commentary on the Noble Eightfold Path
