"This doctrine of mine, as previously stated, is indeed unerring. The unerring nature of this doctrine is to be known by oneself, without relying on others, by practicing this path." This was taught for the purpose of penetrating and knowing the unerring nature of the doctrine. In the Pāḷi text, for the words beginning with "atthi Kassapa," the construction is as follows: A person practicing this path will know and see for himself through direct experience: "The ascetic Gotama speaks at the proper and suitable time; he speaks what is real because it is unerringly true; he speaks what is beneficial because it surely brings welfare; he speaks the Dhamma because it is not divorced from causal principles; and he speaks the Vinaya because it is associated with discipline and because he disciplines others."

There is, Kassapa, a path realized and proclaimed by me through my own higher knowledge, which is the means of escape from the entire suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha); and there is also the preliminary practice which is the means for attaining that path. By that Pāḷi text, it is shown that the doctrine proceeding in the manner of "The ascetic Gotama practices having abandoned these states without remainder" is a true lion's roar (sīhanāda) that cannot be shaken by anyone. In the word "dakkhati," the formation of the word with the suffix "ssati" should be understood as in the Pāḷi passages such as "yatra hi nāma sāvako evarūpaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sakkhiṃ karissati" (where indeed a disciple will know, see, or realize such a thing).

Just as in Sutta passages like "Thus he sees this as it really is with right wisdom," the Buddha, wishing to show the path and the practice together, used the restrictive phrase "ayameva" (this alone) to exclude the multiplicity of paths, to show that it is common to all Noble Ones (Ariyas), and to demonstrate its prominence in the Dispensation (Sāsana). Therefore, he said: "Monks, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings," and "This is the path; there is no other for the purification of vision."
354:
The Blessed One, who guards the welfare of beings and sees Nibbāna—the end of the exhaustion of birth—knows the path that is the one-way road to Nibbāna. In the past, the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, have crossed the flood of the round of rebirths by this path. Those who will cross in the future and those who are crossing now also do so by this path. In all Sutta passages and Abhidhamma passages, this single path is prominent.

## Commentary on the Talk on Ascetic Practices

Because only the ascetic practice (tapa) is to be undertaken or initiated, it is called 'tapopakkama.' Therefore, it is said 'tapārambha' (the initiation of ascetic practice). Here, 'initiation' (ārambha) is shown to be the performance of ascetic practice by the word 'tapokammāni.' 'Samaṇakamma-saṅkhāta' refers to those actions known as the duties to be performed by recluses. The same method applies to the term 'brāhmaṇakamma-saṅkhāta.'

'Niccola' refers to one whose clothes have been discarded, whose garments have been entirely rejected. The words 'cela' and 'cola' are synonyms. Even if someone wears worn-out, discolored rags cut with a knife, they might be called 'niccola' (without clothes) because they lack a proper garment with fringes. To exclude such a person, the word 'nagga' (naked) is used. It means being naked in every way by undertaking the vow of nudity.

The absence of the conduct of well-bred people in the world is called 'abandoned conduct' (vissaṭṭhācāra). This meaning is shown by the words beginning with 'uccārakammādīsu.' How is it absent? It is said 'while standing' (ṭhitakovā), etc. This is merely an illustration. It is because such a person also abandons practices such as rinsing the mouth after vomiting.

'Apalikhati' means licking because of not washing with water. It is said that such a person designates a stick as a 'living being' (satta); therefore, one fulfilling that practice acts in this way, as stated in 'uccāraṃ vā,' etc. There, 'apalikhati' means scraping or wiping (to remove impurity).

The procedure of approaching when called 'Come, venerable' is called 'ehibhaddanta.' One who practices such a procedure is an 'ehibhaddantika.' In this word, the derivative (taddhita) is formed by conventional usage (ruḷhī), just like 'ehipassika.' By rejecting that practice, one is a 'na-ehibhaddantika.' That meaning is shown by the words beginning with 'bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ.' 'Na eti' means not coming. The same method applies to the term 'na-tiṭṭhabhaddantika.'

The intention is that a recluse should be one who follows his own word, not the word of another; thus, he does not do both of those... etc. 'Puretaraṃ' refers to alms-food that has arrived at the place of collection before he himself arrives. He thinks, 'A recluse indeed...'
355:
With the intention that "A monk should accept only alms that are obtained as they come," he does not accept (alms that come first). However, regarding alms specifically prepared for him, he does not accept them with the thought, "Because of me, many small living beings have been brought to destruction." He also does not accept invited alms with the thought, "If I accept this, I will be following their words."

Kumbhī refers to a pot containing cooked alms-food. Ukkhalī refers to a pot for cooking alms-food. Pacchī refers to a basket for holding alms-food. "Tato pi" means (not accepting) even from those pots and baskets. Because that ascetic perceives living beings even in pots and such, it is said, "kumbhīkaḷopiyo," and so on. The same method applies to terms like "ayaṃ maṃ," and so on. Antara refers to the space between two people.

Kabaḷantarāyo means an obstacle to a mouthful of food. In this mouthful also, he perceives living beings. Purisantara-gatāya refers to (a woman) who has come near a man. Rati-antarāyo means an obstacle to sensual pleasure. Because people gather and announce [the food] by way of village commonality and so on, that food is called saṅkitti. Since the food prepared with rice and so on collected in that way is intended here, it is said, "saṅkittetvā katabhattesu."

In the commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, the teacher (Dhammapāla) stated: "It is called saṅkitti because people announce it with this food; it refers to food prepared as a collective action by villagers. Since the announcement of food is intended here, it is said, 'saṅkittetvā katabhattesu'." This (not accepting saṅkitti food) is shown as his excellent practice by the word "ukkaṭṭho" and so on. Just as shown here, in terms like "na ehibhaddantiko," it should be understood as showing the excellent practice. The word sā is a synonym for a dog. Tassa refers to the dog. Tattha refers to that place. Samūhasamūhasārinī means moving or roaming in groups. Manussā refers to people who perform various services.

Sovīraka refers to sour rice-gruel. Although some say "loṇasovīraka," that statement is inappropriate because it is said to be made from all kinds of grain ingredients. In fact, loṇasovīraka is made from ingredients such as all kinds of fish, meat, flowers, and fruits. Surāpānam eva means only the drinking of liquor that has reached the characteristic of intoxication. Here, spirits (meraya) are also included either by the method of lakkhaṇahāra or by the method of ekasesa. Sabbesu pi means (not accepting) sour rice-gruel, liquor, and so on, whether they are blameworthy or blameless. He is called ekāgārika because he approaches only one house for alms. Nivattati means returning; it means that if he receives alms, he does not go beyond that one house. He is called ekālopika because he subsists on only one mouthful of food. It is called datti because it is given with this vessel; it is a small alms-giving vessel that holds only about two or three mouthfuls. Therefore, it is said, "khuddakapātī." Aggabhikkha refers to alms-food that has not yet been touched, or excellent alms-food because it is well-prepared. By way of not eating...
356:
Because it is for one day, it is called ekāhika nutriment; it means consuming that nutriment. Since that nutriment is essentially nutriment that skips one day, it is called "every other day." In terms like "dvāhika," and so on, it should be understood in this same way. Alternatively, eating one day after not eating for one day, or eating once every other day, is ekāhika. Eating for two days after not eating for two days, or eating once every two days, is dvāhika. The same method applies to the remaining two terms (sattāhika, aḍḍhamāsika). Indeed, one who practices the excellent practice of eating meals in turns eats only for one day after not eating for two days. The same should be understood for the remaining two terms. However, in the Majjhima Nikāya commentary, it is said: "It is ekāhika because there is an interval of one day for this eating; the same applies to the remaining terms." As in passages like "The elder monks exhort the bhikkhunīs in turn (pariyāyena)," the word pariyāya has the meaning of a turn or time (vāra). Ekāhavārena means by the turn of one day's eating. It should be understood that the Buddha spoke the words "thus, in such a way" and so on in the Pali text to show the occurrence of the procedure mentioned as "ekāhika" and so on in due order.

Sāmāka is a type of millet. Self-sown grain refers to the type of grain that grows without being planted by humans. That itself is called "vīhi" (grain). Likhitvā means by scraping (plowing). Silesa (resin) also refers to the resin of trees such as the kaṇikāra tree. Kuṇḍaka refers to very small rice fragments (bran). Vinegar made from cooked rice is odanakañjiya. As in passages like "One should bathe with sesame powder (piññāka) scented with perfume," the word piññāka is a synonym for sesame flour. It is as taught: "Piññāka refers to sesame flour." Although some teachers say, "Only the young banana trunk is called piññāka," that statement should not be accepted because it is not stated so anywhere.

Cloths made from hemp fibers are called sāṇa. Hemp cloths mixed with other fibers are called masāṇa according to the method of nirutti (etymology). They are not bhaṅga (hempen) cloths included among the six types of robes. Some teachers, imagining that "masāṇa" refers to special types of cloth, read it as "massakacoḷa." Since the ancient teachers did not say so, such a reading is inappropriate. In the phrase "eraka grass and so on," the word ādi (and so on) includes marū, makaci, banana fiber, and so on. Cloths made from eraka grass and so on are called lowly cloths. Here, the word chava means lowly (hīna). In the previously mentioned alternative, however, it means a corpse. Chaḍḍitanantaka refers to discarded old cloths (worn-out rags). Ajinasseda refers to the skin called ajina (antelope skin). It refers to the natural ajina deer skin. If that skin is split in the middle...
357:
A garment made by splitting an antelope skin (ajina) in half is called an ajinakkhipa. The Papañcasūdanī Commentary states that this very garment is also called "sakhuraka." It is the intention of those teachers that if two or three skins are joined and sewn together, it is also called an ajinakkhipa. However, in the Vinaya Commentaries, the ajina skin that is intact and not split is itself called an ajinakkhipa. "Kanditvā" means spinning by inserting into an axle. There is also the reading "ganthetvā," which means rolling and knotting. Only in this way is the reference to the bark garment (phalakacīra) appropriate. "With reference to which it was said" refers to the Buddha's teaching in the Aṅguttara Nikāya regarding the hair-blanket (kesakambala) made of human hair, intended as a simile to show how extremely loathsome the doctrine of the ascetic Ajita is.

"Tantāvutāni" means garments woven by spreading out a loom. "Paṭikiṭṭho" means something inferior. Why is it inferior? Because it is described starting with "hair-blanket" (kesakambala), and so on. The meaning of the word "ubbaṭṭhako" in the Pāḷi text is "standing upright" or "standing on the tips of the toes," as stated in the Commentary to the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya. The word "ubbha" is an indeclinable (nipāta) meaning "above," as in the word "ubbhajāṇumaṇဍalaṃ." Indeclinables have many measures and express many meanings.

Because the practice of squatting is undertaken only through wrong effort, it is said "he is devoted to the effort of squatting." Not only while sitting does he squat, but even when moving, he goes by jumping while remaining in a squatting position. "Ayakaṇṭake" means thorns made of iron. "Pakatikaṇṭake" means natural thorns [or bamboo splinters]. The word "thaṇḍila" is defined as "on high ground" because it occurs on elevated land. This is an alternative method to the Commentary: as in passages like "patthaṇḍile pāturahosi," level ground is called "thaṇḍila." In the Amarakośa and Nighaṇṭu texts, it is said: "An altar is enclosed ground; thaṇḍila is beautiful on level ground." Therefore, it means he makes his bed on the bare ground without any covering. With reference to that meaning, the Nighaṇṭu itself says: "One who sleeps on level ground by the power of his practice is called a thaṇḍilasāyī." Because dust itself is filth, it is called "rajo-jalla" (dust and dirt). Therefore, it is stated as "the body," etc. "Laddhaṃ āsanaṃ" means whatever seat is obtained for sitting. "Akopetvā" means staying in that very place without going elsewhere. For that reason, it is said "he is one who habitually sits in that very place." Sitting in this way is called not abandoning that place.

Among the four great foul things (mahāvikaṭa), since only excrement is intended here, it is explained as "it refers to dung (gūtha)." Because that excrement is naturally produced in a repulsive state, it is called "vikaṭa." "Sāyaṃ tatiyaṃ" means the third time, which is called the evening. "Assa" refers to the practice of descending into the water. Like the word "pāto," the word "sāyaṃ" is also an indeclinable.
358:
(The word sāyaṃ) is an indeclinable. With the elision of the niggahīta, the reading "sāyatatiyakaṃ" is also found.

In these Pāḷi passages, from "he is a naked ascetic" (acelako hoti) up to "he drinks rice-husk water" (thusodakaṃ pivati), these terms describing practices constitute a single section (vāra). However, passages such as "he is one who accepts food from one house" (ekāgāriko vā hoti) belong to various sections or various times. Similarly, passages such as "he is a consumer of greens" (sākabhakkho vā hoti) and "he wears hempen garments, he wears hemp-mix garments" (sāṇānipi dhāreti, masāṇānipi dhāreti) also belong to various sections or times.

For this reason, the words "vā" and "pi" are used here. Here, the word "pi" should also be understood in the sense of an alternative (vikappa). In the preceding terms describing practices, however, neither of these two (vā or pi) is used. By doing so, there is no contradiction in saying "he wears hempen garments" after saying "he is a naked ascetic," or in saying "he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water" after saying "he is a wearer of dust and dirt." Or else, what is the use of trying to avoid contradiction here? The doctrine of the heretics is like a madman's basket. Alternatively, it should be understood that the naked ascetic Kassapa said "he wears hempen garments," etc., starting from "he is a naked ascetic," merely to show the self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) which is inherently self-contradictory.

## Explanation of the Futility of Practicing Asceticism

"Sīlasampadādīhi" means (being devoid of) these supramundane attainments: the accomplishment of virtue, the accomplishment of concentration, and the accomplishment of wisdom. "Vinā" means either because of being devoid of them, or because without those three (accomplishments), neither the state of a recluse (sāmañña) nor the state of a brahmin (brahmañña) can ever occur; thus, it is construed with the remaining Pāḷi to show the futility of those heretical ascetic practices. "Dosaveravirahitaṃ" means being free from the enmity called anger (dosa). This is said because anger is the direct opposite of loving-kindness (mettā).

The teacher of the Old Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) said: "By the word dosa, all defiling states (saṅkilesadhamma) that are opposites of jhāna are taken. By the word vera, beings who are enemies are taken. To the extent that one is free from anger, to that extent one is free from enemies." That statement should be re-examined because only the word vera exists in the Pāḷi text, and in the Commentary, the word dosa is used only to explain the meaning of that word vera.

"Ettakamattaṃ" means merely such things as the practice of nakedness. It is called "pakati" because it makes the meaning known through its manifest state; it is a well-known view in the world. Therefore, he said, "This is common parlance (pakatikathā)." Just like the word "mattā" in passages such as "mattā sukhapariccāgā," the word "mattā" is a term denoting measure because it carries the internal meaning of "a little."
359:
(The teacher) having made a statement indicating the measure, said "By this" and so forth. By that small measure of practice, the sequence of practice that has come into the context is indeed to be abandoned. Alternatively, he shows the meaning that it is understood by this other word "by exertion in austerity" (tapo-pakkama) through this phrase "by the sequence of practice" (paṭipatti-kkama). "From that" (tato) means because it is extremely difficult through only a small sequence of practice in that state of a recluse or a noble brahmin. Intending this causal connection, it is said "together with the connection of words" (padasambandhena saddhiṃ). "Everywhere" (sabbatha) means in all cycles.

"Otherwise" (aññathā) means if recluseship or brahminhood were to consist of things like being a naked ascetic, then a recluse would be easily known, and a brahmin would be easily known. But because you [Sirs] speak of recluseship in a way other than this [naked asceticism], and speak of brahminhood in another way, therefore a recluse is difficult to know, and a brahmin is difficult to know—this is the meaning. Therefore, (the teacher) says, "He said this intending this matter." "Having rejected that natural view" (taṃ pakativādaṃ paṭikkhipitvā) means: keeping in heart the recluseship and brahminhood that were ordinary in the past, that Acelaka Kassapa said "It is difficult, it is extremely difficult," and the Blessed One also, intending only that ordinary recluseship and brahminhood, spoke "This is indeed natural" and so forth; having rejected only that speech which has ordinary recluseship and brahminhood as its object in this world, and wishing to make manifest the difficulty of knowing a recluse and a brahmin by nature and in the ultimate sense, (the Blessed One) spoke again "Indeed, natural..." and so forth. "Even there" (tatrāpi) means even in the views of recluses and brahmins. "Connection of words" (padasambandha) means the connection of preceding and following sentences together with the causal term.

## Description of the Attainment of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom

400-1. "Wise" (paṇḍita) refers to one endowed with wisdom accomplished through the fulfillment of the cause, which is the triple-rooted rebirth. "How does he learn?" means that because of the maturity of his knowledge, like a lamp shining inside a pot, he perceives the meaning taught by the Blessed One in various contexts with the clarity of wisdom shining within, and he attends to and remembers that teaching. Because he learns and remembers, therefore... [pe]... "having known" is the connection. "And of him" (tassa ca) refers to one who is a naked ascetic. "Tassa ca" is the word-break; it means one who is a naked ascetic and lives devoted to the practice of descending into water. Or "tassa ce" is the word-break, and the construction is "if it is not yet developed, not yet realized." "I ask about those attainments of virtue, concentration, and wisdom by which one becomes a recluse and a brahmin"—this is the intention of Acelaka Kassapa. "For the purpose of knowing the attainment of virtue, etc." (sīlasampadādivijānanattha) means for the reason of wanting to know the attainment of virtue and so forth. For it is said, "Why does he ask?" In this sentence, the word "atha" is used in the sense of cause. In such cases, it is the same. In the phrase "by the attainment of virtue" (sīlasampadāya), the word "iti" has the meaning of "and so forth."
360:
In this context, the word "iti" is an indication by way of illustration (upalakkhaṇa); by that word "iti," the two terms "attainment of mind" (cittasampadā) and "attainment of wisdom" (paññāsampadā) are included. Therefore, the teacher says, "There is no other (attainment) than the attainments of virtue, mind, and wisdom." Since the three aggregates of one beyond training (asekkha-kkhandha), such as virtue, are included by these, it is said "only the fruition of arahantship." The reason for that fruition of arahantship is shown by "ending in the fruition of arahantship" (arahattaphalapariyosānaṃ) and so forth. This statement is like a crow's eye, looking both ways.

## Description of the Discourse on the Lion's Roar

It is called "unsurpassed" (anuttara) because it is not shared with others and because its subject matter is not shared with others. "Great Lion's Roar" (mahāsīhanāda) refers to the great, bold speech of the Buddha. It is "supremely pure" (paramavisuddha) because it is exceedingly and ultimately pure. "Parama" means noble; thus the teacher said "utmost" (uttama). The teacher's intention is that the word "parama" is a synonym for "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha). "Only virtue" (sīlam-eva) refers to ordinary virtue because it is merely mundane virtue. Just as the Blessed One's supramundane virtue is not shared with others because it destroys opposing states along with latent tendencies, mundane virtue is also not shared with others because it proceeds in accordance with that [supramundane virtue]. Only in this way is the Pali statement "I am not there [in that virtue]" appropriate. "Kassapa, as far as there is noble, supreme virtue"—this statement shows the manner in the context of "they speak the praise of virtue." "This which is higher virtue" (yadidaṃ adhisīlaṃ) is an indefinite statement regarding the two terms "there" (tattha). "Yadidaṃ adhisīlaṃ" is said by combining both types of the Buddha's virtue, mundane and supramundane, into one. Therefore, to show that the word "ta" (that) also refers to both, he said "in that virtue and in the supreme virtue" and so forth. "Equal to the equal" (samā-sama) means equal to the virtue which is the qualifier; to make this meaning known, it is said "equal to me by virtue equal to my virtue." "In that virtue" (tasmiṃ sīle) means in both types of virtue. "Iti imaṃ" means thus this subject of virtue. "First" (paṭhama) is the first because it occurs first according to the order of arising.

"He burns" (tapati) means he torments the defilements, he destroys them—this is the meaning. By the word "tadeva," he states a coordinate compound (tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa). "He is disgusted" (jigucchati) means he scorns, he places it in a low position. They are called "Noble Ones" (ariya) because they are far from defilements and are faultless. "By way of the grounds for effort" (ārambhavatthu-vasena) means by way of the eight grounds for effort. "Reckoned as the energy of insight" (vipassanā-vīriya-saṅkhātā) means reckoned as energy associated with insight. Because it is merely mundane, it is just the "disgust of austerity" (tapo-jigucchā). The "disgust of austerity" reckoned as energy associated with the path and fruition is (the noble disgust of austerity)—this should be connected by way of the context.
361:
It is called parama (supreme) because it is superior to all efforts. Just as the state of one who has age is called yobbana (youth), the state of one who loathes is called jeguccha (loathing). Adhijeguccha refers to the Buddha's effort that loathes defilements, which is of two kinds—mundane and supramundane—as in the case of virtue (sīla). In the word 'therein' (tattha), it refers to both jeguccha (mundane) and adhijeguccha (supramundane). Kammassakatā-paññā (knowledge of the ownership of kamma) is the knowledge that functions in the way of 'there is benefit in giving, there is benefit in sacrifice,' and so on. As taught in the Vibhaṅga: 'Therein, what is the knowledge of the ownership of kamma? There is benefit in giving, there is benefit in sacrifice, there is benefit in offerings, there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds... excluding the insight knowledge that is in accordance with the Four Noble Truths, all wholesome wisdom accompanied by taints is called the knowledge of the ownership of kamma.'

All unwholesome deeds, whether one's own or another's, are not called 'one's own property' (saka). Why? Because they destroy welfare and produce harm. Similarly, all wholesome deeds are called 'one's own property.' Why? Because they destroy harm and produce welfare. Thus, the wisdom that functions in the state of kamma being one's own property is called kammassakatā-paññā. Vipassanā-paññā (insight wisdom) is called saccānulomika (conformity to truth) because it is in accordance with the Truth of the Path and the Ultimate Truth; it is simply wisdom occurring in the world. Here, the change from feminine gender to neuter gender is called liṅga-vippallāsa (reversal of gender). Adhipaññā (higher wisdom) refers to the Buddha's wisdom, which is of two kinds—mundane and supramundane—as in the case of virtue. In the word 'therein' (tattha), it refers to both paññā (mundane) and adhipaññā (supramundane).

It is called vimutti (liberation) because of its limited (paritta) or exalted (mahaggata) nature as appropriate. The absolute cutting off and subsequent tranquilization of defilements by the power of the Path and Fruit are called samuccheda-vimutti (liberation by cutting off) and paṭippassaddhi-vimutti (liberation by tranquilization). Alternatively, since the abstinences (virati) such as Right Speech and so on are included under the term adhisīla, Right Effort under adhijeguccha, and Right View under adhipaññā, then Right Intention, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration, which are included in the Path and Fruit but not yet mentioned, should be understood as samuccheda-vimutti and paṭippassaddhi-vimutti. Nissaraṇa-vimutti (liberation by escape), however, is only Nibbāna. Adhivimutti is of two kinds, as explained in the section on virtue. In the word 'therein' (tattha), it refers to both vimutti (mundane) and adhivimutti (supramundane).

Here, suññāgāra (empty dwelling) refers to any place secluded from people. To show that there is no other person there except the one roaring (one who speaks boldly like a lion), it is said 'alone,' and so on. The eight assemblies are: the assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three gods, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmas.
362:
To establish that meaning, he said "Cattārimāni" and so forth, citing the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta (M. i. 150) in the noble Majjhima Nikāya. In that text, "vesārajjāni" means the state of being intrepid (bold); it refers to the state of having no trepidation or fear from any cause when teaching the Dhamma concerning knowledge, things to be abandoned, things that are obstacles, and the way of deliverance. In truth, "vesārajja" is the name for the knowledge accompanied by joy that arises in the Blessed One when reflecting on the absence of fear in four areas. To show its uniqueness, not shared with other Paccekabuddhas and disciples, it is said, "tathāgatassa tathāgata-vesārajjāni" (the Tathāgata's Tathāgata-intrepidities). Alternatively, because the second word "tathāgata" is used in an appositional sense, it is said thus: "intrepidities that have come (āgata) just as (tathā) intrepidities came to previous Buddhas through the fulfillment of their accumulation of merit." This is the method of the Commentaries. Grammarians, however, say that it is stated thus because of its commonality when the compound is formed, and because it is a proper name.

Āsabha-ṭṭhāna means the noble position, the supreme position. Because they go forward by way of claiming omniscience, or because they approach the eight assemblies, the Buddhas are called "āsabha" (bull-like); their position is thus called āsabha-ṭṭhāna.

Furthermore, there are three types of bulls: a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called an usabha; a bull that is the leader of a thousand cows is called a vasabha. Or, a bull that is the leader of a hundred pens is an usabha; a bull that is the leader of a thousand pens is a vasabha. Or, a bull that is the leader in the territory of one village is an usabha; a bull that is the leader in the territory of two villages is a vasabha. A bull that is superior to all cattle, a leader everywhere, able to endure all dangers, white and graceful, capable of bearing great burdens, and unshakable even by hundreds of thunderclaps, is called a nisabha. In this context, only the nisabha is intended by the term "usabha." This word nisabha is also a synonym for that usabha. It is called āsabha because it belongs to the usabha (bull). Or, it is called āsabha because this position is like that of a nisabha bull. Indeed, just as the bull known as nisabha, endowed with the strength of a bull, stands in an unshakable position, pressing the earth with its four legs, so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, stands in an unshakable position in the world with its devas, pressing the earth of the eight assemblies with the four legs of intrepidity (vesārajja), unable to be shaken by any enemy or adversary. While standing thus, he claims that noble āsabha position, reaches it, and does not reject it but takes it upon himself. Therefore, it is said, "He claims the āsabha position."

Regarding "He roars the lion's roar" (sīhanādaṃ nadati), it means he speaks a noble speech, a fearless speech. Alternatively, he utters a sound similar to a lion's roar. This meaning should be understood through the Sīhanāda Sutta found in the Khandhavagga Saṃyutta. Or else, just as the lion, the king of beasts, is called "sīha" because it can endure dangers and because it can subdue and kill buffaloes, elephants, and so forth, so too the Blessed One, the king of monks, is called "sīha" because he endures worldly conditions (lokadhamma) and because he can subdue and destroy the doctrines of others. He utters the speech of the Blessed One who is thus called a "lion." In that simile, just as a lion, endowed with the strength of a lion, roars the lion's roar in all places boldly and without horripilation, so too the Buddha-lion, endowed with the ten powers, roars the lion's roar with his omniscient knowledge, which is adorned with various methods of teaching such as form and so forth, boldly and without horripilation in the eight assemblies. Therefore, it is said, "He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies." "Pañca abhisaṅkhārikā" refers to the creation of other desired things according to his own knowledge; and "taṅkhaṇaññeva" means at the very moment of asking and answering questions.
363:
A lion is called 'Sīha' because it can endure dangers and because it is capable of subduing and killing animals such as bulls and rutting elephants. Similarly, the Buddha, the King of Sages, is called 'Sīha' because He endures the worldly conditions (lokadhamma) and because He subdues and destroys the doctrines of others (parappavāda). The Buddha, who is thus called a Sīha, roars the 'Lion's Roar' (sīhanāda), which is His courageous speech. In that simile, just as the lion, the king of beasts, being endowed with the strength of a lion, is courageous in all places and roars the lion's roar without fear or trembling, so too the Buddha, the Lion King, being endowed with the Ten Powers of a Tathāgata, is courageous in the eight assemblies and, without fear or trembling, roars the Lion's Roar, which is endowed with the elegance of various methods of teaching, such as 'Thus is form (rūpa)', and so forth. Therefore, it is said, 'He roars the Lion's Roar in the assemblies.'

'Pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā' means having prepared the meaning to be known according to the power of His own knowledge. 'Taṅkhaṇaññeva' means He answers with the sharp analytical insight (paṭibhāna) that arises at that very moment of questioning. Because He answers according to the inclinations of the questioners and according to the benefit and the Dhamma, He truly causes the mind to be greatly pleased. 'Assa' means 'of that ascetic Gotama'. 'Sotabbaṃ maññanti' means that since the human existence is obtained in the ninth moment (the arising of a Buddha), excluding the eight inopportune moments, they think, 'Whatever our Teacher instructs, we shall listen to that.' Thus, with a sense of reverence, they consider it something to be listened to and accepted with great effort. 'Kallacittā muducittā' means that due to the great increase in devotion, their minds are free from defilements and thus become ready and soft. 'Muddhappasannā' refers to vain devotion or fruitless devotion. What is called the 'manner of devotion' (pasannākāra) is the honor and offerings (sakkāra) to be made by those who are devoted. That honoring is of two kinds: material offerings (āmisa-pūjā) and practice offerings (dhamma-pūjā). Among them, the material offering is shown by the words 'paṇītāni', etc. The practice offering is shown in the Pali text itself by the words 'tathattāya paṭipajjanti' (they practice for the sake of suchness).

'Tathābhāvāya' means for the sake of escaping from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha), for which purpose the Dhamma was taught. To show that very meaning, it is said 'dhammānudhammapatipattipūraṇatthāya' (for the purpose of fulfilling the practice in accordance with the Dhamma). Indeed, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapatipatti) ends in the escape from the suffering of the round of rebirths. That practice in accordance with the Dhamma must be practiced in a specific sequence; for those who practice, when the internal factors are complete, the fulfillment of that practice is certain. To show that sequence of practice, He said 'keci saraṇesu', etc. As to how those who fulfill the practice are able to fulfill it, it is said 'sabbākārena pana pūrenti' (but they fulfill it in every way) to show that manner of fulfillment.

'Imasmiṃ panokāse' refers to the section of the Pali text where the fulfillment of the function of the Lion's Roar is shown, stating 'those who practice also please Me'. 'Samodhānetabbā' means they should be combined and counted. 'Ekaccaṃ... passāmi' means the Buddha's unique Lion's Roar, which is not shared with others...
364:
...because it is a noble sound and a fearless sound that cannot be turned back by others. This method applies to the remaining ones as well. Furthermore, the word 'tapassiṃ' is a governing term (adhikāra) that carries forward. 'Of the first ten' refers to the ten primary Lion's Roars, starting from the Lion's Roar stated as 'I see a certain ascetic reborn in hell' up to the Lion's Roar stated as 'There is no one equal to Me in liberation (vimutti)'. This is a genitive of specification (niddhāraṇa-chaṭṭhī). Therefore, it is said (in the commentary), 'of each one'. The ten Lion's Roars starting from 'He roars in the assemblies' and ending with 'Those who practice please Me' are the attendant roars (parivāra). 

Indeed, the Blessed One, while roaring the Lion's Roar 'I see a certain ascetic reborn in hell', roars in the assemblies, roars being courageous; there they ask questions, He answers the questions, He pleases the minds of others with the answers, having heard they deem it worthy to be heard, having heard they become devoted to the Blessed One, being devoted they perform the manner of devotion, they practice the practice He teaches for the sake of that practice (or for the sake of liberation), and those who practice please Me—thus, the connection of the meaning by surrounding it in this way is appropriate. This same method applies to the remaining nine as well.

By the word 'evaṃ' and so forth, the aforementioned Lion's Roars are shown in combination. 'Those ten' refers to the ten Lion's Roars starting from 'He roars in the assemblies'. 'Of the first ten' refers to the aforementioned ten primary Lion's Roars. 'By way of attendants' means that by making the primary ones the base and associating each with its attendants, there are one hundred Lion's Roars. 'And the first ten' means that if the first ten primary ones are added without associating them by way of attendants, then there are one hundred and ten Lion's Roars. In another Sutta, such as the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, it is called 'Mahāsīhanāda' because of that greatness in number. Because it is a great Lion's Roar, this Sutta is called 'Mahāsīhanāda'; however, the intention is that it is not called so by depending on (comparing with) a Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, as is the case with the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Probation for Sectarians

'Paṭisedhetvā' means having rejected by showing the existence or non-existence of such states. In the Udumbarika Sutta of the Pāthika Vagga, the Blessed One, while showing the division of defilements (upakkilesa) and the division of purity (pārisuddhi), roared the Lion's Roar in front of the wanderer Nigrodha and his assembly, starting with 'Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic...'; to show that, the word 'idāni' and so forth is said. 'Naditapubbaṃ' means previously to the wanderer Nigrodha, according to the method that comes in the Udumbarika Sutta...
365: (He) has roared (like a lion's roar). Tapabrahmacārī means one who usually practices the supreme practice, or one who practices the holy life through austerity or energy. The word 'idaṃ' refers to the statement in the Pali: 'In the city of Rājagaha... asked a question.' The teacher (the sub-commentator) examines and explains only the aforementioned words of the commentary. In this context, although when Nigrodha the wanderer asked the question and the Blessed One answered it, the Blessed One was not staying on Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) but was staying in Queen Udumbarikā's park near the city of Rājagaha. This is because the asking and answering took place only in that park. Nevertheless, the Blessed One's residence at Vulture Peak had not yet ceased. Therefore, the words 'tatra maṃ' (me there) etc. are used in the Pali, and the words 'me staying at Vulture Peak in that city of Rājagaha' etc. are used in the commentary. This meaning should be understood as being made known by the words 'yaṃ taṃ bhagavā' etc. The phrase 'gijjhakūṭe pabbate' is shown to refer to the monastery (Mahāvihāra) built on that mountain by the words 'gijjhakūṭe mahāvihāre.' Udumbari-kāya refers to the park of that name. Uyyāne refers to the park of the wanderers (paribbājaka-ārāma) made in that park. Nigrodha is a clothed wandering ascetic. Sandhāna is an Anāgāmī lay follower with a retinue of five hundred lay followers. Kathāsallāpaṃ refers to the conversation such as 'Indeed, householder, you should know, with whom does the ascetic Gotama converse?' etc. The word 'paraṃ' is an indeclinable in the sense of 'excessively.' The word 'viya' is a mere filler particle (padapūraṇa), as in the word 'ativiya.' Andhabāla means a fool who is blind in the eye of wisdom. Yoge means in the method, in the sense of the means to escape from suffering. Anena refers to the Blessed One. Khandhake means in the Pabbajjā-khandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga; it should be connected as 'stays for the probation (parivāsa) which...'. The teacher, Venerable Sāriputta, said: 'Because he was formerly a titthiya outside the Sāsana in the past, he is called aññatitthiyapubba.' The teacher says 'one established in the stage of a novice (sāmaṇerabhūmi)' because one must stay for probation only after first taking the novice ordination. Taṃ refers to the probation spoken of in two ways. Pabbajjāṃ refers to the taking of the novice ordination spoken of here: 'He desires the novice ordination (pabbajjā), he desires the higher ordination (upasampadā).' The word 'diratta' (two nights) is mentioned here only for the sake of euphony, just as the word 'diratta' is used in the phrase 'one should make a shared bedding for two nights or three nights.' However, since one must stay for probation only while established in the novice stage and not as a layman, one receives the novice ordination (pabbajjā) without having stayed for probation. In the phrase 'one must not enter the village, etc.,' the word 'ādi' (etc.) includes: not going to the presence of prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, and bhikkhunīs; being skillful and not lazy in the duties of fellow practitioners; having keen desire in learning and questioning; and rejoicing when the faults of one's former titthiya teacher are spoken of.
366:
One who has come to this Dispensation from a sectarian background should be known to encompass these seven duties: being pleased when his former sectarian teacher is criticized, being displeased when the Buddha, etc., are criticized, being displeased when the sectarian teacher is praised, and being pleased when the Buddha, etc., are praised.

'Should reside undergoing probation' means that while undergoing probation, one should reside fulfilling the duties. One should reside by fulfilling the eight aforementioned duties. 'In this matter' refers to either the probation or the higher ordination. 'Rubbing and striking' is like rubbing and striking gold for the purpose of testing the inclination (of the person). 'For the sake of the going forth (pabbajjā)' is merely an illustration. By that word 'pabbajjā,' the higher ordination (upasampadā) is also included.

'Sitting in the midst of the group' means the Teacher said that he sat like a senior Elder of the Saṅgha in the midst of the monks sufficient for the act of higher ordination (upasampadākamma) in order to favor that person. Nowadays, however, in many manuscripts, the reading 'taṃ nisīdāpetvā' (having caused him to sit) is found in the causative sense. 'To one who is recently ordained' means an acirūpasampanna (one who has not been ordained for long). To show the meaning, it is said, 'having become ordained, not long ago.'

In this context, only physical seclusion (kāyaviveka) and mental seclusion (cittaviveka) are intended, because this is the stage of practice for the sake of detachment from the substrata of existence (upadhiviveka). Therefore, it is said, 'both by body and by mind.' 'Vūpakaṭṭha' means secluded. For such a person, heedfulness (appamāda) in purifying virtue is established even without being mentioned; therefore, only heedfulness in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is shown.

'One whose mind is sent forth' means one whose mind is sent forth towards Nibbāna, meaning one whose mind is inclined, sloped, and directed towards Nibbāna. Such a person is called one who has relinquished the body because of having no regard for other things; to clarify this meaning, it is said, 'one who has a relinquished self (attabhāva).' Here, 'self' (atta) refers to the mind, because the material body (rūpakāya) is not the object of inclining towards Nibbāna.

'Yassa' (for the sake of which) refers to the sake of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). Sons of good family by birth (jātikulaputta) also look forward to the going forth to attain Arahantship only when they are endowed with proper conduct. Therefore, wishing to group those sons of good family by birth together with sons of good family by conduct (ācārakulaputta), he said, 'ācārakulaputta.' By this, sons of good family by birth who are endowed with proper conduct are also included. That only those endowed with proper conduct are intended is known by the other word 'sammadeva' (thoroughly/rightly). The word 'sammadeva' is used in reference to the going forth according to the instruction, preceded by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), in the manner of 'I am submerged in birth,' etc. Therefore, he said, 'only by the root cause, only by the reason.' In that context, 'hetunā' means by the way or method. 'Kāraṇeneva' means...
367:
The phrase "kāraṇeneva" is an explanation of the meaning of the word "hetunā." "Taṃ" refers to the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). Indeed, only that Fruit of Arahantship deserves to be called "the unsurpassed end of the holy life" (anuttaraṃ brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ). This is because such a state does not exist in any other states besides the Fruit of Arahantship. By the grammatical rule that the words "yaṃ" and "taṃ" are always connected, this meaning is also shown by the words beginning with "tassa hi." The meaning is: "For the sake of which... they go forth"; for the sake of that Fruit of Arahantship mentioned previously, sons of good family (kulaputta) go forth. Therefore, it should be understood that the Fruit of Arahantship is intended here. One who has no other person to rely on (besides the Buddha) in such realization is called "aparappaccaya" (not depending on others); it refers to such a person. Intending that the prefix "saṃ-", like "upa-", follows the meaning of the root, it is said "pāpuṇitvā," meaning "having reached" or "having attained." Alternatively, intending that the prefix "upa-" follows the root's meaning while "saṃ-" qualifies it, it is said "sampādetvā," meaning "having accomplished" or "having fulfilled" the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training (asekha).

"Niṭṭhāpetuṃ" means to bring to a conclusion by way of a summary. With these words, "the end of the holy life... he dwelt," the teaching is concluded, crowned with the Fruit of Arahantship. To summarize that teaching, the words "a certain... became" were spoken by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka). Here, "aññatara" (a certain) refers to a single individual; it is not said because he was obscure in terms of name, clan, etc. The word "arahantānaṃ" is a genitive case in the sense of exclusion (niddhāraṇa), excluding [worldlings and those in training]. To show the meaning that, by being so excluded and distinguished, he became one among those Arahants, the words beginning with "bhagavato" were spoken. Some teachers, however, say that the word "arahantānaṃ" is a genitive case merely in the sense of relation (sambandha); therefore, the words beginning with "bhagavato" were spoken to show the meaning along with the rest of the text. In this sutta, words not specifically analyzed in terms of meaning are easily understood.

Thus ends the Līnatthappakāsanī, the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta Commentary, which clarifies the hidden meanings of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī (the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya), also known as Sādhuvilāsinī, which explains the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-understand meanings and generates pure and extensive wisdom.

## The Explanation of the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta Commentary is finished.
368:
## 9. Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta
## Commentary on the Story of Poṭṭhapāda the Wanderer
Having thus commented on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, now wishing to comment on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, the words of the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta beginning with "Thus have I heard... at Sāvatthī" are stated, either to show the opportunity for sequential commentary or to show that the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta is the sutta recited immediately after the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. To show that the word "Sāvatthiyaṃ" is a locative case in the sense of proximity, it is said "depending on the city of Sāvatthī." The meaning is "having made a dependence" because of being bound to requisites such as robes. There was a prince named Jeta; because it was planted, nurtured, and protected by him, it is called Prince Jeta's grove (park), hence "in Prince Jeta's Grove." The householder named Sudatta is called Anāthapiṇḍika because he gives food to the helpless (anātha). That merchant Anāthapiṇḍika bought the park from Prince Jeta by covering the ground with eighteen crores of gold, spent another eighteen crores to build the dwellings, and another eighteen crores to complete the dedication ceremony of the monastery. Thus, by relinquishing fifty-four crores of gold, he donated that monastery (ārāma) to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Therefore, it is said, "The monastery was built and donated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika." It is called "ārāma" because it is endowed with qualities such as flowers, fruits, and foliage, or because it provides comfort for living beings, and especially because monks come from various places and dwell there delightfully without weariness. Alternatively, it is called "ārāma" because, due to the aforementioned qualities, it causes one to delight within one's heart even when one has gone to various places.

One on whose feet boils (blisters) have arisen is called Poṭṭhapāda. "Phoṭa" and "poṭṭha" are synonyms. Wanderers (paribbājaka) are of two types: clothed wanderers (channa-paribbājaka) and naked wanderers (acchanna-paribbājaka). Among them, naked wanderers are also of two types: Acelaka and Ājīvaka. Of these two, the Acelaka is completely naked, while the Ājīvaka carries a single cloth on the upper body, tucked under the armpit, but is naked on the lower body. Since this Poṭṭhapāda the Wanderer was neither of those two, he is called a "clothed wanderer" (channa-paribbājaka). The meaning is that he is known as a clothed wanderer because he entered the wandering life covered by the shade of clothing. "Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla" refers to a brahmin who has reached great substance (wealth) due to having great fortune.
369:
The word 'Gaṇācariya' is a compound because it implies dependence (on the word 'gaṇa'). The designation 'Samayaṃ' is a general designation or a designation with one remaining; it means various doctrines. 'Pavadantī' means they speak in various ways; the meaning is that they speak of doctrines according to the traditions they have learned. 'Tārukkha' is the name of that Brahmin. By the word 'pabhuti,' Brahmins such as Todeyya, Jāṇussoṇī, Soṇadaṇḍa, and Kūṭadanta are included; by the word 'ādi,' the wanderer Channa and others are included. 'Tinduka' is the ebony tree with a black trunk. 'Cīra' means a row. Because there are rows of Tinduka trees in this park, it is called Tindukacīra. Similarly, because there is one hall in this park, it is called Ekasalaka. Desiring to show that meaning in detail according to what happened in the past, he said 'Yasmā,' etc. 'Iti katvā' means for this reason. By the words 'Tasmiṃ,' etc., the case endings are shown in accordance with the text.

Because of the analytical knowledge of all knowable things in many ways without remainder, and because of successive occurrences, the Buddha's knowledge seems to spread throughout the world; thus it is said, 'having spread the knowledge of omniscience.' Therefore, that knowledge is called the 'Net of Knowledge' (Ñāṇajāla). The fact that those to be tamed (veneyya) are included within that knowledge has been mentioned below (in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta). When he applies his mind to distinguish the beings to be tamed, first their status as being tamable appears in his knowledge. Then, investigating the accomplishment of tasks such as the establishment of the refuges, he said, 'investigating what will happen.' 'Nirodha' means the cessation of perception (saññānirodha). 'Nirodhā vuṭṭhāna' means emerging from that cessation (the re-arising of perception). The meaning is: having compared how all Buddhas explained cessation and emergence from cessation, and how they will explain them. 'Katipāhaccayena' means after the lapse of two or three days. The Pali text itself will state this meaning. 'Saraṇaṃ gamissatī' means he will go for 'refuge.' 'Hatthisāriputto means the son of an elephant trainer,' said the Teacher (Dhammapāla). Now, however, the reading 'Citto Hatthisāriputto' is seen. It means the son of an elephant trainer named Citta.

'Surattadupaṭṭa' means wearing a double-layered undergarment well-dyed with dye, by turning it over. The phrase 'wrapping around Mount Yugandhara' is a metaphorical statement, meaning 'if such a thing existed, it would be like that.' 'Meghavaṇṇa' means having the color of a red cloud, resembling a cloud illuminated by the twilight glow. The first word shows the perfection of shape, and the second word shows the perfection of color. 'Ekaṃsavaragata' means being placed on the noble left shoulder. This is also stated in the commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā.
370:
"Ekaṃsa" is the name of the robe worn covering the left shoulder. [Commentary on Sutta Nipāta, Nigrodhakappa Sutta (Vaṅgīsa Sutta) explanation]. In that commentary, "etaṃ" refers to the phrase "ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā." It should be connected as: the meaning of this term is to be understood as having arranged the robe in such a way that the left shoulder is covered.

"Paccaggha" means a bowl that is individually very valuable during the time it has not yet been determined (adhiṭṭhita), or it means a brand new bowl, or a bowl produced at that very moment. Of these two meanings, some teachers do not accept the former meaning (being very valuable). For that reason, the Teacher (Dhammapāla) stated in the Udāna Commentary: "Paccaggha means brand new; some say it means individually very valuable, but that is not good. This is because the Buddha Blessed Ones do not accept or use very expensive requisites." In this context as well, that teacher takes only the latter meaning (being new). Calling it "paccaggha" because it is new is said because it has acquired such a designation from the beginning, and because it is not used by others. Alternatively, because of the Buddha's determination (adhiṭṭhāna), that bowl is always called "paccaggha" (new).

"Selamayapatta" refers to a bowl made of stone the color of mung beans, given by the Four Great Kings. Indeed, this is the bowl constantly used by the Blessed One, as stated in the commentary on the Samacitta Sutta and other places.

"Attano" means according to his own wish or inclination, not urged by others. The phrase "atippagabhāvameva disvā" (seeing that it was still very early) is a statement of fact, intended to show that the time for alms-round had not yet arrived. In truth, the Blessed One had left the monastery early at that time, intending, "I will favor Poṭṭhapāda with a discourse that is conducive to his latent tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya)."

In the Pali text, in the phrase "atippago kho," the term "pago" is formed according to the Kaccāyana grammar by the arrival of the letters "o" and "ga" after the prefix "pa". The word "pa" alone expresses the meaning of "pāto" (early). According to other grammarians, it is an indeclinable (nipāta) just like the word "pāto". For that reason, in various commentaries, it is explained as: "atippago kho means extremely early." Furthermore, the derivation (nibbacana) is shown as: "pago" because it goes first or occurs as the beginning of the day. Just as the word "khalu" is of two types as a noun and an indeclinable, the word "pago" is of three types as a noun, an indeclinable, and a prefix. Only if this is so, the phrase "atippagabhāvameva disvā" in this context will be appropriate.
371:
The particle “Yaṃnūna” usually indicates doubt in other contexts, but here it indicates only the appearance of doubt. If one asks, “Why is it said to ‘indicate doubt’? Do the Buddhas not have no doubt?”, the answer is given starting with “Buddhañca,” etc. There is no such thing as doubt for the Buddhas, as it was completely eradicated at the foot of the Bodhi tree. “Parivitakkapubbabhāga” refers to the thought occurring prior to the intended action. This mental process of “I shall do it, I shall not do it,” etc., occurs in all Buddhas through the power of investigation, but not through the power of doubt. Because it occurs in all Buddhas (through investigation), the Blessed One spoke thus, using this very Pali as evidence for this meaning.

This is another method from the Commentary— “Yaṃnūna” is a particle meaning reflection (parikappa). This word highlights the meaning expressed by the verb “upasaṅkameyyaṃ” (I should approach). Therefore, the construction is: “If I were to approach, it would be good.” The phrase “Yadi pana” is also stated to have the same meaning as that (yaṃnūna), as in “Yadi panāhanti attho.”

“Assa” refers to the assembly of wanderers (paribbājaka). “By way of going upwards” means the occurrence of sounds rising higher and higher. “By way of spreading in the directions” means spreading to all directions through the succession of the great elements in a vast manner. In this Pali, just as a sound that mostly rises upwards is called “unnāda,” a sound that occurs successively in a vast manner is also called “unnāda.” Therefore, combining both, it is called “unnādiniyā,” and then separating those two, it is called “uccāsadda-mahāsaddāya.” Thus, it should be understood that the meaning is explained in accordance with the method of the Pali. Now, wishing to show the reason for the high and loud noise of the assembly of wanderers and the manner of its occurrence, he said “Tesañhi,” etc. “Bālātapa” refers to the heat of the newly risen sun. “Kāmassa-āda” is the enjoyment of the cords of sensual pleasure. “Bhavassa-āda” is the enjoyment of existences along with sensual craving, etc.

Regarding the lack of radiance like a firefly when the sun rises, it is said “khajjopanaka-ūpamā jātā.” The meaning “our gain and honor have also declined” should be understood through the Bāveru Jātaka. “Parisa-dosa” is the fault occurring in the assembly.

“Saṇṭhapesi” means he settled them well through the power of restraint. Here, “settling” (saṇṭhapana) means teaching conduct by making them abandon animal-talk (tiracchānakathā) and disrespect for one another, and also concealing the aforementioned faults of the assembly.
372:
Because it involves teaching conduct and concealing the aforementioned faults of the assembly, it is said “sikkhāpesi,” etc. “Naṃ” refers to the assembly. “Appasaddaṃ” means being noiseless, without high or loud sounds. “Eko nisīdati,” etc., shows the fault that has arisen in terms of meaning. “Vuddhiṃ” means the increase of gain and virtuous qualities. “Patthayamāno” is due to the cause of desiring. Scholars of grammar desire the suffixes -māna and -anta in the sense of characteristic (lakkhaṇa) and cause (hetu). Now, to elaborate on that meaning, he began with “Paribbājakā kira,” etc. “Aparaddhaṃ” means having offended. “Nappamajjanti” means they do not fall into negligence; it means they do not show disrespect.

It means there is joy (ānanda) when the Blessed One comes to us. The statement “Venerable Sir, it has been a long time since the Blessed One came to this wanderers’ park” is like a statement made because he had been there before. Having raised such an objection, wishing to dispel it, he said “Kasmā āha,” etc. “Piyasamu-dācārā” means speaking endearing words. Therefore, it is because of speaking such endearing words. Not only this Poṭṭhapāda wanderer alone shows respect, but other monks also mostly show respect to the Blessed One. Therefore, to accomplish that meaning of respect through the common behavior of others, he said “Bhagavantañhi,” etc. The reason for such respect is stated as “uccākulīnatāya,” meaning because of being of a Khattiya lineage unmixed with other castes since King Mahāsammata. Thus, the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa said, “Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is one who has gone forth from a high family, from an unmixed Khattiya family.” By this statement, even those not yet confident in the Dispensation show respect to the Blessed One out of respect for his lineage. “What talk was there in this interval?” means within the aforementioned limit, what kind of talk had started but was not yet finished? By asking “What talk is unfinished?”, he acknowledges the conclusion of that talk in meaning. By asking “What talk?” without specification, he has acknowledged the conclusion of any talk whatsoever. Since such an acknowledgment is not the domain of one who knows only a part, he said “yāva... sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi.” “Esā” refers to the talk about kings, etc., spoken in the assembly of wanderers. “Nissārā” means they are devoid of essence because they are useless.

## Commentary on the Talk on the Cessation of Higher Perception

Wishing to show the meaning that has arrived for the phrase “tiṭṭhatesā,” he said “sace,” etc. “Sukāraṇaṃ” means a good cause that brings about benefit and welfare. “Yattha” means...
373:
It occurred in a certain hall without a specific name. Because they are associated with views called 'various views,' they are called 'nānātitthiya.' (In that word,) by using the suffix 'ṇika' and changing the letter 'ka' to 'ya,' it is called 'nānātitthiya,' similar to the word 'antiya.' Because there was a noisy curiosity (kotūhala) and uproar, with people asking, 'What is this person saying? What is that person saying?', that hall is called 'kotūhalasālā.' Therefore, the teacher said, 'Because it is the place where curiosity arises.' The word 'abhi' is merely a prefix (upasagga) because it follows the meaning of the root. Since this teaching is based on perception (saññā), all states associated with perception are included. Among those states, because the mind (citta) is primary, it is said, 'in the cessation of the mind.'

Because they do not desire absolute cessation (accantanirodha) through abandonment, and because it is not within their scope, it is called 'momentary cessation (khaṇikanirodha).' Indeed, even that momentary cessation is not within their scope. However, according to the meaning, when the discourse on cessation is spoken, it stands only in that momentary cessation. Therefore, it should be understood that it was said so just by reaching the meaning. 'Tassā' refers to the discourse on the cessation of higher perception (abhisaññānirodhakathā). 'Fame (kittighosa)' means the sound of praise that spreads as far as the highest plane of existence (bhavagga), saying, 'Oh, the power of the Buddha is wonderful! He clearly shows the cause hidden in another life as if it were an emblic myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, and he establishes his disciples in such restraint (saṃvara).' This was said by the teacher (the ancient sub-commentator). Now, however, the reading is found: 'The fame of the Buddha's discourse spreads throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.'

'Paṭibhāgakiriya' refers to an effort made in imitation through rivalry. 'Bhavantarasamaya' means they speak of their own views based on some falsely imagined cause occurring in various lives. 'A certain training rule' (kiñcideva sikkhāpadaṃ) means they prescribe a portion of training based on some reason, such as 'there must be a single root' or 'one must sit in one place for this much time.' 'Nirodhakathā' refers to the talk concerning the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

'Tesu' refers to the various sectarian ascetics and brahmins assembled in the Hall of Curiosity. 'Some' refers to those who hold the view, 'The perceptions of a person arise and cease without cause or condition.' Among these four types of theorists, it refers to a person in this five-constituent realm (pañcavokārabhuṃ). 'Samāpatti' refers to the preliminary work (parikamma) for the air kasiṇa or space kasiṇa that leads to the realm of non-percipient beings, or the attainment of the fourth or fifth fine-material jhāna. 'In cessation' means in the cessation of perception as mentioned above. 'Because of not seeing the cause' means not seeing both the cause by which perception absolutely ceases in the realm of non-percipient beings and the cause by which perception arises again in this realm after passing away from that realm, because these are not within the scope of one's own knowledge...
374:
...because of not seeing the cause of the arising of perception in the five-constituent realm, as both causes are not the objects of one's own knowledge.

The second theorist is one who holds the view, 'O sirs, perception is indeed the self of a person,' and so on. 'Naṃ' refers to the first theorist. 'Nisedhetvā' means rejecting by saying, 'O sir, this cessation of perception will not be as you say.' 'Migasiṅgatāpasassa' refers to the ascetic of that name. It is heard that two topknots in the shape of deer horns grew on the head of that ascetic Migasiṅga; he was also named 'Isisiṅga.' 'Asaññakabhāvaṃ' refers to reaching the state of being without perception through the perception produced by the act of falling into a faint. For it will be said later, 'having become non-percipient (visaññī hutvā).' To briefly show the story of the ascetic Migasiṅga according to the method in the Cattālīsanipāta, it is said, 'The ascetic Migasiṅga, it is said,' and so on. He is called 'self-tormenting (attantapa)' because he burns away the defilements by way of abandonment through suppression (vikkhambhana). He is called 'severe in austerity (ghoratapa)' and 'intense in austerity (tibbatapa)' because of his difficult practices. He is called 'one with supreme faculty of steadfastness (paramadhitiindriya)' because he withered the sharp faculties such as the eye in every way by bringing about a state of non-indulgence in defilements. 'Sakkavimāna' is said in reference to the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. That stone seat, due to such causes, sometimes becomes hot, sometimes hard, and sometimes trembles. Sakka, thinking unwisely, 'He aspires to [my position],' sent [a celestial maiden]. 'Bhagga' means one whose wholesome intention has been broken. Nowadays, however, some write the variant reading 'lagga' (attached). 'By that divine touch (tena dibbaphassena)' means by the divine touch of merely holding the hand. 'Taṃ' refers to regaining perception in that manner. 'Evamāha' means speaking of the cessation of perception in this way: 'O sirs, perception is indeed the self of a person,' and so on. In this same way, the connection should be understood by bringing in the Pali text in the next two places from here.

The third theorist is one who holds the view, 'O sirs, there are indeed recluses and brahmins,' and so on. 'Āthabbaṇapayoga' refers to the practice of those skilled in the Atharva Veda, as prescribed in the Atharva Veda, which brings about a state of non-perception. 'Upakaḍḍhana' means bringing or drawing towards. 'Apakaḍḍhana' means removing or taking away. 'Āthabbaṇam payojetvā' means speaking of the cessation of perception by demonstrating things like the cutting off of the head, using mantra verses preceded by fire-offerings as found in the Atharva Veda. 'Tassa' refers to that person to whom the cutting off of the head, etc., was shown.

The fourth theorist is one who holds the view, 'O sirs, there are indeed deities of great power,' and so on. 'Yakkhadāsīnaṃ' refers to spirit-maidens (spirit mediums), who are also called 'Yogavatī.'
375:
They are also known as yoginīs. Madanidda means sleep caused by intoxication from liquor. Devatūpahāra refers to making offerings to deities through dancing, singing, and so forth. Surāpāti refers to a bowl full of liquor. Divā means when the sun is high, or midday. Waking up from such sleep is referred to as 'taṃ'. The meaning is that while one is asleep, because the deities removed perception (saññā), one reaches cessation (nirodha); and upon waking, because the deities bring back perception, one is thought to have emerged from cessation.

The speech of those who consider themselves wise is like the speech of the blind or the foolish; thus it is said, 'eḷamūgakathā viya'. The four cessations that are mutually contradictory are called 'cattāro nirodhe'. Since cessation must have a single nature, it is said, 'ekena bhavitabbaṃ'. Since there should not be many mutually contradictory natures, it is said, 'na bahunā'. That cessation, which has a single nature, must be of a different kind than what they say. No one except the All-knowing Buddha can know that cessation which has a single nature. Saying "This is cessation, this is cessation" twice in this Debating Hall (Kotūhalasālā) was done by Poṭṭhapāda to indicate that the Blessed One, by the power of His teaching, would clarify cessation in its many aspects. In the phrase 'aho nūna', 'aho' is a particle meaning wonder, and 'nūna' is a particle meaning recollection. Therefore, 'aho nūna bhagavā' means that because His teaching is unique, the Blessed One would preach cessation in a wonderful way and satisfy the listeners. The same method applies to the phrase 'aho nūna sugato'. It is repeated twice to make the wonder clear. Poṭṭhapāda took this word 'aho', which has the sense of wonder, primarily in the sense of recollection. Thus it is said, "two particles in the sense of recollection (anussaraṇa)". Since it arose primarily from recollection, it should be connected as: "With the words 'aho... sugato', this thought occurred." To show the connection with the meaning that the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' are always related, he said 'yo etesaṃ', etc. Because these states of cessation are numerous due to distinctions of time, place, person, etc., the genitive plural 'imesaṃ nirodhadhammānaṃ' is used. Since it is associated with the word 'kusala', it should be seen in the locative sense (bhummattha). Kusala, nipuṇa, and cheka are synonyms. 'Aho nūna katheyya' means the expectation that He would preach in a wonderful way. That Sugata (the Blessed One), having mastery (vasībhāva) practiced in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), knows the nature of cessation as it really is.
376:
## Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising and Cessation of Perception Without a Cause
Just as men wishing to go out from a house, before reaching the road, slip on the level floor or the open courtyard inside the house, so should the meaning of the fulfillment of this simile be understood. The distinction that an uncommon cause is called hetu and a common cause is called paccaya is mentioned elsewhere. However, here there is no benefit in such a distinction; because it follows a challenge rejecting the causelessness of perception, it is said "only because of a cause."

In the Pali text, in the statement "Poṭṭhapāda, a man's perceptions arise with a cause and cease with a cause," the phrase "they also cease" is said to show the meaning that perceptions that have arisen merely vanish and do not remain forever. It is not said to show that cessation has a cause. Only arising has a cause; cessation has no cause. If cessation also had a cause, then that cessation would have to cease again, just as a sprout arises again from a sprout. But there is no further cessation of that cessation. Therefore, the meaning of the Pali should be understood only by the method already stated.

This method is stated in terms of momentary cessation (khaṇanirodha). There is a cessation that never arises again (anuppādanirodha) by way of a determined period; because that cessation cannot occur without such training (sikkhā), it should be understood as "having a cause." Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Through training, a certain perception arises; through training, a certain perception ceases." For this very reason, it is also said in the Commentary: "To show the arising and cessation of perception with a cause." These words of the Pali and the Commentary should be understood as referring to cessation without re-arising.

The word "sikkhā" is in the nominative case (pathamāvibhatti) in the sense of a cause (hetu). Or, it is the elision of the letter ya, as in "saṅkhāpi tamhā vanapattā pakkamitabbaṃ," etc. How this training acts as a cause will be made clear later. The word "eka" is also a synonym for "añña" (other/some); it does not denote a number. It is like in the phrase "a certain being in this world," etc. Therefore, it is said, "Through training, certain perceptions arise." The same method applies to the remaining words.

"Vitthāretukamyatā" means due to the desire to elaborate. "Pucchāvasena" means by way of questioning with the desire to preach. Or, it should be understood as a compound (samāsa) meaning "by way of questioning with the desire to elaborate." Because there might be doubt that "this question is only Poṭṭhapāda's question," it is said in the Pali, "The Blessed One said." Showing those trainings to demonstrate the causal arising and cessation of perception...
377:
The construction should be made. In that statement, 'tattha' means in that teaching which will be spoken of above. 'Tatiyā' should be construed as 'the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā) has come.' In this text, 'Ayaṃ...pe... desito,' it comes by way of right view (sammādiṭṭhi) and right intention (sammāsaṅkappa). If it is asked why it comes, the meaning is that it is because it is included, by its nature, and by way of assistance, it is appropriately counted and included within the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). For this very reason, it was said in the Cūḷavedalla Sutta: 'Friend Visākha, whatever is right view and whatever is right intention, these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom.' Although all three trainings (sikkhā) come in the manner mentioned here, the cessation of perception is shown only through the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā). The remaining trainings, however, are brought in as requisites for that training in higher mind; this meaning should be understood by the power of the Pali.

'Pañcakāmaguṇikarāga' (lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure) is the lust that arises with respect to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Asamuppannakāmacāra' (un-arisen sensual conduct) is the occurrence of any indefinite sensual defilement or any arising of greed that is not currently arisen in the present time. At present, however, there is a reading 'asamuppannakāmarāga'; that reading is inappropriate because it is contradictory in meaning. Here, 'kāmarāga' (sensual lust) should be understood as greed having the strands of sensual pleasure as its object, because it is restricted by the power of the object. 'Kāmacāra,' however, is the occurrence of all types of greed, such as attachment to jhāna (bhavarāga) and so forth. It is called 'kāmacāra' because of the sense of being desired and because of the sense of occurring in sensual objects. Indeed, all states belonging to the three realms are called 'kāma' in the sense of being desirable. Since the state of 'kāmasaññā' (perception of sensuality) occurs by way of the method of association for both, it should be understood that the term 'kāmasaññā' is extracted to indicate both. The statement beginning with 'tattha' is either to show the distinction of 'pañcakāmaguṇikarāga' from 'asamuppannakāmacāra,' or to show that only 'asamuppannakāmacāra' is intended here. Even if 'pañcakāmaguṇikarāga' is also un-arisen and is eradicated by the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga), even when that lust is eradicated, not all lust reaches total eradication, because that [remaining] lust is only eradicated by the highest path (arahattamagga). Therefore, since taking 'pañcakāmaguṇikarāga' does not include all the remaining lust, both are included by the figurative method common to both, and the term 'kāmasaññā' is used in the Pali. Therefore, showing both by their nature and by their distinction, it is said that 'asamuppannakāmacāra is appropriate in this place' in the sense of encompassing all. Therefore, this meaning should be understood because only 'asamuppannakāmacāra' is appropriate here.
378:
The construction 'should be understood' is applied. 'Tassa' refers to the person possessed of the first jhāna. 'Sadisattā' means because of being similar to the state of sensual perception and so forth; by this, it is shown that the word 'purimā' (former) in the Pali is spoken by way of conceiving similarity. Indeed, the future perception is said to 'cease' here in the sense that non-arising (anuppāda) is intended. Therefore, to show only the future [perception], it is said: 'what has not yet arisen does not arise.'

'Vivekajapītisukhasaṅkhātā' means the perception described together with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion; it does not mean the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion themselves. Indeed, only the perception associated with those is intended here, not the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Alternatively, it means [perception] having the constituent of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Here, the word 'saṅkhāta' has the meaning of 'constituent' or 'group' (koṭṭhāsa), as in the passage 'taking what is not given, reckoned as theft' (theyyasaṅkhāta). It is called 'subtle' (sukhuma) because it is more refined than the perception of diversity (nānattasaññā) and perception of resistance (paṭighasaññā) by way of abandoning gross factors such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda). It is called 'true' (saccā) because of its reality. That very meaning is shown by the word 'bhūtā.' It means having an undeceptive nature by way of its subtlety and its ultimate (paramattha) state. Having thus shown the meaning according to the text in detail, the author says 'atha vā' (or else) and so forth, wishing to show it according to the text in summary as well. Indeed, the text is seen in two ways: by way of summary and detail. By the phrase 'by way of abandoning gross factors such as sensual desire,' it is shown that the refinement and subtlety of perception, which is accomplished by the power of the development (bhāvanā) of associated states, is known by way of the displacement of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). 'Bhūtatā' means because of being undeceptive by way of its subtlety and ultimate state, or because of its existence in the ultimate sense. 'Vivekajehi' means by those [rapture and pleasure] born of seclusion from the hindrances. Now, to show the meaning of the second term spoken by way of the person possessed of jhāna, the passage beginning with 'sā assā' is stated. 'Sabbattha' means in all cycles (vāra).

Just like the attainment and resolution of jhāna, emerging from jhāna is also included in the jhāna, just as the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhana) of phenomena is included in those phenomena. However, reflection and reviewing (āvajjana, paccavekkhaṇā) are not included in the jhāna. Therefore, taking only the mastery (vasībhāva) that is included in the jhāna, it is said: 'he trains attaining, resolving, and emerging.' 'Taṃ' refers to the first jhāna. The phrase 'tena...pe... jhāneana' is also an explanatory term for 'sikkhā' (training). In the word 'tena,' the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause (hetu); it means 'by reason of the first jhāna.' Here, the causal state (hetubhāva) of the jhāna is its being a conascent condition (sahajātappaccaya) and so forth for the arising of the subtle true perception associated with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. For the cessation of sensual perception, however, it is only a decisive support condition (upanissayappaccaya). And that is indeed by way of the Suttanta method. Likewise, below...
379:
Below, the explanation 'Because it cannot be without such practice' has been clarified.
