'By this method' refers to the method I, the commentator, stated in the text: 'Through training one perception arises, through training another perception ceases,' by means of the first jhāna and the perception that is its opposite. 'In all places' means in all the sections on jhāna.

Now, wishing to clarify the reason for showing the perception that has the Sphere of Nothingness as its limit, the text says 'Yasmā pana,' etc. The connection should be made as: 'Because this contemplation of perception as perception by way of factors has been expounded.' However, to the question 'By way of which person's jhāna factors does this contemplation occur?', the text says 'Aṭṭhasamāpattiyā,' etc. 'By way of factors' (aṅgato) means by way of jhāna factors. This phrase 'by way of factors' is a characteristic description of insight into states in successive order (anupadadhamma-vipassanā). For a monk who practices insight into the formations of the three planes in successive order as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, does so by reaching a meditative attainment and contemplating only by way of the jhāna factors as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Although perception is not a specific factor of the jhāna attainment, because it is said 'this contemplation of perception as perception by way of factors has been expounded,' this statement is merely a characteristic description. 'By way of factors' (aṅgato) means by way of parts; it means in successive order. 'By way of a group' (kalāpato) means as a whole. Since the arising and cessation of various perceptions are spoken of here by way of meditative attainments, they are spoken of by way of jhāna factors; thus, it should be understood that by 'Idañca,' etc., contemplation by way of factors alone is shown. Because contemplation by way of factors is expounded only by means of perception, 'Tadeva' refers only to the Sphere of Nothingness, not the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, because there is no distinct perception in that Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.

Where 'Yo' should be said, 'Yato' is said; thus it says 'Yo nāma.' It is like saying 'Ādito' where 'Ādi-mhi' should be said. When the meaning is grasped, the suffix '-to' is obtained with the appropriate case ending. This word 'nāma' is merely for euphonic purposes, like the word 'kho.' 'Sassedam' means one's own property, the jhāna. The perception in the jhāna one has attained is called 'one's own perception' (sakasaññā). Because that person has that perception, he is called 'one possessing his own perception' (sakasaññī); therefore, it is said 'one possessing perception by means of one's own first jhāna perception.' In this term 'sakasaññī,' the 'ī' ending should be understood as indicating the presence of an extraordinary jhāna perception which is the basis for the cessation of perception to be mentioned later. For this very reason, it is said 'He touches the peak of perception in due order,' etc. Therefore, it should be understood that by taking the possession of one's own perception in each jhāna, the mastery (vasībhāva) well-practiced in every way in those respective jhānas is shown.

The word 'Lokiyānaṃ' is a genitive case in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa), or simply in the possessive sense. Because the Sphere of Nothingness is the best among those mundane jhānas in that respect, it is the best of them; thus the genitive case is used in the possessive sense. Or, it is the genitive case in the sense of the ablative (apādāna).
380:
It is the genitive case (sāmivacana). Here, the qualification 'mundane' (lokiyānaṃ) is made because the Sphere of Nothingness is not superior to the supramundane attainments. The remaining qualification 'of attainments that perform a function' (kiccakaraka-samāpattīnaṃ) should be understood as being made because the Sphere of Nothingness is not superior to the attainment that does not perform a function. The fact that the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception does not perform a function is understood from the statement in the commentaries regarding the absence of distinct perceptual function: 'Just as there is perception there, so too there are contact and so on,' and 'Because the states there have reached the state of residual formations and exist in a form that those practicing ordinary insight are unable to contemplate, they are not capable of performing a distinct function like the states of the lower attainments.'

This meaning is specifically stated by the Teacher in the section on the Formless (Āruppakathā) in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā named Paramatthamañjūsā; therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated there. Some teachers, however, say: 'Just as the lower attainments perform the function of serving as a basis (adhiṭṭhāna) for the higher attainments, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception does not serve as a basis for any jhāna; therefore, it is non-functional, while the others are functional.' That statement is incorrect, because the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception also performs the function of serving as a basis for taming the mind for insight and so on. Therefore, only the previously stated meaning is appropriate. To the question 'Why is this [Sphere of Nothingness] the peak of those states?', the text says 'Ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiyaṃ,' etc. Having said 'Iti,' the meaning is stated as 'Because it is the peak of the mundane... etc.'; or in the word 'aggattā' (being the peak), this 'iti' is merely an illustration.

'Pakappeti' means he arranges or prepares. One who enters jhāna is said to arrange the bliss of jhāna within himself. 'Abhisaṅkharoti' means he strives or accumulates. The sense of accumulating is the sense of a group. Since the function of volition (cetanā) reaches its peak by way of attachment (nikanti), the text says 'Nikantiṃ... etc.,' showing the cause by way of metonymy of the result (phalūpacāra). 'These perceptions of the Sphere of Nothingness' refers to the perceptions of the Sphere of Nothingness currently obtained. Only by transcending that perception can there be the volitional processing for the sake of the higher jhāna; thus, they should cease. 'Other' means perceptions other than those of the Sphere of Nothingness. 'Gross' (oḷārika) means perceptions that are coarser than that. To the question 'What are they?', the text says 'Bhavanga-perceptions.' For only after emerging from the Sphere of Nothingness can there be volitional processing for the sake of the higher jhāna. In this way, the perceptions of the Sphere of Nothingness would cease. Emergence from jhāna occurs by way of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Even after that, until the attainment of the higher jhāna, bhavanga-perceptions would arise at intervals. The intention is that those bhavanga-perceptions are grosser than the perceptions of the Sphere of Nothingness.
381:
‘Cetentovā’ (even while intending) means only the arranging by way of attaining the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaānāsaāyatana-jhāna) for one or two thought-moments. ‘Na ceteti’ (does not intend) means it is not called ‘arranging’ in that manner because there is no prior reflection (pubbābhoga) as there is in the lower absorptions. Indeed, one who arranges the absorption by way of prior reflection is said to ‘intend’ (ceteti) here. ‘Abhisankharontovā’ (even while constructing) means only the striving according to the unabandoned attachment (nikanti) in that absorption. ‘Nābhisankharoti’ (does not construct) means it is not called ‘striving’ because there is no prior reflection as in the lower absorptions. Such construction (processing) as ‘I will produce this absorption, I will attain it, I will enter it’ occurs only for one who has longing (ālaya) for that absorption, not for one without longing. Therefore, one who produces the absorption for even one or two thought-moments is said to be ‘even while constructing’ (abhisankharonto eva) because of the unabandoned attachment to that absorption. Because that monk has no prior reflection in that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as he had in the lower absorptions, it is said ‘he does not construct’ (na abhisankharoti).

The passage beginning with ‘imassa bhikkhuno’ (of this monk) is an explanation of the meaning already stated. In that sentence, the meaning is: because this monk has..., therefore it is said ‘he does not intend, he does not construct.’ ‘Ābhogasamannāhāro’ means what is called reflection (ābhoga), or the bringing of the mind towards the object, or the bringing of the object towards the mind by the power of reflection. The passage beginning with ‘svāyamattho’ explains that same meaning with a simile. ‘Puttagharācikkhaမena’ means by the method of pointing out the son’s house.

It is connected as ‘having gone, having taken, he came.’ ‘Pacchābhāge’ means at the back of the father’s house, which is situated to the west of the refectory (āsanasālā). ‘Tato’ means from the son’s house. ‘Laddhagharameva’ means only that son’s house from which the monk received alms. The attainment of the sphere of nothingness (ākiမcaāyatana-samāpatti) should be understood as the refectory, because from there one approaches the attainments of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), which are like the father’s house and the son’s house. The attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should be understood as the father’s house, because it is not to be reflected upon and because it is situated in the middle. The attainment of cessation should be understood as the son’s house, because it is to be reflected upon and because it is situated at the end. ‘Pitugharaမ amanasi-karitvā’ means without reflecting on the father’s house which he had entered and passed through. Just like pointing out only the son’s house, one should understand the reflection only for the sake of the attainment of cessation ahead, without reflecting on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception which is to be entered for only one or two moments. In this way, the relationship of simile and the thing illustrated (upamā-upameyya) is stated through the similarity of non-reflection and the similarity of reflection, because even by pointing out, only reflection is illuminated. Indeed, pointing out is not possible without reflection.
382:
‘Those perceptions of jhāna’ (tā jhānasaāti) refers to the perceptions of the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception occurring for one or two thought-cycles. Indeed, in the attainment of cessation, the fourth immaterial wholesome or functional impulsion (javana) occurs only twice as appropriate, and not beyond that. ‘They cease’ (nirujjhantĩti) means they cease by their own nature; however, due to the power of prior construction (pubbābhisaᅅkhāra), there is no further arising above that. To show that just as the jhāna perceptions do not arise, so too other perceptions do not arise, he said ‘And others’ (aā ca) etc. The meaning is that they do not arise for the duration of the determined time. ‘The monk who has practiced thus’ refers to the monk who has practiced by way of standing at the culmination of perception (saagga) as mentioned. That monk is either an Anāgāmġ or an Arahant, endowed with two fruits; the meaning is that he has practiced the path leading to cessation by way of the subsiding of the three formations, the sixteen types of knowledge-conduct (āᅇacariya), and the nine types of concentration-conduct (samādhicariya). The non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors by way of successive cessation is called ‘the cessation of perception and feeling’ (saāvedayitanirodha), taking perception and feeling as the heads. ‘He touches’ (phusatĩ) here means experiencing or obtaining, as shown by the words ‘he experiences, he obtains.’ In essence, according to the method mentioned, it is the total non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors for the duration of the determined time.

Since it is meaningless, the word ‘abhi’ is merely a prefix (upasagga); therefore, the meaning is simply ‘perception’ (saā). Regarding the placement of the word ‘sampajāna’ (clearly comprehending) between the words ‘nirodha’ (cessation) and ‘samāpatti’ (attainment), he said ‘it is stated by separating it from the word nirodha.’ Therefore, the commentary ‘anu...pe... attho’ is stated. By that, he shows that this direct reading is an irregular compound (ayutta-samāsa). ‘There too’ (tatrāpi) is construed as: even in such a sequential placement of words, this is the specific meaning. ‘Of one who clearly comprehends’ (sampajānantassa) means of the person who, having entered and emerged from various attainments, knows by way of reviewing the formations therein. ‘At the end’ means at the conclusion of the practice leading to the attainment of cessation as mentioned. In the second alternative, ‘of one who clearly comprehends’ means one who acts with clear comprehension; by this, the knowledge that accomplishes the purpose is shown through its function, along with the knowledge of all-round miracles, starting from the beginning for the monk who enters the attainment of cessation. Therefore, he said ‘of the wise monk’ (paᅇᅃitassa bhikkhuno). The difference between the two alternatives is the regard or disregard for the remaining words. Since the opportunity for explanation has arrived, the discourse on the attainment of cessation should be told. In every way (sabbākārena) refers to the specific nature of the attainment of cessation, the person who enters it, the place of entry, the cause of entry, the manner of entry, and so forth...
383:
In every way (the attainment of cessation is shown). In that word 'sabbappakārena', because it has been spoken of in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.307), the phrase 'kathi-tatovā' means 'only from the place already spoken of,' referring to the twenty-third chapter. The meaning is that it is not explained here in this Sīlakkhandhavagga Commentary to avoid repetition and to prevent the text from becoming too voluminous.

In the Pali, in the phrase 'evaṃ kho ahaṃ,' the word 'evaṃ' has the sense of 'mode' (ākāra) because it shows the mode of what has been grasped. However, in the phrase 'evaṃ Poṭṭhapāda,' it has the sense of 'acceptance' (sampaṭicchana) because it signifies agreement in the same way. Therefore, the Teacher said, 'It has been well grasped by you,' while giving his approval.

In this attainment of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), because perception is the culmination or the highest, it is called 'saññagga' (the summit of perception). When it is said that 'saññagga' exists in the remaining attainments as well, it refers to the state of being the summit of perception. Alternatively, it can be understood as a tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa (appositional compound) meaning 'perception itself is the highest.' The word 'puthū' is either a gender transformation (liṅgavipallāsa) or an elision of the letter 'ni' (nikāralopa); therefore, the Teacher explained it as 'bahūni' (many). By the word 'yathā,' a specific kind of mode known as the mode of cause is taken, not just a general mode; this is shown by the words 'pathavīkasiṇādīsu' (in the earth-kasina, etc.). The phrase 'idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti' (this is what is meant) and so on is the detailed explanation of that concise statement.

Firstly, the causal state of the jhānas is appropriate because it is the most effective means for achieving the cessation of perception. If it is asked, 'How is the causal state of the kasinas appropriate?'—that too is certainly appropriate. For the reason that the jhānas are the most effective means for achieving cessation, the kasinas are also so, because they are inseparable from those jhānas. Furthermore, there is indeed action with multiple causes, just as it is said, 'He goes by another path, by a vehicle, and with a torch.'

'Ekavāraṃ' means once. 'Purimasaññānirodhaṃ' means the cessation of sense-perception (kāmasaññā), not the cessation of perception known as the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). 'Ekaṃ saññaggaṃ' means one perception that is the summit, or it refers to the single state of being the summit of perception because it is superior to the lower perception. For it is 'saññagga' because it is both perception and the summit; it does not mean the highest among perceptions.

Just as in this sphere of nothingness, perception is the culmination or the highest and is thus called 'saññagga,' so it is with the remaining jhānas. Whatever causal sign (nimitta) leads the jhāna to be called 'saññagga,' that very sign known as perception is intended here, either by eliding the word 'state' (bhāva) or by emphasizing the state. 'Dve vāre' means twice. The indication 'sata-sahassaṃ saññaggāni' (a hundred thousand summits of perception) is an explanation using the 'method of following deer tracks' (migapadavaḷañjana-niddesa). By the term 'sesakasiṇesu' (in the remaining kasinas), only the kasinas are taken because they are the subject of the discussion on cessation. For that reason, it should be understood that even when 'jhāna' is mentioned here, only the kasina-jhānas are taken. Just as in the phrase 'pathavīkasiṇေna karaṇabhūtena' (by the earth-kasina as the cause), it is stated without directly mentioning the jhāna that has that as its object...
384:
...thus, the Teacher says, 'by the first jhāna as the cause,' without directly referring to the earth-kasina which is the object of that jhāna. With the word 'iti' and so on, he concludes by summarizing that meaning. 'Sabbaṃ' refers even to the perception of a jhāna attained only once. 'Having encompassed' (saṅgahetvā) means encompassing it because it does not deviate from its nature by the characteristic of perceiving; it means oneness (unity) through the power of attainment and the characteristic of perceiving. 'Aparāparaṃ' means repeatedly. Many summits of perception (saññaggāni) occur.

In the first method, the perceptions and knowledges are shown by way of a person developing insight (vipassanā) which has jhāna as its proximate cause. In the second method, because the path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) arises for one who, having exerted effort in insight, joins it with the Path, the perceptions and knowledges are shown by way of the Path of Insight. In the third method, because the first method is coarse and the second method is mixed (mundane and supramundane), the Teacher shows the perceptions and knowledges by way of the Path and Fruit, without praising those two, in order to show only the extremely subtle, profound, and purely supramundane. These three methods are shown by way of purifying the Path.

'This third method alone is the essence here'—to clarify this, the view of the Elder Mahāsīva, a bearer of the Tipitaka, is brought forward. Indeed, the meaning is explained above in accordance with the Elder's view, starting with 'due to the arising of the perception of the Fruit of Arahantship.' 'These monks' refers to the monks who held the previous views. At that time, while reciting the Dīgha Nikāya Pali, having reached this point and speaking of the three methods in the order mentioned, the Elder said this referring to those monks. After asking about cessation and having it explained, asking about the arising of perception and knowledge immediately after that is, in essence, asking about the emergence from the attainment of cessation. Emergence from the attainment of cessation occurs either through the arising of the Fruit of Arahantship or the Fruit of Never-returning. In that context, perception is primary, and immediately after it, reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) arises. Wishing to extract those two, the Elder said, 'Poṭṭhapāda, below,' and so on. In that speech, 'Bhagavā' is a word of address.

Just as in the cognitive process of the Path (maggavīthi), when the Path and Fruit knowledges have arisen, reviewing knowledges that contemplate the Path and Fruit occur by necessity, so too in the cognitive process of the attainment of the Fruit (phalasamāpattivīthi), the reviewing knowledge that contemplates the Fruit occurs; thus the Teacher said, 'afterwards, the reviewing knowledge.' The statement 'This is the Fruit of Arahantship' shows the mode of arising of the reviewing knowledge. In the phrase 'ayam-eva paccayo' (this very cause), the letter 'm' is changed to 'd', becoming 'idappaccayo.' Some grammarians desire the original word to be with the letter 'd'. That word (idappaccaya)...
385:
In the Theravāda (the view of Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsiva), it is said "phala-samādhi-saññā-paccayā" because it is only the perception associated with the concentration of fruition. It means "due to the condition of perception associated with the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship." The particle "kira" is used in the sense of recollection (anussaraṇa). This is because reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) has the characteristic of repeatedly recollecting the states one has attained. Here, with concentration as the head, the entire fruition of Arahantship is taken by the method of association (sahacaraṇa-ñāya). Since reviewing cannot occur without that fruition of Arahantship, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "idappaccayā" (due to this condition). Thus, in this commentary, the absolute necessity of reviewing the fruition is shown according to the view of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas (reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya).

However, in the Commentary on the Cūḷadukkhandha Sutta, it is said: "That reviewing is not complete for everyone. For one person reviews only the abandoned defilements, another only the remaining defilements, another only the path, another only the fruition, and another only Nibbāna. Among these five kinds of reviewing, it should not be said that one or two cannot be obtained." This is stated according to the view of the Majjhima-bhāṇakas (reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya). The Abhidhammikas say:
"The wise person reviews the path, the fruition, and Nibbāna;
As for the abandoned defilements and the remaining defilements, they may or may not review them."

## Explanation of the Commentary on Perception
By the term "village pig" (gāmasūkara), the wild pig is excluded. Only in this way is the metaphorical statement fully appropriate. Due to the smoothness of the teaching, it cleanses the stains of arrogance, disparaging, envy, etc., and thus the knowledge consisting in learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa) is like being bathed; due to its subtlety, it is like being anointed; and because it bears the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), it is like being adorned with ornaments such as earrings. Because the knowledge that enters into that talk on cessation (nirodha-kathā) has such a nature, the person possessing that view also attains such a state. The fact that Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer did not find happiness in the talk on cessation is like putting a pig on a majestic bed; therefore, it is said "saṇha-sukhuma... ārāpitopi."

"Tattha" means in that talk on cessation. Not finding happiness means not obtaining it or not knowing it due to dull wisdom. Being corrupted by stains, it is like a cesspool. "One's own view" refers to the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi). "Taking consent" (anumatiṃ gahetvā) means taking permission, making one admit "This is my self," and establishing them in one's own view.
386:
In the Pāḷi, the phrase "kaṃ pana" means: among the three types of self based on the three doctrines of self—gross, mind-made, and formless—which self do you believe in? By the phrase "desanāya sukusalo" (skilled in teaching), it shows the reflection of Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer: "The Blessed One will surely destroy my view." "Pariharanto" means wishing to avoid the destruction of his view, thus intending to hide his own view by saying "the self is formless."

In the words of the wanderer starting with "oḷārikaṃ kho" in the Pāḷi, the meaning is as follows: Because the proponent of the self-doctrine takes the continuity of the fourfold material groups as a single entity and believes "the self is gross" because it has form. Imagining the self as the basis for food and drink, he considers it "eternal." Because it has form, the distinctness of perception is understood appropriately. Those who follow the Vedas refer to that self in two ways: "made of food" (annamaya) and "made of drink" (pānamaya). Therefore, the wanderer, referring to that self-conceived by the proponents of the self-doctrine, said "oḷārikaṃ kho" and so on.

In the words of the Blessed One starting with "oḷāriko ca hi te poṭṭhapāda attā abhavissā," the meaning is this: If the self had form, then form would be the self. It would not be possible for it to be percipient (saññī), because perception is immaterial and material phenomena have the nature of not perceiving. If the self with form were eternal according to your view, and perception were impermanent because it breaks up here and there as it occurs successively, then even so, because "perception is one thing and the self is another," the self would be unconscious (acetana) due to the absence of perception. Therefore, this self would be neither the doer of kamma nor the enjoyer of the result; it would fall into this fault. To show this fault, the Blessed One spoke the words starting with "oḷāriko ca."

In that context, "tattha" refers to the doctrine of "the self having form." In the word "paccāgacchato," if it regards the remaining action, it should be in the accusative case (kamma-attha). Alternatively, "paccāgacchato" means of one who knows, or of one who exists by clinging to a doctrine. Why is it said "one perception arises and another perception ceases"? To resolve the objection that "cessation is preceded by arising, and there is no such thing as an arisen state that does not cease," the words "cutunnaṃ khandhānaṃ" etc. are spoken. Although those aggregates have the same object and same base, because they are the subject of arising and cessation, it is stated that they have a common arising and cessation. "Aparāparaṃ" means successively (ponkhānupoṅkha).

## 418-420. In the Pāḷi, "manomayaṃ" means made by the mind, by the power of the jhanic mind. That self which arises by the mind alone, without depending on external conditions, is called "manomaya." It refers to the body born in the fine-material realm (rūpa-loka). Proponents of the Vedas [refer to] that self...
387:
The Vedic proponents use two designations: "made of bliss" (ānandamaya) and "made of consciousness" (viññāṇamaya). "Even in that case" refers to the doctrine of a "mind-made self" (manomaya-attā). "When the fault is shown" means that when a fault is pointed out, such as "perception will be of another kind," the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, intending only his own doctrine, says "formless (arūpī) self," and so on; this is how the words are connected.

In this doctrine of a mind-made self, according to the method stated in the previous doctrine of a gross self (oḷārika-attā): "If the self were mind-made, produced by jhāna-consciousness, complete in all its parts and limbs, and not lacking any sense-organ, then in that case, form (rūpa) would be the self. Since perception is not form (being mental), it is impossible for there to be a self possessed of perception." All such demonstrations of faults should be understood. Desiring to show this meaning, the Blessed One said, "Poṭṭhapāda, your self is mind-made," and so on.

Why does this wanderer first assert a gross self, then abandon that view and assert a mind-made self? And why, after abandoning that mind-made self, does he again assert a formless (arūpī) self? In this question, the reason "At that time, even though he held the view of a formless self..." has indeed been stated below. Nevertheless, to show another reason—that these sectarians (titthiyas) have unstable minds, being as shaky as a stake driven into a heap of chaff—the phrase "Just as..." was spoken.

"Perception does not stand" means that perception does not stand by way of recognizing the object; it means one cannot perform perception on the object. In the phrase "when perception stands," it should be understood in the same way. "Even in that case" refers to the doctrine of a "formless self." "Of perception" means of natural perception; thus it was stated by the Elder Dhammapāla. "Arising and ceasing in another sectarian context" is the connection of words. By this, it shows that according to the view of the Vedic proponents, they desire the arising and ceasing of perception which has various objects arising at various moments.

Some teachers read "ācariyasaññāya" (by the teacher's perception). Such a reading is inappropriate because it contradicts the meaning and because the Elder Dhammapāla did not extract it. Because of seeing the arising and passing away of perception occurring successively, he desires arising and ceasing. However, taking the common designation "perception, perception" as "self," and imagining its continuity, he thinks it is eternal (sassata). Therefore, the teacher said, "But he thinks the self is eternal."

"Therefore" means because he thinks it is eternal by the mere name of the perception occurring successively. The meaning is that the Blessed One shows the fault because, instead of stopping at the mere arising and ceasing of perception, he goes beyond that and grasps the eternalist view. "In the same way" means just as in the two doctrines of "material self" (rūpī-attā) and "mind-made self" (manomaya-attā), it is difficult to avoid the consequence of faults such as the self being impercipient or unconscious (acetana); so it is in this perception-made self doctrine.

"By showing that meaning" is because of being overwhelmed by the wrong reflection called the view of self (attadiṭṭhi). "Because of being overwhelmed" means being oppressed by habits cultivated for an beginningless time, and being blocked from the range of wisdom. A fool, deceived by continuity and mass, reflects on the collection of mind and matter occurring by way of the mental-material process as "self" or "eternal" due to wrong view. The analytical knowledge that correctly distinguishes that continuity (santatighana) and mass (samūhaghana), which are perceived as one, is called "vinibbhoga" (analytical dissection). This vinibbhoga is entirely absent in sectarians. Because of the absence of this vinibbhoga, this wanderer Poṭṭhapāda also lacked such maturity of wisdom, and thus could not understand the distinction even when taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, the teacher said, "He did not know that distinction." This thing called perception, having various objects, arises and disappears at various moments.
388:
The meaning is that being difficult to restrain is the same in this doctrine as well. 'By wrong view' means by the wrong conviction known as the view of self (attadiṭṭhi). Abhibhūtatta (the state of being overcome) means being overwhelmed due to habits cultivated since time immemorial, and thus the range of knowledge is obstructed. The fool, deceived by the compactness of continuity (santatighana) and the compactness of mass (samūhaghana), perceives the collection of mental and physical phenomena occurring in succession as 'self' and 'permanent' through wrong grasping. Analyzing and knowing this compactness of continuity and mass, which is perceived as a unity, according to reality is called the 'resolution of compactness' (ghanavinibbhoga). This resolution of compactness does not exist at all for the sectarians (titthiyas). Therefore, this wanderer (paribbājaka), lacking such maturity of knowledge, cannot understand the distinction (nānatta) even when it is taught; thus it was said, 'because of not knowing that distinction.'

Those who hold Vedic views believe that this perception (saññā) arises and vanishes at various moments with various objects. Even though they see the arising and ceasing of perception, they imagine a self made of perception or consisting of perception. Lacking the aforementioned resolution of compactness, they regard it as permanent and perceive it through the conceit of views (diṭṭhimanyanā). The Buddha, seeing that the subtle, profound, and deep nature of this Dhamma cannot be known by such a person, said 'It is difficult to know,' etc., and to show this reason, He said, 'Then the Blessed One,' and so on.

Among the terms starting with diṭṭhi, the wrong conviction that 'it is thus' is called diṭṭhi (view). The acceptance through reflection that 'it is thus,' which occurs prior to that view, is called khanti (patience/acceptance). Similarly, liking is called ruci (preference). 'Only in another way,' etc., is the explanation that distinguishes those terms like diṭṭhi. In that context, 'only in another way' means not as seen through the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) in the Noble Dispensation without approaching the two extremes, but in a way other than that. 'Only another thing' means that you accept and prefer the non-existent self and permanence instead of the truly existent aggregates (khandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) which are impermanent. Great exertion is called āyoga. Therefore, it is said 'yuttappayuttatā' (the state of being devoted and exerted). 'In the practice' means in the practice of the wanderers, such as contemplating the noble meaning. The state of being a teacher is ācariyaka. There is proper advice and instruction (ovāda anusāsana). Because he possesses that teacher-hood (or instruction), that wanderer is called ācariyaka. It is like the word 'saddho.' Therefore, it says 'in another place,' etc. It should be connected as: your teacher-hood exists in the fold of sectarians outside the Dispensation. The phrase 'Therefore,' etc., is shown in accordance with the sentence structure along with the word connection. Because it is difficult to distinguish 'this is the ultimate truth, this is the conventional truth,' this distinction (nānatta) is difficult to know. Thinking, 'If this matter is difficult to know, let it be; I will ask the Blessed One about another matter,' and to show that he practiced accordingly, it is said 'Then,' and so on.
389:
It is said 'paribbājako,' and so on. 'Añño vā saññāto' means let the self be of a nature other than the nature of perception. However, at present, the reading 'aññā vā saññā' is seen. 'Assa' means his own (of the self).

In this (self), merit, demerit, and their results are manifest or established; therefore, this self is called 'the world' (loka). It is desired as the doer (kāraka) and the feeler (vedaka). The view that arises as 'the self and the world are eternal,' etc., is called diṭṭhigata. This wrong conviction (micchā-abhinivesa) is not based on the welfare of the present life, etc., because it does not lead to that welfare. If a conviction could lead to that welfare, it would deserve to be called 'based on that,' like the accumulation of merit and knowledge. In this same way, it should not be described as being based on the supramundane Dhamma either.

The beginning of the holy life (brahmacariya) is ādibrahmacariya. Just as 'Vinaya is itself venayika,' that ādibrahmacariya is ādibrahmacariyaka. Therefore, it is said 'known as the three trainings,' and so on. Every sentence inherently contains the sense of limitation (the word 'eva'), so it is said 'only the beginning' (ādimattaṃ). Here, it refers only to the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā). That this training in higher virtue is the beginning in the Dispensation's holy life, which is comprised of the three trainings, is shown by the phrase 'only the training in higher virtue.' It shows that it is not ādibrahmacariyaka like other virtues such as those with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamakasīla).

'Nibbindanatthāya' means for the sake of disenchantment. 'Abhijānanatthāya' means for the sake of direct knowledge through the power of full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). 'Sambujjhanatthāya' means for the sake of full enlightenment through the power of full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā) and full understanding by abandonment (pahānapariññā), so say the teachers. Alternatively, 'abhijānanatthāya' means for knowing through the power of higher knowledge (abhiññā). Since such knowing is the direct realization of the round of rebirths, it is said 'paccakkhakiriyāya' (for direct realization). 'Sambujjhanatthāya' means for the sake of penetration through the power of the breakthrough of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya). Adherence to wrong views (diṭṭhābhinivesa) does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and peace in the round of rebirths because that view is included within the round and is connected to the round. Similarly, it should be understood that it does not lead to higher knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.

Although craving (taṇhā) is indeed of the nature of suffering, it is mentioned separately as the origin (samudaya); thus it is said 'excluding craving.' 'Pabhāvanato' means because of producing. Even though craving produces suffering, it does so only when accompanied by other conditions such as ignorance (avijjā), and not alone; hence it is said 'with conditions' (sappaccayā). 'Appavatti' means the cause of non-occurrence. In this Nibbāna, suffering and its origin do not occur, or if this Nibbāna is attained, suffering and its origin no longer occur; thus it is called appavatti. Because it reaches Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering, and because it should be practiced for the sake of that Nibbāna, it is called the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā).
390:
Maggapātubhāvo means the arising of the Path. Phalasacchikiriyā means the realization by means of the attainment of the Fruit. Taṃ ākāraṃ means it is as if announcing the manner and appearance of his departure, which is called silence; it is not, however, a direct announcement.

Sannitodakaṃ refers to pricking or piercing by means of oppression from all sides. Because the word qualifying the group of mind (manogaṇa) etc., is indicated in the neuter gender, it is said: "vācāya sannitodakena". Therefore, [the sub-commentator] said: "vacanapatodakena". Alternatively, the word "vācāya" should be understood as an instrumental case (third case) in relation to "sannitodakena". "Vacanapatodakena" means by the goad of speech; or, connecting the word "vācāya" in the genitive sense (sixth case), it should be construed as "they have made it completely filled with the action of piercing by oppressing from all sides of speech." The word "sajjhabbharitaṃ" should be analyzed as "saṃ adhi abhi aritaṃ", meaning being intensely filled from all sides. It means they pierced with the goads of various wanderers' words, as if piercing with sticks having a hundred points. Therefore, it is said: "they pierced from above."

Sabhāvato vijjamānaṃ means a phenomenon that is obtained (manifestly exists) in the ultimate sense; it is not a phenomenon that cannot be obtained like the prakṛti (primordial nature) etc. Taccham means the true truth. Tatham means the non-erroneous nature. In terms of meaning, all three words are synonyms. The phrase navalokuttaradhammesu is in the locative case in the sense of a domain (visaya); it means taking those nine supramundane states as the object (domain). Ṭhitasabhāvaṃ means having a stable nature, meaning that which brings about those supramundane states. Lokuttaradhammaniyāmaniyataṃ means fixed by the fixed way that leads to the supramundane states. Nowadays, although there is the reading "lokuttaradhammaniyāmataṃ", that reading is not an ancient one because it was not extracted by the former teachers. As to why this practice is dhammaṭṭhitatā and dhammaniyāmatā, it is stated beginning with "buddhānañhi". Sā refers to that practice (paṭipadā). Edisā refers to the practice of the kind already described as dhammaṭṭhitataṃ etc.

## Commentary on the Story of Citta Hatthisāriputta and Poṭṭhapāda

He is called Hatthisārī (elephant tamer) because he tames elephants; it means an elephant trainer (hatthācariya). Sukhumesu atthantaresu refers to phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana), which are the domain of subtle knowledge. It is said that Citta Hatthisāriputta was an expert in the Abhidhamma. Kusalo means he was skilled and proficient because of his previous familiarity in the dispensations of former Buddhas. Tādise citte refers to a mind that yearns for the lay life. The meaning is that the other [monk], upon merely hearing those words, did not disrobe but delighted only in the monkhood. In this context, "because of speaking about the advantages of the lay life," since such talk to a virtuous monk amounted to encouraging him to disrobe, now, although he himself was virtuous, for the six...
391:
The meaning should be taken as disrobing at every turn. For the result of an action must be similar to the action performed. The word 'kathanentānaṃ' is in the genitive case in the sense of disregard (anādara). It means that when the Great Disciple, the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika, spoke in a censuring manner, [the listener] was unable to find a footing in that discourse. The statement 'having disrobed, he became a layman' is said as if it were the seventh turn. However, in the Dhammapada Commentary and the Kuddāla Jātaka, the turn of disrobing is said to be only six times. 'Gihi-sahāyaka' means a companion during the time of being a layman. 'Appasakkantopi nāma' is a word of censure towards Poṭṭhapāda, meaning 'he has indeed moved away.' 'Going forth is appropriate' means the state of a monk is suitable.

It means due to the absence of the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu) which is capable of seeing what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, and what is even and uneven. To show the kind of eye by which that person is called 'one with eyes,' the words 'subhāsitā' etc., are spoken. This is another method besides the Commentary. 'Ekamsika' means those teachings that are certain and definitive, firmly determined as leading to Nibbāna. 'Paññattā' means teachings that are defined. 'Na ekamsika' means those teachings that are not certain, not determined as leading to Nibbāna, because they are included within the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). This meaning accords and agrees with the Sutta passages such as: "Poṭṭhapāda, why have I taught and defined the certain (ekamsika) teachings? Poṭṭhapāda, these teachings are connected with the goal... they lead to Nibbāna."

## Explanation of the Certain Teachings (Ekamsika-dhamma-vaṇṇanā)

Having asked the reason, "Why did he strive?", the benefit is answered as "to show the state of not leading out [of saṃsāra]." Since the cause is established when the result is achieved, this is the opinion of the Teacher. Other teachers, however, desire the meaning: "In such places, the word 'attha' occurs in the sense of cause, and the nominative case is in the sense of reason; therefore, in the phrase 'aniyyānika-bhāva-dassana,' it is because of the reason of showing the state of not leading out."

It means the path of liberation from the defilements that has been made known. Because one reaches the end of the suffering of the round of rebirth by that path, liberation (vimutti) is called 'niṭṭhā' (the end). Just as the word 'ṭhā' in the passage "goṭṭhā paṭṭhita-gāvo" in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta occurs in the sense of going. Here, 'niṭṭhā' is intended as 'niṭṭhā-magga' (the path to the end) with the final member of the compound elided. Only that path has the quality of leading out [of saṃsāra].
392:
The state of not leading out from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) is also stated; however, the state of not leading out (aniyyānika) of the Path, which leads to Nibbāna—the end of the suffering of the round—is not stated. It is called 'niyyānika' because it leads out from the suffering of the round; here, the letter 'ya' is changed to 'ka'. The word 'aniya' mostly denotes the agent; that which does not lead out is 'aniyyānika', and the state of that is 'aniyyānikatā'. Alternatively, 'niyyāna' (departure, escape) refers to the cessation of the suffering of the round; 'niyyāna' itself is 'niyyānika'. That which is not leading out from the suffering of the round is 'aniyyānika', and this should be construed to show the nature of that 'aniyyānika'.

## 'Sabbe hi' etc. is the detailed explanation of that meaning.

'Sabbe hi' and the following words are the detailed explanation of that meaning. It should be connected as: 'Just as Nibbāna, the deathless, is designated as the end (niṭṭhā).' Those who designate the end by way of the Brahma realm, which is the pinnacle of the world, etc., do so by merely taking the common term 'Nibbāna, Nibbāna'. The Brahma realm is called 'Lokathūpikā' because it is conceived as being like the pinnacle (thūpikā) of the world. Although some teachers say that the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is 'Lokathūpikā', it is inappropriate because it is not stated so in the Commentaries. Here, by the word 'ādi' (etc.), the following are included: the knowledge that 'the person (purisa) is one, and nature (pakati) is another' is called liberation (mokkha); the abiding of the self (atta), which is devoid of qualities such as wisdom, in a non-self is called liberation; the non-occurrence [of existence] by way of avoiding the destruction of the body, destiny (gati), birth (jāti), and bonds is called liberation; the state of being destroyed by another person is called liberation; proximity to that person is called liberation; and union with that person is called liberation. In those various doctrines, there is no one who does not designate an end (niṭṭhā). In the doctrine of the Brahmins, the Brahma world of the first jhāna is the end. Just like Baka Brahma, they wrongly cling to that realm as being permanent. In the doctrine of hermits such as Vekhanasa, the Ābhassara Brahma realm is the end; in the doctrine of wanderers such as Sañjaya, the Subhakiṇha Brahma realm is the end; and in the doctrine of the Ājီvakas, the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), conceived as having 'infinite mind', is the end. In this Dispensation (Sāsana), however, Arahatship (arahatta) alone is the end. All these people, by the power of their own views, mistake the Brahma realms etc. for Arahatship and designate them by merely taking the name 'Nibbāna, Nibbāna'. Since, in reality, the designation of Nibbāna cannot be found in their doctrines, it is said: 'That [view] does not lead out from the round,' and so on. 'Yathāpaññattā' means having the various forms as they have been designated. 'Na niyyāti' means it does not lead out because that end cannot be reached by the way they have made known, thinking 'the end is reached by this way'. 'Paṇḍitehi paṭikkhittā' means it is rejected by wise men such as the Buddha, saying, 'This practice does not lead to the end because it does not transcend the suffering of the round.' The word 'nivattati' (recedes/turns back) is stated as the reason for the rejection. Because the end (niṭṭhā) they designate...
393:
That practice does not lead out (to Nibbāna), it does not go there. Indeed, it only causes the person endowed with that practice to wander in saṃsāra and sink down. Therefore, it means it is rejected by the wise. The word 'taṃ' refers to the state of not leading out.

In the terms 'jānaṃ' and 'passaṃ', the teacher said 'jānantā passantā' because there is a change from singular to plural. In such Pali passages as 'Yā pana bhikkhunī jānaṃ sabhikkhukaṃ ārāmaṃ anāpucchā paviseyya' (Whatever bhikkhunī, knowing...), there is a change by the power of gender, meaning 'jānantī' (a bhikkhunī who knows). In such Pali passages as 'yācaṃ adadamappiyo', there is a change by the power of case-ending, meaning 'yācantassa' (to one who begs). Here, however, it should be understood as a change by the power of the plural number. Knowing by direct perception (paccakkha) is primary, so it is called 'knowing' (jānana). Seeing (dassana) is not primary because it is often associated with doubt. Therefore, it is stated in this order: 'jānaṃ passaṃ'. Thus, here, 'seeing' is qualified by 'knowing'. In this way, the expression of the intention as a whole—'Have you ever seen the bodily forms etc. of humans in that world?'—is well-accomplished. The intended meaning here is: 'Do you have knowledge and vision by direct perception of the world of absolute happiness?' Alternatively, by the word 'jānaṃ', the object known by inference (anumāna) regarding that world is meant; by the word 'passaṃ', the object known by direct perception is meant. This means: 'Do you know that world by direct perception or by inference?'

Since an object that is present to the senses in the world is evident as a sphere of the faculties, 'diṭṭhapubbāni' etc. is stated to show the intention through an evident object. Alternatively, it should be noted that it is stated thus to clarify the intention with both meanings, taking 'seeing' by the word 'diṭṭha' and 'knowing' which follows that seeing. 'Diṭṭhapubbāni' means: 'Have you previously grasped [it] by seeing and by the knowledge that follows that seeing?' By doing so, the statement 'sarīrasaṇṭhānādīni', together with its limitation, is accomplished. The teacher said 'appāṭihīraṃ taṃ' because this exposition 'appāṭihīrakataṃ' is an exposition where the nasal (niggahīta) is dropped. It should be connected as: 'That statement becomes one that is devoid of the beyond (cannot lead out).' Some say that in the word 'appāṭihīra', the nasal is dropped and it is a single word with 'kataṃ', but that is inappropriate because a compound (samāsa) is possible and the dropping of the nasal should not be asserted [in that way]. Here, they explain thus: It is called 'paṭihāriya' because it removes opposition; that same thing is 'pāṭihāriya'. It means a statement that itself lacks a superior (is definitive). Here, 'pāṭihāriya' itself is called 'pāṭihīraka'. That which is not 'pāṭihīraka' because it can be countered by the words of others is called 'appāṭihīraka'.
394:
In this word 'appāṭihīrakaṃ', the syllable 'a' denotes the sense of absence (viraha). Therefore, the teacher said 'paṭiharaṇavirahita' (free from the removal of speech by counter-speech). The reason is that a speech that is excessive (or accompanied by excess) is removed or overturned by that counter-speech. Therefore, counter-speech is called 'paṭiharaṇa', and it means being free from that 'paṭiharaṇa'. For that very reason, due to the absence of the path (magga) that leads out of suffering (or removes opposing defilements), it attains the status of being called 'aniyyānika' (not leading to emancipation). Thus, it is called 'aniyyānika'.

'Vilāsa' refers to the grace or charm of women (itthi-līḷā); this 'vilāsa' is also called 'actions born of a passionate nature' (siṅgāra-bhāva). 'Ākappa' refers to specific modes such as the styling of hair and the wearing of clothes, or the arrangement of one's appearance. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), gestures (hāva) and so on are included. 'Hāva' refers to charm or dalliance (cāturiya).

## Description of the Three Acquisitions of Self (Tayo Attapaṭilābha Vaṇṇanā)

In this context, it is called 'attā' (self or person) because the conceit of 'I' (ahaṃmāna) is attributed to (or established in) it; therefore, it is called 'attapaṭilābha' (acquisition of self). How is this shown? It is stated as 'oḷārika-attapaṭilābha' (gross acquisition of self) and so on. It shows the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) because it is grosser than the acquisitions of self in the other two types of existence. It shows the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) because it arises through jhāna and is obtained in a form-possessing state. It shows the immaterial existence (arūpabhava) because it is obtained in a formless state. The twelve types of unwholesome consciousness (akusala-cittuppāda) are called defiling states (saṃkilesikā dhammā); this is because in their absence, no defilement can occur to anyone. Calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are called purifying states (vodāniyā dhammā); this is because through their power, the complete purification of the mind can be achieved.

As long as the opposing unwholesome states cannot be completely eradicated, the fulfillment (pāripūrī) or the abundance (vepulla) of faultless wholesome states can never occur. It can only occur when they are completely eradicated; therefore, it should be understood that only the wisdom of the Path and Fruition (magga-phala-paññā) are referred to. This is because once these Path and Fruition wisdoms are fulfilled, they remain fulfilled forever as they are of a non-declining nature. 'Taruṇa-pīti' (tender rapture) is weak rapture that has just arisen and has not yet obtained repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya). 'Balava-tuṭṭhi' (strong satisfaction) is very firm rapture that has obtained repetition-condition through repeated arising and serves as a cause for the attainment of higher distinctions. Now, wishing to show the essential meaning in brief, he said 'kiṃ vuttaṃ' (what was said) and so on. In that sentence, the connection is: 'We have said that... he will dwell [having realized] that dwelling himself.' The meaning is: 'I will dwell having personally realized through my own knowledge, without depending on others, in this very life, that dwelling which is the fulfillment and abundance of Path and Fruition wisdom, and which is the culmination of the abandoning of defiling states and the development of purifying states.'
395:
“We have said, ‘He will dwell having personally realized and accomplished it through his own knowledge.’ ‘Therein’ means in such a dwelling. ‘To him’ means to the monk who follows the advice and instruction. ‘To one who dwells thus’ means because of dwelling in the manner described, or to the one who is dwelling. Based on that dwelling, there will be gladness (pāmojja); rapture (pīti) which has gladness as its precursor; the two kinds of tranquility (passaddhi)—bodily and mental—which have that rapture as their cause; likewise, well-established mindfulness (sati); supreme knowledge (uttamañāṇa) due to reaching the pinnacle; and it will be a happy dwelling (sukhavihāra). This is how the words should be connected.

Bodily tranquility and mental tranquility are called ‘passaddhi’. Alternatively, this Pali word ‘passaddhi’ itself is the original reading. Some teachers read it as ‘nāmakāyapassaddhi’, but that is inappropriate because the two kinds of tranquility are inseparable from each other. Why is this dwelling called a happy dwelling? To show that among all types of dwellings, such as dwelling in postures, only this dwelling deserves to be called a ‘happy dwelling’ because it is peaceful and sublime, he said ‘sabbavihāresu’ (among all dwellings) and so on. How is it happy? It means ‘it is peaceful and supremely sweet.’

In the mere attainment of the first jhāna, rapture is weak and belongs to the side of gladness (pāmojja) because of its inferior state. However, when that first jhāna is well-developed and mastered, that rapture becomes sublime and strong, capable of fulfilling its function. Therefore, it is said, ‘In the first jhāna, the six states beginning with gladness are obtained.’ ‘Gladness ceases’ means that gladness, known as weak rapture, diminishes among the six states. In the second jhāna, which is classified by the fourfold method and is free from the disturbance of initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra), rapture is always strong. It is never weak as it sometimes is in the first jhāna. This is the intended meaning.

Because the third jhāna is obtained only by abandoning that rapture, it is said, ‘Rapture ceases.’ By the phrase ‘happy dwelling’, concentration (samādhi) should be taken; thus it is said, ‘likewise in the fourth.’ However, in the view of those teachers who say, ‘By this phrase happy dwelling, the feeling of pleasure (sukha-vedanā) is taken,’ it should be understood that even equanimity (upekkhā) in the fourth jhāna is spoken of as ‘happiness’ because of its peaceful occurrence.

To define the method taught in this sutta by extracting the various methods of teaching found in this Dīgha Nikāya, he said ‘imesu’ (in these) and so on. Teaching by ‘Suddha...’ (pure) means teaching only the jhāna which is the basis for insight, without mentioning the higher paths. Teaching ‘by the four...’ means having taught the jhānas as the basis for insight, all four paths preceded by insight are taught. ‘The fruition attainment of the fourth jhāna is taught’ means that the fruition attainments of the first jhāna and so on are not taught, but only the fruition attainment of the fourth jhāna is taught.

‘Making it merely a synonym of rapture’ means that since gladness and rapture cannot occur together in a single thought-moment, gladness is treated as a figurative synonym (pariyāya) of rapture, and the two are intended without distinction. It is said that ‘the fruition attainment associated with the second jhāna is taught’ because rapture and pleasure are not abandoned, and because the phrase ‘happy dwelling’ takes the most excellent happy dwelling. Although rapture and pleasure can indeed be obtained in the first jhāna, in that first jhāna, those rapture and pleasure are not peaceful or sublime due to the disturbance of initial and sustained thought. In this second jhāna, however, only peaceful and sublime rapture and pleasure are brought forth. Therefore, it should be understood that only the fruition attainment associated with the second jhāna is taken, and not the fruition attainment associated with the first jhāna."
396: Since pīti (rapture) and pāmojja (gladness) do not arise together in a single thought-moment (cittuppāda), pāmojja is treated merely as a synonym for pīti, and the teaching is given by making the two identical without distinction. Because pīti and sukha (pleasure) are not abandoned, and because the term 'sukho vihāro' (happy abiding) refers to an exceedingly excellent happy abiding, it is said that 'the Fruition Attainment (phala-samāpatti) associated with the Second Jhāna is spoken of.' Although pīti and sukha are indeed obtained in the First Jhāna, they are not peaceful and sublime there due to the disturbance of vitakka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). However, in this Second Jhāna, only peaceful and sublime pīti and sukha are intended. Therefore, it should be understood that only the Fruition Attainment associated with the Second Jhāna is taken, not that of the First Jhāna.## 432-437. Vibhāvanattho means for the purpose of making clear, for the purpose of describing by way of its own nature. This is like in the passages: 'The ascetic Gotama does not pay homage to, or rise for, or invite with a seat, aged brahmins...' and so forth. Therefore, He said 'Ayaṃ so' (This is that), etc. Having thus made clear and manifested by way of its own nature, saying 'This acquisition of self (atta-paṭilābha) is that very acquisition of self.' By the word 'Ayaṃ' (this), the Blessed One refers to the acquisition of self previously mentioned as being immediate and present. By the word 'So' (that), He refers to the acquisition of self being asked about by others as being remote. In the phrase 'Na naṃ evaṃ vadāma' (We do not say so of it), 'naṃ' (it) refers to the gross acquisition of self. In the word 'Sappāṭihīrakataṃ', the meaning should be understood according to the method previously stated. A speech that includes an answer capable of refuting the words urged by others is called sappāṭihīraka (with a marvel/effective); this is the distinction. 'Tuccho' (empty) means false or unreal speech. 'So' (that) refers to the acquisition of self that is mind-made (manomaya) or formless (arūpa). 'Svevā' means that very gross acquisition of self. Because it exists in that present time, it is said 'Tasmiṃ samaye sacco hoti' (At that time it is true). By the word 'atta-paṭilābho' (acquisition of self) alone, He concludes it; the meaning is that He does not show the designation (paññatti) by extracting its own nature, saying 'this acquisition of self does not come under the reckoning.' In this world, only phenomena such as form (rūpa) and feeling (vedanā) are ultimate realities (sabhāva-dhammā). 'Nāmamattametaṃ' (this is merely a name) means that based on the five aggregates such as form, this name 'acquisition of self' is merely a designation (paññatti). 'Evarūpā vohārā' (such expressions) refers to expressions like 'gross acquisition of self' and so forth. 'Nāmapaññattivasena' (by way of name-designation) is said to complete the meaning that it arrives at the name 'acquisition of self' merely by way of a designation that has become a name.## Evañca pana vatvā means having stated this meaning—that based on form and so forth, this acquisition of self is merely a designation—by the words 'Yasmiṃ citta samaye' (At whatever mental moment), etc.
397: Paṭipucchitvā (having cross-questioned) means having asked about the practices by distinguishing the time in various ways, just as others might ask. Vinayanatthaṃ (for the purpose of discipline) means for the purpose of instructing by way of making known the meaning of what was asked. 'Ye te atītā dhammā' (Those past states) refers to states such as form which were the basis (upādāna) for the acquisition of the past self in the past time. Those states do not exist now because they have ceased. Only because they have thus ceased do they come under the reckoning 'they have been.' Therefore, because the basis is obtained only in the past time, 'that acquisition of self also' means my acquisition of self obtained based on those aggregates. 'At that very time' means only in the past time. 'Sacco ahosi' (was true) means it was as if it were real and existing. 'Anāgatapaccuppannānaṃ' (of the future and present) refers to the future and present states such as form which are the basis. 'Because of non-existence at that time' means because they were not manifest in that past time. The meaning is that the future acquisition of self and the present acquisition of self based on those aggregates were void, empty, false, and non-existent in that past time. Atthato means by way of the meaning of the designation. Nāmamattameva means merely a common name (samaññāmatta). Because it is not found in the ultimate sense (paramattha), one acknowledges it as 'acquisition of self.' By the phrase 'Eseva nayo' (This is the same method), He indicates this meaning: 'Those future states do not exist now, but they come under the reckoning "they will be"; therefore, that acquisition of self of mine will also be true only at that future time. Since the past and present states do not exist then, at that time one acknowledges the acquisition of self as merely a name in terms of meaning, saying "the past is void, the present is void." Those present states come under the reckoning "they exist" now; therefore, this acquisition of self of mine is true now. Since the past and future states do not exist now, at present one acknowledges the acquisition of self as merely a name in terms of meaning, saying "the past is void, the future is void."' He thus extends this meaning.## 439-443. Saṃsandituṃ means for the purpose of comparing or bringing together. Gavā means from a cow. Tattha means among those five products of the cow (pañca-gorasa), such as milk. 'At the time when there is milk' means at the time when, based on the specific basis called primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādāya), the designation 'milk' occurs. At that time... etc... it does not come under the reckoning [of curds, etc.], because the primary elements and derived matter that are the basis for the designation of milk are not taken as the basis for the designation of curds and so forth. Indeed, these worldly expressions (loka-samaññā) have their respective fixed objects. Therefore, He said 'Ye dhamme upādāya' (Based on whatever states), and so forth. It is called saṅkhā (reckoning) because it is reckoned or spoken of by this designation. It is called nirutti (expression) because the meaning is expressed or stated by extracting it through this designation. It is called nāma (name) because beings bend towards those respective meanings by that name; likewise, they use it in common speech (vohāra).
398:
## 
"Etena" refers only to the designation which is a common usage (vohāra). With the words "At which time," etc., the method already mentioned regarding milk is also applied to curd and so forth, as "This method applies in all cases."

"Samanujānanāmattakāni" means that just as one accepts the worldly designations handed down by tradition for specific types of primary and derived matter, such as "This is milk, this is curd," without rejecting them; similarly, based on the collection of aggregates like the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) distinguished by specific conditions, terms like "acquisition of a gross self," "acquisition of a mind-made self," and "acquisition of a formless self" are merely modes of acceptance in those various ways. It means that in the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no other entity apart from these five aggregates or apart from grasping (upādāna).

"Niruttimattakāni" means they are merely means of recognition through linguistic expression (sadda-nirutti). By taking up the designation that follows the sound after hearing terms like "being" or "contact," one penetrates and understands the meaning. Therefore, it is said:
"First, one knows the sound with the ear,
The past sound with the second consciousness,
The name with the third consciousness,
And the meaning with the fourth consciousness."

"Vacanapathamattakāni" is a synonym for "niruttimattakāni." Linguistic expression, which reveals the meaning, is called a "pathway of speech" (vacanapatha) because it serves as the cause for others who follow what they have seen. "Vohāramattakāni" means they are merely modes of common usage in various ways. "Nāmapaññattimattakāni" is a synonym for "vohāramattakāni," meaning they merely make known various names. All these terms like "acquisition of self," "being," or "person" are merely common usages. If asked why they are merely common usages, it is said "Because (yasmā)," etc., to show that they are not found in the ultimate sense. "Suñño" means empty of ultimate reality.

To resolve the objection, "If so, why did the Buddhas also speak these words?" the phrase "But for the Buddhas (buddhānaṃ pana)," etc., is stated. Speaking through conventional usage is called "conventional discourse" (sammuti-kathā). Speaking of ultimate realities (sabhāva-dhamma) is called "ultimate discourse" (paramattha-kathā). Because they are discourses based on ultimate reality, discourses on impermanence (anicca), etc., are also called "ultimate discourse." Only ultimate realities are called "impermanent" and "suffering," not conventional things.

According to the words:
"All formations (saṅkhāra) are impermanent,
Conditioned things (saṅkhata) are suffering and non-self,
Nibbāna and designation (paññatti)
Are determined to be non-self,"
this conventional reality is called "non-self" (anatta). Designations such as the aggregates (khandha) are based on ultimate reality like appropriate designations (tajja-paññatti) and are very close to it, unlike personal designations (puggala-paññatti) which...
399:
## 
...are distant. Therefore, discourse on the aggregates, etc., is also called "ultimate discourse" (paramattha-kathā). Alternatively, it should be understood that by taking the aggregates as the head, only the ultimate realities that are the nature of grasping those aggregates are taken. An objection might be raised: "Do not ultimate realities also enter into the teaching only through the medium of conventional designation, and not through the medium of the ultimate? Therefore, should not all teachings be only conventional discourse?" This should not be understood in this way. The reason is that the classification of discourse is intended according to the classification of the Dhamma to be taught. Furthermore, a word does not manifest a meaning without some basis for its occurrence.

To resolve the inquiry "Why does the teaching of the Buddhas proceed in these two ways?" by clarifying the reason, the phrase "Therein, he who (tattha yo)," etc., is stated. [One] is able to understand the meaning, to penetrate the Four Truths, to escape from the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), and to seize the victory known as Arahantship. Since the penetration of the truths occurs only through ultimate discourse, and the discourse on the Noble Truths (ariyasacca-kathā) is the pinnacle of the teaching, the Blessed One, though teaching conventional discourse at the beginning according to the disposition of the individuals to be led (vineyya), teaches only ultimate discourse later. Thus it is said "Of that (tassā)," etc. By saying "He teaches conventional discourse at the very beginning," it is shown that he also teaches ultimate discourse later. In other cases, by not saying "He teaches only at the beginning," it shows that he teaches it in all places.

With the word "Thus (tathā)," etc., another method of teaching the two types of discourse is clarified. "Having awakened (bodhetvā)" means having made known the meaning to be taught in various ways according to the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those to be led. By this, the following meaning is shown: in some teachings, conventional discourse precedes ultimate discourse according to the person's inclination; in others, ultimate discourse precedes conventional discourse. Thus, the Teacher, who is skilled in guiding those to be led, brings forth the teaching in various ways according to their inclinations.

In all teachings, the Blessed One follows convention without abandoning the natural law (dhammatā). Without discarding convention, he clarifies the natural law. There is no running into wrong views or overstepping in that convention. Thus, it was said by the Blessed One: "One should not adhere to local dialects, nor override common usage."

The teaching of conventional discourse first is generally the practice of the Buddhas according to the capacity of those to be led. To show that practice along with the reason, the phrase "By nature, however (pakatiyā pana)," etc., is stated. "Lūkhākārā" (rough in appearance) means they are like something rough because those to be led cannot yet penetrate the Dhamma. An objection is raised: "Is not convention untrue because it does not exist in the ultimate sense? If so, why do the Buddhas speak conventional discourse?" To address this, the phrase "Even while speaking conventional discourse (sammuti-kathāṃ kathentāpi)," etc., is stated. "Saccamevāti" means...
400: It means only what is true. In terms of worldly convention, it refers only to the nature of that worldly convention. Therefore, the teacher says, 'It is not a lie.' However, regarding the ultimate sense (paramattha), which is the supreme and unerring truth, there is nothing even to be said. What is the difference between these conventional designations and ultimate realities? When a certain name or concept is destroyed, or when it is analyzed into parts by wisdom, if that name or concept no longer exists, that term—such as 'pot' or 'cloth'—is called 'conventional' (sammuti). The nature that is opposite to that convention is called 'ultimate' (paramattha). This principle cannot be applied to natures such as the hardness (kakkhaḷa) of the earth element or the contact (phusana) of touch. Even though it cannot be applied thus, because conventional designations also possess the nature of truth in the aforementioned way, teachers say, 'He taught two truths,' and so on. In that phrase 'He taught two truths'—just as a teacher who is skilled in the languages of various regions and can explain the meaning of the three Vedas, the Blessed One, being skilled in various types of conventional and ultimate truths, taught only two truths, namely conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) and ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca), according to the inclinations and dispositions of those to be tamed. He demonstrates these two truths both in essence and in extent with the words: 'There are only convention and the ultimate; a third is not found.' 'Vadatā varo' means the most excellent among all those who speak. Convention (sammuti) is established merely by worldly symbols. The ultimate (paramattha) is the supreme, unerring, and true nature of reality. Now, to show the true nature of these two along with their reasons, the verse beginning with 'Saṅketavacana' is spoken. The connection should be made thus: because it is the cause of worldly convention, conventional speech is true; and because it is the true characteristic of phenomena (dhamma), ultimate speech is true. 'Loka-sammuti-kāraṇaṃ' is a statement showing the reason for the truthfulness of conventional speech. It means that convention established by worldly usage is the reason for the non-deceptiveness of conventional speech. Because it is not deceptive, conventional speech is said to be true. 'Dhammānaṃ bhūtalakkhaṇaṃ' is also a statement showing the reason for the truthfulness of ultimate speech. It means that whatever true and unerring nature exists in ultimate phenomena, the marking or making known of that nature is called its 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa). It means that ultimate speech is true because it proceeds by way of being factual and non-deceptive. In the Anangaṇa Sutta Ṭīkā, however, the teacher himself, using the ablative case and skipping over words, says: 'Loka-sammuti-kāraṇā' means because of proceeding in dependence on worldly designation; 'Dhammānaṃ' means of ultimate phenomena; 'Bhūta-kāraṇā' means because of proceeding in dependence on the true nature of reality. In other texts, however, a verse showing this quality is found: 'Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in usage, no lie arises when he employs conventional usage.' In that verse, it is explained that because of the two types of truth, or because of the truthfulness of conventional speech, when he teaches convention...
401:
This verse illustrating this quality is also seen. In that verse, "tasmā" is used either because there are two kinds of truth, or because worldly conventional speech is true. "Sammutiṃ voharantassa" means that for the Blessed One who teaches according to worldly conventions such as "person" or "being", what is called false speech (musāvāda) does not occur. Furthermore, the reasons stated in various commentaries for why the Blessed One speaks words related to a person should also be included here, namely: (1) to illustrate shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), (2) to illustrate that kamma is one's own property (kammassakatā), (3) to illustrate the individual effort of men, (4) to illustrate the heinous crimes (ānantariya), (5) to illustrate the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), (6) to illustrate the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa), (7) to illustrate the purity of offerings, and (8) for the sake of not abolishing worldly convention.

If the Tathāgata, even though he stands having fully awakened to the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca), speaks only by taking worldly convention (sammuti-sacca) as a basis, one might ask what the difference is between him and worldly people; therefore, the words beginning with "yāhi" are spoken. This is the connection with the Pali text. The meaning is: Worldly people, because they have not abandoned misapprehension (parāmāsa), speak with clinging, saying "this is mine," and so on. The Tathāgata, however, having entirely abandoned all misapprehension, speaks without clinging. Because the worldly meaning is difficult for worldly people to understand without worldly conventions, he speaks to them using those conventions. Even while speaking thus, through his own elegance of teaching (desanā-vilāsa), he establishes the beings who are fit to be tamed in the ultimate truth. "Desanaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā" means having turned away and separated from the discourse on the cycle (vaṭṭa-kathā) associated with the adherence to wrong views mentioned above. "Arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhāpesi" means that by the word "aparāmasaṃ", he illustrated the abandonment of craving, conceit, and misapprehension, and concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of the Path of Arahatship which abandons those things. Those words whose meanings have not been analyzed here are easily understood.

Thus concludes the Līnatthappakāsanī, the sub-commentary named Sādhuvilāsinī, which explains the hidden meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī—which illustrates the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-perceive meanings, and generates pure and vast wisdom and skill—specifically the explanation of the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta.

## Poṭṭhapādasutta-vaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
402:
## 10. Commentary on the Subha Sutta
## Commentary on the Story of Subha the Young Brahmin
Having thus commented on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, [the teacher] now wishes to comment on the Subha Sutta. To clarify that the time has come to comment on it in due order, or to show that the Subha Sutta is the sutta recited immediately after the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, he said: "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... Sāvatthiyaṃ."

In the phrase "acira parinibbute," the meaning "aciraṃ parinibbute" is shown by the elision of the niggahīta. It is like "appāṭihīrakaṃ taṃ bhāsitaṃ sampajjati" in the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta. Alternatively, "aciraparinibbuto" refers to the Blessed One who had not long attained Parinibbāna. It is like the terms "acirapakkanto" (one who has recently departed) and "māsajāto" (one who is a month old). This is said merely to show the meaning. By the word "aciraparinibbute," it indicates only the closeness of the time of the Teacher's Parinibbāna, rejecting a long duration; it does not show the specific time limit. To show that time, he said "parinibbānato" and so on. Referring to the period from the full moon of Vesākha to the full moon of Jeṭṭha, it is said to be "about a month." By the word "matta" (about), it indicates that the period was slightly incomplete.

The village called Tudi was this person's residence, hence he is called "Todeyya." This Brahmin Todeyya lived [in Tudi] just as Soṇadaṇḍa lived in Campā and Kūṭadanta lived in Khāṇumata. Therefore, it is said, "because he ruled that village," meaning because of his lordship. He was also the chaplain (purohita) of King Pasenadi of Kosala. Wishing to admonish the young Brahmin Subha, he also spoke to his son.

"Añjanānaṃ" refers to a collection of collyrium sticks ground for eye ointment. "Vammikānaṃ" should be connected as "having seen the collection of anthills gathered by termites." "Madhūnaṃ" refers to the collection of honey from bees. "Samāhāraṃ" is the gathering of nectar. A wise person should live at home. Why? Because even if very small amounts are taken, wealth can be exhausted; and even if very small amounts are gathered, it increases. Therefore, seeing these three aforementioned similes with wisdom, a wise person should live at home and maintain a household, producing income without wasting even a little wealth. Thus, he teaches the practice directed by greed.

Having taught only non-giving, and being overcome by greed resulting from that teaching, he was reborn as a dog in that very house. For one who follows the power of greed, a miserable rebirth (duggati) is to be expected.
403:
Just as with collyrium sticks in grinding collyrium, or anthills gathered by termites, or honey gathered by bees (wealth should be accumulated). A wise person should live at home. Even very small amounts of wealth will be exhausted if taken and used; even very small amounts of wealth will increase if gathered.
