Therefore, seeing the three aforementioned similes with wisdom, a wise person should live at home, making wealth increase without wasting even a little. In this way, the practice based on greed is pointed out. (The Brahmin Todeyya) taught only non-giving, and because of being overwhelmed by greed, he was reborn as a dog in his own house. For one who follows the power of greed, it is certain that they will reach a miserable rebirth.

The meaning should be understood in the manner stated in (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary 1, 150): "He was reborn as a yakkha named Janavasabha." Due to the familiarity of the previous life, [Subha] was extremely fond of [the dog]. For it is said: "By previous association..." and so on (Jātaka Pali 1, 2, 174). "Nikkhante" refers to when [Subha] had gone out for some business. The Blessed One, wishing to favor the young Brahmin Subha, entered for alms alone. "Bhukkāraṃ" means making the sound of a dog, "bhu bhu." It was because of the insult [to the Buddha] using the Brahmin's address "Bho Bho" that he became a dog. For it is said: "If there is the trouble of passion, etc., he is called a Bhovādi, one who habitually says Bho" (Dhammapada 396, Sutta Nipāta 625).

If it is asked: "Since it was said below that he was reborn as a dog because he taught only non-giving, why is it said here that he became a dog because he insulted me with 'Bho Bho' in the past?" The answer is: Because being reborn in such a way is the result common to both causes. It should be understood that the beneficial result (āniśaṃsa-phala) can arise from combined actions, unlike the result of ripening (vipāka-phala) which arises from a single action. "You will go to the Avīci hell," because it is impossible to prevent the action that has found its opportunity. Becoming remorseful, thinking "The ascetic Gotama knows me." "Uddhanantare" means between the tripods (hearth). "Naṃ" refers to the dog.

"Taṃ pavattiṃ" refers to that matter spoken by the Blessed One. Wishing not to diminish the Brahmin tradition and thus exalting his father in that manner, [Subha] said, "He is reborn in the Brahma world." "Mukhāruḷhaṃ" refers to words that came out of his mouth according to what appeared in his own intuition. "Taṃ pavattiṃ pucchi" means he asked: "Venerable Gotama, I have heard that you said my father was reborn as a dog; is this true or false?" "Tatheva vatvā" means [the Buddha] spoke in the same way as he had previously spoken to the dog. "Avisāṃvadanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of verification; it is said to show his own non-deceptive nature by making the statement "The Brahmin Todeyya was reborn as a dog" unerring.

"Appodakaṃ" refers to milk-rice prepared with a little water. "Madhupāyāsaṃ" refers to milk-rice that has a good taste or is mixed with honey. He did exactly as the Blessed One said. "Sabbaṃ dassesi" means that by the power of the Buddha, that dog led him and showed all that treasure; it was not because of Jātissara (recollection of past lives). However, the barking upon seeing the Blessed One was due to the power of the habit (vāsanā) established in the previous life, as stated by the teacher in (Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīကā 1, 444). But in the Commentary on the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsaka, it is said: "The dog, thinking 'I am known by him,' cried and made the sound 'huṃ huṃ,' then went to the place where the treasure was buried and showed the mark by scratching the ground with its feet," thus stating the manner of Jātissara. This point should be understood by investigation and reflection.
404:
(In the Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 3, 289) It is stated that by making the sound "Hum hum," going to the place where the treasure was buried, and scratching the earth with his feet, he gave a sign. Therefore, it should be understood through investigation that this refers to the manner of Jātissara (recollecting past lives).

"This kind of rebirth as a dog, though concealed by another life, is evident to the recluse Gotama; surely he is the Omniscient Buddha." Thus, a mind of devotion towards the Blessed One arose. It is said that this young man Subha was an expert in the science of bodily marks (Aṅgavijjā). Because he was skilled in that science, the thought occurred to Subha: "I will make this Dhamma a gift and ask the recluse Gotama questions." From there, he prepared fourteen questions and asked the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, "having asked fourteen questions."

Those fourteen questions are: "Master Gotama, among human beings, some are seen to be short-lived and some long-lived; some are sickly and some healthy; some are ugly and some beautiful; some are of little influence and some are of great influence; some are poor and some are wealthy; some are of low birth and some are of high birth; some are of little wisdom and some are wise. Master Gotama, what is the cause and what is the reason why human beings, though they are all humans, are seen to be inferior and superior?" These are the fourteen questions found in the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta.

At the conclusion of the explanation given both in brief and in detail, starting with "Young man, beings are owners of their kamma, heirs to their kamma," he took refuge in the Blessed One. Although he was named "Subha" (Beautiful) because of his physical grace, he was still addressed by the term "Māṇava" (young man) even in his old age. Because he came from his estate in Tudigāma and was staying there at that moment, it is stated in the Pāḷi text as "on some business."

By the words "I have one doubt," he shows that he had prepared the question he would ask later in advance. "Māṇavaka" refers to a small boy. This is like the use of the suffix '-ka' in the sense of smallness in words such as "ekaputtako" (an only son) and "piyaputtako" (a dear son). "Vissabhāga-vedanā" refers to painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). That painful feeling is called "vissabhāga-vedanā" because it is the opposite of the pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) that arises in the personality produced by wholesome kamma; it is also called "ābādha" (affliction) because it enters the body intensely and oppresses or pains it.

Regarding the question of what the nature of that painful feeling is, the text says "yā ekadese" and so on. Because it arises in one part of the body and makes it impossible to turn this way or that, it is as if one is bound and held by iron plates. By this, it is shown that a strong disease is called "ābādha." "Kicchajīvitakaro" means it brings about an unhappy life. By this term, it is shown that a weak or slight disease is called "ātaṅka." "Uṭṭhānaṃ" means...
405:
Uṭṭhāna refers to rising from lying down, sitting, and so on. By this term 'uṭṭhāna,' it refers to the ability to turn the body properly from side to side. 'Garuka' has the meaning of heavy or that which prevents the completion of a task. The connection (sambandha) is: "Strength does not exist only in the body of one who is ill." Here, the absence of illness is inquired about through 'lahuṭṭhāna' (lightness in rising). Although the state of not living uncomfortably was asked about with the four preceding terms, now the state of living comfortably is asked again. Therefore, it should be understood that a special kind of 'living comfortably' (phāsuvihāra) is being asked here. Even if there are no words expressing an intensive meaning, the intensive meaning is obtained through the power of the sense. For example, when it is said, "The maiden should be given to the [very] handsome youth," (even if the word 'very' is not with the maiden), the sense of a very beautiful maiden is understood. Therefore, he said "gamanatthāna" and so on. The former speech was a command, while this speech shows the manner of questioning. This distinction between the former and latter speech is shown by the Pāḷi starting with "athassā."

447. 'Kāla' is the appropriate and proper time for approaching. 'Samaya' is the harmony of conditions for that time. In terms of meaning, 'samaya' refers to the physical strength suitable for that journey and the absence of dangers resulting from it. Grasping those 'kāla' and 'samaya' with wisdom is called 'upādāna.' Therefore, he said "paññāyā" and so on. By the phrase "Tomorrow will be the time for going," he shows the 'kāla' (time), and by the phrase "kāye" etc., he shows the 'samaya' (occasion) in its true form. "Pharissati" means it will remain by way of pervading.

448. "Cetiyaraṭṭhe" means in the Ceti country. The word is spoken this way by expanding it with the letter 'ya.' Some also say it is a separate country other than the Ceti country. Because the death (Parinibbāna) of the Ten-Powered Ones (Buddhas) occurs only through the power of disease, the words "Bho Ānanda" and so on are spoken to show how he engaged in a pleasant conversation related to death, such as: inquiring into the nature of that disease, inquiring into the cause, inquiring into the mental distress caused by death, the commonality of that distress to the whole world, and the inability to remedy death. By "ko nāmā" etc., he asks about the disease; by the words "What did the Blessed One partake of?" he asks about the cause; by "api ca" etc., he asks about the mental distress; by "satthā nāmā" etc., he shows its commonality to the whole world; and by "ekā dānī" etc., it should be noted that he shows the inability to remedy death.

"Mahājānī" means a great loss. "Yatra" means 'because of which cause' the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna; it should be connected as: "Since he has attained Parinibbāna, who else now can be free from death?" and so on. The word "idāni" (now) is also spoken as a mere conventional term based on one's own reflection. "Lazzissati" means it will be as if ashamed. "Vijjissati" means it will be avoided or shunned.
406:
The meaning is that eating food suitable for the purgative medicine taken is the practice of the ancients; therefore, it is said, "pīta...pe... datvā."

The word "hutvā" is a remaining part of the text, serving as a qualifier to distinguish the state of wandering near [the Buddha]. The evil Māra does not seek faults as a fault-seeker would, nor does he have the intention to test as the youth Uttara would; rather, he is one who wanders nearby as an attendant. "Na randhagavesī" means one who does not habitually seek flaws or openings. "Yesu dhammesu" refers to the dhammas that lead to liberation from the round of rebirth, which are the causes of vimokkha. "Dharanti" carries the meaning of whether they exist or occur at the present time.

Because the meaning of the words is connected with the application, the three Piṭakas, characterized by the sequence of words, are counted by the three aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue (sīla), which are the meanings of those Piṭakas; with this intention, it is said, "Having grouped the three Piṭakas into the three aggregates." "Taught in brief" means that it was taught concisely, both by number, such as "Youth... of the three aggregates," and in a general sense. The question "Which three?" is only an adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā (a question to illuminate what is not seen), not a kathetukamyatāpucchā (a question asked with the desire to explain). Since this is the question of the youth Subha and not of the Elder, it is said "māṇavo," and so on. In other texts, however, in such instances, only the kathetukamyatāpucchā is found, not the adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā. Nevertheless, since it is stated thus in this Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), that statement should be accepted according to the authority of the Commentary. This is because they performed the Council (Saṅgāyana) by witnessing the words occurring at that time. If it were considered a kathetukamyatāpucchā, those words would only be the words of the Elder Ānanda.

## Sīlakkhandhavaṇṇanā

450-453. In this word "Sīlakkhandhassa," the word "iti," which can cause a change in the meaning of the term, is elided; or it is a reference to the word itself, just as it refers to the meaning. Directly speaking, the word "iti" has the meaning of "beginning" or "variety." By that word "iti," it should be understood that this text "ariyassa samādhikkhandhassa...pe... patiṭṭhapesi" is taken. Therefore, it is said "tesu dassitesu," meaning when those three aggregates are shown by way of brief exposition. "Just as the Blessed One said" refers to the method taught in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and others; by those words, it should be understood that the Buddha-spoken nature of this Subha Sutta is shown. "Virtue alone is not the essence in the Sasana" means that in the Sasana of the Blessed One, which has the Noble Path as its essence, virtue as shown is not the essence itself, just as in a great tree that has heartwood...
407:
...because of its standing in the bark, shoots, and sapwood. Indeed, the word "eva" (only/alone) applied to what is not the proper place should not be applied in its usual place. If it is not the essence, why is that virtue taken here? In response to this objection, it is said "entirely," and so on. It is merely the foundation for one who desires to attain the remaining superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) such as the jhānas; for those states such as the jhānas cannot occur for one who is not established in that virtue. Therefore, the Blessed One taught, "A wise man, established in virtue," and so on.

Alternatively, in saying that virtue alone is not the essence in the Sasana, although the supramundane virtue (lokuttara sīla) known as the Path and Fruit is indeed the essence in this Sasana, the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) alone is not the essence; rather, the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha) and the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) are also the essence. Thus, the meaning should be understood by the word "eva" as applied here; however, the former meaning is more appropriate. For that reason, the teacher said, "higher than this," and so on. "There is still more to be done" refers to the remaining two aggregates of concentration and wisdom.

## Samādhikkhandhavaṇṇanā

Why, in this context, did the Elder Ānanda answer regarding sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara) and so on, even though he was asked about the aggregate of concentration? Does this not mean that by answering one thing when asked another, it is like answering about a breadfruit (labuja) when asked about a mango? To show that such an objection has no place here, he said, "How... and so on." By those words, he shows that sense restraint and so on are also pointed out as part of the aggregate of concentration because they are helpful to concentration. "Those dhammas such as sense restraint" is the connection.

Since it is the opportunity for the teaching on higher powers (abhiññā) immediately after the teaching on the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), only the rūpa jhānas appear, not the arūpa jhānas. Indeed, the six higher powers, along with their requisites, have the fourth rūpāvacara jhāna as their basis. However, since mundane higher powers cannot be perfected without training the mind in fourteen ways across the eight attainments (samāpatti), when the higher powers are taught, the arūpa jhānas are also considered taught because of their immediate succession.

Therefore, it is said, "They should be brought forth and shown." The meaning is that the commentators should reveal what has been taught by the aforementioned method. In the Commentary, however, to show that the arūpa jhānas are also included by the words "attains and dwells in the fourth jhāna," it is said "by the fourth jhāna," and so on. Indeed, only the fourth jhāna occurring by way of meditation on detachment from form is called "arūpa jhāna."

471-480. In this phrase "not by one-pointedness of mind alone," the meaning appropriate to the word "eva" applied to what is or is not the proper place should be understood according to the method mentioned above.
408:
Because the mundane aggregate of concentration (lokiya-samādhikkhandha) is intended, it is said: "na cittēkaggatā...pe... atthī" (there is no one-pointedness of mind... etc.). In the phrase "ariya-samādhikkhandha" (noble aggregate of concentration), the word 'ariya' is merely a synonym for purity (suddha), and not a synonym for the supramundane (lokuttara). As it is here, so it is also in the phrase "ariya-sīlakkhandha" (noble aggregate of virtue). "Ito" (from this) refers to the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). Since that aggregate of wisdom is specifically included within the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), it is said: "arahattapariyosānaṃ" (ending in Arahantship), and so on. Even without mundane supernormal powers (lokiya-abhiññā) and analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), once Arahantship is attained, it can be said: "There is nothing further to be done." This is because the Fruit of Arahantship, for the sake of which the holy life (brahmacariya) is lived under the Blessed One, has been accomplished. In this context, however, mundane supernormal powers are indeed included. The rest of the text here is easy to understand.

Thus, the Clarification of the Hidden Meaning (Līnatthappakāsanā) in the sub-commentary named Sādhuvilāsinī—which illuminates the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-fathom meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumangalavilāsinī, and which generates pure and vast intellectual clarity—the explanation of the Subha Sutta is concluded.

## The Explanation of the Subha Sutta is finished.
409:
## 11. Kevaṭṭasutta-vaṇṇanā
## Explanation of the Story of Kevaṭṭa, the Householder's Son
Having thus explained the Subha Sutta, the Kevaṭṭa Sutta is now to be explained. To show that the opportunity to explain it in the sequence of the Suttas has arrived, or to show that the Sutta recited [at the Council] immediately after the Subha Sutta is the Kevaṭṭa Sutta, he said: "Evaṃ me sutaṃ...pe... Nālandāyaṃ," which is the Kevaṭṭa Sutta. "Pāvārikassa" means [in the grove] of the merchant named thus. "Ambavane" means in the park where mango trees are abundant. It is said that the merchant, having prepared a Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi) suitable for the Blessed One, as well as huts, pavilions, etc., for the night and day residences of the Saṅgha of monks, and having enclosed it with a wall and provided it with a gatehouse, offered the monastery to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. However, according to former usage, this monastery is simply called "Pāvārikambavana."

"Kevaṭṭa" is just a name. Some teachers say he was so called because he was protected by fishermen (kevaṭṭa) or because he grew up among them. In the phrase "gahapatiputtassa" (of the householder's son), although Kevaṭṭa was at that time established in the position of a householder, he is referred to by the former designation "householder's son" because his father had not been dead for long. Therefore, it is said: "gahapatimahāsālo." It means a householder who has the "essence" (sāra) of great wealth. By changing the letter 'r' to 'l', it is called "mahāsāla." It is like the word "palibuddha." "Saddho pasanno" (faithful and confident) means being endowed with faith in the Triple Gem by the power of a worldling's faith, and for that very reason, having confidence in the Triple Gem. Or, "saddho" means having faith in kamma and its results, and "pasanno" means having much confidence in the Triple Gem. "Saddhādhikattāyeva" (due to the predominance of faith) gives the reason for such a thought. Indeed, one in whom faith is predominant can become like one who is mad.

"Samiddhā" means well-prospered. It is full, having reached an abundance of wealth and success. Regarding the meaning that this city of Nālandā is crowded with many people, it is said: "aṃsakūṭena" (by the shoulder-joint), and so on. "Come, monk, every half-month, every month, or every year, perform a miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya) to inspire the people"—this commanding or exhorting of a monk is called "samādisana." Since such commanding is like appointing someone to a position, it is said: "ṭhānantare ṭhapetuṃ" (to place in a position). "Uttari-manussānaṃ" (of superhuman beings) refers to those superior to ordinary humans, such as the Buddhas and other Great Beings, meditators (jhāyī), and Noble Ones (ariya). "Dhammato" means from the attained states (dhamma) such as jhāna, abhiññā, path, and fruit. This word has the fifth (ablative) case ending in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). Indeed, it is the showing of a miracle of psychic power drawn from those states.

Having thus formed a compound (samāsa) by joining the word "uttari" with "manussa," he now wishes to show the separate word related to "pāṭihāriya," and thus said: "dasakusala-saṅkhātato vā" (or from what is called the ten wholesome [courses of action]), and so on. "Manussadhammato" means [superior to] the ten wholesome courses of action of ordinary humans. Just as pouring oil into a bright lamp, regarding the gift of the sandalwood bowl by the merchant of Rājagaha, [it was said]: "Monks, to the people, [the miracle] of superhuman..."
410:
"From the states of jhāna, abhiññā, magga, and phala" means from among the states that are to be attained, specifically jhāna, abhiññā, magga, and phala. Here, the word 'dhammato' is in the ablative case (nissakkavacana) in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). This is because the miracle of psychic power is selected and shown from those states of jhāna, abhiññā, magga, and phala.

Thus, after combining the word 'uttari' with the word 'manussa' to form a single compound (samāsa), the teacher says "or more than the ten wholesome courses of action," etc., wishing to treat the word 'uttari' separately as it relates to the word 'pāṭihāriya'. 'Manussadhammato' means more than the states of ordinary humans (the ten wholesome courses of action). 'Pajjalitapadīpo' refers to a burning lamp. 'Telasnehaṃ' refers to the pouring of oil. 'Rājagahaseṭṭhivatthusmiṃ' refers to the story of the merchant of Rājagaha donating a sandalwood bowl. 'He laid down the training rule' means he laid down this training rule prohibiting the miracle of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi), saying: "Monks, the miracle of psychic power, which is a superhuman state, should not be shown to laypeople. For one who shows it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)."

The teacher shows that this statement is made with reference to not falling away from the fulfillment of virtues such as morality (sīla) and concentration (samādhi), by saying "not by destroying virtue." Therefore, he said "the breaking of morality," etc. "There is no such thing as one who is capable" means there is no one who can make an effort in a matter that is prohibited. Although there is no such person, to show that this Kevaṭṭa is making an effort for this other reason, he said "But this person," etc. Because he is an intimate friend, the sentence should be connected as "having increased the intimacy." "Vaḍḍhetvā" (having increased) means having expanded and made it clear.

## Explanation of the Miracle of Psychic Power (Iddhi-pāṭihāriya-vaṇṇanā)

483-4. "Ādīnava" means fault. Because it was asked how that Gandhara ascetic did it, or where it arose, he said "It is heard there," etc. "By a single person" means by the ascetic named Gandhara alone. Only by taking it this way do the preceding and following words harmonize. This science called Gandhārī is of two kinds: Cūḷagandhārī and Mahāgandhārī. Among them, Cūḷagandhārī is the science that can know the destination (gati) of beings who died within three years. The story of the brahmin Vaṅgīsa is the evidence here. Mahāgandhārī is the science that not only knows that destination but can also accomplish the task of the knowledge of various psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) beyond that. Generally, this science accomplishes the function of the knowledge of various psychic powers. It is said that a person who masters that science, having recited the mantra at a suitable place and time, can show himself in various ways, show elephants, etc., become invisible, perform fire-prevention (aggithambha), perform water-prevention (jalathambha), and show himself in the sky. Everything should be regarded as like a magician's trick (indajāla). "Aṭṭa" means one who has reached suffering, one who is oppressed. Therefore, he said "pīḷita" (oppressed).
411:
## Explanation of the Miracle of Mind-reading (Ādesanā-pāṭihāriya-vaṇṇanā)

The word "cetasika" is indeed a collective term for states associated with the mind, those that are thoroughly conjoined with the mind. However, when such a collective term is taken, it is said to show a specific state of mind. General manifestation also rests on a specific detail. Therefore, wishing to show the intended meaning of the word "cetasika," the teacher says "joy (somanassa) and grief (domanassa) are intended." Here, by taking somanassa, the unwholesome states such as lust (rāga) and the wholesome states such as faith (saddhā) that exist in the same thought-arising (cittuppāda) as that somanassa are shown. By taking domanassa, states such as hatred (dosa) are shown. As for initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), they are shown by their own nature (sarūpa).

Because the meaning of the word "pi" as connecting what is to be said is well understood, he says "Thus is your mind." This means "In this manner, your mind has arisen." In what manner has it arisen? It is said "whether conjoined with joy," etc. "Thus also is your mind" is merely to show the state of being conjoined with joy, etc. However, it does not show the specific mind by which there is conjunction with joy or conjunction with grief. To show that mind, it is said in the Pali text, "Thus also is your mind." Here, the word "iti" has the sense of pointing out (nidassana), as in the Pali passages like "Kaccāyana, 'it exists' is one extreme," etc. Therefore, he says "this and that exists." The word "pi" here also has the sense of connecting what has been said.

Because it knows the thoughts of others, it is called "Cintāmaṇi." The letter 'na' is changed to 'ṇa'. That same science is also called "Maṇikā" by removing the preceding word. Since what is called thought (cintā) cannot occur without the mind, he says "he knows the minds of others." Some teachers say, "A person who accomplishes that Cintāmaṇi science, having recited the mantra at such a place and time, if he wishes to know the mind of a certain person, he predicts the behavior of the mind by comparing and inferring through the recognition of specific details such as what was seen or heard." Other teachers say, "He makes the person utter words and speaks by means of noting the syllables in those words." That science should be understood through the Padakusala Jātaka.

## Explanation of the Miracle of Instruction (Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya-vaṇṇanā)

"Pavattentā" means being those who cause to occur; the meaning is "think by way of causing to occur." The word "evaṃ" (thus) is a reflection on the mode of occurrence by way of prescription and by way of prohibition, according to the method of the instruction (anusāsanī) that has been given. That instruction also occurs for the purpose of clarifying the benefits and the dangers in those thoughts, by showing the mode of occurrence of right thoughts (sammā-vitakka) and wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka). One should attend only to the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), not to the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā).
412:
The use of the word 'eva' (only) is for the purpose of excluding the opposite (paṭipakkha). Here too, the meaning and purpose of the word 'evaṃ' should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The same applies to the use of the word 'idaṃ'. The phrase 'lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure' (pañcakāmaguṇikarāga) is merely an illustration. This is because the abandonment of lust other than that for sensual pleasures, as well as the abandonment of hatred and so forth, is desired; and because the abandonment of that lust for sensual pleasures is the means (upāya) for eliminating other types of lust and so on. It is like how extracting bad blood is the means for removing previously formed bad flesh (pus).

In the phrase 'lokuttaradhamma-m-eva', the restriction (by the word 'eva') should be understood as primarily intended to exclude blameworthy states (unwholesome states) because they are opposites. This is because other blameless (wholesome) states, which are the means to and the benefits of attaining that supramundane Dhamma, are inseparable from it. Considering that psychic power itself is a wonder, 'iddhividha' (modes of psychic power) is presented as 'iddhipāṭihāriya' (the wonder of psychic power). The same method should be understood for the remaining two terms (ādesanā and anusāsanī).

Regarding the definition (vacanattha) of the word 'pāṭihāriya', some say: "It is called pāṭihāriya because it removes the opposing defilements such as lust." However, in the Blessed One, there are no opposing defilements like lust that need to be removed. Even for worldlings (puthujjana), psychic power (iddhividha) occurs in a mind that is free from impurities (upakkilesa), endowed with the eight factors, and has suppressed the opposites. Therefore, it cannot be called 'pāṭihāriya' here based on the usage applied to the minds of those worldlings.

If it is said to be 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes the defilements that are the opposites existing in the mental continuities of those to be tamed (veneyya) by the Great Compassionate Blessed One, then such a statement is quite appropriate. Alternatively, it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it suppresses (removes) the sectarians (titthiya) who are opponents of the Blessed One and the Dispensation (Sāsana). Those sectarians are removed and suppressed by psychic power, mind-reading (ādesanā), and instruction (anusāsanī), both by the removal of their wrong views and by their inability to manifest their own doctrines.

In another way, the word 'paṭi' conveys the meaning of 'pacchā' (afterwards). This is like the phrase in the Pārāyana Sutta: "When he had entered afterwards (paṭipaviṭṭhamhi), another brahmin arrived." Therefore, it is called 'paṭihāriya' because it is performed afterwards by one who has completed his task, when the mind is concentrated and free from impurities. Or, it is called 'paṭihāriya' because it occurs after one's own impurities have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the Path. Psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction are performed again for the benefit of beings by one who is free from impurities and has completed his task. Because the removal of the impurities of other beings occurs after one's own impurities have been removed, they are called 'paṭihāriya'. 'Paṭihāriya' is the same as 'pāṭihāriya'. Or, each individual element within the collection of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction, which are 'paṭihāriya', is called 'pāṭihāriya'. Or, it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because it occurs in the fourth jhāna and the Path, which are called 'paṭihāriya' due to their removal of opposites, or because it occurs with that fourth jhāna and Path as the cause, or because it originates from them.
413:
It is called 'pāṭihāriya' because, through psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction, it removes the defilements that are the opposites of faith and so forth in the mental continuums of others, according to the method already stated. 'Constant teaching of Dhamma' (satataṃ dhammadesanā) means the Dhamma teaching that is to be given at all times.

In the term 'iddhipāṭihāriyena', the instrumental case is used in the sense of association (sahādiyoga). It means 'practiced together with that miracle of psychic power'. The same method applies to the other terms [ādesanā and anusāsanī]. It should be construed as 'the practice of the General of the Dhamma' (Dhammasenāpati Sāriputta). To prove this point using the story from the Cullavagga Khandhaka, he said "Devadatte" and so forth.

Gayāsīsa is a large stone slab resembling an elephant's frontal globe (hatthikumbha) located not far from Gaya village, where there is space for even a thousand monks. [The Buddha taught] on that stone slab. By the phrase "knowing the movement of the mind," the miracle of mind-reading (ādesanā-pāṭihāriya) is shown. By the phrase "he taught the Dhamma," the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya) is shown. By the phrase "having shown a psychic transformation," the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya) is shown.

'Mahānāga' refers to the great Arahants whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava). 'Nāga' is a designation for an Arahant because he has no evil (āgu). As stated in the Sabhiya Sutta:

"He does no evil (āgu) at all in the world,
Having abandoned all fetters and bonds;
He is not attached to anything, being liberated,
Such a one is called a 'Nāga' because of his suchness."

However, in this regard, the Commentary (Atthakathā) states: "Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the General of the Dhamma [Sāriputta], five hundred monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, they were established in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala)."

But in the Saṅghabhedaka Khandhaka Pali, it is stated: "Then, while those monks were being exhorted and instructed by the Venerable Sāriputta with the miracle of mind-reading and instruction, and by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna with the miracle of psychic power and instruction, there arose in them the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma (dhamma-cakkhu): 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.'" Thus, it shows the attainment of the Eye of Dhamma by the teaching of both Elders. This discrepancy in statements should be understood as a difference of opinion between the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīgha-bhāṇaka) and the reciters of the Khandhaka (Khandhaka-bhāṇaka). For this Pali text was spoken by the redactors of the Council (saṅgāhaka), and the Commentary was also established by those same redactors. Alternatively, in the Pali text, the higher Paths and Fruits are also included under the term 'Eye of Dhamma'...
414:
The word "udapādi" should be understood as stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta and the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta.

The statement "The miracle of instruction is the constant Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas" is said because of its excellence. Because they can be overwhelmed by counterfeit versions as previously mentioned, [the miracles of psychic power and mind-reading] are "with reproach." Because they are not the means for completely cutting off the faults attributed by others, they are "with fault." Precisely because they are with fault, they do not endure for a long time; they are not long-lasting. Because they do not endure for a long time, they do not lead out [from suffering]; this is an inference of the cause from the effect. Indeed, because they do not lead out, they are not long-lasting. The miracle of instruction is "without reproach" because it originates from purity and relies on purity. For that very reason, it is faultless. In that miracle of instruction, there is no possibility of faults such as internal contradiction. Precisely because it is faultless, it endures for a long time, as it cannot be oppressed or destroyed by the winds of others' criticism or the winds of defilements. Because it endures for a long time, it leads out [from suffering]; here too, it is an inference of the cause from the effect. Indeed, because it leads out, it is long-lasting. The word "tasmā" (therefore) is due to the aforementioned reason; by that word, both "with reproach" etc. and "without reproach" etc. are considered respectively as the causes for being blameworthy or praiseworthy.

## Description of the Story of the One Seeking the Cessation of the Elements

"Aniyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ" means that although the monk seeking the great elements was proficient and highly skilled in the first two miracles, he did not realize Nibbana, which is the cessation of the great elements without remainder. Therefore, because those two miracles do not bring about the leading out [from suffering], they are "not leading out" (aniyyānika); this is said for the purpose of showing their non-leading nature. "Niyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ" means that for the one who practices it, the miracle of instruction definitely brings about the leading out; this is said for the purpose of showing its leading nature alone.

Having thus shown the primary purpose of this teaching, "apica" etc. is now begun to show the incidental purpose. Indeed, the leading out [from suffering] is the primary purpose of this teaching, because that is its objective. The greatness of the Buddhas, however, is the incidental purpose, as it is to be understood by implication. Because it was asked, "What is the nature of this monk?", [the Buddha] said "yo mahābhūte" etc. "Pariyesanto" means seeking the great elements by way of cessation without remainder, desiring to investigate the absolute cessation of those great elements.
415:
"Seeking the great elements by way of cessation without remainder, investigating their cessation without remainder" is what is meant. "Vicarītvā" means having wandered, being urged by the nature of things (dhammatā). It is said that this is established by nature, namely, that monk's wandering in such a way, just like the great earthquake etc. at the time of the Buddha's birth. "Vissajjokāsaṃ" means the place for answering. There is also a variant reading "vissajjakaraṃ," which means one who answers. "Tasmā" means that because of the absence of doubt from having asked only the Buddha, and because only the Buddha is capable of answering, this is what is meant. "Mahantabhāvappakāsanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of illustrating the greatness and the great majesty of the Buddhas, which is not shared by others in the world including the devas. "And this reason" means this reason also: that in the dispensation of all Buddhas, there is always one such monk who illustrates that majesty.

The word "kattha" is in the locative case in the sense of cause (nimitta). To show the meaning "due to what cause," it is said "kiṃ āgamma." It means "having reached what object as a condition, as the cause of attainment." Therefore, he said "kiṃ pattassa." It should be connected as: "To the person who has reached what object do the great elements cease?" This is an adjective containing the cause. "Te" refers to the great elements. "Appavattivasena" means by way of not arising again. "Sabbākārena" means in every way: by way of word-meaning (vacanattha), characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), origination (samuṭṭhāna), group (kalāpa), particles (cuṇṇa), diversity (nānatta), unity (ekatta), separation (vinibbhoga), non-separation (avinibbhoga), similar (sabhāga), dissimilar (visabhāga), internal (ajjhattika), external (bāhira), inclusion (sangaha), condition (paccaya), attention (samannāhāra), and analysis of conditions (paccayavibhāga); and by way of summary with constituents (sasambhārasankhepa), analysis with constituents (sasambhāravibhatti), summary of individual characteristics (salakkhaṇasankhepa), and analysis of individual characteristics (salakkhaṇavibhatti).

In the word "dibbaṃ," those who wander, play, and shine while being endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure are called "devas" (gods) and "devaloka" (heavenly world). Because they go to that heavenly world by this [psychic power], it is called "devayāniya." Just as in the word "niyyānika," the suffix "anīya" is in the sense of the agent (kattu), here it should be understood as being in the instrumental sense (karaṇa). For it is said, "te na hesā" etc. In the phrase "vasaṃ vattento," "vasavattana" means going to any place as desired. "Taṃ" refers to the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividha-ñāṇa). Because those gods have the four great kings as their lords, they are called "Cātumahārājikā." Why did this monk approach the distant gods without asking the Blessed One, the light of the world including the devas, who was standing nearby? This objection is removed by the words "samīpe ṭṭhitaṃ" etc. "Even those gods who have attained the paths and fruits might know that matter in part, but this question was asked as it is the domain of the Buddhas," so they thought.
416:
After reflecting, (the gods) said, "We do not know." Therefore, the words beginning with "Buddha-visaye" were spoken. "Na labbhā" means being unable. In this question, the act of pressing or harassing by asking is called "ajjhottharaṇa," thus it means "asking repeatedly." The phrase "letting go from the hand" is spoken by way of worldly idiom; it means "now we shall remove this monk to a distance." In the word "abhikkantatarā," the prefix "abhi" has the sense of the word "ati" (surpassing), hence it is said "atikkantatarā." It means being more desirable to others, surpassing us in terms of physical perfection and qualities such as wisdom and intuition. "Paṇītatara" means more sublime (uḷāratara). Therefore, it is called "uttamatara" (most excellent).

491-493. Why did Sakka, the thousand-eyed one, who has realized the Four Noble Truths, attained the fruit of Stream-entry, and understood the Dispensation, urge that monk through a stratagem? This question is dispelled by the words beginning with "Ayaṃ pana viseso."

"Khajjopanaka" refers to a firefly that glows at night. "As if blowing" means as if giving out breath from the mouth. "Atthi cevā" means such a person seeking the great elements would indeed exist; the intention is "he will only know later after I have sent him." "Tato" means after such thinking. Since only the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) is intended, it is just like the path leading to the gods (devayāniya). The statement "Whether called the divine path (devayāniya-magga)... or higher knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa), all these are names for the knowledge of psychic powers" is spoken in the Pali and Commentaries according to the conventional names (ruḷhī) found in various places. For in all higher knowledges, names such as "divine path" and "absorption (appanā) of a single mind-moment" are applicable as appropriate.

"Āgamanapubbabāge nimittaṃ" refers to the sign that arises prior to the arrival of the Great Brahma. It should be connected by bringing in the analogy of "prior to sunrise" (like the dawn). "Ime" refers to the hosts of Brahmas. "Veyyākaraṇena" means by way of explanation. "Anāraddha-citto" means having a dissatisfied heart. "Vādaṃ" means fault. "Vikkhepaṃ" means various ways of tossing words aside (evasion).

"Kuhakattā" means because of deceitfulness, wanting to amaze others with what is not true. Some read it as "guhakattā," meaning because of wanting to hide.
417:
## Tīradassī-sakuṇūpamā-vaṇṇanā
"Padesena" means partially, by way of "clung-to matter" (upādinnaka-rūpa) included within the continuity of beings. "Anupādinnake" means also in matter not connected with the faculties (inorganic). "Nippadesato" means without remainder (completely). "Tasmā" means because it was asked in that way, implying the inappropriateness of the question. "Pucchā-mūḷhassa" refers to one who is confused in questioning because of not knowing how to ask. Indeed, just as one confused on a journey is called "magga-mūḷha," one with a distorted problem is called "pucchā-mūḷha." "Pucchāya dosaṃ dassetvā" means having clarified the fault in the manner of the monk's questioning. "Pucchā-vissajjanaṃ" is the answer to the undistorted question as taught. Since an answer must correspond to the question and be given in a manner consistent with the question, and since the Tathāgatas do not answer in a distorted way corresponding to a distorted question, and because questioners might become confused not understanding the meaning due to the nature of the answer, it should be understood that it is the habit of the Buddhas to teach the proper question first and then answer the undistorted question. Therefore, the teacher said "Kasmā," etc. "Duviññāpayo" means difficult to make understood for the reasons mentioned.

"Na patiṭṭhāti" means it does not stand by way of a condition. The word "kattha" is the locative case in the sense of a cause/sign, hence it is said "kiṃ āgamma" (depending on what). "Appatiṭṭhā" means having no condition, in the sense of having completely cut off all causes. "Upādinnamyeva" refers only to matter connected with the faculties. Because the perception of "long" (dīgha-saññā) occurs in a continuity of matter that stands extensively in one direction, and depending on that perception of long, the perception of "short" (rassa-saññā) occurs in matter that stands less than that, and both are grasped primarily through the perception of visible form, therefore "saṇṭhāna-vasena" (by way of shape), etc., is said. The perception of "fine" (aṇu-saññā) occurs in a mass of matter of small dimension, and depending on that, the perception of "gross" (thūla-saññā) occurs in matter larger than that. Since these two are also grasped primarily through the perception of visible form, "imināpi," etc., is said. Here, teachers say that with the word "pi," the meaning "even here, only color/appearance is spoken of" is included in the phrase "derived matter is spoken of by way of shape." Here, the word "vaṇṇa" is just a synonym for the visible-form base (rūpāyatana). "Subha" means beautiful or desirable. "Asubha" means not beautiful or undesirable. Therefore, it is said, "Thus the pleasant and unpleasant objects are described." In the three instances of long, short, fine, gross, and beautiful/ugly, it should be understood that only derived matter (upādā-rūpa) is taken, using the visible-form base as the starting point, because the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa) have been taken separately. For the primary elements are taken separately in the phrase "Where do water, earth, fire, and air find no footing?" "Nāma" refers to the four mental aggregates, such as feeling (vedanā). It is called "nāma" because it bends (namana) towards the object and because it makes a name. Below...
418:
The phrase beginning with “dīghaṃ rassaṃ” (long and short) refers to the derived matter (upādā-rūpa) already mentioned, which is taken here as the perception of form (rūpasaññā) due to its nature of being deformed (ruppanaṭṭhena); this is shown by the words “dīghādibhedaṃ” (the variety of long, etc.). The word “ādi” (etc.) also includes the water element (āpo-dhātu) and so forth. Alternatively, it is because designations such as “long” and so on are not only based on the visible-object base (rūpāyatana), but in fact, are also based on the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa). This is true because shape (saṇṭhāna) can also be perceived through the tangible-object base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana). Therefore, to make it understood that by taking “long, short,” etc., the primary elements are also included, it is said: “dīghādibhedaṃ rūpaṃ” (form consisting of the variety of long, etc.). “Kiṃ āgamma” means: by attaining what? Or, because of what reason of attainment? The word “uparujjhati” (ceases) is said with reference to the cessation without further arising (anuppāda-nirodha, i.e., Nibbāna), and not with reference to momentary cessation (khaṇa-nirodha); to show this, it is said: “all this does not occur anymore without remainder.”

“Therein, the answer is” is merely a connecting phrase. The meaning is that after stating the prose passage (cuṇṇiya-pāṭha), the verse beginning with “viññāṇaṃ” (consciousness), which constitutes the answer, is spoken. “Viññātabba” means it should be known by distinguished knowledge; the meaning is that it should be known through direct realization by the Path Knowledge of the Noble Ones (ariya-magga-ñāṇa), which is supreme among all knowledges. Therefore, it is said: “This is a name for Nibbāna.” Because it can be seen, it is called “nidassana” (a visible object cognizable by eye-consciousness). Because it cannot be seen, teachers say it is “anidassana” (Nibbāna, which is not cognizable by eye-consciousness). Alternatively, “nidassana” means a simile or example. Since such a simile does not exist for Nibbāna, it is called “anidassana.” Indeed, a simile similar to Nibbāna—which is permanent, unique, and of an extremely refined nature—cannot be found anywhere. That conditioned thing (saṅkhata) which arises without having existed before and perishes after having existed, is called “sa-anta” (having an end) because it has the ends of arising and falling. However, in the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) and permanent Nibbāna, both those ends do not exist. For that very reason, decay (jaratā), characterized by the departure from the state of being new, also does not exist in it; thus it is said: “uppādanto vā” (the end of arising, etc.). Therein, “uppādanta” refers to the moment of arising (uppāda). “Vayanta” refers to the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga). “Ṭhitassa aññathattanto” refers to decay (jaratā). By the inclusion of the remainder, the moment of presence (ṭhī) is also acknowledged. “Tittha” refers to a watering place (pānatittha). The etymology of that word is shown by “tañhi,” etc. “Papanti” means they drink in various ways. Thus, the teacher said: “It is called papanti because they drink there; here, papanti means a watering place” (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.499), according to the method of linguistics (nirutti), or by the rule of phonology where the letter ‘pa’ is changed to ‘ba’. “Sabbatoto” means through every entrance of the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). Therefore, it is said: “through whichever entrance among the thirty-eight meditation subjects.” This is another method from the Commentary: “pabhā” means shining or illuminating in various ways; it is “sabbatopabhaṃ” because it has radiance from all sides. The meaning is that it is radiant and pure all around because it is not defiled by anything. In the word “nibbāne,” the locative case (sattamī) is shown to be in the sense of cause (nimitta) by the phrase “having Nibbāna as the cause.”
419:
By whichever Path Knowledge Nibbāna is attained, it is meant that only for the phenomena included in that continuity (santati) is the cessation without further arising (anuppāda-nirodha) intended here; therefore, it was said: “the group of clinging-phenomena ceases, it does not occur again.”

“Tattha” refers to that word which was taught as “viññāṇassa nirodhena” (by the cessation of consciousness). Consciousness is extracted and shown separately because it is to be analyzed. “Carimaka-viññāṇa” (final consciousness) is the parinibbāna-consciousness, known as the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) of an Arahant. “Abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa” (karmic-formative consciousness) is the volitional consciousness of merit and so forth. In this Nibbāna, this name-and-form ceases through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). Therefore, it was said: “extinguished... reaches the state of...” “Vijjhātadīpasikhā viya” means like the flame of a lamp that has been extinguished. By the passage beginning with “abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇassāpi,” the Nibbāna element without remainder is spoken of by way of the Nibbāna element with remainder (saupādisesa), because the intended meaning is the cessation of name-and-form without any remainder. Therefore, it was said: “it ceases by way of not arising again.” The word “sotāpattimaggañāṇena” (by the knowledge of the path of stream-entry) is a word with the third case ending (instrumental) in the sense of either the agent (kattā) or the instrument (karaṇa). The word “nirodhena,” however, is in the sense of cause (hetu). “Ettha” means in Nibbāna. All the remaining words have meanings that are clear and obvious.

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, for the purpose of illuminating the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-understand meanings, and for the purpose of generating the courage and proficiency of very pure and vast wisdom, the clarification of the obscure meanings (Līnatthappakāsanī) of the Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta, in the sub-commentary named Sādhuvilāsinī, is completed.

## The Explanation of the Kevaṭṭa Sutta is finished.
420:
## 12. Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta
## Commentary on the Story of Lohicca the Brahmin
Having thus commented on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta, the commentator, now wishing to comment on the Lohicca Sutta, speaks the Lohicca Sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... pe... Kosalesu" either to clarify the opportunity to comment in due order or to show that the Sutta recited immediately after the Kevaṭṭa Sutta is the Lohicca Sutta.

"Sālavatikā" is the name given to that village by way of the feminine gender without any special reason. Some say it is called Sālavatikā because there was no village headman. "Vatiyā" refers to a fence made of thorn branches and such. The person named "Lohita" was the first ancestor in that brahmin's lineage. Because he was of the lineage of that Lohita, he is called "Lohicca," the son of Lohita, a name derived from the brahmin's clan (gotta).

The view "What can one person do for another?" is a base view because it is devoid of compassion for others. However, because it is not specifically one of the views of annihilationism (uccheda) or eternalism (sassata), it is stated as "Na pana," etc. "Diṭṭhigataṃ" refers merely to a view. Otherwise, since there is no wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) that is free from the grasp of annihilationism or eternalism, it would have to be one of those two. The phrase "uppannaṃ hoti" (it has arisen) is shown by "Na kevalañca," etc., to be a word common to arising in both the mind and in speech. That this view is well-known in the world is meant by the words "bhāsatiyeva." Since a person other than oneself is "para" (another), the one to be admonished is "para" from the perspective of the admonisher, and likewise, the admonisher is "para" from the perspective of the one to be admonished; this is stated as "paro," etc., to show this. Here, the future tense "karissati" (will do) is used in consideration of the word "kiṃ" (what). Or, it is to show that even in the future, there is nothing that person needs to do for the other.

"Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ" means the faultless Dhamma, the Dhamma free from defilements, the Dhamma of liberation (vimokkha—Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna). What is the benefit of wandering around surrounded by others, saying "I will preach the Dhamma to others"? This cannot happen without an increase in desire (āsayavuddha). Therefore, it means one should live by oneself. Thus, he says, "I call this an evil state of greed of such a nature."

By the words "itthilingavasena" (by way of the feminine gender), it is shown that although the meaning is masculine, it is designated with a feminine name. "So" refers to Lohicca the Brahmin. "Bhāro" (burden) means it is heavy and difficult to perform because of the large number of the Buddha's assembly and because of having many of one's own duties to perform.
421:
'Kathā-phāsukatthaṃ' means for the sake of ease in conversation; the meaning is to be able to speak and listen to the discourse with ease. "This lay follower" refers to Rosika the barber. In the phrase 'appeve nāma siyā' (if it could only be), it should be understood as a repetition (āmeḍita) spoken twice by the power of joy (pīti). Such a double utterance is called 'Buddha-gajjita' (the Buddha's roar). For the Buddha, in such instances, especially feels joy and gladness; therefore, he first roars by the power of joy and then roars a second time in follow-up. The distinction between the roar and the follow-up roar is shown by 'ayaṃ' etc. Speaking at the beginning is called 'allāpa'; if followed by a conjunct consonant, it is made short. Speaking together beyond that is called 'sallāpa.'

## Explanation of the Inquiry of Lohicca the Brahmin (Lohicca-brāhmaṇānuyoga-vaṇṇanā)

'Samudaya-sañjāti' means the arising of revenue (bhoguppāda). 'Tato' means from the village of Sālavatikā. 'Lābhantarāyakaro' means one who creates an obstacle to the acquisition of wealth and grain. The prefix 'anu' before the word 'kapi' shows the sense of desiring, as indicated by the word 'icchati.' This is another method besides the Commentary: 'Hitānukampī' is so called because one favors with excessive welfare. 'Sampajjati' means it is accomplished through repeated practice, becomes strong, and is without obstruction (avaggaha). Therefore, it is said to be 'fixed' (niyatā hoti).

510-511. 'Dutiyaṃ upapattiṃ' refers to the second possible logical reason stated in such words as "Is it not King Pasenadi of Kosala?" For the Blessed One shows the root cause by way of a simile. By showing it in this way, including the Brahmin Lohicca, he creates a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvejanā) in you and others. The construction is: "Those sons of good family who bring to maturity the divine wombs." They are unable to do so either because of the lack of perfection in the supporting conditions (upanissaya) or because of the lack of maturity of knowledge. In the verb 'paripācenti,' due to the grammatical transposition of cases (vibhatti-vipallāsa), the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative in the second meaning. Some teachers read 'paripaccanti' in the passive form; in their view, there is no need for case transposition because it is a reflexive-passive (kamma-kattu), but the meaning should be understood as a special merit such as giving (dāna), as mentioned in the second alternative. The desire for harm (ahitānukampā) etc., occurs by the power of beings who possess such a nature. It is called 'dibba' (divine) because it exists in heaven. It is called 'gabbha' (womb) because they are bound to themselves by the power of maturing; this refers to the celestial realms. "The six celestial realms" is just an illustration. For even the Brahma world can be considered a divine womb because it is caused by the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra). Because of this, the phrase "developing the meditation" is also...
422:
The expression "bhāvanaṃ bhāvayamānā" is complete. After stating "fulfilling the practice that leads to the deva world," the teacher says "giving gifts (dāna)," etc., to demonstrate that practice in detail. Because devas, endowed with happiness as they desire, arise in mansions (vimānas), the mansions are called "bhava" (planes of existence). Because they bring about the state of a deva, they are called "dibba" (divine). By the same method already mentioned, they are called "gabbha." This refers to specific merits such as giving (dāna) that lead to the deva world. Here, "divine planes" (dibba bhava) refers to the "rebirth-process" (upapatti-bhava) included within the deva world. Since the "action-process" (kamma-bhava) that leads to that deva world was taken previously, the teacher says "resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandhā) in the deva world."

## Explanation of the Three Teachers Worthy of Reproof

"Aniyāmiteneva" means without specifically pointing out, such as saying, "You have such a view; you are the doer of harm to beings."

Because the view has spread throughout the entire world, the pride that rises up to the highest plane of existence (bhavagga) is the "pride of the wise" (paṇḍita-māna) which occurs as "I know this, I see this." The meaning is to destroy and abandon this pride.

"Three teachers" refers to: a teacher who has not achieved his own benefit and whose disciples do not follow his advice; a teacher who has not achieved his own benefit but whose disciples follow his advice; and a teacher who has achieved his own benefit but whose disciples do not follow his advice. The fourth, the Fully Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha), is not a teacher worthy of reproof. Therefore, with the intention of answering only when asked by the brahmin Lohicca, the Buddha first shows the three teachers worthy of reproof and later shows the fourth teacher.

Although the fourth teacher is unique, without a peer, and unlike other teachers, he is called the "Dhamma-made body" (dhammamaya-kāya) by virtue of those superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). Although he is the collection of those superhuman states, the Blessed One, wishing to show those qualities as being in the position of a teacher, said, "Lohicca, this teacher also..."

The designation "aññā" is a designation where the letter 'ya' is elided, as in "sayaṃ abhiññā," etc. The teacher shows that this is the dative case (sampadāna) in that sense with the words "aññāyā," etc. Because they remain having professed discipleship, they follow his teaching only partially; thus it is said, "without constantly following his teaching."

"Turning away, turning away" (ukkamitvā ukkamitvā) is a repetitive expression (vīcchā) referring to sometimes doing so and sometimes not doing so. It means they do as they please. "They shrink back" means they move away due to lack of delight or lack of respect. For that reason...
423:
The meaning of "paṭikkamantiyā" is moving away due to lack of delight or lack of respect. For that reason, it is said "aniicchantiyā" (an unwilling woman), etc. "Ekāya" means with a woman who is alone. "Sampayogaṃ" means engaging in sexual intercourse. "Eko iccheyya" means a man who is alone (not the husband) would desire engagement in sexual intercourse; the words should be brought in and connected thus. Showing the union of man and woman through the metaphor of shrinking back, etc., serves the purpose of showing the practice of that teacher's disciples in terms of whether they depend on craving or not. It refers to a woman who, being extremely detached, does not even wish to look and stands with her back turned. "Lobbhena" means with greed for gains and honor (lābha-sakkāra) that arises depending on having a following. "Īdiso" means a teacher of such a nature. "Yena" means by that greed. "Tattha sampādehi" means establish them in that practice and make it complete. Make it straight by removing the crookedness of the body, etc.

514. "Sassarūpakāni tiṇāni" refers to grasses such as wild barley that resemble crops.

515. "Evaṃ codanaṃ arahati" means he deserves reproof by way of urging them to reach a state of lack of concern for the disciples in the manner already mentioned. He is not worthy of reproof like the first teacher with words such as "Your greed is of such a nature," nor is he worthy of reproof like the second teacher with words such as "First make yourself complete in that practice." Why? Because the third teacher has already achieved his own benefit.

## Explanation of the Teacher Not Worthy of Reproof

In this context, "na codanāraho" (not worthy of reproof) is because reproof arises due to the misconduct of the teacher, the misconduct of the disciples, or the misconduct of both. None of these types of misconduct exist in this teacher (the Buddha); therefore, to show this meaning, the words "ayañhi," etc., are said. "Assavā" means being obedient (listening respectfully).

"Mayā gahitāya diṭṭhiyā" refers to the evil view that leads to hell, wrongly held by way of attributing non-existent faults to a teacher who is blameless in every way, who practices rightly, and who also shows the correct practice to others. "Narakapapātaṃ" means the great precipice known as hell. It is called a precipice (papāta) because beings fall into this place. "Dhamma-desanā-hatthena" means with the hand known as the teaching of the Dhamma. "Saggamaggathale" means on the dry land of the merit that is the path to heaven. (Alternatively, it means on the dry land known as the celestial realms like Cātumahārājikā and the paths like Stream-entry). The rest should be understood well.

In the Sādhuvilāsinī, which is the Tika on the Dīgha Nikāya Atthakatha (Sumangalavilāsinī) that explains the subtle and profound meaning and generates wisdom, the explanation of the Lohicca Sutta is here finished.

The explanation of the Lohicca Sutta is complete.
424:
On the high ground of meritorious Dhamma, which is the path to heaven, or on the high ground known as the path starting with Stream-entry and the heavens starting with Cātumahārājika (let it fall). The rest is easy to understand.

Thus, in the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) named Līnatthappakāsanī, which is an explanation of the Sādhuvilāsinī—the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) on the Dīgha Nikāya that clarifies the very subtle, deep, and difficult-to-understand meanings, and generates the swiftness and sharpness of very pure and extensive wisdom—the explanation of the difficult meanings of the Lohicca Sutta Commentary is finished.

## Lohicca Sutta Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

13. Tevijja Sutta. Having thus explained the Lohicca Sutta, now wishing to explain the Tevijja Sutta, the teachers spoke the Tevijja Sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... Kosalesu" to show that the turn to explain according to the sequence of suttas has arrived, or to show that the Tevijja Sutta was recited immediately after the Lohicca Sutta. "Nāma" means just a name.

The word "ena" used after the word "uttara" (denoting direction) is intended in the sense of "near". Because of its association with the word "ena", the genitive case (sāmivacaṇa) is used in the sense of the ablative (pañcamī). Therefore, to show the sense of "near" and the sense of the ablative through the word "uttarena", the teacher said the explanation "not far from Manasākaṭa, on the northern side".

In the Pali "uttarena manasākaṭassa", since the word "ena" in "uttarena" expresses "near", the genitive case in "manasākaṭassa" is in the sense of the ablative (apādāna). Because it shows the sense of "near" from the ablative case following the word "uttara" (north), the Līnatthappakāsanī says the teacher spoke the words "on the northern side of Manasākaṭa" with the word "ena" to show the sense of "near". Some teachers say that the word "uttarena" is in the locative case (sattamī).
425:
## 13. Tevijja Sutta Vaṇṇanā
Having thus explained the Lohicca Sutta, now wishing to explain the Tevijja Sutta, the teachers spoke the Tevijja Sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... Kosalesu" to clarify that the opportunity to explain in sequence has arrived, or to show that the Tevijja Sutta is the sutta recited immediately after the Lohicca Sutta. "Nāmaṃ" means just a name. The word "ena" used after a word denoting direction is intended in the sense of "near"; because of its association with that "ena" word, the genitive case (sāmivibhatta) occurs in the sense of the ablative case (pañcamī). Therefore, to show the sense of "near" with the word "uttarena" and to show the occurrence of the genitive in the sense of the ablative, it is said "not far from the village of Manasākaṭa, on the northern side". "Because the ablative case from a word denoting direction expresses the sense of proximity, this was said with the word 'ena' to show proximity"—so say some. As in "pubbena gāmaṃ ramaṇီyaṃ" etc., this word is the third case (instrumental) in the sense of the locative. "Grammarians (Akkhara-cintakā), however, desire the accusative case (dutiyā) in a word denoting a limit when associated with the word 'ena', but the meaning is desired only by the power of the genitive case; therefore, here it is spoken only by the power of the genitive case"—this is the teacher's opinion. "Taruṇa-ambaru-kkha-saṇḍe" means in a grove of young mango trees. A collection of trees is indeed called a forest (vana).

In the word "kulacārittādisampattiyā", the word "ādi" includes accomplishments such as the recitation of mantras, beauty of appearance, and so on. "Tattha tattha" means in those various places or in those various families. Wishing to distinguish those brahmins by their place of residence, he said "tattha" etc. "Mantasañjhāyakaraṇatthaṃ" means for the purpose of performing the recitation of the Atharvaṇa mantras. Therefore, it is said "preventing the entry of many others". "Nadītīre" means on the bank of the Aciravatī River.

## Maggāmagga-kathā-vaṇṇanā
"Jaṅghacāraṃ" means wandering here and there by walking (caṅkama). Since such wandering is for the purpose of dispelling fatigue in the calves, it is called "jaṅghavihāra" or "jaṅghacāra". Therefore, in the Pali, it is taught as "anucaṅkamantānaṃ anuvicarantānaṃ". "Cuṇṇamattikādi" refers to bathing materials such as fine clay powder. In saying "tena vuttaṃ", it is said because both (Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja) were able to walk up and down and wander about. Here, "magga" is the straight path, which is the practice that is the means for going to the Brahma-world. Because it goes straight to the desired place...
426: Because one reaches the desired place straightly by this path, it is called 'magga' (path). A path other than that is called 'amagga' (non-path). Or, the word 'a' should be understood in the sense of growth (vuddhi-attha). Because it is so, by the words beginning with "Katamaṃ nu kho," He shows only the straight path. 'Paṭipadā' refers to the practice that occurs in the preliminary stage of the path leading to the Brahma-world. 'Añjasāyana' is a synonym for the straight path. It is because of showing a distinguished meaning by combining two synonymous words, like the term 'padaṭṭhāna'. In the second method, the word 'añjasa' is a synonym for straightness (ujuka). Because it leads out, it is called 'niyyāniya'. That 'niyyāniya' is indeed 'niyyānika' is shown by the word "niyyāyanto". Both 'niyyānika' and 'niyyāti' mean definitely leading out. It means "being one who goes, he goes." Why is the path said to "niyyāti" (lead out)? One might ask, "Does this path not lack activity (byāpāra) in going?" True, although it is true that there is no activity, because the state of leading out is obtained by the power of the person who travels that path, the path that is the cause of leading out is said to "niyyāti" by the power of the practice through the wise attention of the person who is leading out. 'Karoti' means causing to arise in one's own continuity (santāna). Only such causing to arise is called practicing that path. Because it occurs together, it is called 'sahabya'; it attains the state of occurring together (sahavattanaka). The state of that occurring together is called 'sahabyatā'; therefore, it is explained as "sahabhāvāya". 'Sahabhāva' should be understood as being in the same world (salokatā) or being in the vicinity (samīpatā) in the Brahma-world. For that very reason, He said, "for the sake of appearing in the same place" (ekaṭṭhāne pātubhāvāya). 'Sakameva' refers only to the path taught by one's own teacher, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti. 'Thometvā' means having praised, saying "This path alone is the straight path, this path alone is the añjasāyana," etc., and thus extolling it. It should be construed that Bhāradvāja also wanders about, praising and extolling only the teacher's doctrine taught by his own teacher, the Brahmin Tārukkha. 'Tena vuttaṃ' means it is stated in the Pāḷi text because of the state of being firmly convinced and attached in such a manner. 521-522. 'Aniyyānikāva' means they are only non-liberating (appāṭihārikā), unable to remove the opposition of one another. It means they are devoid of transcendence in order to show the fault in another's doctrine and to show the undistorted, true meaning. 'Tulaṃ' refers to the scales used for comparison. Taking up opposition to each other's doctrine from the very beginning is called 'viggaha' (quarrel). That very 'viggaha', when it arises successively by the power of disputation, is called 'vivāda' (dispute). Therefore, He said "pubbuppattiko," etc. 'Duvidhopī eso' refers to this opposition (virodha) which is stated in two ways as 'viggaha' and 'vivāda'. 'Nānāācariyānaṃ vādato' is because it is the doctrine of teachers who have various inclinations. Although the intended meaning is 'nānāvāda' because it is a various and diverse doctrine, at present the reading is "nānāācariyānaṃ vādo nānāvādo" (the doctrine of various teachers is nānāvāda).
427: "Ekassāpi" means even in one of you two. "Ekasmim" means even in one doctrine among one's own doctrine and another's doctrine. "Saṃsayo natthi" means there is no doubt such as "Is this the path or not?" However, there is doubt regarding the state of being the path or not. Therefore, He said "Esa kira," etc. "Evaṃ sati" means if they perceive all as the path; if it is so, the Blessed One asks, "In what do you have a quarrel?" Here, by the word "iti", 'vivāda' and 'nānāvāda' are included. "Because it leads straightly to the desired place, it is called magga (path); it is a straight path. A path other than that is called amagga. Or, the word 'a' should be seen in the sense of vuddhi (growth)," as stated below. In this term "anujumagga" also, the word 'a' is appropriate in the sense of growth. "That very object" refers to the object called the state of being a path of all the Brahmins' paths, and the object called the state of being a straight path of one's own path. "All those" refers to all the paths shown by various teachers mentioned in the Pāḷi text as "Addhariya Brahmins," etc. Here, the meaning of the Pāḷi is: 'Addhara' is a specific sacrifice. Because they are useful for that sacrifice, the sacrifices are called 'addhariya'. Because they recite those sacrifices, they are called 'Addhariya' (those proficient in the Yajurveda). The Vedas composed by the sage named Tittiri are called 'Tittira'. Because they recite those Vedas, they are called 'Tittiriya' (also those proficient in the Yajurveda). This Tittira Veda is a branch (sākhā) of the Yajurveda. Specifically, the Sāmaveda is called 'Chanda'. Because they chant that Veda with melody, they are called 'Chandoka' (those proficient in the Sāmaveda). They also read it as "Chandoga" with the third letter 'ga'; the meaning is the same. Because there are many praises (iriya) in this Veda, it is called 'Bavhāri' (Ṛgveda). Those who learn and master that Veda are called 'Bavhārijjhā'. In this word "Bahūni," the comparison is: just as those various paths are certainly for entering that village or that market town, similarly, the various paths prescribed by the Brahmins are certainly for reaching the Brahma-world and for being together with Brahma. "Having admitted, when they are later refuted, they deny it" means: after admitting it first, perceiving it as faultless, when they are later refuted due to its faulty nature, they deny it, saying "This is not my word," and they no longer admit it.
428:
527-529. 'Te tevijjā' refers to those Brahmins who have mastered the three Vedas. Since the meaning conveyed by the word 'eva' is not present here, the letter 'va' is taken. This letter 'va' is merely an insertion (āgamasandhi) without its own meaning, as indicated by the phrase 'āgamasandhimattaṃ.' It is used only to connect one word to another through the insertion of a letter.

'Andhapaveṇī' refers to a lineage or row of blind men. The phrase 'fifty or sixty blind men' describes the situation where this long row of blind men is suitable for wandering around a large thicket of bushes. In this way, those blind men think, 'We have been traveling on the path for a very long time.' The lack of a guide (one with sight) who would hold a staff and lead them is shown by the words beginning with 'yaṭṭhigāhaka,' referring to the blind men holding onto each other in succession. To illustrate this, the passage beginning with 'eko kira' is started. 'Anupariyantvā' means wandering around in succession for some time.

'Kacchaṃ' refers to the hem of the loincloth tucked in at the back. As in places like 'kacchaṃ bandhanti,' the word 'kaccha' is a synonym for a specific way of wearing clothes. Alternatively, 'kacchaṃ' refers to the armpit. As in places like 'sambhādho nāma ubho upakacchakā,' the word 'kaccha' is a term denoting a part of the body. 'Cakkhumā' refers to the guide who holds the staff. 'Purimo' and others should be understood according to the order already mentioned. 'Nāmakanyeva' means it is a mere name because it lacks essence or meaning. Although those Brahmins perceive it as having essence, because it is a mere name, it is essence-less and inferior, as shown by the meaning of the word 'lāmakanyeva.'

530. 'Yo' refers to the world of Brahmā. The word 'yato' is a term with a fifth case ending (ablative) used in the sense of the seventh case (locative). To show that it refers to a specific instance from a general statement, 'yasmiṃ kāle' is said. The meaning obtained according to the context is stated with 'uggamanakāle' and so on. 'Āyācanti' means longing for the rising of the sun and moon. Why do they long for it? Because it is of great benefit to the people of the world. The same applies to praise and so on. 'Sommo' means having a cool appearance. It is said to be the belief of the Brahmins that 'in ancient times, due to the prayers of the Brahmins, the moon and sun came and illuminated the world.'

532. 'Idha pana kiṃ vattabbaṃ' means: what is there to be said regarding the teaching of the path for union with Brahmā, who is not present to the senses (unseen), when they cannot even teach the path for union with the moon and sun, who are present to the senses? This is the intended meaning. The word 'yattha' refers back to the meaning already stated as 'idha.'
429:
## Commentary on the Simile of the Aciravatī River
'Samabharitā' means being full all around. Only because it is full all around to the level of the banks is it a river where a crow can drink (kākapeyyā). 'Pāra' means the far bank; to show that this word is a vocative used in calling out, 'ambho' (friend/sir) is said. 'Apāra' means the near bank. 'Ehi' means 'come.' 'Vata' means 'certainly.' If one is to go, then 'come' is used in that context. The words beginning with 'atthime' are the reason for calling out.

The wholesome states of the path of action, such as the five precepts, are to be known as the qualities that make one a Brahmin (brāhmaṇadhammā) because they are included in the Brahmin virtues such as yama and niyama. 'Tabbiparītā' refers to the five enmities and so on, which are the opposite of the five precepts and so forth. 'Inda' refers to the deity named Inda or Sakka. By the words 'sitting on the bank of the Aciravatī river,' it is shown that the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, having perfectly penetrated the Dhamma-element, takes the very river on whose bank He is sitting and uses it as a simile. Saying 'aparaṃ pi' after 'puna pi' is for the purpose of including another river simile.

'Kāmayitabbaṭṭha' is because of the state of being desirable. 'Bandhanaṭṭha' is because of the state of binding the minds of beings due to being desired. Although it is true that this word 'guṇa' is used in other senses, since those meanings are not possible here, this extraction of meaning is undertaken to show that only the sense of 'binding' is appropriate according to the method of remainder (pārisesa). 'Ahatānaṃ' refers to new clothes that have not yet been washed. In this 'Khandhaka Pāḷi' passage, the meaning of 'paṭala' is the meaning of the word 'paṭala,' or it means what is called a layer or film. 'Guṇaṭṭha' is the name for the meaning of the word 'guṇa.' This method should be understood in the remaining words as well. 'Accenti' means they proceed by surpassing. This is in the 'Somanassa Jātaka' Pāḷi passage. 'Dakkhiṇā' is the volition of giving (dāna-cetanā) to animals. This is in the 'Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta' passage. 'Mālāguṇa' refers to a garland of flowers. This is in the 'Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta' and 'Dhammapada' Pāḷi passages. This is merely an illustration, because it also occurs in the senses of a portion, a primary thing, virtue, purity, fulfillment, a bowstring, and so on.

And here it is said:
