'The word guṇa occurs in the senses of a layer, a multitude, a benefit, a portion, and binding; in virtue, purity, and so on; in a primary thing, fulfillment, and a bowstring.'
430:
In this context, 'guṇa' means only the sense of 'bond' (bandhana). When speaking of the desirable nature of forms and so on, the meaning of 'layer' (paṭala) is not suitable, because the desirable nature is not intended in that sense of 'layer'. The same logic applies to the sense of 'mass' (rāsi) and others. By process of elimination, only the sense of 'bond' is suitable. This is because to the extent that those objects are desirable, to that same extent, they possess the nature of a bond.

In this context, the sense of 'portion' (koṭṭhāsa) is also suitable. This is because those objects are desired in the form of portions such as those known by eye-consciousness. The word 'guṇa' is also found in the sense of 'portion', as in 'it should be increased twofold' (diguṇa) and so on.

However, in passages such as: 'The names of the Great Sage are innumerable through his qualities of perfection (sampadā-guṇa); his name can be expressed through his qualities even from among a thousand names,' the word 'guṇa' expresses the sense of 'perfection' (sampadā). Since that sense of perfection is not suitable in this context of the cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa), the teacher did not mention it.

Intending that 'knowing' (vijānana) here is only 'seeing' (dassana), it is said: 'to be looked upon.' The meaning of 'to be heard by ear-consciousness' and so on is indicated by the phrase 'by this method.' Although objects that are sought after are also called 'iṭṭha' (desirable), to show that those sought-after objects are not intended here, it is said: 'whether they are sought after or not.' In this context, only desired objects are called 'iṭṭha.' Therefore, it is said: 'being desirable objects,' which means being objects of pleasure (sukha-ārammaṇa). 'Kāmanīya' means to be desired. They are called 'manāpa' (charming) because they increase the mind through their desirable nature. 'Piyajātika' means having a lovely nature. 'Making an object' means making oneself the object. Since lust (rāga) arises when there is an object, to point that out as the cause, it is said: 'being the cause for the arising of lust.'

'Gedha' means by greed (lobha). The sentence should be connected as: 'being oppressed by greed, they enjoy the five cords of sensual pleasure.' 'Mucchākāra' means the manner of delusion. 'Adhiosanna' means taking excessively, swallowing, and being immersed. Therefore, it is said: 'immersed' (ogāḷha). 'Sāna' means the end. 'Pariniṭṭhānappatta' means having reached the end by way of swallowing and finishing. 'Ādīnava' (danger) means not seeing the fault that will occur both now and in the future in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. That by which one escapes from the defilements caused by the enjoyment of food, clothing, and so on is called 'nissaraṇa' (escape). It refers to the wisdom of enjoying those sensual pleasures after reflecting wisely. To show that 'anissaraṇa-paññā' means the absence of such wisdom of reflective enjoyment, it is said: 'in this matter, thus' and so on. 'Paccavekkhaṇaparibhogavirahita' means being devoid of enjoyment through the aforementioned wisdom of reflection.
431:
548-9. 'Āvaranti' means they obstruct the arising of wholesome states from the very beginning. 'Nivārenti' means they hinder without remainder. 'Onandhanti' means they envelop as if sinking in. 'Pariyonandhanti' means they envelop completely in every way. 'By the power of obstructing and so on' means by the power of the aforementioned meanings of obstruction and so forth. Because of the strength of repeated practice (āsevana), the later obstructions become much more firm and stable than the earlier ones.

## Saṃsandanakathāvaṇṇanā

When there is the possession of a woman, a man's possession of the five cords of sensual pleasure is indeed complete; therefore, it is said: 'one who has possessions through the possession of a woman.' The phrase 'one who has no possessions through the possession of a woman' is to show the absence of the most gross possessions among the possessions evident in the Brahmins who know the three Vedas. How can such Brahmins who know the three Vedas be compared with Brahmā? For Brahmā is entirely without possessions in every way. He is one without enmity because he has no mind of ill-will; the meaning is: where would there be the practice of enmity for that Brahmā? 'Cittagelanyasaṅkhātena' means by that which is known as sickness in the arising of thoughts (cittuppāda); by this word, it is meant that the Brahmā has no sickness of the physical body (rūpakāya). 'Vyāpajjhena' means by suffering. In the phrase 'by restlessness, remorse, and so on' (uddhaccakukkuccādīhi), the word 'ādi' (and so on) includes the defilements (saṅkilesadhamma) that exist in the same single mind along with restlessness and remorse. Therefore, the statement 'due to the absence of restlessness and remorse' (uddhaccakukkuccābhāvato), which mentions only the absence of those two defilements, is complete. When there is doubt (vicikicchā), which is the cause of non-practice, the mind never follows the man's will; only after that doubt has been abandoned can the mind follow the man's will; therefore, he said 'vicikicchā' and so on. 'Cittagatikā' means they follow the will of the mind. Therefore, it is said: 'they exist under the power of the mind.' 'Na tādiso' means he is not one who follows the will of the mind like the Brahmins; rather, having mastery over jhāna and higher knowledge (abhiññā), he brings the mind under his own control; therefore, he is called 'vasavattī' (one who has mastery).

552. 'Brahmalokamagge' means in the path to be practiced, or in the path to be designated, that leads to the Brahma world; the meaning is that they designate that path. 'Upagantvā' means by approaching through wrong practice, or by claiming. 'Samatalanti saññāya' means with the perception of level ground because the surface of the mud is dry for about a finger's breadth or half a finger's breadth. 'Paṅkaṃ otiṇṇā viya' means as if they have entered a great mire deeper than a man's height. 'Anuppavisanti' means they enter the path leading to the states of deprivation (apāya) with the perception that it is the path to the Brahma world. Because of that entry, they sink and reach the destruction of their limbs, great and small. 'Evaṃ' means by the aforementioned method of 'level ground' and so on. 'Saṃsīditvā' means...
432:
Nimuajjitvā means having dived or having sunk. Marīcikāyā means because of the mirage, which is an object of the eye. Vañcetvā means deceiving by showing what is similar to a river. Vāyamānā means being one who exerts effort; or rather, this text 'vāyamamānā' is the explanation. Sukkhataraṇaṃ maññe taranti means they consider themselves to be crossing as if crossing a dry river without water. This is a statement describing exhaustion.

Tasmā means because those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, having approached (accepted) through wrong practice that which is not the path to the Brahma world as 'the path,' they sink; therefore, it is said. Yathā te means just as beings who have entered the mud with the perception of 'level ground' reach the destruction and ruin of their hands, feet, and so on.

Idheva ca means also in this very individual existence. Sukhaṃ vā sātaṃ vā na labhanti means they do not obtain the bliss of Jhana or the pleasure obtained through Vipassana; how then could they obtain the bliss of the Path or the pleasure obtained through Nibbana? This is the meaning.

Maggadīpakaṃ means it is only what those Brahmins desire (understand) as 'showing the path to the Brahma world.' Tevijjakaṃ means making known the meaning of the three Vedas. Pāvacanaṃ means the recited text designated as the noble word. Tevijjānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ is the genitive case (of) in the sense of connection. Iriṇaṃ: because it is a name for a great forest (araññāni), the teacher says it is a great forest without a village. Anupabhogarukkhehi means with poisonous trees such as kimpakka, which are unfit for use even by deer, antelopes, and so on. Yattha means in which forest. Due to the thickness of many thorny bushes, it is impossible even to turn around. The destruction of relatives is called ñātivyasana. Similarly, it should be understood in the cases of bhogavyasana and sīlavyasana. Because disease itself oppresses, it is called rogavyasana. Similarly, it should be understood in the case of diṭṭhivyasana.

The objection 'Is this meaning not already established by the word jāta alone?' is rejected by 'Yo hi,' etc. 'Having been born and then grown up' is called jātasamvaḍḍho, as stated by the teacher (the author of the old sub-commentary). However, 'one who is born and is also grown up' is called jātasamvaḍḍho; this is appropriate because the qualifier samvaḍḍho follows after. Because of the lack of familiarity, they are not entirely evident. Ciranikkhanto means having departed from the village, a long time has passed. Indeed, because there is a long time for that person who has departed from the village, he is called ciranikkhanto. Because the meaning is not complete with the two words jātasamvaḍḍho, the object tamenaṃ is further qualified by tāvadeva avasaṭaṃ.

Dandhāyitattaṃ means slowness in answering (being slow and sluggish); because such slowness is called 'taking a long time due to doubt,' the teacher says 'taking a long time due to doubt.' Vitthāyitattaṃ means hesitation (sārajjitatta). In the Commentary, however, Vitthāyitattaṃ is intended as stiffness (thambhitatta), so it is stated as 'taking the state of being stiff.' It shows the state of being unobstructed because of the very nature of that unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). The doubt 'Might this also be obstructed by an obstacle?' is rejected by 'Tassa hi,' etc. In the phrase mārāvaṭṭanādivasena (by way of Mara's turning, etc.), periods of confusion, fainting, and so on are included.
433:
Because that omniscience is included within the four things that are not subject to obstacles, no one is able to cause an obstacle to that knowledge.

When associated with the prefix 'u', the word luṃpa or lupi has the meaning of extracting (pulling out); therefore, it is said 'uddharatu'. Indeed, due to the distinction of the prefix, verbal roots express distinct meanings, just like the word 'ādāna'. Because the word pajā is understood from the context, it refers to a child; thus, it was said 'brahmaṇadāraka' (a Brahmin youth).

## Explanation of the Teaching on the Path to the Brahma World

556-7. By the word 'apubbaṃ', the reason for what is to be commented upon is shown. One who has excessive strength is called balavā (strong); therefore, it is said 'balasampanno' (endowed with strength). One who blows a conch is a saṅkhadhamaka (conch-blower); he is one who, having blown the conch, produces sound from it. To the question 'What is the purpose of the qualifiers such as balavā?', it was said 'dubbalo hi' (for a weak person), etc. It should be connected as 'the conch-sound of a strong person.' Only absorption (appanā) is appropriate because the mind is well-freed from the opposites (hindrances); this is the intended meaning of why it was said thus.

Limited action (pamāṇakata-kamma) refers to sense-sphere action (kāmāvacara-kamma), because it cannot suppress the defiling states that cause limitation. Indeed, that sense-sphere action, which is the preliminary stage of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), cannot be developed by way of pervading specific or non-specific persons and directions, having transcended the limitation. Conversely to what was stated, fine-material and immaterial sphere action is called immeasurable action (appamāṇakata-kamma). Therefore, it was said 'tañhi', etc. There, among the fine-material and immaterial sphere actions, in the immaterial sphere action, pervading by way of specific or non-specific persons is not obtained, nor is pervading the directions. Some teachers say that it is obtained by way of arrival, but that is incorrect. For the immaterial attainment (āruppa) is not the result of the divine abidings, but rather the result of the kasiṇa. Therefore, whatever immaterial attainment has been well-developed and brought to mastery should be understood as immeasurable action. Alternatively, others say: 'That immaterial sphere Jhana which has arisen in a continuity processed by an excellent development of the divine abidings, and which is entered upon after emerging from the attainment of the divine abidings, is called immeasurable (appamāṇakata) by way of the extent of pervading in this manner.' This should be accepted after investigation.

'Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakamme' means when there is fine-material sphere action and immaterial sphere action. 'Na ohīyati na tiṭṭhati' means that even accumulated sense-sphere action, as long as the attained lofty Jhana (mahaggata-jhāna) is not lost, is suppressed and blocked, and it itself remains behind (unable to produce results)...
434:
It no longer exists in a state capable of providing rebirth. The meaning of the word 'na avasissati' is 'nothing remains.' This phrase is a qualifying term or a synonym for the word 'na avatiṭṭhati.' Therefore, it was said, 'What is meant by this?' and so on. 'Laggituṃ' means to obstruct or to forbid. 'Ṭhātuṃ' means to be capable and to endure. 'Pharitvā' means having spread repeatedly. 'Pariyādiyitvā' means having exhausted the power of that kamma. 'Okāsaṃ gahetvā' means having taken the opportunity to produce its result (vipāka). By this, it should be understood that the phrase 'laggituṃ vā ṭhātuṃ vā' is merely being elaborated. The phrase beginning with 'atha kho' shows the attainment of the meaning. The exhaustion of kamma means obstructing the arising of the result of that kāmāvacara (sensual-sphere) kamma and causing only the arising of its own result; thus it was said, 'tassa' and so on. 'Tassa' means having obstructed the result of kāmāvacara kamma. 'Sayam eva' means only the rūpāvacara (fine-material sphere) or arūpāvacara (immaterial sphere) kamma. The meaning is that if there is no specific mental aspiration (cetopaṇidhi) in such individuals, it leads to companionship with the Brahmās. It should be understood that, due to the specific mental aspiration of those with great merit like Tissa Brahmā and others, the mahaggata (sublime) kamma does not obstruct the result of the limited (paritta) kamma.

How does a kāmāvacara wholesome kamma of little power, by obstructing the result of a weighty (garuka) mahaggata kamma, create an opportunity for its own result? In all three versions of the Vinaya-gaṇṭhipada, it is stated: 'Jhāna declines only through the power of craving (taṇhā) that delights in the sensual realm. Because of that decline in jhāna, the limited kamma finds its opportunity.' However, some teachers say: 'The decline of jhāna due to delight in the sensual realm at a moment free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa) should be accepted after careful investigation.' The most appropriate reason in this matter is this: even if there is no kāmāvacara kamma capable of obstructing the result of mahaggata kamma, according to the Buddha's teaching, 'Monks, the mental aspiration of a virtuous person succeeds because of the purity of their virtue,' the mental aspiration for the sensual realm obstructs the result of mahaggata kamma and provides the opportunity for the result of the limited kāmāvacara kamma. In this way, 'mettādi-vihārī' refers to one who dwells by the power of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra) such as loving-kindness that has reached absorption (appanā) according to the method already described.

In consideration of the first refuge, what does the second refuge depend upon? In response to this question, the phrase beginning with 'paṭhamam eva' was said. In the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, the word 'saṅgītaṃ' (recited/chanted) should be brought in and connected. Taking refuge repeatedly is especially firm and brings greater fruit. Therefore, it should be understood that taking refuge for a second time was also performed. 'Katipāhaccayena' means after the lapse of two or three days.
435:
'Pabbajitvā' means taking the novice ordination (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā). The Buddha taught the Aggañña Sutta also with reference to this young man Vāseṭṭha; the phrase beginning with 'Aggañña-sutte' was stated to make it known that it does not refer to anyone else. It means that they attained both the higher ordination (upasampadā) and Arahatship according to the method found in that Aggañña Sutta. Whatever has not been explained in detail here in terms of its meaning is easily understood by the wise.

Thus, in this sub-commentary (ṭīkā) named Sādhuvilāsinī, which clarifies the subtle, profound, and difficult-to-perceive meanings of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary (Sumangalavilāsinī), and which generates pure and extensive wisdom and skill—the explanation of the meaning of the Tevijja Sutta Commentary is completed. This work was composed by the Great Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati, who is endowed with the qualities of integrity, gentleness, serenity, faith, mindfulness, wisdom, patience, and energy; who possesses courageous knowledge that is unattached and unshakeable regarding the Three Piṭakas along with their commentaries; who has delved into the depths of various systems of his own and other traditions; who is a great leader of a community (mahāgaṇi) and a great grammarian; and who was the preceptor of the Great King of Dhamma (Mahādhammarājādhirājagaru).

## The Commentary on the Tevijja Sutta is finished.

Regarding the name 'Sādhuvilāsinī' in this Sādhuvilāsinī Ṭīkā, it is said:
In this sub-commentary, there is no word, meaning, or decision stated in any way that is devoid of supporting evidence.
Therefore, it especially delights the hearts of the virtuous (sādhu) who look with the eye of wisdom.
Because it thus delights the hearts of the virtuous, it is called 'Sādhuvilāsinī.'
436:
## Concluding Remarks

By this sequence of words, this sub-commentary, which is an explanation of the Sīlakkhandhavagga Commentary, undertaken for the sake of proficiency in the True Dhamma and for the growth of the Dispensation (Sāsana), is entirely completed.

Because there is no word, meaning, or decision in this sub-commentary that is explained without supporting evidence, and because it especially delights the hearts of the virtuous, it is named 'Sādhuvilāsinī.' This sub-commentary consists of over fifty (approximately 515) bhāṇavāras in length.

The Great King (King Bodawpaya), who possesses many white elephants, who is endowed with an immeasurable army of elephants and horses, who bears the title beginning with Siripavara, and who rules over various countries,

Founded the capital named Amarapura in the country of Tampadīpa, in the pleasant land of Myanmar within the continent of Jambudīpa.

That capital is situated near Mandalay Hill, relying on the Irrawaddy River; it is the dwelling place of many people and is adorned with golden palaces.

While reigning justly after receiving his consecration in that capital, he built the venerable Mingun Great Stupa (Pahtodawgyi) for the benefit of humans, devas, and brahmās.

That Great King, having discarded what was not in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya, purified the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Conqueror (Jina) according to the truth, with a constantly firm heart.

That same Great King built and offered a pleasant monastery, endowed with cool shade and water, surrounded by two layers of walls, and suitable for the practice of meditation.

In the Asokārāma monastery complex, which is pleasant and free from sorrow, located directly to the south and near the golden palace where the famous Mahāmuni image resides—an image cast in the very presence of the Living Buddha—he built a great five-storied monastery known as Ratanabhūmi, adorned with a Dhamma palace.

Likewise, in the monastery named Jeyyabhūmi, built by the Chief Queen of the Southern Palace near the northeast corner of the capital...
437:
In the same manner, the Northern Queen built and offered a golden monastery named Parimāṇaka near the Soṇṇaguha Stupa within the city. Furthermore, the Crown Prince also built and offered a monastery named Maṅgalāvāsa near the Mahāguha Stupa in the western part of the city.

Thus, residing in turn at many golden monasteries, being honored by all kings, and having received royal titles three times; being well-known as Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati; having mastered the two Vibhaṅgas (Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga) and attained the status of a preceptor (upajjhāya); and being one who taught the Piṭaka Dhamma to monks arriving from the island of Laṅkā as well as to monks residing on other islands, and who encouraged them in the practice—that Great Maungdaung Sāsanabaing, relying on this great King [Bodawpaya] who purified the Sasana, composed this Abhinavaṭīkā (New Sub-commentary) which is perfect in both meaning and phrasing.

That Abhinavaṭīkā named Sādhuvilāsinī reached its successful completion when two thousand three hundred and forty-five (2345) years had passed since the Parinibbāna of the Buddha.

By the merit I have accumulated through the cultivation and composition of this new Sādhuvilāsinī Sub-commentary and the beautiful new Netti Sub-commentary called Peṭakālaṅkāra, may I in the future attain the supreme Bodhi, and having rescued many beings from the suffering of the round of rebirths, may I liberate them from the bonds of existence.

May the kings always protect these beings in accordance with the Dhamma. May they constantly delight in meritorious deeds and cause the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jina-sāsana) to shine like the sun and the moon. May all living beings be forever free from dangers and calamities; may they always possess noble intentions and reach the deathless state of Nibbāna.

## Thus, the Abhinavaṭīkā named Sādhuvilāsinī,
## which is the explanation of the Sīlakkhandhavagga of the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, is completed.
## The Sīlakkhandhavagga Abhinavaṭīkā is finished.
